title: AI vaginas, customisable personalities and fake bruises: the sex doll market is booming. Does it matter how the dolls are treated? | Sex | The Guardian
description: As the sex doll industry grows and AI changes the products available, what does it mean to engage in any kind of relationship with a woman-shaped thing?
Author: Madison Griffiths
Headline: As the sex doll industry grows and AI changes the products available, what does it mean to engage in any kind of relationship with a woman-shaped thing?
Content: ‘In a global context, where I believe gender equality has gone backwards, sex dolls are actually just the extreme end of that,’ says Prof Kelly Richards of the Queensland University of Technology Centre for Justice.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘In a global context, where I believe gender equality has gone backwards, sex dolls are actually just the extreme end of that,’ says Prof Kelly Richards of the Queensland University of Technology Centre for Justice.Photograph: Getty ImagesSexAI vaginas, customisable personalities and fake bruises: the sex doll market is booming. Does it matter how the dolls are treated?As the sex doll industry grows and AI changes the products available, what does it mean to engage in any kind of relationship with a woman-shaped thing?Madison GriffithsSat 29 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 16.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo weeks ago, two distressed citizens stumbled across what they assumed was the mangled corpse of a woman, stuffed into a suitcase in a small town about three hours south of Sydney. They called the local police, who in turn issued a statement that a body in a suitcase had been found. The wider public waited sombrely for Australia’s tally of dead women to tick up by one.But instead, a day later, after forensic analysis, it was determined that the woman in question wasn’t a woman at all. The “body” was that of a sex doll, marked with fake bruises, left to rot on a lonely dirt road. In Australia, as in the UK and some other European countries, it is not illegal to own a sex doll unless it resembles a child. Given the doll’s seemingly mature presentation, police investigations were called off.The sex doll trade is flourishing. A2026 market analysisestimates that the global market currently was valued at US$6.6bn in 2025, with a projection that it will more than double, to US$13.4bn, by 2033. As the market booms, and involves increasingly lifelike facsimiles of women, does how these dolls get treated matter?And when a sex doll with “bruises” and rain-matted hair is tucked into a suitcase and left on a roadside, should we be concerned?From the classroom to the locker room: nine days of ‘deeply disturbing’ sexual assault allegations shake AustraliaRead moreJohannes Fuss, chair of forensic psychiatry and sex research at the University of Duisburg-Essen, tells the Guardian that “the disposability and desecration of the female form in these contexts cannot be viewed entirely in isolation from broader cultural hostilities toward women”. Working with researcher Jeanne C. Desbuleux, Fuss has published papers on the link between the anthropomorphisation of sex dolls and gender-based violence.The research remains inconclusive. “We currently lack robust longitudinal data to definitively prove whether such doll use is protective or, conversely, is a behavioural stepping stone that increases real-world offending risk. I think we urgently need research on this question as more and more technologies enter the market to simulate human sexuality,” Fuss says.However, he is suspicious of their appeal. “To put it provocatively: it boils down to total availability, a youthful and attractive body, and zero emotional demand or dialogue.”A quick scroll on The Doll Forum website finds members regularly pit real-life women against their silicone knock-offs, one writing that “girlfriends are for guys who haven’t found the right doll yet”, and that “no matter how pretty she is, there is a man out there who is sick of her shit”.View image in fullscreenOne sex doll company suggests their doll can offer ‘routine companionship’, help with ‘building confidence through judgement-free connection’ and allow for a ‘safe expression of your wildest fantasies’.Photograph: Kevin Frayer/Getty ImagesTammie Paine, owner of Naughty by Nature Adult Store, a sex doll retailer based in Adelaide, regularly engages with sex doll enthusiasts. “One of the biggest misconceptions is that they all fit a particular stereotype, or that owning a doll automatically says something negative about someone’s character,” she says.“This hasn’t been our experience at all. The recent image from Goulburn [a town near where the sex doll was found in the suitcase] understandably attracted attention because, without context, it looked confronting. But I don’t think one unusual image should be used to characterise an entire group of consumers.”While the market for sex dolls may be heterogenous, what does it mean to engage in any kind of relationship with a woman-shaped thing?“From my conversations with professionals and police, there are definitely men with adult-like companion dolls who see that doll as a person. They might see their dolls as women,” Prof Kelly Richards, a criminologist in the School of Justice at the Queensland University of Technology Centre for Justice says. “But do they see women as humans?“This is going to sound really dark. But in a global context, where I believe gender equality has gone backwards, sex dolls are actually just the extreme end of that.”Central to the industry’s rise is sophisticated technology. Lifelike sex dolls are now increasingly customisable. Prospective buyers can render themselves an ideal companion from scratch, courtesy of 3D printers. In 2017, the sex-doll brand RealDoll paved the way for the future of AI-generated sex robots by introducing “Harmony” to their coterie. In its newest model, which its website says will be available this year and for which it is running a waitlist, buyers can assign personality traits to her – attributes like “spiritual” or “insecure” – from an app on their phone. “She’s far more than a beautiful body. Harmony listens to you,” the website reads.The new Harmony also has an AI vagina – described on the RealDoll site as “an electronic insert that pairs via Bluetooth to the X-Mode App. It detects touch, movement, and speed, transitioning naturally from mild arousal to climax, with synchronised vocal responses that make every moment feel real.”At the 2026 annual Consumer Electronics Show, a major international conference that unveils breakthrough technologies, the Singapore-based sex tech company Lovense introduced Emily, an AI-powered companion doll, to participants. She is customisable, offering “personality switching” from modes including “co-worker”, “gym crush” and “tradwife”, is able to send AI-generated selfies on request, and remembers past conversations. The Lovense website outlines built-in sensors around the doll’s body which elicits a moan when touched, and suggests the doll can offer “routine companionship”, help with “building confidence through judgement-free connection” and allow for a “safe expression of your wildest fantasies”. The site is running a waitlist, with shipping expected in the first quarter of 2027.Coeros, an online sex doll accessories brand based in Los Angeles, offers customised sex doll heads. According to their website, they are able to model each head on “photos of a real person, an original character, or an AI-generated image”. Customers are able to upload reference photographs to a submission form on their site, when ordering their very own ersatz woman. The Coeros website claims they are able to “achieve around 90% resemblance” to the woman in photographs provided, depending on the quality of the images. The entire process of making the doll’s head, it says, is about one to two months.View image in fullscreen‘There’s an understanding, in the case of child sex abuse dolls, that their use extends to the harm of actual children. This same recognition of harm does not extend to adult women dolls,’ says author Caitlin Roper.Photograph: David McNew/Getty ImagesAsked about the company’s responsibilities or processes if a doll was asked to be modelled on a real person without their knowledge, a spokesperson at Coeros told the Guardian: “The fact that a custom design can be created from reference images should not be interpreted as permission to use another person’s likeness without their consent. We do not encourage or support the use of our customisation service for harassment, impersonation, or other non-consensual purposes.” Details for prospective buyers on the website include specific services from eyebrow hair implantation to shipping, but do not appear to include any directions as to obtaining the permission of women in any photographs uploaded. One member of The Doll Forum wrote of Coeros’s invention: “The most obvious candidates are the ones who turned you down, the ones that got away, the ones you had no hope of winning.”A custom sex doll head is available for approximately US$1,790. Caitlin Roper, Australian author ofSexDolls, Robots and Woman Hating: The Case for Resistance, calls these kinds of dolls“replica female sex slaves”.Roper actively campaigns for adult sex dolls to be prohibited as well as childlike sex dolls. “There’s an understanding, in the case of child sex abuse dolls, that their use extends to the harm of actual children. This same recognition of harm does not extend to adult women dolls. Women are being reduced to a set of penetrable orifices,” she says, before referencing a case currently being tried in South Korea involving Jang Yoon-gi, a 23-year-old man who last month admitted to therape and murder of a 16-year-old high school studentin May. A damaged sex doll was reportedly found in his apartment, withdamage to its neck and chest.There was much speculation about why the sex doll was abandoned on the quiet country road south of Sydney. Was it a prank? A dark, violent fantasy? Or possibly, even, a clumsy way of discarding a large and bulky item – garbage?Families need to openly talk to children about misogyny, consent and sexual violence. Here’s how to start | Stephanie Wescott and Jane Gilmore for the ConversationRead moreAs a large, potentially embarrassing, item, disposal of a sex doll can present its own set of issues. In March, a man from Adelaide posted an advert for his 5’6” tall sex doll onThe Doll Forum.This is because it can be easier to give away a doll, even one with a mutilated vulva, than it is to dispose of one. This particular owner had cut holes out of his doll’s vagina and had never gotten around repairing it by glueing new thermoplastic elastomer to the area.On Reddit, there are many other dolls looking for adoption, and a trove of pictures can be found. Their list of injuries are interminable: macerated nipples, perforated limbs, mouths encrusted with mould. The users authenticate listings for their used sex dolls by positioning them next to blank pieces of paper, inscribed with username details and the date. It makes for a grisly tableau of lifeless hostages.Jerry Siew, owner of SxDolled, a sex doll retailer in Australia, has seen the same listings. “I went through forums – I saw the demand of people wanting to dispose of their dolls. I see it as very important,” he tells the Guardian.Siew’scompany is the only one in Australia that offers a discreet lifelike doll disposal service.“For owners, it gives them a dignified way to part with a beloved doll, whether the doll is beyond repair or they are simply moving and unable to take the doll with them. You just have to look at the incident in Goulburn,” he says. “It caused 20 hours of police time, and stress for the community. I’ve also seen articles of dolls thrown into oceans and rivers. That causes panic and wastes emergency resources.”These glass-eyed companions have little to say about their treatment, but their owners frequently do. While discussing how best to dispose of a lifelike doll, one member of The Doll Forum recommended investing in a chainsaw. “Live out your wildest chainsaw massacre fantasy!” he wrote.Explore more on these topicsSexWomenSexual violenceSexual consentGenderfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I wanted to find the slowest fashion imaginable’: the woman growing her own dress | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Looking for an alternative to fast fashion, Eve Ogden Schaub decided to create a garment from homegrown flax
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Looking for an alternative to fast fashion, Eve Ogden Schaub decided to create a garment from homegrown flax
Content: Eve Ogden Schaub harvesting her flax.Photograph: Stephen SchaubView image in fullscreenEve Ogden Schaub harvesting her flax.Photograph: Stephen SchaubFashion‘I wanted to find the slowest fashion imaginable’: the woman growing her own dressLooking for an alternative to fast fashion, Eve Ogden Schaub decided to create a garment from homegrown flaxNicola DavisScience correspondentSat 29 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom crop tops to shorts and brightly patterned dresses, many of today’s clothes are the result of fast fashion. But one woman is taking a radical approach to challenging this trend by growing her own dress.Eve Ogden Schaub is in the midst of a project to create a linen garment made from flax she is growing at home, documenting the process in videos sharedon her Instagram account.“I had this idea that I wanted to find the slowest fashion imaginable. And that’s when I had the idea I could grow a dress from seed in my back yard,” she says.Schaub began the project in April 2025 when she turned a 600 sq ft vegetable garden in Vermont into a plot for growing flax. Having harvested the first crop, Schaub sowed and harvested a second. She is also learning to process the material in steps that would not sound amiss in a Grimms’ fairytale – sometimes enlisting family and friends to help.View image in fullscreenSchaub spinning her flax.Photograph: Stephen Schaub“We retted it, which is a sort of decomposition process, and then you do breaking and scutching and hackling, and you have to spin and scour and then maybe dye your yarn,” she says, adding that she has yet to get to the latter step, but is growing indigo plants for the purpose.Once the flax is spun into linen yarn, Shaub will weave it on a huge loom – not unlike Penelope in the Odyssey – before cutting out and sewing a dress. “So it’s an enormous undertaking, but something that not all that long ago was completely commonplace, and I found that a very attractive, interesting facet of the project,” she says.As Schaub says, it has never been easier to get a cheap, convenient garment delivered to your door.However “fast fashion” has become an environmental and health catastrophe, with garments ending upon huge rubbish dumpsin Ghana and workers in India’s recycling factoriesexperiencing ailments including lung disease.In our current culture, “if you can do something cheaper and faster, it’s always the preferred option,” Schaub says. “And I want to step back and say: but is it? What might we stand to gain if we were to slow down and try to find things that are more meaningful to us, that bring us something that we can’t get from this fast-paced commercial world?”Schaub also wants to explore the value of creativity, and question what benefits people may gain from making more things.A self-described “fibre-person and maker”, Schaub is no stranger to lifestyle experiments, having written books on a number of projects, including her family’s attempts to give up sugar for a year, and to go 12 months without producing any rubbish.The latter, says Schaub, dovetails with her new endeavour, noting that in avoiding waste, she learned about synthetic materials and the issues plastic poses for our environment and our bodies.View image in fullscreenSchaub and her garden.Photograph: Stephen Schaub“Unfortunately, we’re all walking around wearing plastic bags most of the time, and we don’t even realise it,” she says.Schaub hopes her project will shine a light on the implications of modern clothing – including the poor treatment and low pay of those producing such garments: “The whole system, I want to question and say, is this what we want?”In her efforts to go from ground to garment, Shaub has picked the brains of myriad experts, adding that valuing shared knowledge is another facet of the experiment.But she admits some steps have proved easier to get the hang of than others: in one of the many videos capturing her attempts at spinning Schaub is left grimacing at the camera.“There’s something inherently funny in the learning process, because you screw up and you screw up, and you know you’re going to screw up,” she says.The project, she adds, has been an eye-opener for many. “I get so many people commenting on my social media posts saying, ‘now I understand. Now I understand why clothes were so expensive, why cloth was a valuable commodity, why people only owned one or maybe two outfits, because it was so hard to get’,” she says.Schaub says her own views about clothing have changed too, noting she no longer finds department store clothing appealing, and has a greater motivation to appreciate and mend the clothes she already has.As for the final dress, Schaub admits her previous experience in sewing has only run as far as making Halloween costumes. But she is planning to work with an experienced friend to design the linen garment based on historical dress patterns.“I cannot predict when this project will end, but I promise I’m going to wear something at the end of this,” she says, adding that whatever she produces, it will be deeply meaningful to her. “Because of that, I hope it will be beautiful,” she says. “I know it will be beautiful to me.”Explore more on these topicsFashionEthical and green livingFashion industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ve £80k in the account, here’s my pin’: turning the tables on the scammers | Scams | The Guardian
description: Plagued by bank impersonation scams, one Guardian Money reader got even by stringing the fraudsters along … for hours
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Plagued by bank impersonation scams, one Guardian Money reader got even by stringing the fraudsters along … for hours
Content: Illustration: Sean O’BrienIllustration: Sean O'Brien/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Sean O’BrienIllustration: Sean O'Brien/The GuardianScams‘I’ve £80k in the account, here’s my pin’: turning the tables on the scammersPlagued by bank impersonation scams, one Guardian Money reader got even by stringing the fraudsters along … for hoursAnonymousSat 29 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 16.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Acouple of Sundays ago at just past 11am my mobile rang. An automated message purported to be from Barclays Bank, querying a payment to Argos for more than £1,000. Not only had I not made a payment to Argos recently, nor do I bank with Barclays.I am plagued with these kinds of calls. Usually, when possible, I make it clear to the scammers that I know their game. Usually, that call ends there and then.But this time I realised there was a chance to string themalong. It was just a question of how soon they realised I was bluffing. I assumed it would be a couple of minutes. In fact it was three hours.I called the number shown on my phone and, pretending to be a confused, doddery old man – not that difficult for me – I expressed the expected alarm at the bogus payment.View image in fullscreenImpersonation scams where fraudsters ring you claiming to be from your bank are rife.Photograph: Fiordaliso/Getty ImagesThe man who answered, who had more or less a received pronunciation accent, went through what I understand is the usual story: my credit card had been compromised, bankruptcy was on the horizon, remedial action essential. Someone from the investigations team would call me back, he said. Thirty minutes later someone calling himself “Adam” rang. From here on in the number always came up as “No caller ID”.Several times Adam ended the call, presumably to consult his fellow crooks, and rang back later.First, Adam went through several security-like questions. When did I last use my credit card? “Can’t remember,” I replied. What was the last transaction I made? “Dunno.” Did I use internet banking? “No”. Then came the big one: how much is in your current account? “Around £80,000,” I said. (If only.)double quotation markIt was just a question of how soon they realised I was bluffingThere wasn’t a sharp intake of breath. I couldn’t hear a licking of lips. But I could sense that Adam’s vocal cords had tightened, and he was from now on more intense.He explained it was a matter of the utmost urgency my credit card should be cancelled and a new one issued. Would I like to keep the same pin, he asked? I said “yes” and he asked for it. I’d already written down a made-up pin on a bit of paper, and gave it to him. I thought I could sense him trying hard to remain matter of fact.He asked if I had my debit card and credit card with me. I said I couldn’t find my credit card. Adam was stern, insisting I look for it. I couldn’t be bothered to fabricate two false 16-digit numbers, and so I told him my wife must have it and she was out. He let this go.View image in fullscreenScam callers will ask you to read out your bank card number.Photograph: Chris Rout/AlamyI had already taken out one of my debit cards from my wallet, one issued by HSBC, jotted down the first eight digits and made up eight more. To my surprise, and some alarm, Adam read out the first six digits, correctly, saying the card was issued by HSBC. (How did he know I had an HSBC account?)He didn’t bother to explain why he needed the debit card, too – or why he needed the numbers – and, being in character I didn’t ask, just went meekly along. I guess the implication was that both cards were compromised and so the investigations team needed to cancel that one as well.I gave him the made-up number, thinking this would be the end of it. But within a minute he came back and said the number I’d given didn’t seem to be a genuine one.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markI gave him the made-up number, thinking this would be the end of itI assumed concerned bafflement and told him that all I could say was that I was reading out the number on the card in front of me. There was another pause, presumably while he consulted one of his scammer colleagues. To my surprise they decided to keep going.As this was Sunday, as Adam pointed out, the banks were closed. So the only safe procedure was to send round a courier to pick up my debit card – right now. It couldn’t wait until tomorrow. Was that OK with me? I told him it was fine.He said I should put the card in an envelope and address it: HSBC Investigations Team, what he thought was my name, Ref HS844677.He was most insistent on two things: he repeated several times that the courier must, on no account whatsoever, be able to see that a bank card was in the envelope, and that I must seal it extremely carefully.He insisted three times that I read the address back to him. I pretended to be getting a bit fed up with all this but he explained, quite firmly, that banking security was at stake here and there was no room for error.View image in fullscreenSantander says more than £3m has been stolen from its customers so far this year, with an average loss of £6,000.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAA new thought then occurred to him. Did I have a current bank statement, and could I find the most recent one? I noisily opened and shut a drawer. He asked for the balance. I had already written down a precise made-up amount. I told him £81,224.93.Adam told me he’d ring back when he had booked the courier and got an ETA. He’d already asked me for my postcode and I’d given him one where I lived several years ago. Now he asked for my exact address and I gave him a house number that I knew was too high to exist in that street.Fifteen minutes later he rang back, sounding a little flustered. A blue Prius was outside the address I’d given but it seemed to be a block of flats. “That’s not right,” I said, “I live in a house.” Another hiatus, as he communicated with the courier. Could I see a blue Prius? he asked. I paused long enough to have looked out of an imaginary window and said “No, I can’t see a blue car”.What can you see outside your house? he asked. “Nothing,” I said. He rang off again.Five minutes later he called back. Would I mind going out and trying to find the blue Prius? I explained that I had a bad leg and couldn’t leave my house at all. But I would gladly open the front door and have a look. Then another call. The driver was absolutely adamant that the address was in a block of flats.I’d kept this charade up for a lot longer than I’d expected and I was about to go out. “Oh dear,” I said in my best whispery voice, “it looks like I’ve been wasting your time.”What? I switched into my own voice to deliver the – unprintable – coup de grace, and hang up.Adam even had the cheek to ring back later. I didn’t answer. I wish I had. I could have thanked him for the afternoon’s entertainment.AnonymousExplore more on these topicsScamsConsumer affairsBanks and building societiesNuisance callsBankingCrimefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Faster, higher, funnier: what we learned from China’s robot games | China | The Guardian
description: Five-day showcase reveals leaps Beijing has made in humanoid tech, but also its limitations as US rivals come up from the rear
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Five-day showcase reveals leaps Beijing has made in humanoid tech, but also its limitations as US rivals come up from the rear
Content: The five-day robot Olympics staked out China’s claim as the undisputed leader in humanoid robotics.Composite: Alex Mellon for the Guardian : Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe five-day robot Olympics staked out China’s claim as the undisputed leader in humanoid robotics.Composite: Alex Mellon for the Guardian : Getty ImagesThe Saturday readChinaFaster, higher, funnier: what we learned from China’s robot gamesFive-day showcase reveals leaps Beijing has made in humanoid tech, but also its limitations as US rivals come up from the rearRobert Booth, UK technology editorSat 29 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 07.14 EDTShareWith exploding pelvises, enough comic pratfalls for a Buster Keaton show reel and the odd moment of ruthless violence, the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing gripped the world this week with an unsettling mixture of hilarity, trepidation and relief.The five-day showcase staked out China’s claim to undisputed leadership in humanoid robotics as android martial artists landed knockout roundhouse kicks and robot teams marched into the arena heralded by flag-waving captains astride giant robotic dogs. The games’ blue-riband event, the 100m, did not disappoint when the robot-sprinters ranquicker than Usain Boltbefore slamming mindlessly into a padded wall in a blaze of sparks, flames and flying mechanical limbs.0:48Robots run, punch and score at World Humanoid Robot Games in China – videoThere, in a 10-second clip perfect for the games’ global online audience, was proof of what onlooking international experts described as the superpower’s “staggering” engineering progress, combined with comfort that the disintegrating robots might not yet be ready to become humanity’s overlords.“Ready for another big day of fail,” read a typically schadenfreude-laced comment from one of millions who tuned into viral social media clips and livestreams of events from boxing to breakdancing in which the humanoids displayed a jerky mix of ruthless effectiveness and pathetic failure.Others caught themselves experiencing unexpected empathy. One captioned a robot struggling through the 400m obstacle race: “after drinking 4 bottles of wine at 2 a.m”. Another found a weightlifting contest “way more emotional than I expected” as the bots strained to achieve their sporting goals.If the games had a slogan it might be: faster, higher, funnier. The obstacle course involving humanoids scrambling under nets, down stairs and over stepping stones reminded the comedian Charlie Higson of Monty Python’s Upper Class Twit of the Year sketch: “It’s only lacking ‘taking the bra off the debs’ and ‘shooting themselves’.” He came back the next day for more. “They get better and better,” he tweeted as a cheerleader robot wielding glittery pom-poms flailed around like it was having a fit.But the games were not intended to only entertain. Involving over 2,000 humanoids built by more than 660 mostly domestic tech companies, it was a propaganda flex of China’s robotics muscle just weeks before its president, Xi Jinping, lands in Washington DC for a summit with Donald Trump, where the superpowers’ race to tech supremacy will be high on the agenda. Only last monthTrump banned importsof Chinese humanoids and four-legged robot dogs, citing cyber and national security concerns. The event was also a billboard to boost global sales of Chinese robots as US rivals prepare their own launches, notably Elon Musk’slong-hypedOptimus humanoid which is reported to have finally gone into production this month. Last year China produced 12,800 humanoids, about 90% of the global total,accordingto the Mercator Institute for Chinese Studies, a dominance which perhaps gave China the confidence to candidly broadcast so many comic failures, which surprised some onlookers.View image in fullscreenRobots can run fast or box, but they can’t do both.Photograph: Achmad Ibrahim/APThe event reflected the fact that, for the Chinese Communist party, humanoids are a high priority, offering solutions to a looming demographic crunch in the labour market, rising military ambitions and, as they walk more widely among the people, the state’s desire to tighten its surveillance web. Beijing is fuelling an intensely competitive robot industry by seeding hundreds of companies to create an evolutionary survival of the fittest dynamic, with the games creating a hard deadline for competitors to deliver measurable progress. Xi’slatest five-year plan, approved in March, was studded with pledges to boost robotics industries; accelerate the “practical application of … humanoid robots” and explore “embodied AI in roles experiencing labour shortages or high-risk environments” which likely include war. The military potential of the humanoids on display worried some onlookers.“Fascinating, and honestly, a little scary,”saidArun Bothra, a senior police officer in India, which shares a tense border with China. “Watching robots run, play football and compete like humans is one thing. Seeing them on borders someday, carrying guns and making decisions, will be something else entirely.” Or as another viewer concluded while watching a humanoid hoist a loaded barbell in the weightlifting contest: “Humanity is preparing its own end”.Of courseChinais not alone in pursuing robotic warfare. As the Beijing games progressed on Monday, Ukraine was staging a novel military parade in Kyiv made up entirely of robotic weaponry and defence equipment.View image in fullscreenTiangong Ultra beats Usain Bolt’s record in the 100m sprint.Photograph: Tingshu Wang/ReutersBut how to explain the numerous crashes and fits in the Olympic speed skating arena where the competition took place? Experts said the games revealed how China was making the most rapid strides in developing humanoids’ bodies rather than their minds.“The progress they have made from last year is staggering,” said Thrishantha Nanayakkara, a professor of robotics at the Dyson school of design engineering at Imperial College London. “Everything seems to be coming together …. by 2030, it will be a very different world.”The fastest sprinter, Tiangong Ultra, completed the 100m more than twice as fast as last year, while the peak standing jump rose from 0.96 m to 3.40m. Liquid cooling has allowed Chinese engineers to increase the torque of the motors that drive their limbs creating more twitchy and powerful force.“This execution is incredible,” said Ingo Keller, head of robotics at the National Robotarium, based at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh. “You would not have expected the speed of development. [But] does it move the goalpost in utilising humanoids? Not necessarily.”View image in fullscreenAn Honor Lightning humanoid robot caught fire following the 100m final race.Photograph: Tingshu Wang/ReutersExperts stress the games revealed progress in specialist, not generalist, humanoids: the robots were fast runners or good boxers, not both, partly because the AI models that govern their decisions are yet to be able to process the physical world’s full complexity. The industry talks aboutreaching a ChatGPT moment– a tipping point when humanoid technology becomes generally useful and explodes into the mainstream. By one definition, that comes when a robot can succeed at 80% of tasks in an unfamiliar home, instructed by voice or text. The event coincided with asobering speechfrom Wang Xingxing, founder of Unitree, one of China’s leading robotics companies, who said it could be a decade before that ChatGPT moment.“Humanoids are not yet capable enough for mass deployment,” he said. “The limitations in the AI models that power robots’ decision-making and interactions remain the industry’s biggest bottleneck.” Amid uncertainty about the impact of robotics and bubble fears, his company’s share price has been oscillating wildly since it listed in Shanghai earlier this month.Georg Stieler, a consultant who advises multinational companies on robots, said he did not see much progress on robots’ autonomy when he was in Beijing this week. He reported that some Chinese robotics companies were also privately cynical about the five-day showcase, complaining about a lack of funding for commercial long-term pilot projects “to do something useful in a factory”.“It’s not so difficult to make a stunt, which people will share on LinkedIn or X,” Stieler said. “The major challenge is to do something that’s really useful.”Humanoid robot dexterity requires much more work and there was little focus on the events testing it. There was little obvious coverage of a Monty Pythonesque category that included power tool assembly, powder weighing, bottle opening, cap prying, box unpacking and tweezer bean-picking. One such challenge was briefly featured on Wednesday when the race track was occupied by the unspectacular sight of a humanoid struggling to pick up a small object from a table and spilling water in a pouring challenge. The cameras panned away to find a humanoid martial artist carving the air with kicks.

title: ‘In walked this big bundle of energy’: the day Dolly Parton came to Rotherham | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: Country star came to South Yorkshire town in 2007 for UK launch of the Imagination Library, her book donation scheme
Author: Esther Addley
Headline: Country star came to South Yorkshire town in 2007 for UK launch of the Imagination Library, her book donation scheme
Content: Dolly Parton with newborn Emma, the first baby in Rotherham to receive a book from the Imagination Library programme.Photograph: The Rotherham NHS Foundation TrustView image in fullscreenDolly Parton with newborn Emma, the first baby in Rotherham to receive a book from the Imagination Library programme.Photograph: The Rotherham NHS Foundation TrustDolly Parton‘In walked this big bundle of energy’: the day Dolly Parton came to RotherhamCountry star came to South Yorkshire town in 2007 for UK launch of the Imagination Library, her book donation schemeEsther AddleySat 29 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 09.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShane Jarman was up a ladder decorating a Christmas tree at the school where he was deputy headteacher when he got a call asking him to come toRotherhamhospital ASAP. It was December 2007 and Jarman’s wife, Claire, had given birth the previous day to their first child, a girl called Emma, so of course he rushed to the phone. All was well, he was told, but that “everything would become clear” when he got to the hospital.Once there, his wife told him – somewhat unexpectedly – that they were going to meet Dolly Parton. “And literally within what felt like five minutes,” he recalled, “there weregreat camera flashes, lots of noise, lots of clicking and in walked this real big bundle of energy.”View image in fullscreenShane Jarman and his wife, Claire, watch as Dolly Parton holds newborn Emma.Photograph: The Rotherham NHS Foundation TrustJarman said that as his wife handed over their tiny 4lb 6oz baby to the country star, “all I remember is seeingDolly Partonwith my little girl’s head in her hand and these great big red nails”.Dolly Parton brought divided Americans together. What can we learn from her? | Margaret SullivanRead moreWas he a little nervous about the nails? “I was very nervous about the nails to be quite honest.”Parton was in the SouthYorkshireformer mining and steelworking town – not principally known for its razzle-dazzle – for the British launch of the Imagination Library, the book donation programme the musician had started in her Tennessee home of Sevier County a little over a decade earlier, and which she had been invited to extend to children in Yorkshire.View image in fullscreenDolly Parton performs at the launch of her children’s literacy scheme in Rotherham.Photograph: Rui Vieira/PAIf Rotherham – or at least a gathering of local dignitaries that assembled later in a disused steelworks – was a little bemused by the singer, Parton knew places like this, and of course knew how to charm.“I gotta make sure I say your town name right – it’s Rother’m?” she said, flattening the famous southern twang to something approximating flat Yorkshire vowels. “Did I get it right? I’ve been practising because it don’t look like that on paper. In the States, anything that’sh-a-mwe have to say Rother-ham.”Among the torrent of tributes to the entertainer, businesswoman and philanthropist since her death on Monday, Rotherham toohas been rememberingthe impact of a woman who, for all her own glamour, cared deeply about places that had a little less of it.Parton may have jested when she said she had considered buying a South Yorkshire pied-à-terre (“so you may be walking down the streets of Rotherham and see me coming out of a little cubbyhole somewhere”), but her description of the post-industrialist town as “a heart spot for me” was sincere, thanks to the similarities she saw to her own outsider upbringing.“I totally related to Rotherham,”she saidsome years later. “I know that it’s out in an industrial area … When they were making fun of me for going out there, I thought, you know what? Don’t make fun of me.”The scheme ensured that every child in Rotherham was posted a free book, in their own name, for each month of their life until they were five, funded partly by Parton’s foundation and partly by the local authority and other local funders. Deborah Bullivant, who took over leading the Rotherham Imagination Library shortly after Parton’s visit as part of a wider literacy drive, said that despite some initial scepticism from locals, it “changed the culture” for many.View image in fullscreenDolly Parton meets young children at the Magna Science Adventure Centre in Rotherham in 2007.Photograph: Getty“Some people were very suspicious: Why Dolly Parton? What is this thing?” she said. “[But] can you imagine receiving a book, from registering your child’s birth, your baby in their own name receives the book every month through the letterbox? For many families who didn’t really have a background in reading, it changed the culture within their homes to being more of a reading culture and embracing books and using books and sharing books.”The fact that the literacy drive was so personal to the singer was “the best way to counter any of the suspicion or worries that people had about it”, Bullivant said. “Why is Dolly Parton doing this? Who is she? She doesn’t know about this? Well, she does. She understood she needed to drive her own work herself from scratch. She got the importance of the imagination, of reading, of telling stories.”Though the Rotherham scheme was wound up in 2015after the council withdrew support, it would be rolled out to other places in Britain, including Doncaster, North Lincolnshire, the London borough of Southwark (“Hello Suth’rk!This is Dolly!”) and Nottingham (which even coaxed an“Ay up me duck!”from the singer).View image in fullscreenShane Jarman and his daughter, Emma, now 18, today.Photograph: Family HandoutIn total, 6.3m books have been given to children across the four UK nations since one-day-old Emma Jarman received the first one in 2007, a copy of The Tale of Peter Rabbit, which Parton autographed for her. (Globally, the figure is 300m).Emma, now 18, will shortly be going to university to study biomedical science, “and, if I know Emma, [the book] will go to university with her so that she can show her friends there,” said her father.Explore more on these topicsDolly PartonRotherhamLiteracyYorkshireChildrennewsShareReuse this content

title: The battle over RAF Barnham: how ominous anti-asylum protests engulfed a small Norfolk town | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Thetford has a welcoming history. So why have there been so many demonstrations this summer over plans to house asylum seekers at a nearby military base – as well as nights of violent disorder?
Author: Tim Burrows
Headline: Thetford has a welcoming history. So why have there been so many demonstrations this summer over plans to house asylum seekers at a nearby military base – as well as nights of violent disorder?
Content: A protester on a march from Thetford to RAF Barnham.Photograph: Harry Murray/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA protester on a march from Thetford to RAF Barnham.Photograph: Harry Murray/The GuardianImmigration and asylumThe battle over RAF Barnham: how ominous anti-asylum protests engulfed a small Norfolk townThetford has a welcoming history. So why have there been so many demonstrations this summer over plans to house asylum seekers at a nearby military base – as well as nights of violent disorder?Tim BurrowsSat 29 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 05.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Idon’t talk to mainstream media,” says a young man in an Arsenal shirt. I’ve just asked what brought him to the latest protest against the housing of asylum seekers in Thetford,Norfolk, and his disdain is clear as he goes to warn other protesters of the Guardian’s presence. This isn’t exactly the unity promised by the flyer advertising today’s march: “Everyone welcome: families, friends, dogs. Including the media.”The protest is planned as a two-mile march from Thetford’s market square to RAF Barnham, a site just over the border in Suffolk, which is due to house asylum seekers while they progress through the system. It is the latest part of a campaign that has lasted the whole summer. Banners line the square, the largest succinctly describing why people are gathering here today: “Thetford and Barnham says no to asylum seekers.”View image in fullscreenProtesters march out of Thetford towards RAF Barnham, two miles away.Photograph: Harry Murray/The GuardianSome of the protesters are from Thetford, others from farther afield, but mostly Norfolk or Suffolk. I have been visiting Thetford in the weeks before the protest and, while the reasoning of the protesters varies, many say it comes down to numbers. How can this site house 1,250 people when the nearest village has a population of only 600?Some say the country can’t afford to keep housing asylum seekers as they wait to be processed, or that there are simply too many coming in, or that we don’t know who they are. Asylum seekers are referred to by some here as “boat people” and “invaders”. The suggestion that Britain has lost control of its borders is nothing new. But new theories still materialise. At a protest the week before the march, one attender suggested that people may be being sent intentionally from Iran. “They say that they are sending some of the terrorists over to the UK and we have no idea who comes off the boats,” a protester, David Goulty, told me. “There’s no control on who comes into the country.”In opposition, Labour criticised the Conservative policy of housing asylum seekers on military bases. But in October last year, now in government, it changed tack. The sexual assault of a 14-year-old girl by a resident ofthe Bell hotel in Epping, Essex,had prompted months of angry local protests against the housing of asylum seekers in hotels. Keir Starmer announced thatmilitary bases would be usedonce again.View image in fullscreenThe government has proposed that RAF Barnham house up to 1,250 asylum seekers.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PALabour was explicit aboutthe reason for the U-turn: “We know that communities don’t want asylum seekers housed in hotels, and neither does the government, and that’s why we are determined to fix the mess that we’ve inherited by getting a grip of the issue and committing to close every single asylum hotel, saving the taxpayer billions of pounds.”Typically of Starmer’s time as prime minister, the people he was trying to appease with this policy responded: “Thanks, we hate it.”Now, the Home Office is actively working to expand or open five sites, two of which are already active. MDP Wethersfield, a former RAF airfield in Essex, houses 800 asylum seekers, but could increase its capacity tomore than 1,200. Crowborough training camp in East Sussex plans to increase its numbersfrom 350 to 540; a volunteer vigilante patrol group has been set up in the area to “protect” locals from migrants. Three large military sites are being readiedwith a reported capacity of 1,250 each: MOD Bicester in Oxfordshire; RAF Linton-on-Ouse in North Yorkshire; and RAF Barnham.Much of the classic sitcom Dad’s Army was shot in Thetford, including the external shots of the episode that ends with the show’s most famous joke: “Don’t tell ’em, Pike!” The Guildhall on the market square, where the protesters congregate to start the march today, was often used as a backdrop.The Dad’s Army museum is on the other side of the Guildhall. One of the protesters is an 80-year-old US air force veteran who thinks the UK should emulate Trump’s immigration policy. He sees a group of tourists being led on the Dad’s Army guided tour and invites them to join the march. It’s clear they would rather hear more tales of Jones, Mainwaring and Pike.On the other side of the square, Anwar Noor, 63, is selling ice-creams from his truck to people gathering for the march. Noor came to Thetford from Kenya in the 1980s and worked in the Thermos factory for 17 years, before being made redundant when it closed. (Thermos moved manufacturing to Asia in 2000. Other big employers, such as the factory that processed Danepak bacon, have since closed, leading to the loss of hundreds of jobs.) Noor started another business, a scrapyard, before joining the ice-cream trade a couple of years back as he started his semi-retirement.View image in fullscreenAnwar Noor, a local ice-cream vendor, says blaming asylum seekers is ‘all wrong’.Photograph: Harry Murray/The GuardianYou could argue that Thetford is East Anglia’s capital of integration. In 1903, it elected the first black mayor in the UK, Allan Glaisyer Minns, who was born in the Bahamas and had trained as a doctor at Guy’s hospital in London. There is an established Portuguese community, congregating this morning at a cafe near the square, drinking bottles of Super Bock beer as a very loud wildlife documentary about porcupines plays on TV. The community moved here in their hundreds in the 2000s, after big East Anglian agribusinesses, including the turkey giant Bernard Matthews, set up recruitment offices in the country.There is a statue of Duleep Singh, the last maharaja of the Sikh empire, who was exiled to Britain from Punjab and became a favourite of Queen Victoria, living in Elveden Hall, just over the Suffolk border. His son, Prince Freddy Duleep Singh, became a scholar of Norfolk life and gave Thetford the Ancient House, a home thought to have been built in about 1490, which is still used as a public museum.But, asIan Jack wrote in 2007, during a visit in which he marvelled at Thetford’s burgeoning Portuguese community, while suggesting the town was already paranoid about immigration statistics: “To compare Prince Freddy with the immigrant ham-slicer or turkey-gutter is of course ridiculous.”View image in fullscreenMost people on the march were from Norfolk or Suffolk.Photograph: Harry Murray/The GuardianThere had already been unrest around immigration when Jack visited the town. In 2004, as New Labour’s second of three terms was nearing its end, Thetford was topping tables for deprivation and child poverty while coming bottom for skills and education. That summer, after England lost to Portugal in the quarter-finals of the European Championship, the Red Lion pub on the market square was besieged by more than 200 hooligans, trapping about 120 people – mostly Portuguese – inside the pub. They pelted the building with bottles and stones, smashed windows and tried to force their way in. Police called in reinforcements from all over Norfolk and several officers and pub customers were said to have sustained cuts from flying glass. It was more than two hours before those inside could leave.The Red Lion, now a Wetherspoons, feels more sedate today. It sits on the edge of the market square, which, in the sun, feels like a piazza with added pints. And yet Noor, as he doles out ice-creams, says he can understand why people are angry. “You probably noticed as you walked through the town how many shops are closed, post offices gone. All the banks are gone. You can see the centre hollowing out.” Noor says he understands local people’s frustration and that he has never experienced racism in Thetford. But he believes that blaming asylum seekers is “all wrong. We’re all in the same boat.”At times this August, what has happened in this small Norfolk town has seemed portentous, at risk of provoking another summer of unrest in England, after events inSouthport in 2024andEpping in 2025led to protests around the country.At the start of this month, the addresses of some houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) used to house asylum seekers in Thetford were leaked. This led to crowds of vigilantes targeting the properties on 4, 5 and 6 August.During the second night of unrest, hundreds of people descended on a terrace house on Clover Way in the 70s-built Fairfields estate. Some threw rocks and eggs, smashing an upstairs window, while others attempted to get inside. During these days of disorder, police officers were spat at, while one was hit by a rock and another was bitten. According to police, some of the vigilantes even entered a property andforced out a resident, stealing their mobile phone.View image in fullscreenOne of the homes attacked during the nights of violence in Thetford this month.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianMore than 20 people were arrestedon suspicion of a variety of offences, including racially aggravated public order, inciting racial hatred and conspiracy to commit aggravated burglary, as well as possession of cocaine with intent to supply, possession of cannabis and driving without insurance.On the day of the Thetford to Barnham march, I visit Clover Way. The house that was once home to asylum seekers is immediately identifiable by the dried yolk that remains on the windows, almost three weeks after the eggs were thrown.One of the neighbours comes out to have a cigarette. She tells me she had to flee to a friend’s house over the road on the night the crowds came; since losing her husband last year, she lives on her own. She suggests I speak to her neighbour, John Finch, 91. He says the people who sold the house that was besieged were initially going to sell it to a family, but they were gazumped by a company, which offered more money.View image in fullscreen‘These people have been failed,’ says Terry Jermy, the MP for Thetford.Photograph: Harry Murray/The GuardianOn the night the protesters arrived, the crowds stood on Finch’s flowerbeds and trampled his plants. He saw the melee out of his window, but decided to go to bed. “I slept through it,” he says. He was in the RAF police branch that served in Cyprus when Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots started firing at each other. “I’ve seen worse.”When the disturbances went viral online, it brought infamy to this quiet street. The next day, film crews arrived, as did people keen to see the newly famous house covered in egg. “There were a lot of people coming,” says Finch. “They were coming in cars and stopping and just looking at it. And I think: it’s an empty bloody house, for Christ’s sake.” He shrugs. “Perhaps it was the highlight of their life.” Thankfully, after those three ugly nights, the violent disorder in Thetford fizzled out. But the anti-asylum protests continued.The first protest against the use of RAF Barnham to house asylum seekers was in June 2026. Now, every Sunday, they happen like clockwork at 2pm. The week before the march from Thetford town centre to RAF Barnham, I visit the protest camp at the military base.I park on the dry grass verge and walk towards the protest, noticing a makeshift shed offering drinks to protesters for whatever they can afford. A shirtless fortysomething man with a tan greets me and asks if I want a drink. Clinton Warner grew up across the road from the site and knows its history. He runs a used-car company and each weekend he moves his stock out of the way, so that there is parking space to accommodate the protesters.Warner tells me a contract worker, tasked with servicing the sewers on the RAF Barnham site, gave him a tipoff about the plan to house asylum seekers there. He decided to blow the whistle. “They were asked to recommission it, so the contractors knew about it seemingly before the councillors,” he says. “We put it online.”View image in fullscreen‘It doesn’t matter whether you’re left or right wing. This is not what it’s about’ … Terry Curtis, one of the protest movement’s organisers.Photograph: Harry Murray/The GuardianRAF Barnham has been used in many ways over the years. It has been a logistics hub for the RAF, and during the second world war it was a mustard gas and munitions storage facility. After the war, it was commissioned by Churchill to store nuclear bombs and everyone forgot about themustard gasstored underground. Warner remembers being warned: “Do not remove wildlife from these ponds, do not pick the lilies, do not remove the flowers, leave everything, because it’s all hazardous.”The use of sites such as Barnham to house asylum seekers isn’t only controversial with concerned residents. Two years ago, the UK parliament’shome affairs select committee wrotethat the use of large military sites to house asylum claimants had “generally proved more costly to deliver than hotel accommodation”. Military sites cost more because ofthe cost of refurbishing them; they are often in a poor state of repair.When it comes to the asylum issue, the UK government seldom learns the lessons published by parliament. Rather than respond to the evidence, the government seems trapped in a reactionary loop, apparently keen to be seen to do something punitive.“In policy discourse, there’s this concern about how some asylum accommodation can function as a pull factor,” says Nuni Jorgensen, a researcher at theMigrationObservatory at the University of Oxford. “Politicians often say hotels can work as a pull factor because people imagine that these are fancy hotels and that’s why they come to the UK. But the evidence that we have on that is not very clear.” That hasn’t stopped politicians such as Reform UK’s Nigel Farage making hay with the suggestion. Jorgensen adds, however, that there is a lot of evidence showing that larger sites negatively affect asylum seekers’ wellbeing.View image in fullscreenNo one in Thetford who spoke to the Guardian said anything in support of asylum.Photograph: Harry Murray/The GuardianWhen it comes to housing, asylum planning boils down to three choices. Hotels are cheaper when it comes to housing many migrants at one site. HMOs seem a good option when it comes to integration and infrastructure, but are hampered by the reality of house prices. And then there are military sites, which are notoriously difficult to use for this purpose.Hotels are easier to source than HMOs, says Jorgensen, but they “have been linked to very poor mental-health outcomes among residents”, as the conditions are often cramped and unclean and isolate them from the community. Dispersal to neighbourhood HMOs has, historically, been the Home Office’s preferred option. “They tend to be cheaper than hotels. They tend to produce the best wellbeing outcomes for asylum seekers. The problem is that they are very hard to find in some areas.”The failure of the hotels policy and suspicion around private management of HMOs are among the issues that have led to the use of large military sites.It is clear that these sites are controversial. Along with the volunteer vigilante patrol group in Crowborough, a village near RAF Bicester has voted symbolicallyto leave the UKover the policy. The use of military sites to house asylum seekers has, in a way, united left and right in opposition, but on very different grounds. Human rights campaigners say they amount to a form of“open-prison camp”, while Reform UKlikens them to holiday camps.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn my first visit to RAF Barnham, I meet Terry Curtis, 40, one of the protest movement’s organisers. He was present at the HMO protests in early August, he says, but left “when things escalated … because it’s not what we’re here for”. He says the police were heavy-handed in their tactics; he mentions thata woman on a mobility scooter was pepper-sprayed. No one I speak to who was present at the HMO protests seems to have considered how afraid those living in the affected properties must have been.View image in fullscreen‘Our schools are rubbish and our healthcare system is rubbish. They’re going to be grumpy and they’re looking for somebody to blame.’Photograph: Harry Murray/The GuardianCurtis moved to Thetford from south London when he was 15 and still supports Millwall. London accents can be heard all over Thetford. In the 1950s, the town’s population was 5,000. By the end of the 1960s, due to overspill from the capital, it had more than tripled to 17,000. In that booming decade, when new towns were referred to as “pram towns” because of the amount of children being born, Thetford was the fastest-growing in the country.The Abbey estate was the last to be completed in that period of great expansion. In 1968, it was opened by Labour’s minister for housing, Tony Greenwood, who said the design was “exceptional”. The estate is today the poorest area of Thetford and was one of the locations of the violent protests in early August. Regeneration plans were announced in 2019,which were deeply unpopularwith many residents andscrapped by Reform UKwhen they took over Norfolk county council in May. This was part of a Reform UK surge across the county, except in liberal, urban Norwich.Curtis says he knows what it’s like to go through hard times: “I’ve been homeless myself … I’ve been in hostels.” The movement isn’t affiliated with any political party, he says, which feels like a stretch. Local Reform UK politicians mingle with the protesters each week, including the councillorScott Hussey, a former Sun journalist who has moved back to his home town and seems fully committed to the anti-immigration agenda.View image in fullscreenProtesters outside RAF Barnham.Photograph: Harry Murray/The GuardianIt is clear that the rise of Reform, and Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain, in East Anglia has put the wind in the sails of movements such as these. Reform UK now runs the county councils in Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex, in each case unseating the Conservatives, while Restore-backed candidatesswept all 10 contested seatsthey stood for in the May 2026 local elections.“I feel like we’ve got more inequality than we have equality these days,” says Curtis. “Everybody should be treated the same. And, unfortunately, we’re not. Everything’s going up.Prices are going up. Taxes are going up. But, yeah, people are able to come over here, you know, on boats, seek asylum and then get a home, get a house, get what they want – fed, gas, electric, all paid for by the government, which is inadvertently [sic] the taxpayers. Personally, I think we should close the borders to everybody. Get our own country sorted first.”A failure of political communication, and the rise of social media that reward extreme content, has led to the anti-asylum narrative in UK politics becoming overwhelming. This isn’t lost on Terry Jermy, the Labour MP who represents South West Norfolk, the constituency that includes Thetford.Some MPs parachute into a constituency with barely any knowledge of it. Not Jermy. He shot up the ranks of local politics, from town councillor in 2008 to mayor in 2016, before giving Liz Truss her Portillo moment in 2024, when he was unexpectedly elected MP at the expense of the former prime minister.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Harry Murray/The GuardianJermy’s family has lived in Thetford for hundreds of years. In his maiden speech, in October 2024, he alluded to the fact his dad was one of 13 and his mum had seven brothers. “With nearly 40 aunties and uncles and over 100 cousins, I am sure that I owe at least my first election victory to my grandparents’ love for one another.”After the HMO attacks, Jermy said the violence was “scaring and terrifying people who live in Thetford, particularly people from minority ethnic communities who are contacting me terrified that they are going to be misidentified as an asylum seeker and attacked”.Jermy says he can see why the hotels policy had to change – “it’s not a good use of taxpayers’ money” – and isn’t against the use of military bases in principle. But he strongly opposes the use of Barnham. “I get branded a hypocrite when I say that Barnham’s not appropriate,” he says. “But if you’ve been to Barnham [the village rather than the military base], you will see that it’s relatively small. It’s in the middle of nowhere and it’s going to cost the government a fortune to put in the sewage and electricity and everything else that’s needed to make it work. I suspect, once they’ve done their calculations, they will realise that the cost-benefit rules it out.”He points out that Barnham was only ever an overflow base for Honnington, a much bigger base nearby. Barnham has been empty for a long time and Jermy says a lot of the buildings are in a state of disrepair, “so new modular units will have to be built” to accommodate people.View image in fullscreenTerry Jermy, the Labour MP for South West Norfolk, which includes Thetford.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianThe truth is, like a lot of asylum policy, this plan doesn’t feel very well thought-out. Meanwhile, the language used by the Home Office has been sloppy to the point of stoking rage, he says. “Inthe official government factsheetabout Barnham, they referred to the people due to be based there as ‘illegal migrants’. They are asylum seekers. They are waiting to be processed.”Jermy has flagged this with Home Office ministers, but he is facing an uphill battle with his constituents over a subject that is confusing at the best of times. “Most people don’t understand the difference between refugee, asylum seeker and economic migrant. And we’ve got a lot of work to do in this country to educate people about that, but also to talk more positively about immigration and its contribution to society.”He doesn’t blame local residents for being angry. “These people have been failed,” he says. “They’ve been failed by decades in which people don’t shop in town centres any more and manufacturing is on the decline. And the vast majority of jobs locally are minimum wage. Our schools are rubbish and our healthcare system is rubbish. They’re going to be grumpy and they’re looking for somebody to blame. And rather than us, as a Labour government, articulating, actually, that it’s greed and austerity that are driving this, a lot of the language that we have used, trying to out-Reform Reform, has aided and abetted a lot of those concerns.”At 1.30pm on Sunday, the march from Thetford to Barnham is due to begin. A group of women assemble behind the main banner. The march starts and passes through town. Shoppers stop and stare at the collection of union and St George’s flags.The protesters move past a golden statue of Thomas Paine, the Thetford-born autodidact, founding father of the US and author of Rights of Man. The statue glints in the sunshine as Louis Armstrong’s What a Wonderful World drifts out of a speaker on wheels, being pulled by a female protester. The next track is Vera Lynn’s The White Cliffs of Dover. As we turn a corner, a horse-drawn hearse, crewed by three funeral directors in traditional garb, arrives out of nowhere, carrying a cardboard coffin with “DEMOCRACY” written on its side.A handful of people watch the protesters pass. One or two are clapping. I don’t come across anyone who is vocally against the protests, despite talking to scores of people. It occurs to me later that I didn’t meet anyone who wanted to say anything in support of asylum at all.View image in fullscreenA macabre view of British politics.Photograph: Harry Murray/The GuardianAnd yet, the turnout of 130 people or so tells its own story. Although the march was billed as a community event, it hasn’t attracted a big crowd. One of the main chants as we walk out of town is distinctly un-family-friendly: “Deport, deport, deport the fucking lot.”Jermy isn’t here because, although he agrees that Barnham should not be used to house asylum seekers, the protests have attracted gestures of support from not only Reform UK and Restore, but also the far-right partyBritain First. During the protests at RAF Barnham, says Jermy, “there have been speeches on the stage which have basically been outright racist and disgusting and my presence would be seen as condoning that behaviour”.We are on the straight road out to Barnham when the crowd starts cheering for a young man who is standing on the side of the common, setting off a flare attached to a St George’s flag. Acrid smoke spreads across the march. As two police officers approach the young man, an accomplice on a motorbike arrives, speeding him off towards a housing estate, to more cheers.The march crosses the border from Norfolk to Suffolk, exiting Jermy’s constituency and entering the Bury St Edmunds and Stowmarket constituency of his fellow Labour MP Peter Prinsley. “It’s affecting the whole country,” says Jean Glasdale, 73, who has come to the march from just outside Bury St Edmunds. What does she want the government to do? “I want them to deport them,” she says. “I want to be able to walk safely. I mean, they’re not just raping children, they’re raping pensioners like me. I want to feel safe in my own country.”Talk of rape, amplified and distorted, fills the air at events like this. After we reach Barnham, male speaker after male speaker from Reform UK and smaller fringe parties follow each other on to the small stage with ever greater claims about what rape statistics suggest about migrant behaviour,generating fear about the threat posed by “undocumented, fighting-age men”.View image in fullscreenA protester escapes the police after setting off a flare.Photograph: Harry Murray/The GuardianWhat is clear fromthe statistics is that most rapes are perpetrated bymen already known to the victim. But the image of men marauding the countryside and making women unsafe is potent and heavily exploited. I talk to a 38-year-old woman who lives near RAF Barnham and is on the protest with her small children. She is full of fear, she says, about what she sees as the threat posed by asylum seekers. She is so scared, in fact, that she thinks they should be held in detention offshore: “The safety of people is paramount. If they’re off from the main island – you know, if they’re off, say, Shetland or wherever – it’s another barrier and it’s another bit of protection for us.”Safety concerns trump talk of specific ideologies – and sometimes reality. “No, there’s no far right,” says Curtis, the organiser. “It doesn’t matter whether you’re left or right wing. This is not what it’s about. It’s just about the community – all the communities getting together to feel safe. You know, everybody’s concerned for the safety of the whole area. Because the people that are going to be put here are going to be able to dowhatever they want, whenever they want.”It’s a message that magnifies the threat of foreign-born men. “It’s been going on since for ever,” says Vron Ware, author of Return of a Native, of the exploitation of these primal fears of rape by “others” and “invaders”. Ware’s book is a reckoning with rural England and chancers such as Lowe and Farage who try to exploit its insecurities.In the 1980s, Ware was the editor of the anti-fascist publication Searchlight. “I’ve got a poster of an old fascist march in the 70s where someone’s got a placard that says: ‘75% of rapings are done by immigrants.’ It’s just a trope that never goes away.”After the march, I ask Curtis how he thought it went. He seems a little disappointed with the turnout. He says he is going to take some time out from organising, which has taken its toll.I leave RAF Barnham with Harry Murray, who has been taking photographs for the Guardian. We trudge along the side of the road, articulated lorries rushing past, until we reach a footpath through a field. As we make our way towards town, passing a few cows, I think about how angry everyone is – not just at events like today, but everywhere and all the time – and how draining it feels.Will the rage blowing through East Anglia eventually die down? I think back to Glasdale, to whom I was talking as the march neared the protest camp. When I asked her if she thought the populist party she leaflets for, Restore, could make a dent in the next general election, maybe even win it, she was very positive. “We’ve only got to look at today,” she said. “These people are so …incensed.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘Their whole village has disappeared’: frantic hunt for survivors in Kathmandu hospital | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Family members pin photos of Nepal’s missing to hospital wall as people try not to give up hope on loved ones
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Family members pin photos of Nepal’s missing to hospital wall as people try not to give up hope on loved ones
Content: People search posters of those missing in Nepal floodNepal-Tibet flood disaster‘Their whole village has disappeared’: frantic hunt for survivors in Kathmandu hospitalFamily members pin photos of Nepal’s missing to hospital wall as people try not to give up hope on loved onesNepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updatesHannah Ellis-PetersenandGaurav Pokharelin KathmanduSat 29 Aug 2026 10.11 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 10.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePosters of missing people line the wall of the hospital, the glue still fresh beneath. A schoolgirl smiling in her uniform; a beaming, chubby-cheeked baby; a couple smiling on their wedding day; a young man, hands on hips, atop a mountain peak; a young girl with flowing hair, peaking out from behind a door.These faces are just a fraction of the thousands who have not been seen since deadly flash floods coursed through the Himalayas and wiped away entire villages. By Saturday morning, the toll of the missing had risen to almost 3,000, in both Nepal andTibet.View image in fullscreenRelatives search through lists of people reported missing outside the hospital in Kathmandu.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianSo far,Nepalhas recovered 675 bodies, but many remote areas have only been accessed by army helicopters on the hunt for survivors. Rescuers said it was too difficult to assess how many more people might be buried beneath the mud.The task of identifying the dead is also gargantuan.In the Nepali city of Chitwan, the morgues have been overrun by the sheer number of bodies and a makeshift building has been set up to house the dead.Some of the bodies were carried so far down the river by the force of the floods, they were recovered in neighbouring India.2:02Timeline of how deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – explainerAt Tribhuvan University teaching hospital in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, desperate relatives gathered in the hope of news. Four days on since the disaster struck, people continued to crowd round the police desk to register the names of missing family members. Hundreds of the injured are recovering in the hospital’s wards and people were frantically checking lists of patients, desperate to find a sign that their loved ones were still alive.View image in fullscreenRelatives look through the lists of missing flood victims at the teaching hospital.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianIn the absence of information and with affected areas almost completely cut off, many families have resorted to making posters to appeal for information. Yavraj Lama said his sister, her husband and their two children were missing after their village of Jaydada, in Rusawa district, had been entirely washed away.His eyes filled with tears as he glued a photo of one-year-old Sijan Tawang, a baby in the arms of his mother, to the hospital wall. A picture of 12-year-old Sahil, his brother, hung next to it.“We are numb, we don’t have words to say how sad and distraught we are,” said Lama. “Our main focus is trying to find baby Sijan. He was so sweet and innocent; it’s impossible for us to think he is not with us any more.“But their whole village has disappeared,” he added, “so we have no hope left that any of them survived.”View image in fullscreenMonita Nepali, right, whose husband is missing, is comforted at the hospital in Kathmandu.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianMonita Nepali, 22, howled in grief as a poster of her missing husband, Vishal Nepali, 30, was pinned to the hospital wall. They had married six months ago and his work as a driver regularly took him to the border between Nepal and Tibet. She had spoken to her husband an hour before the floods hit when he was out for a morning walk in Rusawa. He had promised to call her that evening, but his phone has been ever off since.“I don’t want to live on the face of this earth without him,” she said. Four days may have passed, Nepali said, but she had not stopped believing in her husband’s return. “I feel it in my heart he will come back.”10:11‘Erased before their eyes’: desperate rescue efforts continue after Nepal-Tibet floods - The LatestFor some families, the scale of the loss was too hard to comprehend. Tulmaya Tamang, 36, came to the hospital bearing posters of some of her 12 family members, including her five-month-old niece, who lived in a village in Rusawa and have not been seen since the floods.“Our family is under tremendous stress,” she said. “So many are gone, and those of us who are left behind are struggling.”As hopes for their survival faded, Tamang said they were now just hoping the bodies could be retrieved. “If we had the bodies, then at least we could have peace,” she said. “Otherwise, the family will never stop wondering and this pain will go on for a very long time.”At least 900 of those still missing were working on the vast hydropower projects along the Trishuli River corridor, high up in the Himalayas, which were decimated by the floods and mudslides. Many of the workers were low-paid labourers, including at least 63 from India.View image in fullscreenA Nepali soldier rescues a survivor from a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa district, Nepal.Photograph: Nepal Army Handout/EPAOn Friday, dramatic footage showed Nepali soldiers pulling several survivors out through a thick wall of mud from a tunnel in the Trishuli-1 hydropower project. The Nepali army said they believed at least another 100 people were still trapped inside the tunnels, as well as dozens more stuck underground in the Trishuli-3 hydropower plant.Among those missing was 24-year-old Sujan Nepali, who had just finished his night shift at the hydropower project and was asleep in bed when the wall of water came gushing down the valley. At the hospital trauma centre in Nepal, his sister, Sushisha Maluwar, had returned anxiously every day to check if his name was listed.“We haven’t lost hope,” she said. “We are writing down his name at the hospitals and putting up his photographs everywhere, hoping that we might find him somewhere. Maybe he has already been rescued. Maybe he had managed to escape and survive.”Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetFloodingSouth and central AsiaNatural disastersnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s no surprise’: the manosphere mogul convicted of attacking pregnant girlfriend | Domestic violence | The Guardian
description: Podcaster James English is one of many men with far-right ties to have been found guilty or accused of domestic violence
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Podcaster James English is one of many men with far-right ties to have been found guilty or accused of domestic violence
Content: James English at Glasgow sheriff court where he was found guilty of domestic abuse.Photograph: Mike GibbonsView image in fullscreenJames English at Glasgow sheriff court where he was found guilty of domestic abuse.Photograph: Mike GibbonsDomestic violence‘It’s no surprise’: the manosphere mogul convicted of attacking pregnant girlfriendPodcaster James English is one of many men with far-right ties to have been found guilty or accused of domestic violenceGeraldine McKelvieSat 29 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 12.01 EDTShareIn many ways, the case heard this week at Glasgow sheriff court was, unfortunately, not out of the ordinary.
