It was one of thousands of domestic violence trials to have passed through the Scottish courts since new legislation was introduced in 2019 to clamp down on a grimly persistent problem.A woman had testified that her former partner had waged a campaign of terror against her, and that she suffered abuse while she was pregnant with his child.The court heardthat her partner had grabbed her by the throat, pinned her to a door, kicked her off a bed and sent her abusive texts, sometimes calling her a “fat slag” and a “little bitch”.What caught the eye of onlookers, however, was the identity of the man convicted.James English may not be a household name, but in the online world he is a star, a podcaster with millions of followers across several social media platforms for his interview show, Anything Goes.English has won plaudits for securing high profile guests, such as the footballer Paul Gascoigne and Rebecca Loos, who allegedly had an affair with David Beckham.However, he has also attracted controversy for his ties to figures from the far right, particularly the English Defence League founder Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, more commonly known as Tommy Robinson. Last September, English appeared atRobinson’s Unite the Kingdom rally, describing the event as “legendary” and praising Robinson for organising it.View image in fullscreenEnglish has hosted Robinson several times on the Anything Goes podcast.Photograph: YouTubeDuring the course of his podcasting, English has also platformed personalities from what has become known as the manosphere.Other guests on English’s podcast have included men accused of serious sexual offences, such as Andrew Tate, the internet personality recently charged with rape and sex trafficking, and the footballer David Goodwillie.Goodwillie and his former teammate, David Robertson, were ordered to pay £100,000 in damages to Denise Clair after a judge in a civil case ruled they had raped her after a night out in 2011.English, a 42-year-old father of three from Larkhall, Lanarkshire, reinvented himself as an independent journalist after appearing on Glow, a failed reality television show billed as a Glaswegian Towie.Although he says he does not necessarily share the views of his guests, he has given a range of far-right activists a sympathetic platform. As well as hosting Robinson several times, he has interviewed the commentator Katie Hopkins and the Raise the Colours founder Ryan Bridge.View image in fullscreenKatie Hopkins on the Anything Goes podcast.Photograph: YouTubeThe Unite the Kingdom march was “beautiful” and “very patriotic”, English said. “The people that have been on stage speaking, Katie Hopkins, Tommy Robinson, it’s been unbelievable,” he said, on a clip posted on Robinson’s X account. “It’s been great to see so many people getting behind each other and uniting for a better future.”View image in fullscreenPeople at the Unite the Kingdom rally in London in May.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersEnglish is one of many men with ties to the far right who have found themselves accused of intimate partner violence.Project Starlight, a 2021 study commissioned by Counter Terrorism Policing, found that about a third of people referred to the government’s Prevent programme had links to a domestic abuse incident, either as an offender, victim, witness or a combination of all three. In 18% of these cases, extreme rightwing ideology was present.Deniz Ugur, the deputy director of the End Violence Against Women Coalition, said police data had “consistently shown that a significant proportion of men arrested during far-right riots are already known to the police for domestic abuse”.The Guardian previously revealed that 41% of those arrested in the 2024 riots, prompted by the murders of three young girls in Southport,had been reported to the police for alleged domestic abuse. After the riots, 21% were accused of similar offences.English had already been charged with abusing the woman, a model he met on Instagram, by the time he travelled to London for the Unite the Kingdom protest. One of its central themes was the threat supposedly posed by migrant men to British women and girls. “It’s all about saving the children,” English said.Some speakers promoted conspiracies about migration, including the “great replacement theory – the suggestion that there is a plot to replace white Europeans with people from other races. While English described the march as “peaceful”, the Metropolitan police said its officers faced “unacceptable violence” from some demonstrators, more than 20 of whom were arrested.View image in fullscreenPeople gathered in front of parliament at the Unite the Kingdom rally.Photograph: Tayfun Salcı/EPAThis week, Sheriff David Hall, who heard English’s case without a jury, convicted him of engaging in a course of abusive conduct towards his former partner between July 2022 and November 2023. The single charge included 19 allegations, six of which Hall judged to have been proved. He described the woman as “credible and reliable”.Alice Russell Harris, public affairs lead at the domestic abuse charity Refuge, said: “The manosphere, which significantly overlaps with far-right communities, has helped amplify misogynistic narratives that objectify and seek to control women, casting women as subordinate to men and suggesting that those who reject male expectations deserve punishment. These ideas can directly promote abuse – both online and offline – by encouraging men to engage in coercion, control and related harms.”English, who will be sentenced next month, was not in court to hear Hall’s verdict on Tuesday. However, the next day, he used his social media platforms to issue a rallying cry to his followers, sharing misinformation about the legal basis for his conviction.“Men need to be worried, especially inScotland,” he said. “Ladies, if you have a brother or a son, you should also be worried, because women can say anything and it’s a man’s job to prove his innocence.” He added that, in Scotland, “accusations are enough to get the man charged”.double quotation markIt is no surprise to see a convicted perpetrator of domestic abuse and prominent figure in the far right promote deeply harmful misinformation about violence against women and girlsDeniz UgurIn fact, Scottish law is underpinned by the principle of corroboration, where two independent sources of evidence are required to prove a criminal accusation. Defendants are innocent until proved guilty and the testimony of a single witness – no matter how compelling – is not enough to secure a conviction.Neither English nor any of the nine people he claimed could support his version of events took the stand. English said this was because he was “so confident” he would be cleared. “I should never have been charged, never mind convicted,” he said.Ugur said: “It is no surprise to see a convicted perpetrator of domestic abuse and prominent figure in the far right promote deeply harmful misinformation about violence against women and girls.“Most victims do not report to the police, and those who do, know how many hurdles there are to seeing a conviction due to institutional cultures of victim blaming and failures to treat violence against women and girls with the seriousness it warrants.”Despite the headlines his case has generated, English has remained defiant, criticising the mainstream media for covering it. “People need to be wary, because if they want you, they’ll find something to get you on,” he said, adding that he was “tired of men getting fucked over”.He did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian, but vowed on his social media channels to continue broadcasting. “I’m still going to keep doing what I’m doing,” he said. “If anything, it’s just fuelled me to keep raising the bar.”

title: James Cleverly resigns from shadow cabinet to run for mayor of London | James Cleverly | The Guardian
description: Shadow minister for housing, communities and local government to resign with immediate effect
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Shadow minister for housing, communities and local government to resign with immediate effect
Content: Cleverly has held the posts of both home and foreign secretary for the Conservatives.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCleverly has held the posts of both home and foreign secretary for the Conservatives.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianJames CleverlyJames Cleverly resigns from shadow cabinet to run for mayor of LondonShadow minister for housing, communities and local government to resign with immediate effectSammy GecsoylerSat 29 Aug 2026 12.24 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 11.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJames Cleverly has resigned from the shadow cabinet to run for mayor of London.The Tory heavyweight, who was once home and foreign secretary and is shadow minister for housing, communities and local government, told the Sunday Times he will resign with immediate effect.The MP for Braintree, who lost his bid to lead theConservativesto Kemi Badenoch, is considered a more moderate voice in a party that has lurched to the right. On breaking the news to Badenoch, Cleverly told the Sunday Times: “She took it very well. Kemi has been very gracious.”He added: “Our route to getting Kemi in No 10 has got to be through success inLondon,” he said. “It’s a business city, entrepreneurialism, arts, culture. I don’t buy the lazy idea that London is a Labour city. It represents the philosophical heart of the Conservative party.”Cleverly’s resignation comes in advance of the Conservative party conference in October, where he is expected to make his case to party members.According to the Sunday Times, sources close to Badenoch said she was “gutted” about the news but added that she “is delighted that someone of his calibre wants to put himself forward to be Conservative nominee for mayor of London”.Cleverly had kind words for Badenoch. “Frankly, Kemi is doing really well now. She’s getting great cut-through. It took longer than any of us would have liked, but she’s getting it,” he said.Sadiq Khan is halfway through his third term as mayor. He has not stated whether he will run for a fourth term in the contest to be held in May 2028. Susan Hall was the Tory candidate in 2024 but lost to Khan, who was declared the winner with 43.8% of the vote.If Khan does step down, the Labour MP for Brent Central and Brent South, Dawn Butler, is expected to throw her hat in the ring, having previously revealed her desire for the job.Cleverly is the most senior Tory politician to run for mayor of London in recent times. Making his bid, he said Khan was “asleep at the wheel” and accused him of using the role as a stepping stone for a higher-profile position.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Sadiq has been trying to get out of that job for quite a while. He went in with the intention of doing what Boris [Johnson] did, using it as a high-profile platform to get him his next big job in government. There has been lots of posturing, very little delivery. Lots of picking rows with the president of America, less focus on bringing down street crime. It wouldn’t surprise me if he bows out for 2028. He’s lost the passion for the job.”Days before Keir Starmer stood down as prime minister, he handed Khan a peerage, potentially opening the door to him joining Andy Burnham’s cabinet in future. However, while Burnham and Khan have worked closely together over the years and have a shared understanding of the challenges of devolution, it is understood Khan has told the former Manchester mayor that he has no wish to be a minister in his government.Explore more on these topicsJames CleverlyConservativesLondonMayoral electionsLocal governmentLocal politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Palestinian woman and NBC News team reportedly attacked in West Bank | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Matt Bradley and crew assaulted while interviewing woman who said settlers had driven family out of home
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Matt Bradley and crew assaulted while interviewing woman who said settlers had driven family out of home
Content: Matt Bradley of NBC News in the West Bank on 13 August.Photograph: mattmcbradley/NBC NewsView image in fullscreenMatt Bradley of NBC News in the West Bank on 13 August.Photograph: mattmcbradley/NBC NewsWest BankPalestinian woman and NBC News team reportedly attacked in West BankMatt Bradley and crew assaulted while interviewing woman who said settlers had driven family out of homeEdward HelmoreSat 29 Aug 2026 17.55 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 17.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Palestinian woman and an NBC News team are reported to have been attacked and injured by masked Israeli settlers in the Israeli-occupiedWest Bankon Saturday, amid worsening confrontations in the area.Benjamin Netanyahu said he condemned the violence committed “by a handful of rioters”.The attack occurred when four members of the news team wereinterviewingAida Ahmed Abdullah and her family in the Palestinian town of Jalud, near Nablus.Abdullah told the outlet that they had been driven out of their home by settlers, and the team was walking down a hill toward the house.A car with Israeli license plates reversed up the hill toward them. At least four men with their faces covered leapt from the vehicle, hitting them with sticks and throwing rocks.“They jumped out, beat us, then jumped back in the car,” saidNBCNews correspondent Matt Bradley. Bradley was hit twice in the arm and treated at a nearby clinic.Abdullah, 51, was taken for medical care by the Red Crescent. Her injuries were not life-threatening. Three other members of the news team were also injured and treated.“Suddenly a car came to us,” said producer Lawahez Jabari. “The settlers had sticks, I saw a gun, but they didn’t use the gun.”Camera operator Khaldoon Eid said the team had not expected to be attacked in a village.Several violent incidents in the area were reported on Saturday. Palestinian workers were pepper-sprayed in nearby Qusra by masked Israeli settlers.Israeli security forces told the outlet they had received reports that “violent clashes had occurred, including stone-hurling toward Palestinians and additional civilians”.They said “security forces identified dozens of rioters who had barricaded themselves inside a Palestinian home while Palestinian residents were inside”, the statement said.“The security forces who arrived at the scene initially operated to remove the rioters from the home and separate the groups, in order to protect the residents inside. In addition, the security forces confiscated vehicles belonging to the Israeli rioters that were suspected of having been used to reach the area,” the statement said.“IDF soldiers and Israel Border Police forces continue to operate in the areas of Qusra and Jalud to prevent further disturbances and restore order in the area,” it added.Earlier this month, a group of settlers began blocking supplies from entering Palestinian houses on the outskirts of the village near Nablus, trapping residents inside and drawing strong criticism from the US ambassador.Israeli forces continue to operate in the area while settlers still roam the surrounding hills.Netanyahu, whose government has been accused of turning a blind eye to the settler attacks, condemned the “criminal acts of violence” and blamed “a handful of rioters who violate the law, cause enormous injustice to the law-abiding settler public, hinder the IDF in fulfilling its missions and harm Israel’s standing in the world”.According to the United Nations’ office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs, Israeli forces or settlers killed 76 Palestinians in the West Bank in the year to 24 July. Three Israelis were killed over the same period.Explore more on these topicsWest BankNBCIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Far-right media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos deported by ICE from US to UK | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Ex-Breitbart editor has vocally supported immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residency
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Ex-Breitbart editor has vocally supported immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residency
Content: Milo Yiannopoulos in New York City on 21 February 2017.Photograph: Drew Angerer/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMilo Yiannopoulos in New York City on 21 February 2017.Photograph: Drew Angerer/Getty ImagesUS immigrationFar-right media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos deported by ICE from US to UKEx-Breitbart editor has vocally supported immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residencyEdward HelmoreSat 29 Aug 2026 13.08 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFar-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US after beingdetainedon Thursday by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in New Orleans in connection with what the agency said was expired authorization to be in the country and a deportation order.Yiannopoulos’s deportation to the UK occurred on Friday, said a statement on Saturday from a spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE.A DHS spokesperson on Friday said that Yiannopoulos, 41, had been arrested by ICE on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans international airport. The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019 through New York City but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.The spokesperson said that Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”.The spokesperson added: “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”Yiannopoulos – who has previously been a vocal supporter of ICE and immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residency – was believed to have been arrested while heading to a concert by rapper Ye, formerly Kanye West.West performed at New Orleans’s Caesars Superdome on Friday. In 2022, Yiannopoulosworked onWest’s short-lived 2024 White House campaign, and his social media account suggests he was working for a company of the rapper.Yiannopoulos, aformer editor of the conservative media outlet Breitbart News, previously servedas an internfor the former US congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene. He eventually became locked into a feud with fellow far-right commentator Laura Loomer, a Trump administration ally who claimed on Friday that she had reported Yiannopoulos to ICE over his immigration status.At the peak of his influence, Yiannopoulos was offered a speaking slot at the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, in 2017 after he had been supportive of Donald Trump during his run for his first presidency.He fell out of favor in conservative circles after the publication of a video inwhich he condoned sexual relationswith boys as young as 13.Yiannopoulos claimed that his experiences as a victim of teenage sexual abuse gave him license to comment on the subject. He soon resigned as a senior editor atBreitbart.Yiannopoulos was also banned from Twitter, now called X, in 2016 for directing racist and misogynistic tweets against a Black actor in a Ghostbusters remake. His accountwas reinstated to the platform in 2022after it was acquired and renamed by multibillionaire Elon Musk.A little more than a year before his detention by ICE, a social mediapostfrom Yiannopoulos called on immigration checkpoints to be set up at California “supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersection and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally”.He had also sarcasticallyaskedwhether it was impolite for one “to masturbate” in public rather than in private “if you are going about your business and find yourself observing an ICE raid” amid the mass deportation campaign that Trump has pursued throughout his second presidency.Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationFar right (US)ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)BreitbartUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Royal Navy spent three days tracking Russian vessels in UK waters | Military | The Guardian
description: Three vessels and a helicopter deployed to monitor four ships travelling through the North Sea to the Channel
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Three vessels and a helicopter deployed to monitor four ships travelling through the North Sea to the Channel
Content: The destroyer HMS Duncan, pictured in Portsmouth Harbour, was one of three Royal Navy vessels deployed to monitor Russian ships.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe destroyer HMS Duncan, pictured in Portsmouth Harbour, was one of three Royal Navy vessels deployed to monitor Russian ships.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/ReutersMilitaryRoyal Navy spent three days tracking Russian vessels in UK watersThree vessels and a helicopter deployed to monitor four ships travelling through the North Sea to the ChannelGeraldine McKelvieSat 29 Aug 2026 11.06 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 09.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheRoyal Navyspent three days tracking Russian vessels as they passed through UK waters, it has emerged.The “intense” 72-hour operation took place last week, with radars used to monitor four ships that made their way from the North Sea through to the Channel.The fleet was surveilled by HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn, with a Merlin helicopter providing support, officials said.The Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko was observed escorting the cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta, which are under sanctions, towards Dover.In response, Russia deployed its own military resources, including the Neustrashimy frigate, to guard the shipment. Gen Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord, said there was “no room for complacency” as shadow fleet vessels continued to pose “an unacceptable risk” to UK security.“Alongside our allies, this approach is forcing Moscow to divert Russian warships away from their core purpose,” he said. “That is because Russia knows we stand ready to act again, should it be required.”The Royal Navy recently warned ofincreasing Russian activity in UK waters. In July, it spent 21 days monitoring ships from Moscow, an increase of 25% compared with the previous year. Officials say they have repeatedly observed warships in the Dover strait and the North Sea.In June, the Royal Marinesseized the Russian tanker Smyrtos, the first time British troops have directly boarded a shadow fleet vessel, one of more than 500 that have been sanctioned by the UK.The Kremlin hasthreatened the UKafter Andy Burnham visited Kyiv this week in his first overseas trip as prime minister. During the trip, Burnham said the UK would provide Ukraine with military support, including blueprints for components of long-range Scalp missiles.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlthough western officials have tried to play down the prospect of direct conflict between Russia and Nato, the Kremlin has accused the UK and its allies of “playing with fire” in relation to their continued support for Ukraine.Andrei Fedorov, a former Russian foreign minister, said he could not “100% exclude” the possibility of “semi-military” action against Britain in retaliation, raising the prospect of an attack on British drone factories from “unknown sources”.Explore more on these topicsMilitaryRoyal NavyRussiaUK security and counter-terrorismEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Filip Hrgovic stuns Britain’s Moses Itauma to claim IBF world heavyweight title | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Moses Itauma’s hopes of becoming the second-youngest world heavyweight champion lay in ruins as Filip Hrgovic rallied to stop him in the ninth round
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: Moses Itauma’s hopes of becoming the second-youngest world heavyweight champion lay in ruins as Filip Hrgovic rallied to stop him in the ninth round
Content: Filip Hrgovic gets on top of Moses Itauma.Photograph: Richard Pelham/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFilip Hrgovic gets on top of Moses Itauma.Photograph: Richard Pelham/Getty ImagesBoxingFilip Hrgovic stuns Britain’s Moses Itauma to claim IBF world heavyweight title21-year-old Itauma stopped after ninth-round rally34-year-old Hrgovic is first Croat to win such a titleDonald McRaeat the O2 ArenaSat 29 Aug 2026 19.40 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 20.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMoses Itauma’s hopes of becoming the second-youngest world heavyweight champion in history lay in ruins after the extraordinarily tough and resilient Filip Hrgovic stopped him in the ninth round of their IBF title fight. Yet, until the latter stages of round eight, the sheer speed and dextrous power of the Briton had dominated the contest, with the Croat being dropped in the second and caught again and again by jolting combinations.The fight changed course when Itauma’s stamina suddenly dipped and he began to weave in woozy fatigue as Hrgovic fought back with granite-like determination. Itauma could not withstand the dark storm rolling over him in the ninth and he sank back against the ropes as Hrgovic opened up with renewed conviction. Just as the referee stepped in to stop the fight, Ben Davison, Itauma’s trainer, also sent a white towel sailing sadly over the listing ropes to save his man from a knockout.Filip Hrgović completes astonishing comeback to stun Moses Itauma and win IBF title – live reactionRead moreThe shocking twist was too much for the 21-year-old and he left the ring on a stretcher, apparently having injured his knee. But the damage was done by the remarkable fightback from his opponent, who made his own significant slice of boxing history. The admirable Hrgovic is the first world heavyweight champion from Croatia – a country that has no real boxing heritage.The shock result was also a sobering reminder that, for all Itauma’s obvious skill, a heavyweight tyro is always vulnerable to a world-class opponent who simply refuses to surrender. Itauma’s inexperience also cost him badly for, rather than boxing with more care and staying out of trouble from the eighth round onwards, he allowed himself to be caught up in a slugfest.Before the late dramatics, Itauma walked with calm solemnity to the ring, seemingly unmoved by the fact that the crammed and partisan crowd had begun singing his name in raucous harmony even before he left his dressing room.View image in fullscreenMoses Itauma lands a punch on Filip Hrgovic early in their fight.Photograph: Richard Pelham/Getty ImagesFighting out of a southpaw stance, Itauma landed the first meaningful punch, a sweeping right hand. Moving with menacing intent Itauma clipped Hrgovic with fast and cuffing blows. His speed was striking as he backed up the bigger man with a shuddering right cross which nailed and shook up Hrgovic.Itauma missed with a scything left early in the second but Hrgovic walked almost immediately on to a jolting short right hook which dropped him to the canvas for a count of eight. Hrgovic fought back near the end of the round only for Itauma to produce another blistering combination.A sharp left snapped back Hrgovic’s head at the start of the third, as sweat glistened on the faces and torsos of both men. Itauma switched to the body, sinking a cruel blow to Hrgovic’s gut, but the Croat refused to wilt. His vociferous supporters at ringside began screaming their support as he had a measure of success for the first time in the fight to prove that his ambition remained undimmed.Itauma began to grimace occasionally as the pace of the fight began to leave its mark. A beautiful short left snaked through Hrgovic’s defence in the fifth but the older man marched forward with stoic determination. Itauma was starting to breathe heavily and he had to use a glove to slip his black gum shield back into his mouth. It was the first real sign of distress in Itauma’s previously impassive expression. But at the bell a spiteful uppercut rocked back Hrgovic’s head on the plinth of his massive neck.The cut about Hrgovic’s right eye began to seep with a tickle of blood. But just before the bell Hrgovic landed some heavy shots. Itauma absorbed them and fired back as the fight really caught fire.Itauma had never boxed more than six rounds before and he entered uncharted territory in the seventh. But he again forced Hrgovic on to the back foot and landed some deft combinations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe referee raises his hand to stop the fight as Moses Itauma’s team throw the towel in.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersHrgovic ate one meaty blow after another in the eighth round but was resolute as ever. Itauma looked desperately weary as Hrgovic, unbelievably, rallied again. He would soon overwhelm the exhausted youngster and finish a remarkable resurgence.Throughout an intriguing fight week, the 34-year-old Hrgovic had tried to unsettle his complex rival by suggesting that becoming a world heavyweight champion at such a young age would be “bad for his soul”. Itauma, who is so suspicious of fame, engaged fully with those doubts about his readiness for sporting celebrity. It was almost as if the callow prodigy was uncertain, deep down, whether his world title shot had arrived too early.Hrgovic was always going to provide an acid test of Itauma’s much lauded credentials. The experienced Croat had lost only one previous bout in his nine years as a professional. It had been expected that he would not match Itauma’s deft footwork, fast hands, clarity of thinking and the kind of power that is impressive because it arrives from such dizzying and unexpected angles.But Itauma, instead, was rendered helpless by Hrgovic’s superior stamina and bludgeoning will and self-belief. “Let me tell you something,” Hrgovic said afterwards. “It was not me tonight. It was Jesus Christ in me. Holy Spirit. Father, Son and the Holy Spirit. It was not me. I was losing every round. I was outboxed. And I don’t know from where I got energy in that ninth round. And it was really not my strength. It was the Holy Spirit.”He then turned his attention to his fallen opponent. “He’s an amazing fighter,” Hrgovic said of Itauma. “I want to thank him for accepting this fight, to give me a chance to become a new superstar in the heavyweight division. I’m the present and he’s definitely the future.”Itauma is obviously more than young enough to come back from such crushing disappointment but it is Hrgovic who will celebrate victory in the weeks and months to come. The new world champion administered a chastening lesson in the harsh and unforgiving realities of heavyweight boxing.Explore more on these topicsBoxingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sarah Ferguson to return to UK after relocating amid Epstein revelations | Sarah Ferguson | The Guardian
description: Former Duchess of York moved to Swiss chalet during fallout over her friendship with convicted child sex offender
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Former Duchess of York moved to Swiss chalet during fallout over her friendship with convicted child sex offender
Content: Ferguson used to live with her ex-husband, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, at his former home Royal Lodge in Windsor until he was forced to vacate the premises.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PAView image in fullscreenFerguson used to live with her ex-husband, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, at his former home Royal Lodge in Windsor until he was forced to vacate the premises.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PASarah FergusonSarah Ferguson to return to UK after relocating amid Epstein revelationsFormer Duchess of York moved to Swiss chalet during fallout over her friendship with convicted child sex offenderSammy GecsoylerSat 29 Aug 2026 10.32 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 08.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSarah Ferguson will return to the UK after relocating to a Swiss chalet amid the fallout over the friendship between her and her ex-husband,Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, and the convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, according to reports.The pair werestripped of their royal titlesin October over the scandal of their relationship with Epstein. According to the Sun, the former Duchess of York, 66, is renting a six-bedroom gated property in the home counties.Ferguson used to live with Mountbatten-Windsor at Royal Lodge in Windsor until he was forced to vacate the premises and move to Marsh Farm on King Charles’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk.She could “imminently” move into a new home, which has three bathrooms and a “granny annexe”, according to the Sun.It is believed Ferguson has been spending time out of the public eye at a Swiss chalet in Verbier since leaving Royal Lodge, and her belongings were collected from Andrew’s home in Sandringham this week, the newspaper added.Her expected return comes just days after the Duke and Duchess of Sussex arrived back in the UK with their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. The family are expected to enjoy an “extended stay” in Britain, with the children enrolled at school and due to start next week.There is clearly trouble ahead for Harry and Meghan on their return to the UK. Here are five ways to avert it | Stephen BatesRead moreFerguson has faced calls to speak to US authorities about Epstein after last year’s release of millions of documents associated with him shed fresh light on their relationship. One email exchange suggested Ferguson had taken her daughters to see Epstein in the US days after he was released from prison for child sex crimes.A year after his conviction for child sex crimes, Ferguson thanked Epstein for being the “brother” she had “always wished for” in an email.Last September, the Mail on Sunday published emails from 2011, in whichFerguson privately described Epstein as her “supreme friend”and apologised for “letting him down”, despite having publicly called her association with him “a gigantic error of judgment”.The messages were sent less than two months after she had insisted she would “never have anything to do with [Epstein] again”, amid pressure over the ties she and Mountbatten-Windsor had maintained with him – including a £15,000 payment Epstein made to help settle Ferguson’s debts.Epstein has been the downfall of Mountbatten-Windsor, who was stripped of his titles by the King because of “serious lapses of judgment” over his friendship with the late child sex offender and allegations of sexual assault against him by one of Epstein’s victims,Virginia Giuffre.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFerguson lost her courtesy royal divorcee title and reverted to her original name, and also lost the freedom of the city of York after councillors voted unanimously to remove the honour over her links to Epstein. She and Mountbatten-Windsor were given the honour as a wedding present from York in 1987 during a visit to the city.The former duchess has published more than 50 books – largely children’s titles – but after the Epstein revelations, thousands of copies of her latest children’s book were withdrawn from sale and “pulped”.Earlier this year, Ferguson’s international charity, Sarah’s Trust, announced its closure “for the foreseeable future”. Seven charities, including the Teenage Cancer Trust and children’s hospice, have alsocut ties and revoked Ferguson’s patronagedue to her links with Epstein.Six companies linked to Ferguson – S Phoenix Events, Fergie’s Farm, La Luna Investments, Solamoon Ltd, Philanthrapreneur Ltd and Planet Partners Productions Ltd – were wound down in February after more damaging revelations came to light with the release of the Epstein files.Explore more on these topicsSarah FergusonMonarchyAndrew Mountbatten-WindsorJeffrey EpsteinnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tennessee governor says he backs airport name change to honor Dolly Parton | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: Bill Lee says he favors proposal to rename Nashville’s international airport after legendary country singer
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Bill Lee says he favors proposal to rename Nashville’s international airport after legendary country singer
Content: A mural of Dolly Parton in East Nashville, Tennessee, on Friday.Photograph: Justin Renfroe/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA mural of Dolly Parton in East Nashville, Tennessee, on Friday.Photograph: Justin Renfroe/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockDolly PartonTennessee governor says he backs airport name change to honor Dolly PartonBill Lee says he favors proposal to rename Nashville’s international airport after legendary country singerEdward HelmoreSat 29 Aug 2026 15.57 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBill Lee, the Tennessee governor, on Friday said he favored a proposal to rename Nashville’s international airport after legendary country singerDolly Parton, who died three days earlier at age 80.In a statement, Lee said he and the managers of the airport in Tennessee’s capital city – where Parton resided – wanted to create “a lasting tribute to her indelible legacy and the generations of people she inspired”. He said he had spoken previously to the 11-time Grammy winner and her team, who were “touched by the idea”.“Dolly Parton’s extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state,” Lee said, noting that Nashville airport is where Tennessee welcomes the world.He added: “It is fitting thatNashvilleInternational Airport would bear the name of our state’s favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly’s music, generosity, faith, and kindness.”The proposal was scheduled to be addressed at a meeting of the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority (MNAA) on 17 September. A statement from Doug Kreulen, MNAA president, said the Nashville airport shared Parton’s understanding that “dignity, kindness and opportunity should never be defined by where you come from or your socioeconomic status”.“Whether you are boarding a private aircraft or taking your first flight, you deserve to be welcomed, respected and served with the same level of care,” he remarked.Partonhad requested a private funeral for immediate family, and there is not going to be any public memorial. She will be buried beside her husband, Carl Dean, at Nashville’s Woodlawn memorial park and mausoleum.The singertold Entertainment Weeklyin 2014 that she expected Whitney Houston’s rendition of I Will Always Love You to be part of her service. Parton also said she wanted an old gospel hymn, If We Never Meet Again, which was her father’s favorite.In a video statement announcing her death on Tuesday, Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver, her longtime head of security, remarked: “Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because, after a life wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest.”Lee discussed the proposal to rename Nashville’s airport after a plane tugging a banner urging the name change buzzed over theTennesseestate capitol on Friday. A petition was also launched, and it has since gained more than 150,000 signatures.“Everybody is looking for a way to honor Dolly and her legacy,” petition organizer Dan Diontold the Tennessean. “Our airport is so important, and there’s symbolism in flying into Parton Airport. With Dolly’s message of love, acceptance, music, kindness, humor and all these things, people feel that she is representative of what Tennessee truly is.”If it comes to be, renaming Nashville airport will be at least the second airport in a matter of months to make a switch. Palm Beach airport was recently renamed for Donald Trump, withmixed reactionsfrom travelers and locals about naming the facility after the president.Freddie O’Connell, the Nashville mayor, hinted that the proposed name change is only the start of metropolitan tributes in the city. He said the 9 to 5 and Jolene singer had been in the process of developing a hotel and museum called SongTeller “that she called her love letter to Nashville”.“Now it’s our turn to share a love letter to Dolly – by renaming Nashville International Airport to Dolly Parton International Airport in Nashville,” O’Connell told the Tennessean.He also said the city was “working closely” with Parton’s team and family “on appropriate public recognition”.Explore more on these topicsDolly PartonNashvilleTennesseeAirline industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Was it a mistake for 99 Colombian guerrillas to lay down their arms? | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Fighters in legal limbo after accepting ‘total peace’ plan of Petro government just days before hardliner Abelardo De la Espriella took over
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Fighters in legal limbo after accepting ‘total peace’ plan of Petro government just days before hardliner Abelardo De la Espriella took over
Content: Tattoo of a former combatant now in a designated zone in Colombia under the ‘total peace’ plan.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTattoo of a former combatant now in a designated zone in Colombia under the ‘total peace’ plan.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianColombiaWas it a mistake for 99 Colombian guerrillas to lay down their arms?Fighters in legal limbo after accepting ‘total peace’ plan of Petro government just days before hardliner Abelardo De la Espriella took overDaniela Díaz in Valle del Guamuez andTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroSat 29 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 10.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn mid-June, 99 guerrilla fighters were flown by helicopter to a small settlement in a rural area of southernColombiawhere they lined up and, one by one, handed their weapons to government officials: rifles, pistols, machine guns and grenade launchers.They also stripped off their heavy tactical vests, field packs and camouflage uniforms, which were each piled into a bonfire to mark the beginning of a new life away from an armed conflict that has claimed nearly half a million lives in the last six decades.That was precisely what the former president Gustavo Petro’s “total peace” plan had sought to achieve: negotiating with and disarming all of Colombia’s criminal groups, which are estimated to have nearly 30,000 members.But the group of just 99 people was the only one to disarm, and did so just three days before the presidential runoff, which waswon by the far-rightmillionaire lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella, who had campaigned on a promiseto end “total peace” and return to a full-on strategy of jailing or killing criminals.Now, several weeks after the new president took office – and amid efforts to deal with the aftermath of the7.4-magnitude earthquake, as his government hasalready begunthe promised airstrikes against criminal groups – the 99 do not know what will happen to them.“We’re in limbo,” said Natalia Bríñez, 29, one of 13 women among the group staying in the temporary location zone, or ZUT by its Spanish initials, a government-controlled zone where, under surveillance and unable to leave, they were supposed to make the transition to civilian life over the following months.View image in fullscreenNatalia Briñez, a former guerrilla fighter, is one of 13 women in the ZUT.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianThe former guerrillas are housed in beige brick buildings decorated with drawings they painted themselves, including doves of peace, with a communal dining hall where three meals a day are served. No weapons are allowed inside and soldiers guard the ZUT from a perimeter less than a mile away.One former combatant built a makeshift gym with weights made from metal pipes and tins filled with cement and sand, and there is an improvised football pitch, but most of them spend their days on their phones.De la Espriella has repeatedly said his government will no longer negotiate peace agreements and has yet to announce what he intends to do regarding the people at the ZUT. The president has not responded to requests for comment.In theory, any arrest warrants against the group are suspended, and they remain under state protection until 25 December, when Petro’s decree establishing the ZUT expires. But De la Espriella could revoke the decree at any time.Armando Novoa, the former government official who led peace negotiations with the group, said “the worst-case scenario would be for the new government to close the ZUT, launch a military operation and try to capture or kill them. That would be a crime against humanity, because these people are unarmed.”Between 2 and 4 August, days before De la Espriella’s inauguration, Novoa led journalists including the Guardian through the ZUT. The Office of the High Commissioner for Peace, where he worked, has since been absorbed into the newly created National Security Commission – a move expected to result in more than 200 job losses – and Novoa has resigned.For now, at least, the ZUT remains in operation and has a small library run by Bríñez, who has a phoenix tattoo on her left shoulder as a symbol of her rebirth away from the armed conflict.View image in fullscreenNo weapons are allowed inside the ZUT and soldiers guard it from a perimeter less than a mile away.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The Guardian“The hardest thing for me has been being away from my children,” said Bríñez, who has a seven-year-old daughter and a 10-year-old son and speaks to them on video calls, but will only be able to see them in person once her “transition” is complete, a process that includes vocational training and psychosocial support.They were also supposed to receive financial support of about £425 a month, which had not yet been paid. In the meantime, some of them were planning to start achicken-rearing business.The 99 made up a small part of a group of about 1,000 combatants calledCommandos of the Frontier– most of whom remain armed – and are part of the National Coordinator of the Bolivarian Army (CNEB), a former dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) with about 2,500 members which controls the border with Ecuador.The Petro administration said negotiations were also under way with other members of the CNEB, who published anopen letteraddressed to De la Espriella saying they were willing to continue talks with him. It is not known whether the president responded.View image in fullscreenOne of the works of graffiti in the ZUT painted by the former guerrillas.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianThe CNEB’s chief “peace negotiator”, Geovany Andrés Rojas, known as “Araña” (Spider), had been in custody since February under a US extradition request for drug trafficking, which Petro had delayed. Last Wednesday, De la Espriellaorderedextradition.Although such groups emerged in the 1960s as leftwing rebels fighting government abuses and seeking revolution – followed soon afterwards byfar-right paramilitary groups– ideology has long since been overtaken for most of them by economic interests, above all drug trafficking (Colombia is the world’s largest producer of cocaine) and illegal mining.“Here in the ZUT, the vast majority were not in the group because of any ideological commitment, but for economic reasons,” said Novoa. “It even surprised us that most of them simply called the group ‘the company’.”Petro repeatedly tried to negotiate peace agreements with larger groups. The armed factions took advantage of temporary ceasefires to continue expanding, a process that had already begun before he took office. They also clashed among themselves for control of territory and illicit economies, which many security experts say contributed to a rise in homicides, kidnappings and massacres.“Total peace” was an attempt to address what thelandmark 2016 peace dealbetween the government and the Farc failed to resolve, as other armed groups and Farc dissidents remained active.Petro’s administrationfailed to reduce violence, which instead reached its worst levels in a decade, and to reach the disarmament stage with any of the gangs, apart from the 99 former combatants – who handed over their weapons only on the eve of an election thatevery poll indicatedthe government-backed candidate would lose.“They [the government] told us: ‘If this works, you’re opening the door for other groups and will set an example,’” said Bríñez.Some security experts saw the agreementas rushed.View image in fullscreenFormer guerrillas in the ZUT have little to do and spend much of their time looking at their phones.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The Guardian“It was a somewhat irresponsible decision,” said Paula Tobo, a senior researcher at the thinktank Ideas for Peace Foundation, which published anextensive reporton why Total Peace failed.Tobo said the 99 were now in a “legal limbo” because their protection rested on decrees that could be revoked and there is no legal framework for their transition to civilian life. All of the Petro administration’s proposals to regulate surrenders failed in Congress and, under current law, anyone who has committed crimes such as kidnapping or drug trafficking is not eligible for amnesty.“It’s positive that these people wanted to lay down their arms, but it really wasn’t the right time for the government to take that decision … The previous administration clearly put them at risk of this government suddenly deciding to abolish the ZUT and arrest them,” said Tobo.View image in fullscreenA wristband with the logo of the armed group to which Adrián, 19, belonged.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianThe group wrote a letter to De la Espriella reaffirming its “irreversible decision to commit to peace” and inviting him to visit the ZUT. At the time of publication it had received no response.The youngest member of the group, a 19-year-old who asked to be identified only as Adrián, said they wanted “to have a home, a family”.However, he knows what he will do if things do not go according to plan. “Honestly, I’d take up arms again, because we’re keeping our side of the bargain and the government should do the same, shouldn’t it?” he said.Daniela Díaz travelled to Valle del Guamuez at the invitation of the Colombian government’s former Office of the High Commissioner for Peace.Explore more on these topicsColombiaFarcAmericasDrugs tradefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sovereignty, farming and fishing: Iceland votes on its future with the EU | Iceland | The Guardian
description: Country holds a knife-edge referendum that cuts across political divides on taking step closer to Brussels after Trump threats towards Greenland
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Country holds a knife-edge referendum that cuts across political divides on taking step closer to Brussels after Trump threats towards Greenland
Content: The vote in Iceland was brought forward after Trump's aggressive moves towards Greenland. Photograph: Sigga Ella/The GuardianCountry holds a knife-edge referendum that cuts across political divides on taking step closer to Brussels after Trump threats towards GreenlandByMiranda Bryantin Hvammur, Þorlákshöfn and ReykjavíkSat 29 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a long time, the prospect of becoming the third generation to run his family farm was an exciting one, says Davíð Clausen Pétursson.Icelandic farmers were starting to get higher prices for their meat and milk, debt was no longer an occupational prerequisite and innovation was on the rise.Now the 29-year-old is anxiously awaiting the result of a referendum on Saturday, when Icelanders will be asked whether or not they want to restart accession talks with the EU.View image in fullscreenDavíð Clausen Pétursson, a farmer, will be voting ‘nei’ in Iceland’s EU referendum.Photograph: Sigga Ella/The GuardianDavíð believes joining the bloc could have negative ramifications for farmers all over Iceland, slowing down progress made in the sector and reducing profits.Across Europesmall and medium-sized farmshave struggled, with thousands closing each year because of brutal economic circumstances. In Iceland, however, the picture has been somewhat brighter for some farmers who have been able to make a profit and innovate.Since the government announced that it was bringing forward the planned vote, amid Donald Trump’s efforts to take control of neighbouringGreenland, debate has taken in everything from food security to national identity, defence, housing, inflation, language, and natural resources.The latest polls show the two sides – which cut across the political spectrum and generations – are neck and neck. According to Thursday’s Gallup poll, the no campaign is slightly in the lead with 51.6% of the vote and yes at 48.4%.While the yes campaign has strong support, critics of the EU have in some ways been louder in part because a yes vote is less decisive: it is agreeing to begin negotiations, not saying yes to joining the EU.View image in fullscreenCritics of the EU have in some ways been louder than the yes campaign.Photograph: Sigga Ella/The Guardian“Of course I am quite invested in how it goes,” says Davíð at his remote farm in Hvammur, south-west Iceland, overlooked by a mountain that features in the Icelandic sagas. “I want at least to build my life around farming for the next 30-40 years and I would also like my kids to be able to do that as well. I am just not sure that it will be possible if we go that route.”He says a “yes” win would lead to the years of negotiations before the nation votes again on any deal reached, and he fears the resulting uncertainty would put a halt to all the progress and the momentum in farming. Then, they would have to deal with the repercussions of the outcome, where he fears farmers’ interests, drowned out by the more valuable and noisier fishing lobby, would not be prioritised.As Davíð explained to his nine-year-old son – the vote has been a big talking point at school – a litre of milk currently costs them about 100 ISK to produce, which they can sell for 145 ISK.He worries that joining the EU would mean he would have to significantly decrease the price of his milk and other products.View image in fullscreenDavíð Clausen Pétursson with his parents, Pétur Benedikt Guðmundsson and Charlotte Clausen, on their farm.Photograph: Sigga Ella/The Guardian“It is not that I am against anything in the EU at all. I am half Danish, my mother is Danish and we of course buy a lot fromEurope,” he says. “The regulations they have there are suitable for countries that live next to each other, but I am fearful that if it is a yes, the uncertainty will make it quite hard for us to see where we are going, so that will put everything at a bit of a halt.”Iceland’s current farming system was built on the country being a lone independent state in the Atlantic with unique weather conditions, he says. “We can figure it out ourselves. We make trade agreements with everyone around us, we try to take off the tariffs and have free trade with the products we really need, we put tariffs on the products we are trying to produce here.”He understands that high food costs are frustrating for consumers, but believes it is worth it. “There is a high cost to food security in Iceland. But there is an even bigger cost to losing that and being dependent.”The EU vote taps into a sense of lament among some in Iceland that in a globalised, highly connected world the country’s foundation in agriculture and fishing – central to life there until a few decades ago – is being rapidly forgotten.Davíð says that 30 years ago children came to work on the farm in the summer, but machinery and specialisation mean that is no longer possible.View image in fullscreenSigurrós Birta Jóhannsdóttir, an agricultural science student, will also vote no on Saturday.Photograph: Sigga Ella/The GuardianSigurrós Birta Jóhannsdóttir, 22, visited the farm on an educational visit with a coach load of other agriculture students. Jóhannsdóttir, who works on a farm that she will take over in the future, will be voting no on Saturday because she believes that negotiations will only slow down progress and cost money.Supporters believe joining the EU could help bring down the high cost of living and inflation in Iceland, and would be good for the country’s security.View image in fullscreenKári Böðvarsson, a retired fisher, is planning to vote ‘yes’.Photograph: Sigga Ella/The GuardianAt his home by the sea in Þorlákshöfn, Kári Böðvarsson, 79, says he plans to vote yes, despite being right-leaning politically. “It doesn’t matter if you’re on the right or on the left, what your opinion is, people are just voting across politics,” the retired fisher says.He is an outlier at the gym among his training buddies, where discussions can get quite heated. He enjoys provoking them but he will be glad when the debate is over. “We have to trust these people to negotiate well for us because why shouldn’t they?” he says. “But the ‘no’ people don’t trust them.”When it comes to fishing, there is not much the EU can do to win back power over fishing quotas from the big fishing companies to individuals, Kári says. But perhaps it could help with housing costs.View image in fullscreenThe prime minister, Kristrún Frostadóttir, says Iceland should seize the chance to take the first step to join the EU.Photograph: Sigga Ella/The GuardianAt a public meeting in Reykjavík, the prime minister, Kristrún Frostadóttir, told a packed Icelandic-flag-waving house that joining the EU was a “unique opportunity”.“Iceland’s sovereignty is not a museum piece that we keep in a cupboard while isolating ourselves from other countries,” she said, to cheers.She said it was also “good timing” for Iceland’s security – not just in light of the US and its unpredictable economic and geopolitical moves, but also China. “This isn’t about being afraid,” she said. “It’s about being prepared and seizing opportunities when they arise.”View image in fullscreenPsychology students at the University of Iceland, Reykjavík. Saga Gautadóttir, right, agrees with arguments on both sides, while Anna María Magnúsdóttir, second left, says she has not yet made up her mind.Photograph: Sigga Ella/The GuardianBut at the University of Iceland in Reykjavík, Kristrún and the yes campaign still have some convincing to do before polling stations open at 9am on Saturday. The first results are expected between 10pm and midnight.Student Saga Gautadóttir, 20,is considering spoiling her ballot because she agrees with arguments on both sides. Anna María Magnúsdóttir, 20, has not made up her mind yet how to vote, she says, sitting in the sunshine on campus with friends. “I just want the best for our country, whichever one it is.”Explore more on these topicsIcelandEuropean UnionEuropeGreenlandFarmingFishingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Switching channels: will the Edinburgh TV festival’s magic survive the move south? | Edinburgh International Television Festival | The Guardian
description: After 50 years the annual shindig is heading to Manchester – but a new rival could keep the industry’s fringe link going
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: After 50 years the annual shindig is heading to Manchester – but a new rival could keep the industry’s fringe link going
Content: Amol Rajan speaks during the Alternative MacTaggart lecture in Edinburgh.Photograph: Neil HannaView image in fullscreenAmol Rajan speaks during the Alternative MacTaggart lecture in Edinburgh.Photograph: Neil HannaEdinburgh International Television FestivalSwitching channels: will the Edinburgh TV festival’s magic survive the move south?After 50 years the annual shindig is heading to Manchester – but a new rival could keep the industry’s fringe link goingRobyn VinterSat 29 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe summer sojourn toEdinburghhas been a highlight of TV executives’ calendars for half a century, allowing them an annual trip to the UK’s most spectacular city during the world’s biggest arts festival.So there was sadness when it was announced that this year’s 50th Edinburgh TV Festival would be the last to be held in the Scottish capital.High costs fuelling concerns about accessibility – accommodation in the city in August is themost expensive in Europe– prompted the TV Foundation, the charity which runs the annual industry shindig, toconsider a new venue last year.Campbell Glennie, its chief executive, said the move was about “exploring how we can reduce costs for delegates and make the festival open to more people”.However, critics of the decision pointed out that while holding the conference alongside the Edinburgh fringe and international festivals made it so expensive, the chance to see world-class theatre, arts and comedy was a huge part of the draw for attenders.Off the record, some TV figures blamed the Scottish government for the failed attempt to keep the event inScotland. Glasgow had initially been on the table, requiring only a 40-minute train ride west, but Holyrood ministers threw their weight behind a campaign to keep it in Edinburgh.It was ultimately Manchester that had the winning proposition, backed by Andy Burnham, then the Greater Manchester mayor, who promised the necessary “infrastructure, talent, ambition and creativity” to host the festival from next year.At Edinburgh’s valedictory gathering, many delegates did not hide their disappointment.One Scottish television producer said the decision reflected a problem in the industry, where production companies south of the border have brought London-based workers to film in Scotland and failed to hire local talent. “It’s a fucking joke,” they added.The TV Foundation said relocating would “radically reduce the costs” for attendees. The charity makes no profit from running the festival and instead invests the funds into programmes to improve training and widen access, with several sessions this year aimed at tackling the class gap in the industry.Sydney Lima is a documentary presenter and co-founder of the Rich Parents Club, a group providing support to working-class people in arts and media. She said members were reporting that TV was becoming “an increasingly gatekept industry”, suggesting that recent hits from working-class writers such as the Channel 4 series Big Boys would no longer be commissioned.“As funding cuts continue, employers rely on smaller pools of talent, more often than not, from within their own networks – or even gene pool,” she said.In 2024 the scriptwriter James Graham used the festival’s keynote MacTaggart lecture – past speakers have included Armando Iannucci, Dennis Potter and Rupert Murdoch – to lament howimpenetrable the industry was for working-class people.View image in fullscreenPlaywright James Graham delivered the prestigious MacTaggart Lecture at the Edinburgh TV Festival in 2024.Photograph: James Veysey/Shutterstock for Edinburgh TV FestivalA subsequent TV Foundation report found nearly a quarter of TV executives wereprivately educated. Graham’s views were echoedby the presenter Carol Vorderman, who grew up working class, in the alternative MacTaggart slot the same year. (That lecture was delivered by Amol Rajan this year).The move also comes at a time of enormousfinancial pressure on the industry, with theBBC sheddingup to 2,000 staff,ITV and Sky mergingbroadcast operations andChannel 4under pressure.Traditional UK broadcasters are struggling to compete for audiences and advertising money against the rise of deep-pocketed US-based streaming titans, such as Netflix and Amazon.In a sign of the times, this year’s main MacTaggart lecture was delivered by YouTube’s Pedro Pina, who hit back at proposals to makepublic service content more prominenton his platform, now the second most-watched media service in the UK.As British commissioners cut their TV production budgets, freelancers are bearing the brunt, making it harder to find funds for networking events like the TV festival.A full-price ticket cost more than £1,500, though there were bursaries and lower rates for freelancers, Scottish delegates and those under 30. Among this year’s attendees were graduates and freelancers, some of whom had bitten the bullet and forked out in the hope of making connections that would lead to work.Adeel Amini, a freelance executive producer who founded the campaign group The TV Mindset to support casual workers in the sector, said: “The price of the ticket is already ridiculous and unaffordable, especially when the industry has been going through a crisis and so many people are out of work.”View image in fullscreenCirque Éloize, from Canada, at the Edinburgh fringe, which is central to many TV executives’ diaries.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianAmini, who has produced entertainment shows such as Who Wants to Be a Millionaire, Lingo and Catchphrase, praised the TV Foundation’s work but said the conference itself highlighted how “two-tier the industry is”, with a divide between those who pay their own way and executives whose companies pick up the tab.Amini added: “It’s there for commissioners and production companies to go and mingle and have these parties and either lament the state of the industry without doing anything much about it or just give themselves a round of applause without acknowledging the workers at the heart of it.”Daran “Jonno” Johnson, the head writer on this year’s surprise hitSNL UK, spoke on a TV festival panel on Friday morning as part of its new Funny Business strand, focusing on comedy. It was in between performances of hissuccessful nightly Edinburgh fringe standup run.He said the benefit of the two festivals being in the same city was that “so many industry people are suddenly in town in the last week” that it was helpful “to have that pipeline between fringe comedy and telly”.Performers were nervous that their shows – many of which cost tens, if not hundreds, of thousands of pounds to put on – might no longer have the same chance of being seen by commissioners. Kimberly Hart-Simpson, a Manchester-based writer and actor whose one-woman play Amnesia won a Scotsman Fringe First award this year, said her concern was “whether TV industry professionals will continue to commit to attending the arts festival to discover and support emerging talent”.However, the fringe was so integral to many TV executives’ diaries that they would still be here if the schedules clashed, reassured Alex Cartlidge, co-director of Country Mile Productions at an event at the fringe venue Shedinburgh.“The reason you’re coming to Edinburgh, if you’re a TV producer, is for the fringe. The TV festival happens to be on, and you can convince your boss to put a few of those things through company expenses … but if TV companies have the choice next year between going to Manchester or coming here, 99% of people will come here.”There is hope on the horizon for those who do not want to see the link between the fringe and television severed. On Thursday evening, television executives, performers and fringe organisers gathered in a hot room at Edinburgh Fringe Central for the launch of an initiative for the media and creative industries from 2027, funded in part by the Scottish government.View image in fullscreenKimberly Hart-Simpson’s one-woman play Amnesia won a Scotsman Fringe First award this year.Photograph: Jeff Spicer/Getty ImagesSpeaking to the Guardian at the launch, David Smith, director of Screen Scotland, which is partnering with the Fringe Society on the project, said it was not a replacement for the TV Festival. “It will be inclusive of TV, but it won’t be a TV festival,” he said.Having two events risks splitting attendance, but with dates for Manchester yet to be announced there is still the prospect the gatherings could avoid a clash if the TV Foundation does not go for the traditional last week of August slot.The Scottish culture secretary, Màiri McAllan, said that while it was “hugely disappointing that a London-based company took the decision to move the Edinburgh International TV festival”, the SNP government was now focused on Screen Scotland’s alternative and was “working with the TV, media, and festivals sectors to ensure that we deliver an unmissable event”.Smith said plans were still being formed on what that event would look like but added: “I hope to get back to some of the chaos of the original TV Festival, the fact that it was slightly more seat-of-your-pants.”Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh International Television FestivalTelevision industryTelevisionEdinburghScotlandFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The moment I knew: I’d never had romantic feelings for a man – then he touched my hand and it felt electric | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: As a widower and a newly single father of three, Jim Rogers was struggling. Then on a poolside holiday, he sat next to Tyler – and his life changed
Author: Doosie Morris
Headline: As a widower and a newly single father of three, Jim Rogers was struggling. Then on a poolside holiday, he sat next to Tyler  – and his life changed
Content: ‘Tyler has rescued me more than once. I feel so very lucky that we crossed paths’: Tyler (left) with Jim Rogers (right), dementia advocate and author, in 2026.Photograph: Rob PalmerView image in fullscreen‘Tyler has rescued me more than once. I feel so very lucky that we crossed paths’: Tyler (left) with Jim Rogers (right), dementia advocate and author, in 2026.Photograph: Rob PalmerThe moment I knewAustralian lifestyleThe moment I knew: I’d never had romantic feelings for a man – then he touched my hand and it felt electricAs a widower and a newly single father of three,Jim Rogerswas struggling. Then on a poolside holiday, he sat next to Tyler– and his life changedFind more stories fromthe moment I knew seriesJim Rogers, as told toDoosie MorrisSat 29 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 16.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the mid 90s, I was in the prime of my life. I was in my early thirties, married to my soulmate, Lorna, with three kids under three. We’d emigrated from our small town in Worcestershire in the UK to Perth, and life was wonderful. Then Lorna was diagnosed with melanoma. We returned to England and less than a year later she was gone. It was completely unbelievable, as though someone had just come along and smashed my life into a million pieces.The following months were a blur: I was a grief-stricken widower and newly single parent struggling to keep the kids’ life on track and my own head above water. As time went on, it was obvious I wasn’t doing well and my parents insisted on treating me to a holiday in the sun. I didn’t want to go.I remember arriving at this beautiful hotel in the Canary Islands and sitting on the balcony. I was so miserable looking out at all the happy people holding hands.The moment I knew: Days after September 11, we flew through turbulence – all I could say was ‘I love you’Read moreEvery day I’d drag myself down to the pool and sit in the same spot. There was a large group of British tourists there each day who would look at me sympathetically and invite me to join them. I turned them down a few times but eventually I thought “sod it” and joined in, careful not to burden anyone with the tragic details of why I was there all alone.View image in fullscreen‘Over the next couple of days, I noticed I was thinking about him all the time’: Tyler and Jim Rogers in the Canary Islands, 2000.Photograph: SuppliedOver poolside beers I found myself chatting to this lovely English chap, Tyler. When I asked if he was married he surprised me by telling me he was gay. I’d never met an openly gay person in my life.The day went on and as my spirits lifted I agreed to join them for the evening. Tyler and I spent the night chatting and laughing and one by one the group dwindled until it was just the two of us. As we eventually wandered back to the hotel he threw his arm around my shoulder and I just felt this connection. Over the next couple of days, I noticed I was thinking about him all the time. We went out for lunch one day, and I spilled my whole story.Back in England we began chatting on the phone for hours every evening. It became clear that this friendship was lifting me out of the doldrums – our conversations each night made me feel like I wanted to get up the next morning.One day I drove to London to surprise him at work. We went for lunch in this lovely restaurant with views over the Thames. As he reached out and touched my hand in the elevator, electricity ran through me. Then he leaned in and kissed me. I’d never had romantic feelings for a man before. It was so strange; it felt so right, yet so wrong. I was desperately confused but I couldn’t let go of it because it was making me feel something I hadn’t in the longest time – happy.In those days, and in my conservative village, the idea of being openly gay was a complication I couldn’t add to my life. I’d been on a few dates with women, but they were always spoiling the kids and making me cringe; and I never wanted to feel like I was replacing Lorna.Whatever was going on between Tyler and me was different. It didn’t feel like it was spilling over into the children’s lives: it was just for me. When I introduced Tyler to the kids, it was just as “dad’s friend”. They never questioned it, and Tyler didn’t want anything from us: he just wanted to give. He made everything fun and his upbeat personality lifted this dark cloud that had been hanging over us all. He was so comfortable in his own skin, so kind and so spontaneous; it changed everything.Eventually, I told my parents. While my mother was sceptical, my father was amazingly supportive. Still, this was small-town England in the early 2000s and I felt the only way we could be together was if the house next door came up for sale. Miraculously, it did!Ty is the most impulsive person you will ever meet. If he’s in, he’s fully in. He went back to London and called to say if I saw a “sold” sticker on the sign, it was him. A year after we met, he moved in and we became neighbours. Ty’s dad came over and popped a panel out of the garden fence. Out the front, we were a widower and a bachelor living side-by-side; out the back, we were together. We lived like that for years.Several years later, friends from Australia came to visit. They went on and on about how much they loved it there, and how much Lorna had wanted the kids to grow up there. My kids seized on this and would not let it go. For a while I pretended I was looking into it, then I gave in. We returned to Perth when the kids were 12, 13 and 15; they finished high school there and then headed east for their careers. Ty and I soon followed.View image in fullscreen‘We’ve been travelling the world celebrating our 25 years together’: Tyler and Jim Rogers in Santorini, Greece, in 2022.We made a beautiful life for ourselves in Sydney. It was everything you could want from Australia, wrapped up with a bow on it. But I was starting to have problems at work. I’d been managing large scale property projects for decades, but I was getting forgetful – something wasn’t right. At the doctor’s one day, they asked me to turn my phone to silent and I was completely blank; I simply couldn’t work out how to do it. Tests would reveal I had early-onset dementia. I was only 55.I fell into a serious depression. But Tyler has a very positive outlook on life: even in the worst of times you’d very, very, rarely catch him down. It’s just his natural way; some people are lucky enough to be like that.No matter how maudlin I can get, he stays calm, and you will never hear a shortness in his voice. One day, as I continued to wallow about my diagnosis, he said: “Listen, you have to draw a line in the sand and you have to step over it. Because if you stay here in this moment, you’re gonna miss what is right under your nose and all the fun we could have.”We’ve been travelling the world celebrating our 25 years together. Tyler has rescued me more than once. I feel so very lucky that we crossed paths.Jim Rogers is a dementia advocate and author ofHolding On To Happiness, co-written with his daughter, Millie Robinson, available on 1 September through Pan Macmillan (RRP AU$36.99).Tell us the moment you knewShare your experienceShare your love storyDo you have a romantic realisation you'd like to share?
