title: Omar Badawy: Guided Detour review – dizzying tales of decision paralysis | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The comic’s unique tale of assimilation and romance-related limbo has a high joke rate and emotional intelligence
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: The comic’s unique tale of assimilation and romance-related limbo has a high joke rate and emotional intelligence
Content: Budding star quality … Omar Badawy.Photograph: Matt StrongeView image in fullscreenBudding star quality … Omar Badawy.Photograph: Matt StrongeEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewOmar Badawy: Guided Detour review – dizzying tales of decision paralysisPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghThe comic’s unique tale of assimilation and romance-related limbo has a high joke rate and emotional intelligenceAnya RyanSat 29 Aug 2026 15.31 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 15.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwant to tell Omar Badawy to take a breath. This debut moves at a frantic, almost dizzying pace, so much so that you could easily miss a few details in a show that zooms in and out of the time he was accidentally caught in the middle of a Tommy Robinson march while en route to a fancy dress party. But with writing this sharp, does it matter? You can see why SNL: UK came calling.The Cambridge-raised Badawy lays out his identity conundrum: he’s an Anglo-Egyptian Muslim who, as a pupil at a Christian school, was teased for his background. Differences surfaced during Nativity plays, where his culturally accurate interpretations of innkeepers and wise men’s assistants weren’t quite what his teachers had in mind. He also knows his well-spoken accent makes it easier to assimilate. Because of all this, Badawy often feels stuck in the middle. Once, a stranger even asked his ethnicity because he wanted to call him his “correct racial slur”.Perhaps this state of limbo is also why he has a severe case of decision paralysis. He’d rather be pulled into things than actually have to choose a side. But, at university, he started going out with the only Arab girl, and now he’s got a big choice to make. Using the march as the linking framing device feels too neat, but it also gives Badawy a heart-tugging, romcom-style ending.Underground Monk Show review – hysterical visions enrobed in mysteryRead moreWith his delivery veering towards the shrill and over-astounded, he doesn’t yet look totally at ease on stage. The more he tells us he hates leaving the house, the more you start to actually believe him. And yet Badawy possesses a budding star quality and the hour with him is a joy. His voice is unique, emotionally intelligent and generous. He shoves a hell of a lot of jokes in along the way – from having to police his divorced mother’s suitor list to using football chat to placate angry men. It’s an hour about detours, but there’s no question Badawy is going places.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Simple, creamy and crunchy’: the best (and worst) supermarket coleslaw, tasted and rated | Food | The Guardian
description: Too cloying, too sweet or just right? Our tester works through the shop shelves to find the best slaw for your next barbecue, picnic or packed lunch
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Too cloying, too sweet or just right? Our tester works through the shop shelves to find the best slaw for your next barbecue, picnic or packed lunch
Content: The crunch bunch: 10 supermarket slaws were judged on appearance, aroma, texture and taste.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.View image in fullscreenThe crunch bunch: 10 supermarket slaws were judged on appearance, aroma, texture and taste.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterFoodReview‘Simple, creamy and crunchy’: the best (and worst) supermarket coleslaw, tasted and ratedToo cloying, too sweet or just right? Our tester works through the shop shelves to find the best slaw for your next barbecue, picnic or packed lunchThe best supermarket veggie burgersTom HuntSat 29 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIfind shop-bought coleslaw hard to stomach because it’s sharp, gloopy and often made with copious amounts of poor-quality mayonnaise and spirit vinegar. Pungent ingredients, such as cabbage and onion, are better eaten fresh, otherwise they break down and give off a disconcertingly sulphurous and sweaty aroma.I judged each product in this test on appearance, aroma, texture and, above all, taste, and awarded extra points for value. I marked down for an off-puttingly strong raw onion aroma.Preservatives and stabilisers aren’t essential (the better-tasting products don’t use them), and often give a slaw an unappealing, moussey texture. All that said, I was surprised to find some great products out there and most retained a surprisingly satisfying crunch.The best supermarket coleslawBest overall:Waitrose deli-style coleslaw with red onion and chivesView image in fullscreen£1.85 for 300g at Waitrose (62p/100g)★★★★☆A lovely, crunchy, finely shredded slaw with a creamy sauce and with no stabilisers or gums. Red onion and chives are present, but not dominant. The mayo includes a little whipping cream, free-range egg yolk and UK dairy.Best bargain:Aldi Specially Selected rich & indulgent coleslawView image in fullscreen£1.29 for 300g at Aldi (43p/100g), in store only★★★☆☆A creamy, chunky coleslaw that’s unctuous and moreish. Fresh, crunchy and well balanced with sweetness and acidity, this is cabbage-forward, with a little carrot and a subtle onion flavour, and a relatively straightforward mayo made with guar and xanthan gums.And the rest …Lidl Deluxe creamy coleslawView image in fullscreen£1.29 for 300g at Lidl (43p/100g), in store only★★★☆☆A veg-heavy, fine-cut cabbage and carrot slaw with a subtle onion twang and a refreshing sauce. A little tart, but arguably that’s what one wants from a slaw. Free-range egg, too. Flavoured with mustard, but also includes a preservative (potassium sorbate) and stabiliser (xanthan gum).Morrisons The Best extra crunchy coleslawView image in fullscreen£2 for 300g at Morrisons (67p/100g)★★★☆☆A medium-thick, crunchy coleslaw in a rich, free-range egg mayo. Sweet with some mild acidity and a subtle onion flavour. One of the simpler recipes (carrot, cabbage, onion, mayo), but it does contain xanthan gum.Tesco Finest coleslawView image in fullscreen£1.40 for 180g at Tesco (78p/100g)★★★☆☆A thinly shredded slaw that’s simple, creamy and crunchy, and has a nice balance of sweetness and acidity. Onion present, but not overpowering. No cream, but the thick mayo is thickened with citrus fibre, guar gum, xanthan gum and pectin.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionM&S Food deli-style coleslawView image in fullscreen£2.40 for 300g at Ocado (80p/100g)★★★☆☆Medium thick-cut slaw with a strong chive and onion flavour. Attractive with the pink cabbage, and one of the more mayo-heavy contenders. Includes a pinch of soft brown sugar, ground allspice and turmeric, though none is prominent. No gums, but potato starch and citrus fibre are added to stabilise.Asda Exceptional classic coleslawView image in fullscreen£1.94 for 300g at Asda (65p/100g)★★☆☆☆A rich, saucy, medium-thin slaw that’s sweet and crunchy but has a dominant onion and chive flavour. The mayo, made with xanthan gum and citrus fibre, is slightly moussey, though.Iceland Luxury coleslawView image in fullscreen£2.25 for 330g at Iceland (69p/100g)★★☆☆☆Finely shredded crunchy carrots, lots of sweet sauce made creamy by the addition of creme fraiche, and a sharp finish. Contains acetic acid, stabilisers (guar gum, xanthan gum) and a preservative (potassium sorbate).Co-op Irresistible deliciously rich coleslawView image in fullscreen£2.25 for 300g at Co-op (75p/100g)★★☆☆☆A finely shredded slaw with heaps of flavour, a warm dijon undertone, nice acidity from white-wine vinegar and great crunch. Colourful, with pink cabbage, carrot, red onion and chives, and a relatively strong onion flavour, but a slightly overcomplicated ingredients list, including potassium sorbate, maize starch and xanthan and guar gums.Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference coleslawView image in fullscreen£1.50 for 180g at Sainsbury’s (84p/100g)★★☆☆☆A ribbon-cut, saucy coleslaw made with a splash of single cream. Subtle acidity from lemon juice, but a complex recipe including stabilisers (guar gum and xanthan gum), potato starch and citrus fibre.For more, read thebest supermarket kimchi, tasted and ratedExplore more on these topicsFoodThe FilterVegetablesSaladSide dishesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From The Dog Stars to Erykah Badu: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: Jacob Elordi stars as a post-pandemic pilot in Ridley Scott’s sci-fi adventure, while the celebrated soul singer returns with a long-trailed collaboration
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Jacob Elordi stars as a post-pandemic pilot in Ridley Scott’s sci-fi adventure, while the celebrated soul singer returns with a long-trailed collaboration
Content: Pawsing for effect … Jacob Elordi in The Dog Stars.Photograph: © 2026 20th Century Studios. All Rights Reserved.View image in fullscreenPawsing for effect … Jacob Elordi in The Dog Stars.Photograph: © 2026 20th Century Studios. All Rights Reserved.Going out, staying inCultureFrom The Dog Stars to Erykah Badu: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadJacob Elordi stars as a post-pandemic pilot in Ridley Scott’s sci-fi adventure, while the celebrated soul singer returns with a long-trailed collaborationSat 29 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaThe Dog StarsOut nowRidley Scott has got to be one of the most prolific octogenarians working today. The director’s latest, a sci-fi drama based on the 2012 novel, stars man of the moment Jacob Elordi as a former pilot surviving the aftermath of a pandemic, with Margaret Qualley as a medic/love interest and Josh Brolin as a pugnacious former marine.ColonyOut nowWelcome to a Korean zombie horror where the twist is that the undead share a hive mind, making them a formidable threat to the not-so-merry band of survivors hoping to pull through against the odds. Train to Busan director Yeon Sang-ho returns with more gore and action thrills.One Night OnlyOut nowWill Gluck writes and directs a romcom starring zeitgeist-friendly actors Callum Turner and Monica Barbaro. It hit the headlines fornothaving any explicit sex in it despite its The Purge-meets-romance premise: premarital sex is illegal in the US, apart from on one no-holds-barred night each year.I Want Your SexOut nowAnother new release with banging on the brain sees Olivia Wilde and Cooper Hoffman playing, respectively, a provocative artist and the assistant with whom she enters into a BDSM relationship. Being a Gregg Araki film, this one is rather bolder, with the young man soon finding himself in over his head, so to speak.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenBest foot Forwards … Little Simz.Photograph: Rosaline Shahnavaz/The GuardianForwardsThe Downs, Bristol,29 & 30 AugustThe likes of Tems, Little Simz and Amyl and the Sniffers headline this two-day festival in one of the UK’s foremost music cities. The eclectic bill also includes UK legends (Tricky, Goldie) and electronic experimentalists (Oklou, Wesley Joseph).Michael CraggGesualdo Six and the Colin Currie GroupRoyal Albert Hall, London,2 SeptemberTwo British musical trailblazers – a Renaissance-focused vocal consort and a new-music ensemble headed by one of the world’s leading percussionists – join forces for this late-night Prom. The programme mixes centuries-old Christian choral works with Steve Reich’s Tehillim to mark the composer’s 90th birthday.Flora WillsonA$AP Rocky30 Augustto 5 September, tour starts LondonIn the eight years since his last album, Testing, rapperA$AP Rocky ventured into acting, designing and modelling, before releasing his fourth album, Don’t Be Dumb, in January. He now brings that expertly curated shapeshifting record to UK arenas.MCSwansea international jazz festivalVarious venues,3to 6 SeptemberSwansea not only hosts the UK’s longest-running weekly jazz club, but a prestigious weekender too. Guitar maestro Nicolas Meier splices Turkish music, flamenco, jazz and more (3 September), while ever-cool vocalist Claire Martin duets with bass virtuoso Laurence Cottle (4 September).John FordhamGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenFinding a new angle … Jack Guariento’s Bellsmyre Caledonia, part of Selected 16.Photograph: Jack GuarientoSelected 16Nottingham Contemporary,2 SeptemberTouring art venues across the UK, this exhibition celebrates incredibly diverse new moving image work by early-career artists including Rhiana Bonterre, Rosanna Lee, Jack Guariento and Viviana Almas.Mike NelsonLeedsArtGallery,to30 AugustIt’s your last chance to see M62 (East, West) by the ever brilliant English conceptualist Mike Nelson, a minimal display of blown-out car tyres, collected from the verges of the M62 motorway that runs south of Leeds.John AkomfrahWalker Art Gallery, Liverpool,to31 AugustListening All Night to the Rain is a multichannel immersive video installation all about diasporic lives in the UK, dealing with ideas of racial injustice, the climate crisis and colonial history, all in Akomfrah’s signature dramatic, cinematic style.Richard TuttleModern Art, London,3 Septemberto 3 OctoberThis American minimalist once filled the Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall with vast reams of yellow and red fabric, but this show gives viewers a chance to see him operating at a much smaller, but no less radically experimental, scale.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenMaria Friedman in rehearsals for Kimberly Akimbo.Photograph: Marc BrennerKimberly AkimboHampstead theatre, London, to 7 NovemberThis five-time Tony award-winning musical is about a 16-year-old girl who, due to a rare genetic condition, looks 74. It’s all a bit barmy but heartfelt and truthful too. Starring the mighty Maria Friedman.Miriam GillinsonHenry Paker3 Septemberto 30 May; tour starts NorwichMany comedians moonlight as artists, but few do both jobs at the same time. In Pencil Case, Paker – one-third of beloved podcast Three Bean Salad – combines standup with live drawing in what promises to be a gratifyingly clever and gently novel evening’s entertainment.Rachel AroestiBallet NightsTheatre Royal Glasgow,2 & 3 SeptemberHusband-and-wife dancers Harris Bell and Sae Maeda take a break from their day jobs at the Royal Ballet to perform on tour with Ballet Nights. The gala-style show is a smorgasbord of dance from classical pas de deux to new contemporary pieces, compered by ex-Scottish Ballet dancer Jamiel Devernay-Laurence.Lyndsey WinshipKing LearCrucible, Sheffield,29 Augustto 19 SeptemberIan McDiarmid returns to Sheffield to play Shakespeare’s Lear – a king on the wane, surrounded by his scheming daughters, thoughtful fools, fears and frailties. Directed by Titas Halder.MGskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenOutstanding in his field … Chad Powers.Photograph: DisneyChad PowersDisney+,3 SeptemberGlen Powell will continue cementing his Hollywood leading man status next year, with starring roles in new Judd Apatow and JJ Abrams movies; in the meantime he’s back with season two of this sweet comedy about a disgraced college American football player trying to get back in the game.VigilBBC One & iPlayer,30 August, 9pmYou may still think of Vigil as the sickeningly stressful Suranne Jones submarine drama, but these days the thriller takes place largely above ground; series three transports Jones’s intrepid detective to an Arctic research station where a British special forces operative has been murdered.The GentlemenNetflix,3 SeptemberGuy Ritchie’s other gangster streamer series (the one that hasn’t been generating a slew of headline-grabbing behind-the-scenes gossip) re-enters the fray, as aristocrat Eddie (Theo James) expands his drug dealing business into Italy. Hugh Bonneville and Maya Jama join the cast for series two.Live from the Lycett ArmsChannel 4,4 September, 10pmForget post-pub TV, how about actual pub TV? Channel 4’s latest attempt to liven up their Friday night schedule comes courtesy of comedian Joe Lycett, who hosts this new series – part chatshow, part love letter to the great British boozer – from his own pop-up establishment in east London.RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenYou spin me right round … Orbitals.Photograph: Kepler InteractiveOrbitalsNintendo Switch 2, out3 SeptemberLocal co-op games are rare, Nintendo Switch 2 exclusives even rarer. Orbitals is both, with an art style and sci-fi story inspired by anime, and an asymmetrical approach to its puzzle-platforming reminiscent of the likes of It Takes Two. Thankfully for those of us with an original Switch, it’s Gameshare compatible.The Blood of DawnwalkerPC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S, out3 SeptemberThis dark fantasy RPG is set in an alternative 14th-century medieval Europe run by vampires. Player character Coen is a dawnwalker (human by day, vampire by night) whose choices affect how the story plays out as he races against time to save his family.Jordan Erica WebberStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenJumping for Joyce … Flowerovlove.Photograph: Yana Van NuffelFlowerovlove – Mini Skirt WarriorOut nowAfter a string of EPs showcasing her love for occasionally sour bubblegum pop, London singer-songwriter Joyce Cissé finally releases her debut album. The country-tinged American Wedding channels Kacey Musgraves, while the bouncy In My Victoria’s Secret is as sweet as candy floss.Interpol – This Mirror Weighs a TonOut nowSeven albums in there was a sense that the New York doom-rockers had lost their spark. There’s very little evidence of that on the Andrew Wyatt-produced This Mirror Weighs a Ton, with the quintet’s brand of atmospheric balladry and fizzing art-rock anthems infused with newfound energy.Erykah Badu and the Alchemist –Before the World Blows: The Abi and Alan ExperimentOut nowThis near-mythical collaboration between the mercurial soul icon and esteemed hip-hop producer Alan Maman has been on release schedules since spring 2025. Such procrastination, however, isn’t reflected in the gently hypnotic shuffle of lead single, Witch Doctor.Alabama Shakes – I Must Be DreamingOut nowAs their 2018 hiatus extended it was assumed the Grammy-winning US soul-rockers would stay on their own musical journeys. A one-off performance in late 2024 led to this, their eclectic third album, which takes on jazz (Garden) and heartfelt R&B excursions such as single Another Life.MCStaying in:Brain foodView image in fullscreenRecipe ClubPodcastChef Dave Chang and writer Chris Ying host this charming culinary series, which analyses the perfect ways to recreate movie foods, from Pulp Fiction’s burger obsession to the ratatouille from Ratatouille.Ansel Adams: US National ArchiveOnlineIn 1941, photographer Ansel Adams was commissioned by the US National Park Service to create a vast mural. Although never completed, his fascinating reference images are now available to view on the National Archives webstie.Untold Raygun: Breaking BadlyNetflix,1 SeptemberFollowing her chaotic breakdancing performance at the 2024 Paris Olympics, Rachael Gunn became a viral internet celebrity. This often sobering film recounts the massive fallout for Gunn and the breakdancing community who sought sporting legitimacy.Ammar KaliaView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From Dalliance to Billy Strings: the week in rave reviews | Culture | The Guardian
description: Hugo Weaving leads a delightful drama about the trials and tribulations of a bunch of friends of a certain age, and the bluegrass wunderkind returns with a remarkable new album
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hugo Weaving leads a delightful drama about the trials and tribulations of a bunch of friends of a certain age, and the bluegrass wunderkind returns with a remarkable new album
Content: Russell Dykstra and Ryan Panizza in Dalliance.Photograph: Lisa Tomasetti/Paramount+View image in fullscreenRussell Dykstra and Ryan Panizza in Dalliance.Photograph: Lisa Tomasetti/Paramount+The week in reviewsCultureFrom Dalliance to Billy Strings: the week in rave reviewsHugo Weaving leads a delightful drama about the trials and tribulations of a bunch of friends of a certain age, and the bluegrass wunderkind returns with a remarkable new albumSat 29 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTVIf you only watch one, make it …DallianceParamount+; available nowSummed up in a sentenceA beautifully written Australian drama following the heartbreaks and hilarities of a group of old friends in their 60s, starring Hugo Weaving.What our reviewer said“Dalliance is not about plot. There are no murders nor mysteries to be investigated or suspects to be harangued. It’s a mood piece and an array of portraits of characters who have actually lived some life, been formed by meaningful experiences and come out the other side – at a later stage than we are used to seeing on our screens.”Lucy ManganRead the full reviewPick of the restRainbow WarriorNow TV; out nowView image in fullscreenRainbow Warrior.Photograph: SkySummed up in a sentenceA riveting feature-length documentary about the bizarre story of French secret agents blowing up a Greenpeace ship in New Zealand in 1985.What our reviewer said“It’s gasp-inducing stuff, even if the documentary is at pains to keep the mood fizzy via skittish editing and a soundtrack consisting of wine-bar jazz and, inexplicably, Wang Chung.”Sarah DempsterRead the full reviewThe Airport ChaplainNetflix; out nowSummed up in a sentenceAnother moreish Hugo Weaving drama, this time about a do-gooder minister who is always saving the day at work.What our reviewer said“I doubt the lives of real airport chaplains are anywhere near as frenetic as those of this show’s protagonist, Tobias Wallace (Weaving), whose existence is a testament to that old saying: “Not all heroes wear capes.” Sometimes, they wear hi-vis.”Luke BuckmasterRead the full reviewFurther readingShabana Azeez: ‘The most disgusting thing I’ve seen on The Pitt? American coffee’You may have missed …KabulBBC iPlayer; out nowView image in fullscreenKabul.Photograph: BBC/Cinétévé/24 25 Films Télévisions/Domniki MitropoulouSummed up in a sentenceA tense, powerful thriller about an Afghan family and the shameful events of when the Americans withdrew and the Taliban moved in.What our reviewer said“Its thriller tropes, of a race against time and of risks taken under the gaze of an implacable enemy, are utilised effectively to make the story as compelling as it is appalling. August 2021 in Kabul was an awful, shameful moment in history; this show vividly re-lives it.”Jack SealeRead the full reviewFilmIf you only watch one, make it …De Gaulle: RésistanceOut nowView image in fullscreenDe Gaulle: Résistance.Photograph: Entertainment Film Distributors/PASummed up in a sentenceSimon Abkarian plays the great Gallic general and Resistance leader, opposite Simon Russell Beale as Churchill, in the first half of a lavish two-parter.What our reviewer said“This very enjoyable and gallopingly eventful biopic offers a good-humoured, though naturally sympathetic, perspective on France’s great wartime hero. A tiny touch of comedy makes it resemble an old-fashioned 60s war film.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewFurther reading‘The spirit of resistance’: De Gaulle biopic turns into surprise hit for France’s younger viewersPick of the restBitter ChristmasOut nowView image in fullscreenBitter Christmas.Summed up in a sentencePedro Almodóvar’s autofictional and meta drama is about a director writing a film about a director writing a film.What our reviewer said“A candidly personal movie, circling around ideas of grief, loss, the vampirism of art and the betrayal involved in basing fictional characters on real people: a complex, slightly muddled, almost surreally modernist noir-melodrama.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewFurther reading‘It is the riskiest film I’ve ever made’: Pedro Almodóvar on being the villain in his own movieColonyOut nowSummed up in a sentenceFrenzied K-horror action from the director of Train to Busan traps a small group of the non-infected in a tower block swarming with rabid hive-mind zombies.What our reviewer said“Working with a company of South Korea’s top contemporary dancers, movement choreographer Jeon Young makes many of the action and gore scenes resemble something you might see on stage at Sadler’s Wells. Michael Jackson’s Thriller video might have done it first but Colony does it better, more scarily and on an epic scale”Laurence PhelanRead the full reviewShaun the Sheep MovieOut nowSummed up in a sentenceThe first feature-length adventure of cinema’s most adorable ovine hero gets a rerelease ahead of next month’s (18 September) sequel The Beast of Mossy Bottom.What our reviewer said“It’s a quasi-silent film jam-packed with gags, visual ideas and narrative invention and positively bursting with comedy flavour. Like Jim Henson’s muppets, the stop-motion Aardman figures are effortlessly funny, as well as being better performers than most humans.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewFurther readingBaa-hind the scenes on the Shaun the Sheep movie: ‘In a good week we can shoot two minutes’Now streamingMarching in the DarkTrue StoryView image in fullscreenMarching in the Dark.Photograph: SNG FilmSummed up in a sentenceLow prices and rising debt levels have caused a suicide epidemic among agricultural workers in rural India; this documentary is about some of the women left behind.What our reviewer said“Sanjivani not only works in the fields but also performs domestic labour for her extended family – cooking, cleaning and doing laundry. Her resilience is stunning to witness, but even more impressive is the emotional support provided by a tight-knit network of other widows.”Phuong LeRead the full reviewFurther readingSuicides of nearly 60,000 Indian farmers linked to climate change, study claimsskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBooksIf you only read one, make it …View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Riverhead/APThe Disappearers by Marlon JamesReviewed by Yagnishsing DawoorSummed up in a sentenceThis tale of the aftermath of a homophobic mob attack in 1980s Jamaica is longlisted for the Booker prize.What our reviewer said“Few books have mapped the beleaguered realities of queer existence with such psychological depth, harrowing realism and searing condemnation.”Read the full reviewPick of the restView image in fullscreenThe Great Dictator: A Life of Barbara Cartland by Matthew SweetReviewed by Kathryn HughesSummed up in a sentenceAn extraordinary biography of a much-underestimated woman.What our reviewer said“Matthew Sweet pays his subject the compliment of absolute seriousness, regarding her as a cultural phenomenon whose life, stretching the entire 20th century, deserves deep study.”Read the full reviewPassage by Colin ThubronReviewed byJohn BanvilleSummed up in a sentenceA dying woman looks back on her life as she makes a last journey to Egypt.What our reviewer said“Passage is an exquisitely wrought novel which, for all its understated, filigree texture, reverberates in the mind with poetic force.”Read the full reviewBetrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest by Luke HardingReviewed by Lawrence FreedmanSummed up in a sentenceHow the US turned its back on Ukraine, and aided Putin.What our reviewer said“Harding discusses the question of whether Trump might himself be a Russian asset. Is it just that he enjoys the company of tyrants and envies their supreme power, or do they have embarrassing kompromat that he wants to ensure doesn’t see the light of day?”Read the full reviewSophie, Standing There by Meg MasonReviewed by Sam LeithSummed up in a sentenceA heartbroken woman becomes obsessed with an author, in the follow-up to Sorrow and Bliss.What our reviewer said“Mason is brilliant at describing the small but intense joys of everyday life – getting your scalp massaged at the hairdresser, for instance, or owning one really nicely designed pair of trousers.”Read the full reviewYou may have missed …View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Transworld Publishers Ltd/PANobody’s Girl by Virginia Roberts GiuffreReviewed by Emma BrockesSummed up in a sentenceThe searing memoir of a Jeffrey Epstein victim, now out in paperback.What our reviewer said“Giuffre was rightly proud of holding Epstein and Maxwell to account. And yet for any survivor of sexual violence, the cost of recovery – let alone of confronting her abusers in front of the world – can be impossibly steep.”Read the full reviewAlbumsIf you only listen to one, make it …Billy Strings: So Much for GoodbyesOut nowView image in fullscreenSummed up in a sentenceThe introspective fifth album from the bluegrass crossover star – feted by everyone from Bob Dylan to Post Malone to Willie Nelson – is a moving journey through grief following the death of his mother.What our reviewer said“What does cut through the gloom is the lingering thought of how rich and powerful the album you’ve just heard is.”Alexis PetridisRead the full reviewFurther reading‘I was running away from poverty’: the remarkable rise of bluegrass virtuoso Billy StringsPick of the restDahi: Black Boy (Alternative)Out nowView image in fullscreenSummed up in a sentenceAfter creating tracks for a diverse range of artists including Kendrick Lamar, Vampire Weekend and Madonna, California producer Dahi steps into the spotlight on this genre-hopping debut album.What our reviewer said“Twisty, tactile tracks reference Radiohead and Fela Kuti, toy with time signatures and chord changes, and are just as likely to deploy open-hearted sax solos as gnarly vocoder – all in the service of showing off the guitar’s versatility.”Katie HawthorneRead the full reviewKlara Lewis: OpeningOut nowSummed up in a sentenceSwedish musician and self-styled “sound sculptor” Klara Lewis returns with more deconstructed ambient and acoustic experiments.What our reviewer said“Even at their most simple and ephemeral, Lewis’s vignettes build something rich and moving.”Safi BugelRead the full reviewExplore more on these topicsCultureThe week in reviewsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lavish spending fails to fix Tottenham’s big issue – the lack of a soul or spine | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: It might be too early to push the panic button after the 2-0 defeat by Newcastle but Roberto De Zerbi faces a huge task if he is to turn Spurs around
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: It might be too early to push the panic button after the 2-0 defeat by Newcastle but Roberto De Zerbi faces a huge task if he is to turn Spurs around
Content: A dejected Roberto De Zerbi trudges across the pitch after Tottenham’s 2-0 defeat against Newcastle.Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA dejected Roberto De Zerbi trudges across the pitch after Tottenham’s 2-0 defeat against Newcastle.Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty ImagesTottenham HotspurAnalysisLavish spending fails to fix Tottenham’s big issue – the lack of a soul or spineJonathan Liewat Tottenham Hotspur StadiumIt might be too early to push the panic button but Roberto De Zerbi faces a huge task if he is to turn Spurs aroundSat 29 Aug 2026 16.33 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 16.53 EDTShareTime for Tottenham to start panicking? This is, of course, a subtle trick question. Tottenham is one of those clubs that never actually stops panicking. They panic when they concede and they panic when they score. They panic when they have the ball and they panic when someone else does. They have a coach inRoberto De Zerbiwhose face evokes a state of permanent alarm, the expression of a man perpetually having a toilet door opened on him. One year they even managed to panic their way to the Europa League. For the ever-rattled Spurs fan, this club is less a treasured devotion and more a lifelong haunting, broken up by occasional panic substitutions.Elanga and Wissa strike as Newcastle extend Spurs’ miserable start to seasonRead moreYou could intuit that sense of encrusted resignation pretty much from the moment Anthony Elanga’s improvised shot kissed the post and trickled over the line to give Newcastle the lead. Since beating Aston Villa 4-1 in late 2024, Tottenham have gone behind 44 times in all competitions and come back to win precisely zero of them. There is something innate and endemic here, a chronic case of Long Tottenham for which – despite the new coach, the new leadership structure and more than a third of a billion pounds in transfer fees – there remains no proven cure. Yoane Wissa’s clincher was of zero surprise to anyone.And so welcome back to the temple of pain, the Theatre of Everyone Else’s Dreams, a stadium that fittingly still has no naming rights because pretty much every visiting side gets to own the place. Over the past 12 months, Aston Villa have won the same number of domestic fixtures atTottenham HotspurStadium (two) as Tottenham. Unai Emery’s men may well get the chance to retake their lead here in three weeks’ time. In the meantime it was Newcastle, with one clean sheet in their last 18 matches, who feasted on Tottenham’s neuroses, stayed tight and stayed patient, waited for the train that always arrives.Perhaps as Matthias Jaissle’s team climbed all over the duels and the second balls there was also a certain reassuring symbolism here: a lesson in the enduring value of culture over commerce. Newcastle have lost half a team but kept their soul; Tottenham have bought half a team and are still searching for theirs. There were inevitable boos for Sandro Tonali, who was actually fine: one of those rare Tottenham players who actually treasures the ball and wants to do interesting things with it. Alongside him Mateus Fernandes was restless, classy, excellent. Omar Marmoush on his debut looked fit and sharp. But of course the individuals were never the problem here.View image in fullscreenSandro Tonali tussles with Anthony Elanga.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAThe problem was the little things: the lost headers, the fractional pauses on the ball that kill momentum, the rushed shots, the extra touches, the tackles not quite committed to, the barely perceptible signs of a deep-rooted softness. Take Elanga’s goal, which sprang from an unpressed Nico González long ball, a poorly challenged Amar Dedic header, a cool turn and finish. Three very simple things in a row, at least two of which should probably have been prevented. No screaming howler or smoking gun here. Just a run of lost battles, a sum of marginal flaws, a team that for all its moments of promise and competence has not yet been welded together into a coherent whole.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBiggest problem for Spurs is finding right mentality, says Roberto De ZerbiRead moreHow De Zerbi fixes this is anyone’s guess. It feels increasingly clear that for all the new blood there is still a kind of generational trauma here, perhaps dating back to the injury crisis of 2024-25, when a threadbare squad was pushed beyond the boundaries of wellness and sanity. For the veterans of that campaign, your Archie Grays and Micky van de Vens, your Destiny Udogies and Rodrigo Bentancurs, you occasionally glimpse that accumulated tension in the 50-50 tackles and big physical clashes, the sense of players still not quite trusting their bodies. And oppositions really do pick up on this stuff. Right now there is a clear blueprint for beating Tottenham: compete, do the simple things well, and eventually bully them into playing your game.How much worse does this get before it gets better? Are Spurs fans ultimately in for another season of discontent and disgruntlement, of taking an unhealthy interest in the latest score from the Coventry Building Society Arena? The instinct here is still to be patient and wait for the required chemistry to develop. But what if two defeats become four, or six? What if it’s November and the top scorer is still somehow Richarlison with two? How does a club so medicinally addicted to panic possibly avoid it?Quietly, there is now some ridiculous creative talent at this club. The signings of Marmoush and Sávio, the new-look midfield, the return of Mohammed Kudus and Dominic Solanke, the prospect of James Maddison and Dejan Kulusevski and Xavi Simons to come. A World Cup finalist in Marcos Senesi sitting unused on the bench. It feels inconceivable that Tottenham could be in relegation trouble again. But as with so many clubs before them, Tottenham are discovering that buying new footballers is the easy part. Growing a spine will take considerably longer.Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurNewcastle UnitedRoberto De ZerbianalysisShareReuse this content

title: Dan Lawrence hails ‘different mentality’ as he strives to make up for lost time | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: Dan Lawrence said he was ‘desperate’ to establish himself, after his unbeaten 50 helped England to a strong position against Pakistan at Lord’s
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: Dan Lawrence said he was ‘desperate’ to establish himself, after his unbeaten 50 helped England to a strong position against Pakistan at Lord’s
Content: Dan Lawrence hit his second 50 of the series against Pakistan on the third day at Lord’s.Photograph: Sam Mellish/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDan Lawrence hit his second 50 of the series against Pakistan on the third day at Lord’s.Photograph: Sam Mellish/Getty ImagesEngland v Pakistan 2026Dan Lawrence hails ‘different mentality’ as he strives to make up for lost timeEngland all-rounder ‘desperate’ to establish himselfLawrence hits second fifty of Pakistan series at Lord’sSimon Burntonat Lord'sSat 29 Aug 2026 15.27 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 15.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDan Lawrence said he was “desperate to establish myself in an England shirt” after taking some solid steps in the right direction on a rain-affected third day of the second Test against Pakistan.In a chill breeze and with frequent interruptions from the weather, the battle for England’s batting spots heated up in the continued absence of the injured Jacob Bethell. Emilio Gay’s hard-fought 31 was ended by a grubber before Lawrence scored his second half-century of the series – matching Jordan Cox on that metric – to put England in control, 177 for seven at stumps to stand 357 ahead.“I’ve really tried not to think about that,” Lawrence said about the contest for places, after finishing the day unbeaten on 50. “I’ve tried to just enjoy every day of being here and trying to contribute to the team. It’s pointless looking into the future. I’m just trying to give a good showing of myself and thankfully I think I have done.Lawrence stretches lead against Pakistan as weather delays England victory pushRead more“Thoughts creep into your head and I’m desperate along with all the other boys to establish myself in an England shirt. It’s just about trying to take every opportunity you get instead of feeling nervous about the occasion, just have fun and play the cricket that’s got me here this summer.”Lawrence’s last run in the team, three Tests against Sri Lanka in 2024, came as opener and without great effect, three single-digit scores and three in the thirties. “I got wrapped up in a lot of things and I was thinking about my position and what I needed to do to stay in the team, instead of just enjoying it and realising how lucky I am to play for England,” he said.“My mentality since coming back has been completely different. Hopefully, we get a good series win and then we’ll see what happens in the coming months and years.”As a middle-order batter by preference he does not covet Gay’s position as opener – “It has been great fun batting in a position that is a little bit closer to what I’m used to,” he said, after a third outing at No 6 – and certainly took no pleasure in the 26-year-old’s dismissal, trapped lbw by a Mohammad Abbas delivery that kept low. “He played beautifully last night, dug in really hard and fought for the team.“Hopefully that bit of bad luck he got, he gets all the good luck next week. He can take a lot of confidence in how he played.“To get off the mark I had a massive big whooshka and edged it over the slips. That could easily have been caught and I’d have looked really stupid.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOf the four occasions when Pakistan have scored more than 300 runs in the fourth innings to win a Test match, three came against Sri Lanka and only one score exceeded 350. On an awkward pitch and against in-form bowlers their task already seems extremely difficult.“As far as batting is concerned we can only hope,” said Mohammad Ali. “Until the last ball is bowled in cricket, or the last run is made, nothing is decided. Maybe if we can get them out quickly … Miracles do happen in cricket.”Explore more on these topicsEngland v Pakistan 2026England cricket teamPakistan cricket teamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tadej Pogacar requires surgery after crashing out of Vuelta a España | Tadej Pogacar | The Guardian
description: Leader ⁠Tadej ⁠Pogacar ​abandoned the Vuelta a España on ⁠Saturday after breaking his collarbone in a crash ⁠during stage ​eight
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Leader ⁠Tadej ⁠Pogacar ​abandoned the Vuelta a España on ⁠Saturday after breaking his collarbone in a crash ⁠during stage ​eight
Content: A giant screen at the Vuelta a España shows Tadej Pogacar entering an ambulance.Photograph: Josep Lago/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA giant screen at the Vuelta a España shows Tadej Pogacar entering an ambulance.Photograph: Josep Lago/AFP/Getty ImagesTadej PogacarTadej Pogacar requires surgery after crashing out of Vuelta a EspañaLeader abandons on stage eight with broken collarbonePogacar also suffers concussion and ‘stable’ neck fractureAgence France-PresseSat 29 Aug 2026 15.56 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 11.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTadej Pogacar requires surgery on a broken collarbone sustained in a crash on stage eight of theVuelta a Españaon Saturday which forced him to abandon the race.The five-time Tour de France champion hit the tarmac with 31km remaining, ending his bid to complete a career clean sweep of the three grand tours.Pogacar had been leading by 3min 50sec a week into the race and was the overwhelming favourite for victory. Spaniard Enric Mas inherited the overall leader’s red jersey, a minute ahead of Primoz Roglic.“He is stable and, following a thorough medical assessment at hospital, Tadej has been diagnosed with a concussion, displaced left clavicle fracture, a stable C7 cervical fracture, and multiple abrasions,” said UAE Team Emirates-XRG’s medical director, Adrian Rotunno. “Fortunately, no other major injuries and no neurological fallout. He will require clavicle surgery which will be delayed due to concussion precautions. Tadej remains under the care of our medical team and we’ll provide further updates following the surgery.”Pogacar fell after brushing shoulders with another rider and losing control of his handlebars. With his entire team waiting as the peloton carried on without them, Pogacar tried to remount after a couple of minutes but cried out “no” and winced in pain when he touched his bike.He was then led to an ambulance as his teammates set off up the road towards the finish line at Xeraco, near Valencia.View image in fullscreenThe new overall race leader, Enric Mas, holds the red jersey after Tadej Pogacar’s withdrawal.Photograph: Josep Lago/AFP/Getty ImagesIt marks the first time the 27-year-old has failed to finish a grand tour.Mas (Movistar) took the ​red jersey after stage eight, becoming the first Spaniard to lead ​the Vuelta since ‌Jesus Herrada in 2018. ​Roglic (Red Bull-Bora Hansgrohe) moves up to ​second overall with Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM) 71 seconds back in third.At the podium, a sombre Mas accepted the red jersey ​but did not wear ‌it, holding it in ​front of him instead. “I hope he gets better quickly,” he said of Pogacar. “We’ve still got a few races left and I hope he’ll be in good shape for them.“skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn July, Pogacar joined a select group of five-time Tour de France winners in Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Induráin. He is the youngest rider to have won five Tours, more than a year younger than Merckx was in achieving the same feat, and is the first person to finish on the podium seven years running. He is also the only rider to have been on the podium in nine consecutive grand tours.Bryan Coquard (Cofidis) ⁠won the stage after several riders went down in ​another crash in ​the final kilometre. Mads ​Pedersen finished second while Jordi Meeus was third. The race continues on Sunday with a 187.5km mountainous ride from Villajoyosa to Alto de Aitana, before a rest day on Monday.Explore more on these topicsTadej PogacarVuelta a EspañaCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Erasmus tricks and Kolisi magic inspire Springboks to level series with All Blacks | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: South Africa levelled the series against New Zealand with a 33-26 win after Rassie Erasmus made multiple last-minute changes while Siya Kolisi was in inspired form
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: South Africa levelled the series against New Zealand with a 33-26 win after Rassie Erasmus made multiple last-minute changes while Siya Kolisi was in inspired form
Content: Siya Kolisi inspired South Africa to a thrilling victory against New Zealand.Photograph: Rodger Bosch/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSiya Kolisi inspired South Africa to a thrilling victory against New Zealand.Photograph: Rodger Bosch/AFP/Getty ImagesRugby unionErasmus tricks and Kolisi magic inspire Springboks to level series with All BlacksSecond Test: South Africa 33-26 New ZealandHead coach changes front-row just before startGerard MeagherSat 29 Aug 2026 13.28 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 16.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Boks are back. Level at one apiece in the series after a return to what they do best. Blending power and directness, blood and thunder, to edge far enough ahead of New Zealand and withstand a gutsy comeback from the All Blacks. Throw in some brazen mischief from Rassie Erasmus, who swapped his entire front-row just an hour before kick-off, and this was much closer to a trademark Springboks performance after they were unrecognisable a week ago.South Africa were far from flawless but constantly ferocious. It was not a knockout blow – not least given how the All Blacks finished the match – but it was some counterpunch after last week’s humbling. The third Test is scheduled for Johannesburg but they may consider relocating to Manila.South Africa v New Zealand: rugby union second Test – liveRead moreErasmus had been up to his usual games all week. Naming his team on Monday, swapping his fly-halves 24 hours before kick-off by recalling Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu and then coming up with his front-row switcheroo, starting with Gerhard Steenekamp, Deon Fourie and Thomas du Toit and relegating Ox Nché, Malcolm Marx and Wilco Louw to the bench. Nché and Marx were introduced on 36 minutes and promptly won two penalties to set up Siya Kolisi for a crucial try and stretch their half-time lead to 10 points. Marx was inspired thereafter while Cheslin Kolbe, who was drafted into the side on Friday, kicked 18 points.Whether Erasmus should have been allowed to switch his front row so soon before kick-off ultimately depends on the fine print of the tour agreement between the two unions. That he would not have been able to without medically justifying the decisions in the World Cup demonstrates how close to the wind the head coach is sailing.What is not up for debate is just what a savage intensity this Test was played at. The All Blacks were braced for a Bok-lash but could do little to stop South Africa’s opening score inside two minutes. Jordie Barrett did not get enough distance on his clearance after New Zealand received the kick-off and from the resulting lineout, the Springboks’ maul went into overdrive. Jessie Kriel was soon over. Statement of intent made.For all that South Africa were fired up, the All Blacks were not to be cowed. They demonstrated last week how slick they can be showcasing their ability to use the rapier in response to the bludgeon. After a series of wonderfully dextrous passes, Will Jordan found himself in space on the right, releasing Cam Roigard inside him.View image in fullscreenSiya Kolisi roars in delight after scoring a crucial try for the world champions.Photograph: Rodger Bosch/AFP/Getty ImagesThe most significant difference in South Africa’s performance was how direct they were and Kolbe nosed South Africa back ahead with a penalty before the Springboks struck again with another maul leading to Damian de Allende’s close-range score. Again New Zealand responded with a devastating score – Ardie Savea busting up the guts before Damian McKenzie was sent clear to the right-hand corner on the angle. It was another demonstration of how lethal the All Blacks can be.Just as was the case at Ellis Park, the Springboks came on strong towards the end of the first half and some nifty footballing skills from Feinberg-Mngomezulu and Kolbe forced a scrum five metres out. Cue the introduction of Nché and Marx and Kolisi’s try on his comeback to the side. Marx then proceeded to make a thunderous tackle on Luke Jacobson, with the All Blacks threatening on the left, to bring an end to a pulsating half.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideSouth Africa 33-26 New Zealand teams and scorersShowSouth AfricaWillemse (Libbok ht); Kolbe, Kriel, De Allende, Hooker; Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Reinach (Van den Berg, 56); Steenekamp (Nche 35), Fourie (Marx 35), T du Toit (Louw 55), Etzebeth, Nortje (De Jager 67), Kolisi (capt; Esterhuizen 42), PS du Toit, Wiese (Hanekom 67).TriesKriel, De Allende, Kolisi.ConsKolbe 3.PensKolbe 4.Yellow cardDe Jager 79.New ZealandMcKenzie; Jordan, Tupaea (Lienert-Brown 67), Barrett, Carter; Love, Roigard (Preston 51); Bower (Numia 53), Taylor (Aumua 48), Lomax (Newell 48), Holland, Vaa’i, Parker (Lakai 51), Jacobson (Tuipulotu 62), Savea (capt).TriesRoigard, McKenzie, Carter, Savea.ConsLove 3.RefereeAngus Gardner (Aus).Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.A couple of silly penalties allowed Kolbe to stretch South Africa’s lead early in the second and a trademark jackal by Marx gave him the chance to do so again soon after. The Springboks seemed content to hold what they had at that stage, Eben Etzebeth coming up with a crucial lineout steal with the All Blacks threatening to build up a head of steam on the hour mark. Leroy Carter’s speedy finish on the left trimmed the gap to 11 but another Marx penalty at the breakdown was typical of South Africa’s determination. Kolbe duly added another three points before South Africa, who lost Lood de Jager to the sin-bin, survived a grandstand finish after the outstanding Savea bustled over.Explore more on these topicsRugby unionSouth Africa rugby teamNew Zealand rugby union teamShareReuse this content

title: Novak Djokovic feels ‘as best as I can be’ before tilt at 25th grand slam title in New York | Novak Djokovic | The Guardian
description: Novak Djokovic said he was as prepared as he could be for the US Open as he attempts to take advantage of the wide-open men’s draw
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Novak Djokovic said he was as prepared as he could be for the US Open as he attempts to take advantage of the wide-open men’s draw
Content: Novak Djokovic has his eyes on grand slam No 25 as he prepares for the US Open.Photograph: Frank Franklin II/APView image in fullscreenNovak Djokovic has his eyes on grand slam No 25 as he prepares for the US Open.Photograph: Frank Franklin II/APNovak DjokovicNovak Djokovic feels ‘as best as I can be’ before tilt at 25th grand slam title in New YorkSerb hopes to take advantage of wide-open men’s drawElena Rybakina has eyes on No 1 world rankingTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsSat 29 Aug 2026 18.58 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNovak Djokovic said he was as prepared as he could be for the US Open as he attempts to take advantage of the wide-open men’s draw and battle for a potential 25th grand slam title.Djokovic arrived in New York having competed only once after his semi-final run at Wimbledon,losing in his opening match of the Cincinnati Opento Thiago Agustín Tirante while struggling with the humidity. However, he now sees the silver lining in that defeat, which he believes gave him the time to make sure he was in optimal shape for the US Open. “I don’t like early losses anywhere, to be honest, but it gave me time to be prepared for US Open in a most adequate way,” he said. “I had almost a few weeks, actually two weeks, to really train and get my body and mind into the right state, prepared for what’s coming up.‘Why would you want to retire me?’: Novak Djokovic is still driven by doubtRead more“So it remains to be seen. If you ask me if I’m prepared, I feel like I am as best as I can be, but it’s different training and then getting out on the Arthur Ashe Stadium and playing best-of-five.”Over the course of the past two years, nobody other than Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner has been as consistent at the grand slams as Djokovic, who has reached the semi-finals or better in six of his last seven such tournaments. However, Sinner and Alcaraz account for five of those defeats, along with a retirement loss at the Australian Open last year.With Sinner absent because of injury and Alcaraz competing for the first time since being sidelined for four and a half months by a right wrist problem, the field is wide open. Had this scenario unfolded 12 months ago, Djokovic would have been the clear favourite at the start of the tournament, but a year is a very long time at 39 years old and despite how high his level remains, each tournament brings more physical problems for the Serb to manage.Meanwhile, Elena Rybakina declared herself healthy for the US Open as she recovers from a foot injury. She is aiming to take advantage of a golden opportunity to claim the No 1 ranking for the first time. “I didn’t play for exactly a week, and we consulted with different doctors. I have been doing the recovery. Slowly started to go on the court. Just a lot of gym,” she said.View image in fullscreenElena Rybakina had to retire from the Cincinnati Open with a foot injury but has declared herself fit for Flushing Meadows.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty Images“It wasn’t easy, because we didn’t know exactly how the foot was gonna react, since it was very painful for me to go and serve in that match in Cincinnati, because I wanted to try once more. Then for a couple of days, it was painful to even walk. Afterwards we managed to do everything possible for it to get better, and I’m glad how the process is going for now.”Rybakina, the second seed and Australian Open champion, begins the tournament at No 1 in the live rankings and she can be overtaken only if Aryna Sabalenka, who has been No 1 for 97 consecutive weeks, Coco Gauff or Jessica Pegula win the title and Rybakina fails to reach the semi-finals.After a difficult period during the summer, Rybakina found her form again during the North American hard-court swing, reaching the final in the Canadian Open before moving into the last eight of the Cincinnati Open. However, she was forced to retire early in her quarter-final against Swiatek last week by a foot injury.“I don’t check the rankings [for] the point situation, but from the media mostly I know where I should get, how the others should play. It’s all the different scenarios,” she said. “But for me, especially now when I had this injury last week, I feel like the most important thing is to just try to stay healthy, play one match at a time, because this is not the last tournament of the year. Of course it’s a grand slam, and you want to do well. But you have plenty of opportunities after if you’re healthy and you keep on playing. I’m trying not to think about it at all, and just play one match at a time.”Explore more on these topicsNovak DjokovicUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Liverpool’s Andoni Iraola angered by substitution delay before Forest penalty | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Andoni Iraola revealed his frustration after being unable to make substitutions before Nottingham Forest were awarded a penalty at Liverpool
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Andoni Iraola revealed his frustration after being unable to make substitutions before Nottingham Forest were awarded a penalty at Liverpool
Content: Liverpool’s Andoni Iraola looks on as the substitutes Rio Ngumoha, Ryan Gravenberch and Kostas Tsimikas wait to come on.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenLiverpool’s Andoni Iraola looks on as the substitutes Rio Ngumoha, Ryan Gravenberch and Kostas Tsimikas wait to come on.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPALiverpoolLiverpool’s Andoni Iraola angered by substitution delay before Forest penaltyFourth official appeared to struggle with electronic boards‘I wanted to make those substitutions about three minutes before’Andy Hunterat AnfieldSat 29 Aug 2026 11.55 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 15.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndoni Iraola bemoaned a poor first-half display plus a broken electronic board forLiverpool’s disappointing 2-2 draw with Nottingham Forestin the first home game of his Anfield reign. Forest led twice, but were denied a third successive Premier League win at Liverpool by Víctor Muñoz’s emphatic 82nd-minute equaliser.The visitors’ second goal, from a penalty converted by Morgan Gibbs-White, stemmed from a throw-in taken quickly by Liam Delap while Iraola was attempting to make a triple substitution.Iraola’s Liverpool start slow again but Muñoz strike denies Nottingham ForestRead moreHe was prevented from doing so because the fourth official was unable to flash up the substitutes’ numbers due to a malfunctioning electronic board. “I cannot explain because I don’t have an explanation,” said the exasperatedLiverpoolhead coach.“I wanted to make those substitutions about three minutes before. It was two, three, four times the ball had gone out. He [the fourth official] was having some problems with the board. The penalty wouldn’t have happened if I had made the subs.“I had complained the previous time. The supporters were shouting and they were aware of the situation. I’ll leave you to decide whether it was a penalty or not.”Despite his annoyance over the buildup to Forest’s penalty, Iraola conceded that Liverpool created their own problems for the second week in succession with a sluggish start.He said: “The first half was poor, it was not good enough. We haven’t controlled the game and after we improved a lot in the second half. We were much more intense, quicker on the ball and had more urgency, but it hasn’t been enough to win the game and we have to blame the first half.“I am frustrated because we want to win, especially at home. It’s not a good result. We have come back from two results where we were losing and I like what we have done in the second half, but we haven’t been able to complete the comeback.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“In the first half we were too passive without the ball. Afterwards we improved this and intensity gives you the chance to win duels and attack quicker and better. But in the first half there was a lack of intensity and we had issues with throw-ins today.”Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolAndoni IraolaNottingham ForestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 9: Liverpool | Liverpool FC Women | The Guardian
description: Liverpool will hope Germany striker Vivien Endemann and Japanese youngster Mao Itamura can help get them off to a better start than they had last season
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Liverpool will hope Germany striker Vivien Endemann and Japanese youngster Mao Itamura can help get them off to a better start than they had last season
Content: Mao Itamura was named Eredivisie player of the year last season before moving to Liverpool. Photograph: Andrew Powell/Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesLiverpool will hope Germany striker Vivien Endemann and Japanese youngster Mao Itamura can help get them off to a better start than they had last seasonByTom GarrySat 29 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:8th (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:11thProspectsAfter a disappointing 2025-26 campaign, there is renewed positivity at Liverpool. A strong summer transfer window, coupled with encouraging results in pre-season, suggests they will significantly improve on their 11th-place finish, continuing the good run they had in the second half of last season.Gareth Taylor did not take charge until quite late last summer and the squad needed something of a rebuild. This time around, the former Manchester City head coach has been able to spend a full pre-season with his team. The managing director, Andy O’Boyle, has also had three transfer windows since starting his job to try to evolve the squad. The arrival of Germany forward Vivien Endemann, from Wolfsburg, is a very promising signing, while goalkeeper Khiara Keating has been reunited with Taylor, albeit she is not as experienced as Sweden’s Jennifer Falk. Falk was tremendous during a loan spell with Liverpool in the second half of last season, but opted not to make her stay permanent because she wanted to be closer to family.Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 8: EvertonRead moreThere were other notable losses, including the centre-back Gemma Bonner. Nonetheless, Liverpool appear to have a squad that is more than capable of staying up although they still look a long way off challenging for Europe and their budget is dwarfed by the big spenders.It took Liverpool until late January to record their first league win last season and this time around they will want to make an immediate impact. It should help that they begin away to promoted Charlton.Graphic showing where Liverpool finished in the past five seasonsOff-field pictureThe women’s team have never really benefited from the type of cash injections from their owners, Fenway Sports Group (FSG), that Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City’s women’s sides have from theirs. Liverpool have recorded an overall profit of more than £500,000 when the past eight seasons are combined and consistently break even. They also boast top-class facilities at their Melwood training base..The managerTaylor will want to see the team look more accustomed to his style of play. The 53-year-old has yet to win over the fanbase, but he does have a strong CV, winning the Women’s FA Cup and the League Cup with Manchester City in 2020 and 2022 respectively, and very nearly a league title, too. A former Wales international striker, Taylor represented a broad range of clubs, from Bristol Rovers to Nottingham Forest and Wrexham, with spells at Sheffield United and Manchester City in between.Star signingLiverpool were delighted that Endemann decided to make the switch from Wolfsburg. The 25-year-old had a good record in the Bundesliga, as well as 17 caps for Germany, whom she helped finish third at the 2024 Olympics. Endemann won a German Cup with Wolfsburg in 2024 and has Women’s Champions League experience, too.View image in fullscreenVivien Endemann will give Liverpool more threat in front of goal.Photograph: Nick Taylor/Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesStat attackLiverpool improved after a very slow start to the last campaign. They earned 11 points more in the second half of the season than in the first, the widest margin of improvement in the Women’s Super League. Doubling their tally from the second batch of 11 games would have given them 28 points, enough for sixth.Graphic showing points won in the first half and second half of the season by WSL teamsSet for a breakthroughThe 20-year-old Japan youth international Mao Itamura has been signed from Feyenoord. She was named as the Eredivisie player of the year last season and is a versatile forward with great dribbling skills. She should add a fresh and exciting dimension to Liverpool’s attack.What they say“We want to be in the first half of the table because we have really good players and I think we canshow what we are capable of. I believe in every single person in this team. We have good chances to have a great season. And we all have this good feeling; I can feel it in the training” – Liverpool and Switzerland forward Aurélie CsillagWhere are they playing their home games?Liverpool play the vast majority of their home matches at St Helens Stadium, which they share with the rugby league side. It has a modern feel and a capacity of about 18,000. They have announced they will be playing three times at Anfield this season; the first of those games being a derby against Everton in September.Explore more on these topicsWSL season previews 2026-27Liverpool FC WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: No country for old men: Premier League grind is why managers are getting younger | Premier League | The Guardian
description: The boss in the dugout is typically no longer an ageing former player – most are in their 40s on an exhausting treadmill
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: The boss in the dugout is typically no longer an ageing former player – most are in their 40s on an exhausting treadmill
Content: Unai Emery (left) and David Moyes (right) are part of the old guard in the Premier League with most managers, including Matthias Jaissle (centre left) and Fabian Hürzeler, significantly younger.Composite: Guardian Pictures; PA; Action Images/Reuters; Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUnai Emery (left) and David Moyes (right) are part of the old guard in the Premier League with most managers, including Matthias Jaissle (centre left) and Fabian Hürzeler, significantly younger.Composite: Guardian Pictures; PA; Action Images/Reuters; Getty ImagesInside footballPremier LeagueNo country for old men: Premier League grind is why managers are getting youngerJonathan WilsonThe boss in the dugout is typically no longer an ageing former player – most are in their 40s on an exhausting treadmillSat 29 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 16.57 EDTShareOne of the problems with getting older is that you’re never quite sure whether it’s you or them. Is the world really changing, or is it just you, struggling to adapt? There’s a milestone in life, probably as you’re contemplating university or a first job, when you realise you’re watching a footballer who is younger than you. Then, 15-20 years later, you realise you’re watching a manager who is younger than you. And 15-20 years after that, especially if you’re watching the modernPremier League, you realise that almost every manager is younger than you.At which you do two things: give thanks for David Moyes; and check to see whether it’s actually happening, or whether this is just the football equivalent of the policemen-getting-younger cliche.Managerial turnover means we need new ways to predict Premier League fixturesRead moreIt turns out it is true. Managers used to be ashen-faced men with nicotine-grey hair dressed in the sports jackets of grim experience. They spoke with a rasping melancholy of the depths of human fallibility and of fates that were not to be trusted. Now they’re trim, sprightly figures in T-shirts, convinced that analytics can explain the world.There are fewer Premier League managers now aged 50 or over than at any point in the past 20 years: only four, and two of those have only just made it over the threshold. Moyes is 63 (three months younger than José Mourinho, which, like Aberdeen being further west than Bristol, is a fact both true and too counterintuitive to be worth believing). Then there is Unai Emery at 54, Oliver Glasner at 52 and Régis Le Bris at 50. Most Premier League managers are in their 40s, with the youngest two Matthias Jaissle, 38, and Fabian Hürzeler, 33.A chart showing the age ranges of Premier League managers at the start of seasons over the past 30 yearsThis is not coincidence; rather it seems the result of two interconnected trends. Even at the turn of the century, when Mourinho was starting out, it was unusual for a manager not to have played the game to at least a reasonable level, which meant they were starting their managerial careers in their mid-thirties. That’s still the route many take – Andoni Iraola, Michael Carrick, Gary O’Neil or Álvaro Arbeloa, for instance.View image in fullscreenAndoni Iraola’s first appointment as head coach was at AEK Larnaca in 2018, aged 35.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APBut there’s also a recognition, to use Arrigo Sacchi’s phrase, that a jockey does not need first to have been a horse. Coaching is regarded as a job in its own right, requiring a very different skillset to playing. Hürzeler came through the youth systems at Bayern Munich, Hoffenheim and 1860 Munich but, aged 22, in part because of an ankle injury, decided to focus on coaching.Jaissle was a member of the Hoffenheim side that soared through the divisions to win promotion to the Bundesliga before knee and achilles tendon injuries ended his playing career at 26. The early switch into coaching seems particularly common in Germany: Thomas Tuchel and Julian Nagelsmann have similar stories.That greater receptiveness to career coaches explains the wave of younger managers. But there are also fewer older coaches.In part it may be coincidence: an experienced generation – Sam Allardyce, Tony Pulis and Alan Pardew – grew old together. That the process occurred just as many of their tactical characteristics – low blocks, direct play, a focus on set pieces – re-entered the mainstream may not simply be irony. The old must be cast out before it is reinvented as new; the modish cannot be represented by a 60-something football man.But it’s also because modern management is exhausting. At Ipswich, Kieran McKenna would have his coaches present their plans to him for the day at 6am, altering anything he felt wasn’t quite right. That plan would be sent to the staff at the training ground to set up all the various pitches and drills. McKenna would then go to check everything was laid out properly. It was all extraordinarily detailed; everything was marked out, down to where players should stand when they weren’t directly involved and where water bottles would be placed.During sessions, McKenna would walk between each unit, stepping in to offer advice and make amendments. After sessions, coaches would watch them back and report to McKenna on what could be improved before planning the next day’s drills to be presented at 6am the following morning.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKieran McKenna’s relentless coaching at Ipswich was exhausting so it was no surprise he needed a break following their third promotion in five years.Photograph: Cat Goryn/Action Images/ReutersDuring 11 v 11 practice games, McKenna would be the only one who coached. Over his five years at Ipswich, no drill was ever repeated in exactly the same form; repetition and possible staleness were to be avoided at all costs. Little wonder that after a third promotion in five seasons at the club, he felt exhausted, in need of a break rather than taking on an uneven fight in an ungrateful Premier League that could only sap his reserves further.Brian Clough would take holidays during the season. He would turn up only infrequently at training. His input was sharp, erratic, impressionistic. Four decades on, a top-level manager is running a team of coaches and analysts that probably outnumbers the players with whom he has direct contact.He cannot simply ignore the board until he needs money for a signing but has to manage up to whatever structure of sporting directors exists above him. He often will have little autonomy, althoughthe success of Mikel Arteta, who has a more traditional role and seems to micromanage everything at Arsenal, may change that. And he is liable to be sacked after a month of poor form. The pressure is enormous, the margin for error minute.That perhaps explains why so many top managers are nowdrifting into international football. Management, it’s commonly said, is a drug, but perhaps that fix is more palatable when it is delivered in five doses spread over a season, plus a major tournament every other year, rather than in the relentless drudgery of the club game. Carlo Ancelotti took his break from the club game at 66, Jürgen Klopp at 56, Tuchel at 50. None have demonstrated any great desire to return to the remorselessness of the league.The Premier League may be the greatest stage in management. It may be where the best salaries are paid. It may be where every manager wishes to test himself. But it is an exhausting and capricious world that requires extraordinary reserves of energy, physical and mental. It is no theatre for old men.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueInside footballcommentShareReuse this content

title: James Tarkowski pounces at the death as Everton deny Bournemouth win | Premier League | The Guardian
description: James Tarkowski denied Bournemouth their first win of the season with a late leveller in a 1-1 draw at the Vitality Stadium, after Alex Scott had put the hosts ahead
Author: John Brewin
Headline: James Tarkowski denied Bournemouth their first win of the season with a late leveller in a 1-1 draw at the Vitality Stadium, after Alex Scott had put the hosts ahead
Content: James Tarkowski (right) celebrates scoring Everton’s equaliser in stoppage time at the Vitality Stadium.Photograph: Peter Tarry/PAView image in fullscreenJames Tarkowski (right) celebrates scoring Everton’s equaliser in stoppage time at the Vitality Stadium.Photograph: Peter Tarry/PAPremier LeagueJames Tarkowski pounces at the death as Everton deny Bournemouth winJohn Brewinat the Vitality StadiumSat 29 Aug 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 16.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThrough wind and rain, the end of summer and a new era at the Vitality. In the Europa League, Milan will visit Dorset and trips to San Sebastián, Galicia, Norway and Czechia awaitBournemouth. The stadium is under renovation, towering exoskeletons waiting to be filled, new security cordons to negotiate, the team under the new management of Marco Rose.An unbeaten home record that stretches back to 3 January sustains, though so does Bournemouth’s tendency to concede late goals. James Tarkowski’s equaliser came in injury time. Other songs remain the same. Set pieces retain huge importance in thePremier League. From an outswinging corner from Hayden Hackney, Marcus Tavernier and Ryan Christie got in a terrible tangle. Tarkowski, unmarked, stabbed home an unlikely equaliser.Hull maintain flying start as Liam Millar’s winner ruins Coventry’s dayRead more“It’s not even a set-piece goal, it was just slapstick,” said Rose. If Bournemouth’s stance is that Alex Scott remains whatever the offers, his first-half goal and overall performance will only add to the cachet. In a game played at regulation Premier League 1.5x speed, while others skidded on a sodden surface, the Channel Islander made time and space bend to his will. “A top performance,” said Rose of Scott.Everton’s situation is volatile, racked with uncertainty, insurrection bubbling. Before kick-off, the away contingent sang for the 19-year-old Harrison Armstrong, linked with a £40m move to Nottingham Forest. Should he be sold “you’re going to have a riot on your hands”, fans warned.As if joining the protest movement, David Moyes started a player Evertonians hope does not follow the decades-long drain of young players sold. Wayne Rooney, John Stones, Francis Jeffers, the list is long. Selling Armstrong to a peer in Forest will cut yet deeper. “It would be a club decision,” said Moyes, disassociating himself from any sale, though not ruling it out. “I don’t really want to talk about it,” he said, before talking about it.Finances and regulations dictate that every Everton player has a price, is a bargaining chip. The scorer oflast season’s winning goal at Bournemouth, Jack Grealish, may return from Manchester City as part of a swap deal with Iliman Ndiaye. Such are the equations supporters must accept.Still, Everton began confidently enough. Eight shots registered in the first 30 minutes, beginning with an attempt from Jarrad Branthwaite, another jewel, though one whose fitness record dampens interest.When Bournemouth found their momentum, Rayan came to the fore, Vitaliy Mykolenko struggling with the Brazilian’s incursions. Scott increased in influence, socks rolled down, gliding across the turf.
