He was calmness personified in controlling Evanilson’s pass, dropping his shoulder and drilling his shot beyond Jordan Pickford.View image in fullscreenThe impressive Alex Scott scores just before the break to give Bournemouth the lead.Photograph: Matt Impey/ShutterstockMoyes’s fusty reputation belies his indulgence of talent if players marry aesthetics with hard yards. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall is delightful to watch, as can be Tyrique George, while Ndiaye and Armstrong also fit the School of Science ethos. Yet soccernomics, anexpensive legal dispute with Burnleyand squad cost ratios are likely to diminish Everton.The manner of Scott’s goal, the defence far too open to Evanilson’s escape, offered reasons why Moyes, whatever the window brings, might soon cork the fizz. Were he able to add players, Barry clanking wide a chance laid on by Dewsbury-Hall suggested a striker would be high on his want list, despite Barry’s four goals this season.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe first half suggested Rose’s immediate influence on Bournemouth is increased directness, Evanilson chasing plenty of long balls. From the beginning of the second half, with Scott directing traffic and Adrien Truffert galloping from full-back, their interchanges frayed Everton’s resolve.Three points should have been long secured by the time Christie and Tavernier collided. Pickford was kept very busy, he and Hackney combining to somehow deflect goal-bound efforts from Rayan and Evanilson.“We could have scored a second goal two, three or four times and now we have to deal with a point,” said Rose. “I have to get used to the Premier League. It’s quite different. It’s always an open game.”Moyes’s agitation was made apparent as his team ground the gears, only to feel the benefit of Bournemouth’s mishap. By then, Scott had departed to an ovation. It fell short of being a victory lap.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueBournemouthEvertonmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: There is clearly trouble ahead for Harry and Meghan on their return to the UK. Here are five ways to avert it | Stephen Bates | The Guardian
description: With a sceptical public and hostility from a lot of the press, the Sussexes face quite a challenge. Still, they really could help themselves, says former Guardian royal correspondent Stephen Bates
Author: Stephen Bates
Headline: With a sceptical public and hostility from a lot of the press, the Sussexes face quite a challenge. Still, they really could help themselves, says former Guardian royal correspondent Stephen Bates
Content: ‘Harry and Meghan must face up to the fact they will always be newsorthy.’Photograph: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Harry and Meghan must face up to the fact they will always be newsorthy.’Photograph: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty ImagesOpinionPrince HarryThere is clearly trouble ahead for Harry and Meghan on their return to the UK. Here are five ways to avert itStephen BatesWith a sceptical public and hostility from a lot of the press, the Sussexes face quite a challenge. Still, they really could help themselvesSat 29 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 03.59 EDTShareThey’re back! Harry and Meghan’s quiet return to England this week,via Birmingham airport, was much anticipated but scarcely celebrated – no bunting or street parties.So far there are many questions but very few answers: not just “why return now?” and “why so suddenly?”, but also questions of security: who pays if not themselves, given that they are not working royals? And where will the money come from to keep them in the style to which they are accustomed?The bills are mounting: not justthe Daily Mail’s legal costsincurred by Harry’s ill-fated court action, but even the upkeep of their nine-bedroom Montecito mansion, which, with property taxes, mortgage and upkeep (including looking after their chickens), could costabout $80,000 (£60,000) a month. That’s to say nothing aboutthe house in Portugal. Meghan will have to get some pretty meaty and regularacting jobs– and fast.Maybe all will be well, they will readjust to British life and Britain will readjust to them, but on past experience this seems highly unlikely. Can they avert it? Here are five tips that might help.1. Find capable advisers.Not necessarily the pin-striped courtiers who serve at the palace and know a great deal but whom Harry hated, nor the subversives likeMark Bolland, the PR guru,who once advised Charles as prince and seems to have initiated rows with half the rest of the family. Young smart-alec briefers are not required, nor perhaps Americans who don’t have a feel for Britain and its generally pro-royalist population. There are considerable bridges to be rebuilt with the people who feel Harry and Meghan let them down, and especially with the rest of the royal family. The couple need careful guidance over how they should present themselves, when they should speak and what they should say – or not say. No moreinterviews with Oprah Winfreyslagging off the relatives. It makes a splash, but thereafter, it doesn’t exactly help.2. Make peace again with the family, especially William and Catherine.It may be difficult and arduous to restore trust, but they need to do that as quickly as possible. And no setting up a rival court: they must know by now the obligation to choose discreet friends wisely.View image in fullscreenOprah Winfrey chatting to the Sussexes during their 2021 TV interview.Photograph: Harpo Productions/Reuters3. Help out a bit.Not necessarily with the washing-up but with attendance at public events, visits and charities. Not by freeloading, the public hates that, but by generally doing good – not for a few minutes or a day or two between flips to California, but regularly and humbly.4. Breathe deeply and make nice with the media – and not just the networks that have previously been prepared to pay them mega money.Wiser members of the royal family face challenges too, but they know that they need the so-called dead tree media, including newspapers, for their popularity. A smile goes further than a snarl. Remember that you need them more than they need you – they have businesses to run, you have a public perception to shape via their products.If they stop reporting on the royals or all the coverage is negative, the institution’s days of crisis will never end.Think hard about what to communicate and what you try to keep secret. The “secret” – private –christening of Archiewas unnecessary as was William’s attemptto hide the name of a family dogfrom an avid press and public. The media will always ferret even more important things out – such as their new home and the children’s school (especially if, as reported,Harry wants to watch young Archie play rugby every Saturday) and a defensive, sneering approach gains nothing. It just makes ever-fragile media/royal relations even worse. Better to be as open as possible and broker an arrangement for the media to thereafter leave Archie and Lilibet alone – it has worked for William and Catherine’s children. Harry and Meghan must face up to the fact they will always be newsworthy and isn’t that partly what they want to publicise their ventures?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion5. Above all, smile, for God’s sake.Harry and Meghan are both in a very privileged position. People won’t like it if they appear to despise or patronise them, or to feel too sorry for themselves. They have the opportunity to be identified with the great cause of cheering people up. Cometh the hour … perhaps.Steve Bates is a former Guardian royal correspondentDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Sunsets, disasters, dinners: we now record them all with our phones. But what is that doing to our souls?  | Phoebe Greenwood | The Guardian
description: As a war correspondent, I worked with photographers who said the camera was a buffer between them and reality. It is much the same now as we snap and scroll, says journalist and author Phoebe Greenwood
Author: Phoebe Greenwood
Headline: As a war correspondent, I worked with photographers who said the camera was a buffer between them and reality. It is much the same now as we snap and scroll, says journalist and author Phoebe Greenwood
Content: A man takes a selfie in front of a smoking lava flow. But have phone cameras changed how we perceive danger?Photograph: Antonio Parrinello/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA man takes a selfie in front of a smoking lava flow. But have phone cameras changed how we perceive danger?Photograph: Antonio Parrinello/The GuardianOpinionSmartphonesSunsets, disasters, dinners: we now record them all with our phones. But what is that doing to our souls?Phoebe GreenwoodAs a war correspondent, I worked with photographers who said the camera was a buffer between them and reality. It is much the same now as we snap and scrollSat 29 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 03.09 EDTShareIwas sitting on a rooftop in Athens at sunset looking up at Filopappou hill.Athens in August is burning hot. Not so much hotter than London or Paris any more, but the sort of hot that makes it foolish to step out into sunlight before 6pm. Emerging from the air conditioning at dusk, I saw a dense line of silhouettes on the ridge above me. Almost every one of these shadows had its arm raised, holding a cameraphone towards the sunset.Of all the pretty hills in the Greek capital, Filopappou arguably has the best view. The Acropolis stands directly to its north. To its south, where I sat, the city sprawls out towards the sea and a dark horizon of islands – Aegina, Salamina, Agistri.Looking up, the wall of tourist photographers reminded me of something: war zones.I worked as a correspondent covering conflicts and disasters for the Guardian and other newspapers for more than a decade. Over time, every new disaster came to resemble the last: another catastrophic tableau of buildings and bodies with a dense ring of telephoto lenses pointed at it.Print reporters like me could stay at a distance from the gore and the horror because we could describe it. The photographers had to get as close as possible because they needed a clean shot.Later, when I asked them about their work over beers at the American Colony hotel bar or tea at Gaza’s now-destroyed Al Deira hotel – how could they do it? Spend their days gazing at suffering? – most said the same thing. The lens was a buffer, a sort of protective forcefield. They weren’t looking at the fatally injured child, they were looking at the image of one.View image in fullscreenTourists capture a sunset in Oia village on the Greek island of Santorini.Photograph: Dancar/ShutterstockThe illustrious war photographerDon McCullinwas wise to the danger in this distance. “I operate not as a photographer but as a human being,” he said in 1983, 16 years before the first cameraphone. “I try to balance what I photograph not as a photographer but as a person, a man, and photography has got nothing to do with it. It is just something I have learned, it is just a way of communicating.”Now it’s 2026 and almost every one of us – bar the kooks and the luddites – clutches a distancing device.I was late toInstagram, but it quickly became second nature. Now, when an attractive dish is put in front of me, an animal does something cute, a fight breaks out on a ferry, a helicopter lands to race some poor person to hospital, I pull out my phone and record it alongside everyone else.Like the people on the hill, most of us live our lives through lenses: camera first.And they aren’t always pointing outwards.Multi-billion-dollar industrieshave been built on people photographing themselves. Much has been written about the psychological perils of our narcissistic age, but increasingly, the danger is more than psychological.Earlier this month,five teenagers were killedin a car driving the wrong way down a motorway in Ireland. They crashed into another car carrying four members of a family, all of whom were seriously injured. It seems they died taking part in an online trend in which masked young men film themselves driving recklessly at high speed, baiting police into giving chase. The camera is not incidental to the danger: the danger is created for the camera.Forensic cyberpsychologistMary Aiken describes thisas “hybrid behaviour”: filming and driving simultaneously, with “one foot in the real world and one foot in cyberspace”. While the physical car accelerates down a motorway, part of the driver’s mind is watching the finished video, the audience, the likes from other picture-sharers around the globe.View image in fullscreenA lamplighter at work on Charles Bridge in Prague, Czech Republic, December 2024.Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPAThis could also explain thefatal selfiephenomenon.A study identified 332 selfie-related deathsbetween 2014 and 2021, most commonly caused by drowning, falling or some form of transport. These tragedies can’t all be blamed on vanity meeting the smartphone – people have always taken stupid risks – but phone cameras have changed how we perceive danger: a cliff edge becomes a backdrop, death is content.In Afghanistan in 2009,Associated Press photographer Julie Jacobsontook nine frames over two and a half minutes of 21-year-old US L/Cpl Joshua Bernard lying fatally wounded after a Taliban ambush as he was treated by his fellow marines. Jacobson didn’t help them, she photographed.The resulting image of Bernard’s dying face and horrific injuries provoked bitter debate. His family asked for it not to be published. The then US defence secretary, Robert Gates, called AP’s decision to release it “appalling”. The news agency argued that the photograph performed an essential public function: it forced people at home to see the reality of a war being fought in their name.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJacobson’s defence was that in the moment she couldn’t help him and she decided the most helpful thing she could do as a photographer was to document a painful truth.I suspect that for the average smartphone user, their cameras serve the opposite purpose. The world has become too difficult to look at directly.View image in fullscreenA man takes pictures of demolished houses in Hebron in the Israeli-occupied West Bank in 2023.Photograph: Mussa Issa Qawasma/ReutersEvery day, those same screens show us bombed homes in Gaza, burning forests everywhere, celebrities in psychological anguish, self-harming in front ofmillions of TikTok followers. After reels of influencers slurping “the best cacio e pepe ever”, we are shown executions, assaults, maimed and dying children. Phone users are exposed to more suffering than a human nervous system is built to absorb, and we keep scrolling.We’re addicted to our cameras because they have the magical capacity to turn much of what is frightening, painful or just intensely beautiful into something we can frame, edit, caption and share. They allow us to be present but absent.It’s this sort of moral confusion I tried to explore in my novel, Vulture. Its protagonist is a British correspondent in Gaza who finds that documenting other people’s suffering gives her not only purpose but somewhere to hide. Horror becomes a picture byline; every dead body a pull quote. Bearing witness becomes absolution.Not that we should, can or will stop recording. In Gaza,Palestinian journalistsfilming on their phones have provided an indispensable record of a war foreign reporters have largely been prevented from entering. There, picking up a camera is an act of extraordinary courage.“Photography for me is not looking, it’s feeling,” the greatMcCullin said, an approach that has produced some of the most affecting images ever taken in conflict zones.The rest of us may just have to work to remain human behind the lens; to remember to engage with reality once the image is posted.Phoebe Greenwood is a former Guardian correspondent, and the author of the novel VultureDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The rebranding of ‘Lake America’ is Trump’s desperate attempt to distract us | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Ignore Iran, the Epstein files, and your wallet – not to mention Trump’s plummeting approval ratings
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Ignore Iran, the Epstein files, and your wallet – not to mention Trump’s plummeting approval ratings
Content: ‘As well as being a distraction, this pathetic maneuver is supposed to be a middle finger to Canada.’Photograph: Al Drago/Pool/Al Drago - Pool/CNP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘As well as being a distraction, this pathetic maneuver is supposed to be a middle finger to Canada.’Photograph: Al Drago/Pool/Al Drago - Pool/CNP/ShutterstockThe Week in PatriarchyDonald TrumpThe rebranding of ‘Lake America’ is Trump’s desperate attempt to distract usArwa MahdawiIgnore Iran, the Epstein files, and your wallet – not to mention Trump’s plummeting approval ratingsSat 29 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTShareDon’t mention the war! Or the economy, for that matter. Or the Epstein files. Or Natalie Harp. Or “affordability”, which, as Donald Trump recentlysaidat a rally, is a word that was “never used” by the media before he took office. Best not to talk about anything that affects ordinary people or embarrasses the president, really. Instead, let’s all rejoice in Trump’s latest triumph: renaming Lake Ontario, which is shared by Canada and the US, asLake America.On Thursday, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to America-fy the lake’s name on US maps and documents, which is an excellent use of time and resources. I suppose we can at least be thankful that the president, who is trying to slap his own name on everything fromairportsto theKennedy Center, didn’t decree that the body of water be called Lake Trump.This is not an isolated embarrassment: the Lake Ontario name change follows the president’srebrandingof the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America last year. “We have a gulf and we have a lake – now all we need is an ocean. Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific,” Trumptold reporters.Give it a few more months of the disastrous war in Iran and a bruised Trump may well make good on that threat: the man will do anything to distract from his failings.As well as being a distraction, this pathetic maneuver is supposed to be a middle finger to Canada. Trade negotiations between the US and Canada recentlycollapsed, with the Trump administration imposing a 50% tariff on some goods and the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, promising a “dollar for dollar” response. One suspects that Trump thinks Lake Ontario is named after the Canadian province it borders. Ergo he reckons a unilateral name change is a good way of showing the US’s northern neighbour who is boss.However, as Carney was forced topoint outon social media, the name Lake Ontario has been used for more than 400 years and comes from the Indigenous Wendat/Huron word Ontari’io, meaning: “The lake is beautiful, the lake is big.” It predates both the Confederation of Canada and the US Declaration of Independence.A US president ordering the name change of a Great Lake in order to antagonize one of its closest allies would have been headline news for weeks in a normal timeline. Now it’s just another Thursday. Still, this is more than a silly stunt that both Canada and the governor of New York have made clear they are going to ignore. It’s a glaring demonstration of just how desperate, isolated and out of ideas Trump is. His approval ratingshave hit a new low, sliding 14 points from 47% at the start of his second term to 33% now amid rising costs. The Iran war, which was sold as a “little excursion” that would only last a few weeks has hit thesix-month mark, and there isn’t a decent off-ramp in sight. And Canada isn’t the only former ally angry with Trump’s US; the country’s reputation hasplummetedglobally. A 36-country survey conducted by Pew earlier this year found overall ratings for the US are largelynegative; only seven countries rate the US positively, with Israel at the top of the list. Trump is weak and floundering: because he lacks the intellectual and diplomatic ability to reshape reality to his liking, he’s trying to rebrand it instead. But it doesn’t matter how many executive orders he signs; people will be calling Lake Ontario by its original name long after we can all stop calling Trump “president”.Florida ‘deputy of the year’ allegedly used Flock camera surveillance system to stalk exBrevard county’s 2025 deputy of the year has nowresignedfrom the sheriff’s office after an investigation found numerous examples of “egregious misconduct”, including images of him putting a gun in his ex-girlfriend’s mouth and a claim he used the Flock license plate readers to look up his ex-girlfriend. He also appeared to have posted a photo of himself sporting a Hitler-like moustache while performing a Nazi salute. (He denies that he used Flock to stalk his ex, and said the photo was merely a joke.) This is not a one-off: there arenumerous allegations involvinglaw enforcement officers using Flock to stalk people. Just this week a police officer in Kentucky was accused of using the Flock camera system to search for and track his exmore than 2,000 times.Tate brothers reportedly rented supercars to appear ‘uberwealthy’Theself-styledmisogynist Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan were arrested in the US in July as part of a UK police investigation into alleged sexual offences. Part of their lawyers’ strategy to fight extradition seems to be to paint them as posers who just pretended to be “uberwealthy” online in order to generate attention. “[T]he $2.1m Aston Martin and $5m and $7m Bugattis featured in Tristan’s videos were rented,” one legal submissionnotes. “The valuation of Andrew’s watch collection is based on a third-party enthusiast publication.”Women using HRT may be at lower risk of dementiaA studytracked183,450 postmenopausal women in the UK and found that those who had used hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for at least a year were 10% less likely to develop any form of dementia.Female-first music festivals are due for a resurgenceOlivia Rodrigo’s women-led Daisy Chain Fields Festival is taking place in California this Saturday, with net proceeds going to organizations like Planned Parenthood and the Center for Reproductive Rights. “[The festival] creates a necessary and refreshing culture of community, setting up women’s art to be received and valued in a less competitive and capitalist environment,” the pop artist Elitold the Guardian.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIsrael has killed at least 100 Palestinians in Gaza in the last two weeksThis is more than10 months intoa “ceasefire”. Still, that kill count is not enough for Itamar Ben-Gvir, the leader of Israel’s far-right Jewish Power (Otzma Yehudit) party and the minister of national security. “I think we should be doing 30 to 40 targeted assassinations per night,”Ben-Gvir recently saidon a podcast. “Not just those who pose an immediate threat. There are people there who don’t deserve to live … They are not even people.” Ben-Gvir went on to say that he thought Israel should occupy the entirety of Gaza. “I imagine settlements … throughout Gaza, and encouraging as much emigration as possible.” There has been a disturbing lack of outrage about these comments from the international community.A Texas judge has advice for people offended by drag shows“[T]he solution is relatively simple … just don’t go,” US district judge David Hittnerwrote in a rulingthat struck down a 2023 state law trying to restrict drag shows. Hittner ruled on the basis that the law was so vague that it was unconstitutional. As the New York Times noted in apiece last year: “Vagueness has become fundamental to the way Trump operates. It is not so much a legal strategy as a power dynamic.” People are more likely to self-police and comply in advance because they’re terrified they’ll get in trouble.Dolly Parton’s death united the US in griefIt’s not often that you’ll see Donald Trump and the Democratic Socialists of America pay homage to the same person. The Washington Postnotesthat Parton was “the only global figure that a majority of conservatives and liberals both supported in one Marchpoll– and by far – leaving the likes of Taylor Swift in the favorability dust”. RIP Dolly. As Robert Reichwrote in the Guardian, she was everything Trump is not: “Dolly Parton was a huge winner, bless her soul. Trump is the biggest loser on the planet.”Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpThe Week in PatriarchyTrump administrationCanadaAmericasUS politicsFloridaSurveillancecommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: The barbecue is fundamentally unenjoyable. Please, put a lid on it | Max Liu | The Guardian
description: Dress up the barbie however you like – it’s toxic, tiresome and, more to the point, malnourishing, says freelance writer Max Liu
Author: Max Liu
Headline: Dress up the barbie however you like – it’s toxic, tiresome and, more to the point, malnourishing, says freelance writer Max Liu
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onBarbecueThe hill I will die on: The barbecue is fundamentally unenjoyable. Please, put a lid on itMax LiuDress up the barbie however you like – it’s toxic, tiresome and, more to the point, malnourishingSat 29 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 09.44 EDTShare“If you’re invited to a barbecue, have your dinner before you go.” It is the wisest advice my dad has ever given me. Barbecues are one of life’s perennial disappointments. The romance of eating outside quickly degenerates into a recipe for mucky fingers, smelly clothes andmore mess than you bargained for, with grills that you can never get clean, uncomfortable seating that makes your back ache or, dafter still, eating while standing up. Worst of all is the true barbecue legacy – the nagging hunger that follows bitty dining, leaving you with the aggrieved sense that you missed a mealtime you’re never getting back.I grew up in Cornwall, where beach barbecues were a rite of passage. The flame under the sandy grill was blown out by the Atlantic wind, so these gatherings were impractical, unpredictable and interminable. One minute the sausages were raw and looked like they’d never be ready, the next they were hard and black and basically inedible. Rain frequently sent us scrambling to pack up and flee for shelter.Even when it doesn’t rain, and the scene is a suburban garden wheresomething that looks like it belongs in a gastropub kitchenhas been installed to char halloumi three times a year, I find myself wondering: “How is this fun?” Barbecues are terrible for socialising because the food trickles out, with kids served first (why, when they have the most energy?), so guests don’t eat at the same time and instead dine in silos, wondering if they’ll get home early enough to make pasta. As for drinks, they’re warm because ice buckets don’t work – they’re too small and the ice melts almost instantly in the kind of temperatures we’ve seen this summer – and nobody wants to dash back and forth to the fridge.The hill I will die on: Breakfast cereal is for babies – I eat salad in the mornings, like a grownup | Jacq KellyRead moreThe popularity of barbecues is inexplicable yet undeniable, with black smoke puffing from back gardens at the first sniff of a sunny day. When I broached my hatred with an Australian, she reacted as if I wanted to deprive her of her birthright. But just because people keep doing something doesn’t necessarily mean they actually enjoy it.Barbecues are antisocial in other, more important ways. I used to live above a man who liked to come home from work and barbecue steak on his patio, directly below my kitchen. I had to close every window to stop my whole flat stinking of beef. If you live in a densely populated area, it’s not particularly socially conscious to fill the air with meaty smog during hot weather, just so you can clog your arteries.Disposable barbecues, which have beenfactors in wildfiresduring this summer’s heatwaves, are the worst. This month, onecaused a forest fire in the North York Moors, while Dorset and Wiltshire fire and rescue recently told people togo to the pub instead. A spokesperson added: “I’d certainly challenge anybody to say whether they’ve ever had a good meal from a disposable barbecue.” An excellent point which, if we’re honest, applies to all variationsof barbecue.Max Liu is a freelance writerExplore more on these topicsBarbecueThe hill I will die onFoodcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘If it’s made in the US, I don’t buy it’: Canadians on boycotting Trump’s America | International trade | The Guardian
description: Avoiding US goods and services – from tech to whisky to air travel – has forced many to find a new way of living
Author: Jane Clinton
Headline: Avoiding US goods and services – from tech to whisky to air travel – has forced many to find a new way of living
Content: A sign in a liquor shop in Vancouver, British Columbia promotes native Canadian alcohol.Photograph: Chris Helgren/ReutersView image in fullscreenA sign in a liquor shop in Vancouver, British Columbia promotes native Canadian alcohol.Photograph: Chris Helgren/ReutersInternational trade‘If it’s made in the US, I don’t buy it’: Canadians on boycotting Trump’s AmericaAvoiding US goods and services – from tech to whisky to air travel – has forced many to find a new way of livingJane ClintonSat 29 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor William McDonald, 38, a diesel mechanic from Thunder Bay, Ontario, “Canadian is always the first choice,” even if it means his weekly bills are higher.“As soon as Trump started putting those tariffs on in February [last year], I started boycotting US goods,” he said. “Avoiding American products has driven my costs up, and I’m still happy to do it.“I used to drink US beer, but now I drink Canadian beer, and that costs me an extra C$1,000 (£531/US$720) a year. Likewise, groceries cost about C$50 more a week, but you work that extra hour to pay for it.”McDonald likened Donald Trump’s behaviour towardsCanadaas “a lot like the schoolyard bully yelling and stomping their feet when they don’t get the cowering reaction they expect”.View image in fullscreenA shop poster in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada.Photograph: Artur Widak/NurPhoto/Rex/ShutterstockThis week the US imposed 50% tariffs on US$20bn (£15bn) of Canadian goods, and Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, hasvowed to match them “dollar for dollar”after the collapse of trade talks between the two countries last weekend. Donald Trump retaliated on Thursday by ordering the federal government torename Lake Ontario to Lake America.Such actions have added fuel toa widespread boycott of US products and services by Canadiansthat began early last year in response to the president’s trade war andthreats to annex his northern neighbour.More than 3,500 people from across Canada shared with the Guardian via an online callout how they have made changes to their lives in response to the US administration’s political and economic stance. Many expressed deep anger and sadness, but remained resolute that this was now a new way of living.View image in fullscreenA ‘Made in Canada’ sign at a liquor store in Victoria, British Columbia, Canada.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesBuying only Canadian groceries, including fresh produce, and boycotting travel south of the border featured heavily among the responses. Respondents have stopped paying for US technology; streaming services provided by Netflix, AmazonPrime, AppleTV and Disney+; petrol; vehicles such as Teslas; and whiskies including Jack Daniel’s. Social media sites including X, Facebook and Instagram were also being avoided.In July, an Angus Reid survey found40% of grocery shoppers were actively checking where products came from, and most of those avoiding US products where possible.double quotation markI think you need to be in Canada to understand how deep the animosity to the US isDenise, WinnipegThe ABUS (Anything but US) or ABUSA (Anywhere but USA) acronyms and “Elbows Up!” slogan – a hockey term for offering a stiff defence – began appearing in Canada last year.“I think you need to be in Canada to understand how deep the animosity to the US is … even across the political spectrum,” said Denise from Winnipeg, Manitoba.“‘Elbows up’ is a real thing. We don’t fly US airlines, we stay in locally owned hotels, we won’t even connect in a US airport … we’ve moved investments to Canadian companies, and we actively avoid USA products, produce and groceries. It can be pretty inconvenient to do the research and read signs and labels, and often more costly, but BDS [boycott, divestment, sanction] is the only tool ordinary people have to stand up for our values.”View image in fullscreenElizabeth started growing her own vegetables to avoid buying American.Photograph: Elizabeth/Guardian CommunityElizabeth Lorenz, 68, a retired teacher who lives in Nanaimo, British Columbia,said she would change a recipe to work around a lack of certain ingredients.“I read labels on packaged food, and if it’s made in the US, I don’t buy it,” she said. “Annie’s Pasta is an example of a product I no longer purchase.“Grocery stores are increasingly offering more produce from Mexico, Peru, Guatemala, Chile and South Africa. Although this means the transportation of this produce has contributed to more environmental degradation than if I were to buy American produce, my outrage at America’s greed and corruption trumps (apologies for the pun) my environmental concerns.”She has planted yams and sweet potatoes in her garden “since only American-grown yams and sweet potatoes are available”, she said.Jane, 54, a teacher, was one of many who believed the relationship between the US and Canada had been badly damaged, perhaps beyond repair.“I definitely will not support America economically while this administration is in power and, to be honest, I may not ever again,” she said.“The relationship, in my eyes, has been permanently tarnished.”View image in fullscreenA liquor shop in Winnipeg announces its rejection of American produce.Photograph: Ed White/ReutersJane has been buying only Canadian groceries and alcohol for more than a year and has also stopped travelling to the US, opting for a longer journey to see sports in Canada.“I have been vacationing in Mexico and the Dominican Republic and Europe instead,” said Jane, who lives in Camlachie, Ontario. “I used to go to Detroit for sporting events or concerts and would pick up gas and groceries before returning to Canada. For more than a year, I have been driving four hours to Toronto for those events that I normally would drive only an hour to in the US.”She said at first making the changes to non-US goods was “quite challenging” but she uses apps and online forums which direct her to Canadian options.Among the many US products Jane has replaced with Canadian equivalents are Heinz Tomato Ketchup, Kraft Cheese and Charmin toilet paper. She uses the apps CanMade – Canadian Made, Buy Beaver and O SCANada: Buy Canadian. She also uses the websitemadeinca.ca.“Grocery shopping is now easier as stickers are used to indicate place of origin,” she said. “Checking origin of product information has become second nature to me now.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJames Buchan has swapped out all his US tech.Photograph: James/Guardian Communitydouble quotation markI’ve sold all my Apple productsJames Buchan, HalifaxThe same is true of James Buchan, 36, who works in IT, lives in Halifax, Nova Scotia and describes himself as “a habitual label reader”.“All Procter & Gamble and Colgate products have been replaced by Attitude and Lavo products from Quebec,” he said.“Canadian produce is quite easy to get hold of, and we can get food from Mexico, but ready-made meals are more difficult to find, as the US has it on lock. So making the change could be more difficult for some.”He also did a clearout of his tech. “I sold all my Apple products: a year-old MacBook, iPhone, AirTags and AirPods, and replaced them with alternatives,” he said. “Tech was the easiest – I do not miss my iPhone or Mac at all.”He switched his email providers to European-based ones and has done the same for his mapping applications, language-learning apps and calendar. He also left Facebook, Reddit, Instagram and WhatsApp.Kurt, 61, a retired engineer who lives in Calgary, Alberta, said his whiskey-tasting group “spent a small fortune” annually on American whiskies – in the region of US$10,000.“Since‘Liberation Day’and the first round of tariffs, we decided one way of expressing our distaste is not to buy American whiskies,” he said. “So since then we’ve spent US$0.00. Amazingly, we just stumbled on a whole new batch of Canadian equivalents. We didn’t realise the range and quality of stuff available locally. So we’ve got no intention of ever going back.”He is also now a “vigorous” label checker, but added this was not always straightforward, citing the US company Kraft, which has a Canadian operation, employs Canadians, and “uses Canadian materials and ingredients when they can”.“It actually pains me to buy a product that, yes, it’s made here in Canada, but we know their revenues are going back to the company in the States,” he said.View image in fullscreenA billboard in Mississauga, Ontario, Canada promotes Canadian-made pet food.Photograph: Xinhua/Rex/ShutterstockHis wife also no longer drinks California wine, and despite being “frequent visitors for 30-plus years” to the US, Kurt said they have not been there since January 2025.Many who got in touch with the Guardian felt that trust had been broken irrevocably with their US neighbour.double quotation markI won’t go back to buying US products, even if the regime changesSarika, Vancouver“I won’t go back to buying US products, even if the regime changes, because the US is unreliable and untrustworthy,” said Sarika, 61, an academic who lives in Vancouver.“It’s a shame, as many of us in the border regions have friends across the border, and we don’t want to see their businesses and towns suffer, but perhaps Americans will now get a little more involved in voting for and enabling a more fair and just government and trade system.”Vikram, 51, who works at a finance firm and lives in Toronto, said he refused to travel to the US even though he has family there. They visit him instead. He also avoids US products and is now boycotting Amazon.He reflected the sentiment of many who found the turn of events lamentable.“I find it quite sad that Canadians are forced to do this as a protest against these ridiculous threats to our sovereignty, but I’m not sure how else to react,” he said. “We cannot go back to looking at our relationship with the US as it was before, because things have changed. We need to shift focus for our own protection and to maintain our sovereignty and control over our economy.”Kurt, however, sounded a quiet note of optimism.“We’re going to look back, and we’re going to say, you know what, it was painful, and it was a shock, especially to have your best friend turn on you, but it was the best thing that could ever happen to us,” he said. “Canada will be stronger and healthier after all this is over.”William also took some solace from how he feels things have changed in Canada.“After years of internal division in our country, it’s nice to finally see something bind us together again,” he said. “I guess sometimes it just takes a mutual enemy to find one’s resolve.”Explore more on these topicsInternational tradeCanadaUS economyAmericasEconomicsGlobal economyTrump administrationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ireland will be united, says Gordon Brown | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: Former PM believes Northern Ireland will leave UK in the long term – but remains opposed to Scottish independence
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Former PM believes Northern Ireland will leave UK in the long term – but remains opposed to Scottish independence
Content: Gordon Brown said a united Ireland would be ‘a long process where people have got to come together and find a way of agreeing’.Photograph: Victoria Jones/PAView image in fullscreenGordon Brown said a united Ireland would be ‘a long process where people have got to come together and find a way of agreeing’.Photograph: Victoria Jones/PANorthern IrelandIreland will be united, says Gordon BrownFormer PM believes Northern Ireland will leave UK in the long term – but remains opposed to Scottish independence‘I don’t want to be a backseat driver’: Gordon Brown on Burnham, billionaires – and his vision for a better BritainPeter WalkerandCharlotte EdwardesSat 29 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 04.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former prime ministerGordon Brownhas said it is inevitable that Ireland will become united at some point in the future, in a wide-ranging interview with the Guardian.While he added that any union would necessarily be “a long process” and based on mutual agreement, Brown’s comments are notable both because of his vehement opposition to Scottish independence, but also because of his involvement in government in efforts to bring peace toNorthern Ireland.He was Tony Blair’s chancellor when the Good Friday peace agreement was signed in 1998. In 2010, he was prime minister when justice and policing powerswere devolvedto Northern Ireland’s power-sharing government, another major step for reconciliation.But,speaking to the Guardian’s Saturday magazine, Brown argued that Northern Ireland had a potentially different position with regards to the rest of the UK than, for example, Scotland.Asked about continued pressure for Scottish independence, Brown said: “Scotland’s got to find a way of living in cooperation with other countries, and independence would not be the right way forward. We’re geographically, economically, socially, culturally linked to the rest of the United Kingdom, whether it’s Wales, England or parts of Ireland.”Questioned about whether the geographical link of NorthernIrelandwith the Republic of Ireland meant uniting the two made sense, he replied: “Yes. Well, of course, in the long term, Ireland will be united.”Such a process would be, he added, “a long process where people have got to come together and find a way of agreeing. Basically, that is the issue: whether people can actually agree.”Elsewhere in the interview, coinciding with the publication of Brown’s new book,The Future Starts With Us, he said he did not want “to be a backseat driver” in terms of telling Andy Burnham – who served in his cabinet – what to do.He nonetheless made the case for continued oil and gas drilling in the North Sea, one of the most politically sensitive decisions facing Burnham in the coming months, notably over the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields, consultations on which have now closed.Brown argued that decisions over the North Sea had been incorrectly portrayed as a binary choice between fossil fuels and renewables, when in fact it was a question of helping a transition towards the latter.He said: “I think you can support renewables as the future for British energy and support the development of the North Sea to use some of the existing oil and gas.“And in fact, the way to use the North Sea for hydrogen, for wind – it could be floating wind– and for carbon capture and storage, which are three energy products that could come out of the North Sea, the way to make that happen is to keep the infrastructure and skills that you have in the development of the North Sea for oil and gas.“In other words, the transition to renewables in the North Sea should come from keeping the infrastructure and skills that we have in the first instance for oil and gas, and gradually moving them across to doing wind, hydrogen, and carbon capture.”This transition, he argued, could be managed via a “European consortium” also involving Norway, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and Denmark.But more widely, Brown said, environmental policies had “got to be seen as a benefit and not just a cost”.He added: “It’s quite important that renewable costs are coming down all the time. So, 20 years ago it would’ve been cheaper to produce coal and oil and gas, but now of course you have the advantages of solar power and wind power and everything else. So, investing in the environment is potentially a money-saving thing.”Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandIrelandGordon BrownEuropeGood Friday agreementScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Statins can safely cut risk of heart attacks or strokes in healthy people aged over 70, world-first clinical trial shows | Health | The Guardian
description: Australian-led trial finds low risk of side effects from common cholesterol-lowering medication for otherwise healthy older people
Author: Melissa Davey
Headline: Australian-led trial finds low risk of side effects from common cholesterol-lowering medication for otherwise healthy older people
Content: New research shows taking statins can reduce the risk of people aged over 70 suffering heart attacks or strokes.Photograph: Carol Heesen/AlamyView image in fullscreenNew research shows taking statins can reduce the risk of people aged over 70 suffering heart attacks or strokes.Photograph: Carol Heesen/AlamyHealthStatins can safely cut risk of heart attacks or strokes in healthy people aged over 70, world-first clinical trial showsAustralian-led trial finds low risk of side effects from common cholesterol-lowering medication for otherwise healthy older peopleMelissa DaveyMedical editorSat 29 Aug 2026 02.25 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 21.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaking a common cholesterol-lowering medication can reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke for people aged over 70, with a low risk of serious side effects, a world-first clinical trial led by Australian researchers has found.Statins are already commonly prescribed to people under the age of 75 who meet certain risk criteria, such as having diabetes and high cholesterol, to prevent them from having a major heart event such as a heart attack, stroke, or from requiring heart surgery.Statins helping people with obesity match those of healthy weight on key metrics, study findsRead morePeople who have already had a major heart event are also commonly prescribed the drugs, regardless of their age.What doctors did not know was whether it was safe to prescribe a daily statin to people aged 70 and over who were healthy overall, having never experienced a heart attack, stroke or heart surgery, and whether doing so could prevent these cardiac events.A co-author of the study, Adjunct Prof Mark Nelson with the Monash University school of public health and preventive medicine, said it was an important piece of missing information, because the biggest risk of major heart-related events “is increasing age”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“Our society is ageing, and therefore the burden of disease is increasing, making it important to improve our ability to prevent disease in this group,” he said. “So we needed the evidence for this group to see if prescribing statins as a prevention measure works.”But Nelson said older adults were often overlooked in early statin research because 40 years ago, heart disease was most common in middle-aged populations especially if they smoked, leading public health efforts to focus on preventing premature deaths in that group. Elderly populations may also be sick and on other medications, making trialling drugs risky, he said.To address the gap, Monash researchers analysed the cardiovascular outcomes of almost 10,000 study participants over the age of 70 who were given either a daily statin or a placebo, in a scientifically-robust type of study known as a randomised control trial. The participants were enrolled with the help of almost 3,400 GPs across Australia.Most statin side-effects not caused by the drugs, study findsRead moreThe researchers excluded people who had a condition that might make taking a statin unsafe, if they were not living independently, or if they already needed the drug because they had suffered a heart attack.The decade-long study found the medication decreased the risk of a first major cardiovascular event by 30% for those aged over 70.In real terms, this means one major cardiac event such as a heart attack, stroke, or heart surgery could be prevented for every 37 older adults treated with daily statins over almost six years.Prof James Chong, a cardiologist at Sydney’s Westmead hospital, said if the research “leads to increased statin use globally, the absolute reduction of (heart-related) events can be significant”.“One of the major changes that may result, in my opinion, is more elderly patients having confidence to take long term statins,” he said.“However, one thing we have to keep in mind is it was an almost exclusively white population with the mean age around 75 years of age, so the results may not be as generalisable globally without further supporting evidence.”The findingswere published in the New England Journal of Medicineon Saturday and presented concurrently at the European Society of Cardiology Congress in Germany.Lead researcher on the paper, Adjunct Prof Sophia Zoungas, said: “What we hope to see, now that we have provided such strong evidence, are updated treatment guidelines to help clinicians make use of this new finding.”Older patients should have a conversation with their GP about whether statins are appropriate to help them stay healthy, the researchers said.Prof Tom Marwick, a cardiologist at Hobart’s Royal hospital, said there had been a lot of misinformation about statins increasing the risk of dementia, making some older people reluctant to take the drugs.A benefit of the Monash study was that the findings “really close the book on that, in large numbers,” he said. The study found no statistically significant difference in dementia rates among those who received a statin and those who did not.Marwick described it as a “well done, really important trial”.But he said the study also found patients were reluctant to adhere to therapy, with more than 15% of patients in the trial discontinuing their medication.Marwick said “a slight disappointment” in the findings was that although major heart events were reduced, the disability-free survival was the same among the participants whether they took the statin or the placebo.In other words, taking the medication didn’t extend life or its quality.“We can reduce cardiovascular events, but the health burdens of ageing are less amenable,” he said.Explore more on these topicsHealthHeart diseasenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ex-White House teleprompter operator fined $172,000 for Trump speech bets | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Commodity Futures Trading Commission said Gabriel Perez wagered on Kalshi about words president used in speeches
Author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
Headline: Commodity Futures Trading Commission said Gabriel Perez wagered on Kalshi about words president used in speeches
Content: Donald Trump delivers his State of the Union address on 24 February 2026, with a teleprompter panel visible to his left.Photograph: Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump delivers his State of the Union address on 24 February 2026, with a teleprompter panel visible to his left.Photograph: Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty ImagesTrump administrationEx-White House teleprompter operator fined $172,000 for Trump speech betsCommodity Futures Trading Commission said Gabriel Perez wagered on Kalshi about words president used in speechesRamon Antonio VargasSat 29 Aug 2026 09.33 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 18.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA White House teleprompter operator wholeft his postamid accusations that he used inside knowledge to make bets onDonald Trump’s speeches on an online prediction market has been fined $172,000, according to federal regulators.Gabriel Perez illicitly exploited “material, nonpublic information” that he gathered through his work for the president in order to place wagers on the Kalshi platform “for his personal benefit”, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) maintained in anews releaseon Friday.The CFTC ordered Perez to both “disgorge the profits he made from his unlawful [conduct]” totaling $107,539.02 and to pay a civil penalty of $65,000, the agency’s news release said. Such amounts represented “a substantial discount”, the CFTC added, attributing that to what the agency called “Perez’s exemplary cooperation” with its investigation into him.‘Inept, incompetent, craven’: Scott Bessent struggles to clean up the president’s messRead moreAccording to the CFTC, from December to February while working as a White House teleprompter operator, Perez made bets on Kalshi tied to words or phrases that Trump might make during his speeches. Perez’s White House role gave him access to those speeches before the president delivered them, and he “misappropriated that information” to profit, breaching “his duty of trust and confidence”, the CFTC asserted.Perez – besides being fined – “agreed to cease and desist from further violations” of federal laws prohibiting market manipulation and CFTC regulations, the CFTC said. He was also handed a three-year trading ban.The CFTC issued its news release about Perez on Friday, about a month after the White House said he no longer had his job there. It was unclear whether Perez resigned or was fired.Yet his departure came after he was reportedly put onunpaid leaveamid an investigation into whether he had used his inside knowledge to win more than $100,000 betting on what Trump would say on big occasions, including his State of the Union address in February. The White House press secretary at the time, Karoline Leavitt, had described the reports of insider trading by Perez as “deeply unfortunate and, frankly, a disgrace”.Perez earned an annual salary of $175,000 for his teleprompter work, according toWhite House personnel records.The case centering on Perez was only the latest to illustrate the continued proliferation of online prediction markets, which allow users to place speculative bets on public events and trends. That has evidently incentivized insider trading.For instance, about four months before Perez’s fine, federal prosecutors indicted US soldier Gannon Ken Van Dyke for allegedly making a $400,000 bet on Kalshi rival platform Polymarket about whether Nicolás Maduro would be removed from Venezuela’s presidency. Van Dyke had worked on the operation to remove Maduro and extradite him to the US on drug-trafficking charges, according to prosecutors.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFurthermore, Kalshi in April alsoannouncedfines against three political candidates who bet on their own elections, including one who wagered on whether he would run for office before announcing an independent campaign for a US Senate seat in Virginia.Trump hasdefendedthe prediction market industry, to which his family has business ties. He has advocated against individual US states regulating those markets and has argued that the CFTC should instead carry out that function.In its news release on Perez’s fine, meanwhile, the CFTC made it a point to thank Kalshi for its “assistance … in this matter”.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationGamblingDonald TrumpUS politicsWashington DCnewsShareReuse this content

title: Artemis II astronauts receive nation's highest space honor for their successful moonshot | Artemis II | The Guardian
description: Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen receive Congressional Space Medal of Honor
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen receive Congressional Space Medal of Honor
Content: From left, Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, Jeremy Hansen and Donald Trump at the Johnson Space Center in Houston on Friday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFrom left, Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, Jeremy Hansen and Donald Trump at the Johnson Space Center in Houston on Friday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesArtemis IIArtemis II astronauts receive nation's highest space honor for their successful moonshotReid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen receive Congressional Space Medal of HonorAssociated PressSat 29 Aug 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 18.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheArtemis IIastronauts who flew around the moon in April received the US’s highest space honor on Friday.Donald Trumppresented the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the three Americans and one Canadian whose lunar flyby for the US space agency Nasa set a new distance record for humanity.Nasa’s administrator, Jared Isaacman, and other dignitaries took part in the packed ceremony atHouston’s Johnson Space Center, home to mission control. The president used the occasion to announce the creation of a US space academy for the nation’s space force as well as Nasa and the commercial space community.Nasa space telescope set to launch after surviving Trump budget cutsRead more“Space is the hot thing,” Trump told the crowd, adding that the academy’s location had yet to be determined.Cmdr Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen, a Canadian, became the first astronauts to travel to the moon in more than half a century, coming within 4,067 miles (6,545km) while test-driving Nasa’s new Orion capsule. They were the first to launch onboard Nasa’s new moon rocket, a 30-story behemoth that had soared only once before from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center.While they didn’t stop at the moon, the four set the stage for next year’s Artemis III docking rehearsal in orbit around Earth. Artemis IV’s moon landing by two astronauts, near the lunar south pole, could follow as soon as 2028.Trump said Americans will land back on the moon before his second presidency ends. Mars is next – “very shortly”, he said.The president called the newest recipients “four intrepid space heroes”. He pointed out that they did not do it alone, thanking all who contributed to the Artemis II mission.“There are no finer humans we could have sent as our ambassadors to the stars,” Isaacman added.Wiseman and his crew are in good company, with only 30 astronauts receiving the prestigious honor before them. Many of the recipients were honored posthumously following their spaceflight-related deaths.Apollo 11 commander Neil Armstrong – whose phrase “that’s one step for man, one giant leap for mankind” gripped the world when he became the first person to walk on the moon on 20 July 1969 – was the first to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor.President Jimmy Carter awarded six of these medals in 1978, which also went to Alan Shepard, the first American in space; John Glenn, the first American in orbit; and Apollo 8 commander Frank Borman, whose 1968 mission marked humanity’s first lunar voyage.The most recent recipients were Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken, the first astronauts to launch aboard a SpaceX rocket. Coming nine years after the space shuttle program’s close, their 2020 test flight to the International Space Station restored the US’s ability to launch crews from home soil. Joe Biden awarded them the medals in 2023, during the third year of his presidency.Dozens of astronauts participated in the ceremony, including Apollo 17 moonwalker Harrison Schmitt, who is now 91 – and the four men assigned to Nasa’s upcoming Artemis III mission.Schmitt noted that his mission – Apollo’s last moonshot – was the most productive lunar exploration yet.“Soon to be surpassed by Artemis,” he said of active astronauts standing behind him.Nasa plans a sustainable moon base staffed by astronauts and robots near the lunar south pole, where permanently shadowed craters are thought to hold tons of frozen water that could be turned into rocket fuel and drinking water. China is eyeing the same region.“The second space race has begun,” Nasa’s deputy administrator, Matthew Anderson, said.As the two-hour ceremony came to a close, the Artemis II astronauts presented Trump with his own blue flight jacket complete with space patches, which they had promised him while visiting him in the Oval Office after their mission.The president then hustled over to mission control to call the three US astronauts onboard the International Space Station. He informed them of the new US space academy, then briefly handed the phone to two of their spouses for a quick hello.Explore more on these topicsArtemis IIDonald TrumpThe moonSpaceHoustonTexasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Exeter University approves deal with Saudi Arabia to train military officers and officials  | University of Exeter | The Guardian
description: In move that could generate millions, Exeter academics to deliver MA at National Defense University in Riyadh
Author: Sally Weale
Headline: In move that could generate millions, Exeter academics to deliver MA at National Defense University in Riyadh
Content: Saudi guards and officials await arriving dignitaries. The masters degree is for senior military officers and government officials.Photograph: The Canadian Press/AlamyView image in fullscreenSaudi guards and officials await arriving dignitaries. The masters degree is for senior military officers and government officials.Photograph: The Canadian Press/AlamyUniversity of ExeterExeter University approves deal with Saudi Arabia to train military officers and officialsIn move that could generate millions, Exeter academics to deliver MA at National Defense University in RiyadhSally WealeEducation correspondentSat 29 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 06.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUniversity of Exeterhas approved plans for a “formal partnership” with Saudi Arabia to train senior military officers and government officials, despite long-held concerns about the Saudi government’s human rights record, the Guardian has learned.In a deal that could generate millions of pounds for the Russell Group university, Exeter academics will deliver an MA in applied security and strategy (also known as an MStrat) to a cohort at the National Defense University (NDU) in Riyadh.The MA will form the academic component of the NDU’s global strategy and strategic leadership programme, starting in 2026-27, and will be delivered to about 20 individuals per year, over three years. Until two years ago, the NDU was called the Saudi Armed Forces Command and Staff College.The Saudi partnership has come to light at a time when the university is under fire from leading writers, broadcasters, academics and other alumni overplans to cut 150 jobs, primarily in the humanities, arts and social sciences, for which the highly ranked university is renowned.The Exeter branch of the University and College Union (UCU) accused university managers of chasing “dirty money”.A UCU spokesperson said: “We are horrified but hardly surprised to learn that management at Exeter are more interested in flogging military training to despotic regimes than in defending world-class humanities and social sciences teaching.”The Exeter deal has not been widely publicised. It was approved by the university council in February this year, then endorsed by its senate the following month. In council minutes, seen by the Guardian, the partnership with the NDU is marked “Strictly confidential and commercial in confidence”.In its marketing material, the university says the MStrat blends “academic depth with practical application”. It is aimed at working professionals in the armed forces, the government and international organisations and “offers a rigorous yet flexible environment in which to build strategic expertise”.UK universities often sell consultancy and training to foreign governments via contracts worth millions of pounds. All such proposals have to be vetted first by university authorities to assess the legal, ethical and security risks of any potential collaboration.Similar concerns were raised earlier this year when theJudge business schoolat the University of Cambridge put forward proposals to provide “leadership development” and “innovation management” to Saudi Arabia’s defence ministry. Senior academics described it as “horrifying” and a betrayal of the university’s commitments to freedom of expression.Last month, the UK government announced the formation of adefence universities alliance– with Exeter among the 35 founding members – to “bring together academia and the armed forces” as part of a £182m investment to strengthen defence research and build critical skills.A spokesperson for Exeter University said: “The MA in applied security and strategy has been taught at Exeter since 2012 through our strategy and security institute. Its students include serving British military personnel sponsored by the Ministry of Defence and Chevening scholars supported by the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.“We are in discussions to deliver this established Exeter programme to a cohort at the National Defense University in Riyadh. Professional military education has formed part of the UK’s defence relationship withSaudi Arabiafor many years, including through UK government institutions.“Partnerships of this kind are assessed on academic and ethical grounds, through a process separate from budget planning.“Like universities across the sector, Exeter continues to develop external partnerships and educational activity that supports our academic mission and enables our expertise to have impact in the UK and internationally.”The UCU spokesperson responded: “Rather than chasing dirty money like this, we believe a university should be about protecting freedom of speech, upholding human rights and ensuring a wide range of brilliant courses and a fantastic student experience.”Explore more on these topicsUniversity of ExeterSaudi ArabianewsShareReuse this content

title: Man, 41, dies after large sign falls at Christian festival in West Sussex | West Sussex | The Guardian
description: Six more people hospitalised after incident at Big Church festival near Steyning
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Six more people hospitalised after incident at Big Church festival near Steyning
Content: The Big Church festival on the Wiston Estate in West Sussex was cancelled after the incident on Friday afternoon.Photograph: bigchurchfestivalView image in fullscreenThe Big Church festival on the Wiston Estate in West Sussex was cancelled after the incident on Friday afternoon.Photograph: bigchurchfestivalWest SussexMan, 41, dies after large sign falls at Christian festival in West SussexSix more people hospitalised after incident at Big Church festival near SteyningNadeem BadshahSat 29 Aug 2026 05.26 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 41-year-old man has died and at least six other people have been injured after a large sign fell at a Christian festival inWest Sussex, police have said.The man, from Eastbourne, East Sussex, was pronounced dead at the scene after the incident at the Big Church festival near Steyning on Friday afternoon.His next of kin have been told and are being supported by specialist officers, Sussex police said. The force added that at least six other people had been taken to hospital for treatment.DCS Richard McDonagh said: “This is a tragic incident and our thoughts go out to the man’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.”Anyone with any information or relevant video footage has been asked to contact police.In a post on Instagram shortly after 5.30pm, organisers told attenders that the show had been cancelled and all day visitors “must leave the site now”.Organisers later said they had decided to cancel the rest of the festival, which had been scheduled to run until Sunday. “We are devastated by the serious incident that took place at Big Church festival 2026 today, in which a sign fell, injuring at least seven people, one of whom tragically lost their life,” the festival said in an online statement.“First and foremost, all of our thoughts are with those who have been affected, their families and friends, and everyone who witnessed what happened.“Following today’s incident, we have made the decision to bring Big Church festival 2026 to a close.”Officers remained at the scene on Friday night and people were advised to avoid the area.The incident has been reported to the Health and Safety Executive and local authority, Sussex police said.McDonagh added: “I recognise the immense distress this will have caused people at the festival, and we are working with a number of partners as we seek to establish exactly what happened.“We know there were thousands of people at the festival and we’re urging anyone with any information, or any relevant video footage, to please come forward.”Explore more on these topicsWest SussexnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tax promises, defence targets and Iran: Andy Burnham’s budget headaches | Budget | The Guardian
description: As economic circumstances worsen, the PM’s commitments have left him and the chancellor in a tight spot
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: As economic circumstances worsen, the PM’s commitments have left him and the chancellor in a tight spot
Content: Andy Burnham and the chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, pictured in Sheffield in July, face many of the same problems as their predecessors.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and the chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, pictured in Sheffield in July, face many of the same problems as their predecessors.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PABudgetTax promises, defence targets and Iran: Andy Burnham’s budget headachesAs economic circumstances worsen, the PM’s commitments have left him and the chancellor in a tight spotJessica ElgotDeputy political editorSat 29 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenAndy Burnhammade his first speech after returning as an MP, he promised that as prime minister he would oversee “the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years”. His style, direction and communication has been a big shift from Keir Starmer’s approach, but as he heads into the autumn, the new prime minister faces some very similar problems.With anearly budget in late October, and worsening economic circumstances, Burnham has made promises and commitments that put him in a tight spot. Here are some of the constraints over the coming months that Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, must contend with in their autumn budget.1.Fiscal rulesThe biggest risk of Burnham as prime minister was always whether he would spook the bond markets and set in train a Liz Truss-style meltdown.Starmer’s allies often played up this fear but there is no doubt that Burnham had to ensure that markets knew he was a serious operator. Gilt yields rose after an interview last year in which he said the government was“in hock to the bond markets”.So, Burnham has committed to Rachel Reeves’s fiscal rules on debt and borrowing, though he has indicated he will “use, obviously, any flexibility within them” where he can borrow to fund further investment.2.Tax promisesBurnham has said he will “stick to the manifesto”, which promises no increases in income tax, national insurance or VAT, though he cautioned in an interview earlier this week that the public needed to be “realistic” about what needed to be funded and how difficult more spending would be.That decision to stick to no rises in personal taxation had left businesses fearing a tax raid – and Burnham has been urged by some leftwing and union leaders to consider further wealth taxes. But the prime minister told the FT this week he was loth to do more to increase the costs of doing business and did not want to target “wealth creators”. With each utterance, the possibilities of revenue raisers become ever narrower.Burnham hinted in the past that he hoped to unfreeze the personal allowance, which would amount to a tax cut, but has recently been more cautious about this because of the costs.3.Economic turmoilReeves left £23.6bn of “headroom” in her last budget, which gives Healey a buffer to meet the fiscal rule of balancing day-to-day spending with receipts.But the Iran war and subsequent rises in inflation and borrowing costs for servicing Britain’s national debt, which is now almost £3tn, are likely to have an effect on that headroom. Treasury sources say the impact may not be as much as feared, but with the strait of Hormuz remaining closed, growth is sluggish and inflation creeping upwards.4.Cost of livingBurnham has made a number of popular early interventions to help ease the cost of living. Some, such as cutting VAT on energy bills, are ostensibly funded by cutting existing programmes such as the digital ID scheme, though, as the former minister Darren Jones pointed out, that was never properly costed in the first place.Healey has suggested there are no further plans to offer energy support at this October price cap, though prices have risen by 4%, wiping out the impact of the VAT cut.The Treasury will want a contingency plan in place in case more help is needed in January – probably a targeted scheme for more vulnerable households. The Resolution Foundation has suggested that even a targeted scheme for those earning under £25k would cost about £2bn.5.Defence targetsThe Treasury confirmed on Friday that it woulddelay setting outwhen the UK would meet the target of spending 3% of GDP on defence, until next year’s spending review.Healey’s budget to duck setting a date for 3% defence spending targetRead moreBurnham would have had to find an additional £4.7bn over five years for defence in October’s budget, after Starmerannounced £15bn extrawhen he published the defence investment plan, without saying where the cash would come from.The remaining £10.3bn will also have to be raised by “reallocating budget” from across government departments.Healeyresigned as defence secretaryin June under Starmer’s leadership, accusing the then prime minister of being “unable” and the Treasury “unwilling” to “commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country”.Labour has committed to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by the middle of the next decade. But there will be endless pressure to go faster, putting more and more of a squeeze on other departmental budgets.6.Public controlBurnham promised he wanted to place life’s essentials “back under public control” – specifically Thames Water. In June, hetold the Guardianhe favoured public ownership for Thames Water, which is struggling with a £20bn debt. One possible solution is to use the forthcoming water bill to change the terms of the special administration regime, but it could still end up in costly legal action.Burnham told the FT recently that he had intentionally spoken in terms of more public control rather than nationalisation, but the budget is his first opportunity to set out a direction of travel that goes beyond local control of bus routes.7.WelfareTwo big reviews will come back this autumn. One is the second part of the Timms review, which will look at a new system to deliver personal independence payments to disabled people, where the bill is increasing substantially.The other is the Milburn review of youth unemployment and inactivity, also likely to require significant spending to try to solve the structural crisis that is costing the economy £125bn annually.Both are highly emotive and fraught with risk, including a potential backlash from Labour MPs.The Telegraph reportedon Thursdaythat Burnham was likely to push the issue of welfare into the new year at the earliest, and would not be attempting to tackle it in the budget.Explore more on these topicsBudgetAndy BurnhamJohn HealeyEconomic policyLabourTax and spendingUK cost of living crisiskey takeawaysShareReuse this content

title: Fire in California’s Big Sur region doubles in size overnight, forcing evacuations | California wildfires | The Guardian
description: Plaskett fire has swept through more than 5,900 acres in Monterey county and remains un-contained, says Cal Fire
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Plaskett fire has swept through more than 5,900 acres in Monterey county and remains un-contained, says Cal Fire
Content: A firefighter moves an injured animal as the Plaskett fire burns towards Highway 1 on Friday, in Big Sur, California.Photograph: Ethan Swope/APView image in fullscreenA firefighter moves an injured animal as the Plaskett fire burns towards Highway 1 on Friday, in Big Sur, California.Photograph: Ethan Swope/APCalifornia wildfiresFire in California’s Big Sur region doubles in size overnight, forcing evacuationsPlaskett fire has swept through more than 5,900 acres in Monterey county and remains un-contained, says Cal FireUwa Ede-OsifoSat 29 Aug 2026 19.51 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 19.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA fire in California’s Big Sur region doubled in size overnight, forcing the evacuation of nearby residents, in a coastal region where firefighters have battled another blaze for weeks.The Plaskett fire, which sparked on Tuesday, had swept through more than 5,900 acres (2,400 hectares) in Monterey county as of Friday, and remained un-contained, according to Cal Fire. Its cause is under investigation.View image in fullscreenFirefighters watch as the Plaskett fire burns toward Highway 1 on Friday.Photograph: Ethan Swope/APFire authorities have deployed helicopters and air tankers to suppress the flames with targeted water drops, but the remote area’s steep terrain and scarce roads have hindered ground crews’ ability to access the fire.Meanwhile, to the north, the Timber fire continues to burn through more than 24,000 acres (9,700 acres), as authorities have it under 21% containment. The blaze broke past certain containment lines.
