Smoke from the fire and cloud cover prevented officials from mapping the fire’s expansion overnight.View image in fullscreenSage Harvey tosses a rope off the roof of his house as the Plaskett fire approaches on Friday in Big Sur, California.Photograph: Ethan Swope/APBoth fires have prompted partial closures of Highway 1, whose Big Sur stretch offers a scenic route between Los Angeles and San Francisco.Explore more on these topicsCalifornia wildfiresCaliforniaWildfiresWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian drone strike on Kyiv warehouse storing weapons kills at least 37  | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian prosecutors open investigation into why munitions were stored so close to residential buildings
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Ukrainian prosecutors open investigation into why munitions were stored so close to residential buildings
Content: Emergency service workers respond to a Russian strike on a warehouse in the town of Myla, near Bucha, in the Kyiv oblast.Photograph: Aleksandr Gusev/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEmergency service workers respond to a Russian strike on a warehouse in the town of Myla, near Bucha, in the Kyiv oblast.Photograph: Aleksandr Gusev/Sopa Images/ShutterstockUkraineRussian drone strike on Kyiv warehouse storing weapons kills at least 37Ukrainian prosecutors open investigation into why munitions were stored so close to residential buildingsDonna FergusonSat 29 Aug 2026 09.34 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 07.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 37 people have been killed after a Russian drone struck a warehouse near Kyiv’s western suburbs that was storing “explosive objects”.The attack damaged at least 50 residential buildings, including a care home for elderly and disabled people, and sparked a huge fire and explosions in the Bucha district of the Kyiv region. The regional governor, Tymur Tkachenko, said a further 42 people, including four children, had been injured in the strike.More than 370 people have been evacuated from the area and the evacuation process was continuing, the Ukrainian president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said. In a statement, he said a warehouse in the town of Myla had been struck, “followed by a detonation”.The warehouse was a depot owned by the Ukrainian military and stored shells, drones and other munitions, he said in a video address. “The first impact was on a place where ammunition was being stored that absolutely should not have been there – a depot of the defence forces. [There was] detonation of shells, mines, other munitions and drones on a significant scale,” Zelenskyy said.Criminal proceedings had been opened on charges of official negligence, he added.“There are regulations in place; ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas.”He said one of the people killed was the head of the Dmytrivka community, Taras Didych, who died while rescuing others.View image in fullscreenSmoke and flames rise from the warehouse after the strike in the Bucha district of the Kyiv region.Photograph: Libkos/GettyUkrainian prosecutors said they had opened an investigation into the legality of the “storage of explosive objects and materials”.The Ukrainian prime minister, Serhii Koretskyi, expressed regret that mistakes had not been learned from aprevious deadly strike on a munitions depot in Vyshneve, near Kyiv, in July.An investigation into that incident, in which 22 people were killed and fires tore through nearby homes, revealed serious failings on the part of a state-owned company, which did not comply with regulations on the proximity of residential buildings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA man walks past destroyed houses after the Russian strike in Bucha.Photograph: Libkos/Getty“Unfortunately, we can already see that the terrible tragedy in Vyshneve did not become a lesson,” Koretskyi said. “In the fifth year of a full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes is criminal negligence. And all those guilty, without exception, must be severely punished so that such situations do not happen again.”In a statement, Russia’s ministry of defence said it had hit a warehouse in Myla storing components and launch boosters for long-range drones. It said it had also attacked the ports of Mykolaiv and Izmail, as well as a logistics centre and warehouse facilities storing parts for Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles in the Kyiv region.Elsewhere, Russian attacks across Ukraine’s southern Kherson region killed two people and wounded 27 more on Saturday, including a child, a local official said.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeVolodymyr ZelenskyynewsShareReuse this content

title: FBI no longer banning all applicants who have had sexual encounters with sex workers | FBI | The Guardian
description: Bureau to still dismiss those with encounters within past 10 years, three or more times or while in public safety capacity
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Bureau to still dismiss those with encounters within past 10 years, three or more times or while in public safety capacity
Content: The FBI has drawn concern about a perceived loosening of recruitment requirements as it seeks to replenish its ranks.Photograph: Douliery Olivier/Abaca/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe FBI has drawn concern about a perceived loosening of recruitment requirements as it seeks to replenish its ranks.Photograph: Douliery Olivier/Abaca/ShutterstockFBIFBI no longer banning all applicants who have had sexual encounters with sex workersBureau to still dismiss those with encounters within past 10 years, three or more times or while in public safety capacityAssociated PressSat 29 Aug 2026 10.17 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 18.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheFBIis dropping a categorical hiring ban on applicants who have had sexual encounters withsex workersand will instead consider in a more holistic manner at least some candidates who have engaged in the practice in the past, according to people familiar with the matter.The move away from an automatic disqualification falls along a continuum of evolving recruitment standards within federal law enforcement and at the buttoned-up bureau, which several years ago relaxed its approach to candidates’ past marijuana use and has drawn more recent concern among some current and former agents about a perceived loosening of recruitment requirements as it seeks to replenish its ranks.The bureau still intends to dismiss applicants who are revealed during the vetting process to have engaged with sex workers within the last 10 years, three or more times overall, or while in a position of trust, such as in a public safety capacity, according to guidance issued this past spring and described by a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to discuss internal decision-making and spoke on condition of anonymity.Man posed as 49ers player to scam women out of $1.3m, FBI saysRead moreFor others, it will allow for consideration of the context of the conduct rather than treat it as grounds for an automatic rejection during the FBI’s hiring process.The practical impact is not immediately clear since many people who have solicited or accepted sex work may still be either immediately disqualified or weeded out upon further scrutiny from FBI polygraphers and security officials.The FBI said the change was meant to account for the fact that some otherwise suitable candidates, including service members, may have engaged in the practice in places where it is legal – and to accommodate applicants who may have done so when they were much younger or have themselves been victims of sexual abuse.“It is false to suggest criminal behavior like this is no longer disqualifying at the FBI. Any applicant who has engaged in criminal sexual acts like those referenced would of course not be eligible for employment, and it is ridiculous to suggest otherwise,” the FBI said in a statement that described the background check process as “wide-ranging and extensive”.“The FBI has and always will maintain some of the highest suitability standards for its applicants and employees in the US government,” the statement added.Even so, the shift is being made at a time when current and former officials worry that the FBI, and the federal justice department more generally, have eased recruitment requirements while facing a mass personnel exodus brought on by retirements, voluntary resignations and firings. The bureau, for instance, has taken steps to make it easier for its own professional staff to become agents and has offered a truncated training academy for applicants from other federal law enforcement agencies.“If they’re moving the bar for sexual encounters to include prostitution, what is that saying about the applicant pool? They’re trying to bring in more people, which to me indicates that the applicant pool is extremely shallow right now,” said Daniel Brunner, a retired FBI agent who spent two decades in the bureau.In 2015, then attorney general Eric Holder issued a memo reiterating that all justice department employees were prohibited from soliciting or accepting sex work, including in places where it was legal. But both before and since that directive, the FBI and other federal law enforcement agencies have confronted periodic episodes in which agents serving abroad have been accused of sexual encounters with sex workers.As recently as the summer of 2025, for instance, the justice department inspector generalsubstantiatedallegations that a supervisory special agent solicited and engaged with sex workers on multiple occasions while overseas and used a bureau-issued cellphone for the transactions.Chris Piehota, a retired top FBI executive, said he would be more troubled if the bureau were to loosen its standards for current employees who require periodic renewals of their security clearances. But he said he could understand the FBI leaning “toward leniency” for actions taken as a teenager or college student.“I don’t think you get a better or worse candidate from something you did in your college years,” Piehota said. “That’s why they have the screening process, that’s why they have the vetting process. And the people who do the recruiting and hiring, they look at all those things.”Applicants to the FBI undergo a multistep application and vetting process that includes, among other things, a background check, a detailed questionnaire, credit checks, interviews with neighbors and colleagues, and a polygraph test. The comprehensive regimen is meant to uncover any prior criminal conduct in an applicant’s past as well as embarrassing personal information that could make an employee vulnerable to blackmail.Felony convictions, domestic violence convictions, failure of a urinalysis and violating the bureau’s drug policies are among factors treated as automatic disqualifiers.Though the new guidance will allow for a broader and more contextual evaluation of applicants who disclose past experience with sex work during their polygraph admission, such an admission has historically been typically regarded as a “death knell” for potential employees at agencies including the FBI, the CIA and the NSA, said Daniel Meyer, a Washington lawyer with the Tully Rinckey law firm who specializes in the background check and the security clearance process.Explore more on these topicsFBISex workTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nasa space telescope set to launch after surviving Trump budget cuts | Nasa | The Guardian
description: Searching for exoplanets and clues on planet formation, the Roman telescope will lift off Sunday morning in Florida
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Searching for exoplanets and clues on planet formation, the Roman telescope will lift off Sunday morning in Florida
Content: The Nancy Grace Roman space telescope is set to join the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes, which were launced in 1990 and 2021, respectively.Photograph: Jolearra Tshiteya/Nasa/APView image in fullscreenThe Nancy Grace Roman space telescope is set to join the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes, which were launced in 1990 and 2021, respectively.Photograph: Jolearra Tshiteya/Nasa/APNasaNasa space telescope set to launch after surviving Trump budget cutsSearching for exoplanets and clues on planet formation, the Roman telescope will lift off Sunday morning in FloridaRichard Luscombein MiamiSat 29 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA $4.3bn space telescope thatDonald Trumptried to kill is set to lift off from Florida early on Sunday as Nasa embarks on the next stage of its quest to unlock the secrets of the universe.The Nancy Grace Roman spacetelescopesurvived two rounds of proposed White House budget cuts, and will embark on a million-mile journey into deep space from a launchpad at the Kennedy Space Center at 7.26am ET, barring late technical issues or intervention from Florida’s notoriously capricious summer weather.Searching chiefly for exoplanets and clues about planetary formation, it is set to join the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes in the annals of Nasa’s storied history of space exploration.But as next-generation equipment almost 10 years in the making, the Roman telescope, named for the space agency’sfirst chief of astronomy, who died in 2018, is many times more powerful than Hubble and will work to enhance the output of its stablemates, both of which continue to operate.View image in fullscreenAstronomer Nancy Grace Roman, Nasa’s first chief of astronomy.Photograph: NASA/APAccording to Nasa, its 300-megapixel infrared camera will give Roman the same sharpness and resolution as Hubble, but with a field of view at least 100 times larger. The agency says each image will capture a patch of sky about 1.5 times bigger than the apparent size of a full moon.Roman also contains a specialized instrument known as a coronagraph that blocks glare from stars and makes it easier to photograph planets around them in detail.Nasa said it expected the images would reveal “giant worlds that are older, colder, and in closer orbits than the hot, young super-Jupiters direct imaging has mainly revealed so far”.Roman’s destination is Lagrange point 2, a “parking spot” in space about one million miles from Earth, where it will operate in the same complex sun-Earth orbit as Webb, though the two telescopes will remain far apart.It is not entirely a successor to Hubble and Webb, which were launched in 1990 and 2021, respectively, but was designed to support and advance their missions, while making discoveries of its own.View image in fullscreenTechnicians connecting the inner and outer segments of Nasa’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on 25 November 2025, at Nasa’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.Photograph: Jolearra Tshiteya/NASA/APNasa said Roman’s large panoramas would “uncover interesting targets that Hubble could follow up on using infrared, visible, and ultraviolet light to offer a more comprehensive view”, while Webb “can then use its larger mirror and more powerful vision to deliver even more detailed, ultra-sharp observations”.Roman, meanwhile, can view regions around objects Hubble or Webb observe “to offer context”. Its imagery, which Nasa expects will first come in early 2027 after months of calibration and tests in the telescope’s final orbit, will be made immediately public, allowing the agency, professional researchers and amateur astronomers an unprecedented opportunity for analysis.“From objects in our outer solar system and exploding stars, to growing black holes and galaxies by the billions, very little will be beyond Roman’s reach,” Nasa said in anonline explanationof the telescope’s initial five-year mission, which could be extended to 10.“Roman will pair a large field of view with crisp infrared vision to scan vast, deep swaths of sky. This flagship mission is designed to help astronomers explore dark matter, dark energy, and planets outside our solar system.”Julie McEnery, Nasa’s senior project scientist for the Roman mission, said the need for it was conceived at the end of the last century, although it was only in 2016 that Nasa began the development stage, and 2020 before it finally approved the entire project and commenced construction.“One of the motivations for Roman was the discovery that our universe is not just expanding, but that expansion is accelerating,” she said inan interview on Thursdaywith Sophia Roberts, an astrophysics video producer at Nasa’s Goddard space flight center in Maryland.“It’s like if you were to throw a ball in the air, and instead of the ball coming back down, it just keeps shooting away. There’s something really fundamental that we don’t understand about the nature of our universe itself, and Roman is purpose-built to address and provide the data that we need to address these questions.”If the US president had his way, Roman would never have made it to the launchpad. A 2025 White House proposal for what analysts said would be “extinction level cuts” to Nasa’s science budget, including the axing of the Roman project, wasroundly rejectedin January by Congress, which restored the agency’s 2026 funding level to $24.4bn.Seemingly undeterred, the Trump administration istrying againfor the 2027 fiscal year, seeking a 23% reduction in Nasa’s overall budget to $18.8bn, and a 46% chop for science projects that thePlanetary Society saidwould lead to the termination of more than 50 missions.Sunday’s scheduled launch of Roman marks the final flight of SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy rocket, which Elon Musk’s company is phasing out along with its smaller Falcon 9 rockets to concentrate onStarship, its versatile new workhorse that is planned to eventually carry humans to Mars.Explore more on these topicsNasaSpaceFloridaDonald TrumpTrump administrationSpaceXAstronomynewsShareReuse this content

title: Sharp rise in incidents of AI escaping users’ control, research finds | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Number of times AI lies, ignores instructions and pursues goals in harmful ways almost doubles in July
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Exclusive: Number of times AI lies, ignores instructions and pursues goals in harmful ways almost doubles in July
Content: The Loss of Control Observatory monitors reports made by AI users on the social media platform X (image shows models posing as computer programmers).Photograph: Posed by models; Maskot/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Loss of Control Observatory monitors reports made by AI users on the social media platform X (image shows models posing as computer programmers).Photograph: Posed by models; Maskot/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Sharp rise in incidents of AI escaping users’ control, research findsExclusive: Number of times AI lies, ignores instructions and pursues goals in harmful ways almost doubles in JulyRobert BoothUK technology editorSat 29 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIncidents of AIs escaping users’ control to lie, ignore instructions and pursue goals in harmful ways have hit a new high, according to research that also suggests the severity of deception and misalignment is worsening.Analysis of real-world loss of control incidents involving AI models flagged by businesses and individuals almost doubled in July compared with June, with more than 300 cases in the month, according to the Loss of Control Observatory, which monitors reports made by AI users on the social media platform X.The observatory was set up with funding from the UK government’s AI Security Institute (AISI) and began tracking AIs slipping free from their users’ instructions last November. Cases recorded since then include AIs pretending to be their own human controller and mimicking their writing style to effectively grant themselves consent to take actions and bypassing rules requiring human approval for actions. A loss of control incident is defined as having clear evidence suggesting scheming or scheming-related behaviours.The latest findings, shared with the Guardian, come after rising concern about rogue behaviour by leading-edge AI models during testing by OpenAI and Anthropic this summer, which have fuelled calls for a pause to the development of frontier models.Itemergedthis week that Open AI staff observed signs of rogue behaviour among its leading-edge AI agents weeks before they escaped a training environment to launch an unprecedented hacking crusade that spread global alarm. An investigation into their hack on Hugging Face, a software repository, revealed a squad of about 700 autonomous agents collaborating in secret last month and celebrating their hacking breakthroughs on a message board they set up to help them plot with exclamations such as BOOM! and Whoa!AISI this month also uncovered a “serious incident” in which advanced AI models produced by both companies – Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol – executed a hacking campaign against real people during a cybersecurity test.“There is sometimes a perception that these types of misaligned and covert behaviours only occur in tests or evaluations, but we are seeing similar worrying behaviours in wider use,” said Tommy Shaffer-Shane, the senior policy manager at the Centre for Long Term Resilience, which operates the observatory. “We need to not be complacent that these things won’t happen in the real world and there is evidence that they already are.”Chart showing loss-of-control incidentsThe count of loss of control incidents relies on X users posting about incidents that happened so it is only partial, but in the absence of other comprehensive public monitoring it provides a snapshot of how fast-advancing AI models sometimes behave.This month it emerged that a personal AI agent, called OpenClaw, in use by an Australian gym member, conspired without his knowledge to remove another member from a waiting list for a coveted morning class to help him get a slot. It apologised but could not reinstate the member it kicked out.Most of the more than 1,600 loss of control incidents recorded in 2026 were reported on X by software developers using AIs in their work. But with AI companies encouraging the public and businesses of all kinds to experiment with the technology, Shaffer-Shane called for greater transparency from Silicon Valley about when AIs go rogue.“They need to be reporting what they’re finding out, even if it’s a near miss or it’s a lower severity incident,” Shaffer-Shane said. “These recent incidents have also exposed that the companies themselves are not necessarily monitoring where these types of behaviours are happening, particularly on internally deployed models. There needs to be greater emphasis at those labs on systematic monitoring.”The Loss of Control Observatory said that while most of the real-world loss of control incidents it detected did not lead to significant harm, a growing proportion were rated higher severity in terms of how deceptive and misaligned they were with the human user’s intentions.“They evidence AI systems’ willingness to disregard direct instructions, circumvent safeguards, lie to users and single-mindedly pursue a goal in harmful ways,” it said, adding the current loss of control was likely to be underestimated since it was only collecting incident reports from X.It is calling on the government to require AI companies to monitor and report severe loss of control incidents and to introduce emergency powers to manage severe loss of control incidents including temporarily restricting AI services.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Winter panic’: EU gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years | Gas | The Guardian
description: As one of Europe’s biggest consumers of gas the UK may be particularly exposed to heightened price volatility
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: As one of Europe’s biggest consumers of gas the UK may be particularly exposed to heightened price volatility
Content: An LNG (liquefied natural gas) tanker from the US arrives at the Isle of Grain, Kent, last year. The UK relies on imports of gas via pipelines from Europe or tankers from the US and Middle East.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/GettyView image in fullscreenAn LNG (liquefied natural gas) tanker from the US arrives at the Isle of Grain, Kent, last year. The UK relies on imports of gas via pipelines from Europe or tankers from the US and Middle East.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/GettyGas‘Winter panic’: EU gas stores at their lowest level in 13 yearsAs one of Europe’s biggest consumers of gas the UK may be particularly exposed to heightened price volatilityJillian AmbroseSat 29 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEurope is on course to enter the cooler months with gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years, which has triggered “winter panic” among energy traders, experts have warned.The EU’s gas stocks were 63% full in the last week of August, well below the 80% average for late August over recent years and among the lowest levels ever recorded for this time of year.At the current sluggish rate of gas storage injections, the EU is likely to enter the winter heating season with gas stocks about a fifth below the five-year average, and at their lowest level since 2013, according to Greg Molnar, a gas analyst and professor.“Low storage levels are naturally increasing the risk of heightened winter price volatility,” he said, which could be made worse by “cold spells or slow wind patterns” increasing gas usage over the winter.The UK may be particularly exposed to market volatility, because it is one of the biggest gas consumers in Europe but has some of the lowest levels of domestic gas storage capacity.Typically, the UK relies on imports of gas via pipeline from Europe or tankers from the US and the Middle East. Chris O’Shea, chief executive of the British Gas ownerCentrica, said this week the UK had “almost no gas in storage” for the coming winter.The EU’s gas stores have struggled to rise towards a watered-down target of 80% full by the start of winter, since the US-Israel war on Iran triggered severe disruption to exports of oil and gas from the Gulf region.graphA cold end to last winter, and higher-than-usual gas power generation during Europe’s heatwaves this summer, have also contributed to the bloc’s depleted gas stores. In a typical year, owners of storage facilities fill them up during the summer when both demand and prices are lower.Europe’s gas market prices have “stayed relatively calm” this summer in the hope that the strait of Hormuz would be reopened and winter stocks could be rebuilt. However, “no one expects it to happen any time soon”, according to Bjarne Schieldrop, chief analyst commodities at the Nordic banking group SEB.“As a result, the European natural gas market has run into a bit of a winter panic over the past week,” Schieldrop added.Although Europe is not expected to experience physical shortages of gas this winter, traders expect higher prices.Benchmark gas price has climbed to three-year highs above €68 per megawatt-hour (MWh) in recent weeks, more than double the price at the start of the year. Prices have risen sharply on the growing expectation that market traders in the EU will need to compete with Asian buyers to secure cargoes of liquefied natural gas as temperatures begin to cool.Without a return of gas exports from the Middle East, Europe’s benchmark price “would likely need to move above €100/MWh” to attract enough shipments of gas to meet winter demand, according to analysts at Goldman Sachs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGas supply concerns are particularly acute in western Europe, where storage levels are well below those in countries such as Italy and Poland, which have managed to top up their gas stores to over 80% full.In Germany, which has Europe’s largest gas storage capacity, facilities are about half-full, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe. Storage levels in Belgium and the Netherlands, which connect directly to the UK gas market via gas pipelines, stand at 51% and 45%.The UK’s reliance on global gas importsis expected to deepenas declining gas production from the UK’s North Sea sector accelerates, and Norwegian output begins to fall from 2030.The government is considering plans to provide direct financial support to safeguard domestic gas infrastructure, after an official consultation found that homes and businessesrisk running out of gas within the next decade, despite its growing clean energy sources.This could include offering financial support to the owners of gas storage facilities and pipeline operators, to make it economically viable to upgrade and maintain them in the decades ahead.The UK energy regulator, Ofgem, said this week that typical gas and electricity bills willrise by 4%from October under its quarterly cap, afterclimbing 13%at the start of July, to take account of global energy market price rises caused by the war on Iran.Explore more on these topicsGasEnergy industryEuropean UnionCentricaCommoditiesEuropeEnergy billsnewsShareReuse this content

title: How to make a bestseller: insiders reveal the tricks of the book trade | Publishing | The Guardian
description: From cover design to shelf placement and influencer partnerships … how publishers will persuade you to buy their books this autumn
Author: John Self
Headline: From cover design to shelf placement and influencer partnerships … how publishers will persuade you to buy their books this autumn
Content: Illustration: Giacomo Gambineri/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Giacomo Gambineri/The GuardianPublishingHow to make a bestseller: insiders reveal the tricks of the book tradeFrom cover design to shelf placement and influencer partnerships … how publishers will persuade you to buy their books this autumnJohn SelfSat 29 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTShareThink about the last book you bought. How did you choose it? Was it from a recommendation, a review, aTikTokvideo? Did the cover grab you, were you swayed by the quotes on the front, or did you just happen to spot it on an appealing table as you walked into the shop? Did you think about all the nudges that led you to that decision – by the publisher, the bookseller or that person you follow on Insta?The reality is that our reading choices are directed and massaged at every turn. “It’s all about the art of persuasion,” says Philip Gwyn Jones, who was a publisher for more than 30 years and is now a literary agent. And who are the persuaders? They’re the booksellers, the supermarket stock buyers, the publishing houses and their ranks of marketers and publicists. And, more recently, persuasion often comes from BookTokers and online influencers, social media videos, podcasts and Instagram posts. How is all this changing publishing?We all judge books to some extent by their covers, but did you know how much thought goes into finding just the right cover, colour, font and design? These covers are focus-grouped, shown to supermarket buyers and often changed at their behest, according to Jamie Keenan, one of Britain’s leading book designers. “That happens quite a lot,” he says. “If Tesco with commercial books, or Waterstones with literary stuff, don’t like it, they’ve got a tremendous amount of clout.” (Waterstones and Tesco declined to speak to me for this piece.)Meanwhile, online browsing and buying have brought about big changes. “There’s been a move towards more iconic book covers because of thumbnail images [on apps and websites],” Keenan explains. “One very simple emblem or logo that you can see from a distance, even when it’s two inches tall. Nice bright colours and big type,” he adds. “That’s what publishers are doing to attract people’s attention.”It’s true: when I went into Waterstones last week, I felt like reaching for my sunglasses to shield the glare of garish, saturated colours screaming from the fiction shelves: more sweet shop than book store. When I shared a photo on Instagram, a number of authors messaged me. “I hate it,” said one (whose own latest novel has a brightly coloured cover). “It’s just so brash.” Yet ironically, because all these books look the same, the effect is to make them blend in, not stand out. “Jewel tones have the industry in a headlock,” messaged another.And then there are the increasing numbers of copycat covers, so that every cosy crime novel suddenly looks like Richard Osman’s bestsellers – cream background, coloured border, hand-lettering – and all heartwarming Japanese books have to feature a cat. (At his last publishing house, says Gwyn Jones, for Japanese fiction “there was this unspoken imperative to put a cat on the cover even if there wasn’t a major role for a cat in the book. It did seem to make a difference.”) “You quite often get briefs on what are called comparable titles,” Keenan says. “That’s a nod-and-a-wink way of saying, ‘Can you do something that looks a bit like these three?’”View image in fullscreenIllustration: Giacomo Gambineri/The GuardianAfter the cover does its trick, we read the publisher’s description on the back. That’s the work of copywriters. “The cover designer has got them to pick up the book,” says a copywriter for a major commercial publisher. “It’s my job to make sure they don’t put it down again.”The blurb is how we decide if this book is one for us. “You’ve got seconds to grab people,” says the copywriter. One of their tricks is to use Christopher Booker’s bookThe Seven Basic Plots. “Most stories can fit into three or four of Booker’s categories: The Quest, Overcoming the Monster and so on. It gives you tools to tell the story of the book in different ways. You want to say: ‘It’s the same but different.’”What if an author isn’t writing what’s on trend right now? “For the best part of two decades,” the copywriter says, “we had Scandi noir: very dark, psychological thrillers. Now cosy crime is absolutely everything. If a writer is still writing noir and wants their books to be in the supermarkets, it needs to look like the books that are selling in supermarkets.” That means “you’ll find books being packaged rather differently to how they [really] are”. These cosy crime blurbs need to, frankly, make death and violence sound like a minor inconvenience, so they focus on the mystery aspect (the books are “ingenious”, full of “twists and turns”) or the welcoming narrative tone (“delicious’” and “delightful”) or the sense of tradition they follow as “quintessentially British” stories. But “publishers are lemmings,” the copywriter says, “and that’s where the market is.”“There has been a sense since the mid-2000s that popular fiction readers’ tastes have narrowed,” they continue, “following one or two big trends. That parallels [the rise of] social media. Romantasy and cosy crime are the main areas of current growth.”Whatever the genre, “a blurb has to tell a little story,” says Louise Willder, another copywriter, and author of a book on the subject,Blurb Your Enthusiasm. But, “we’re aware not every word we write will get read.” That’s because, explains the commercial copywriter, “People read in an ‘F’ [shape] – they’ll read across the top and then they won’t read the next line, they’ll just drop down to the next paragraph. So you’re trying to hit your marks at the start of each paragraph.” Cliches have always been rampant, they just shift with time. So “witty” becomes “whip-smart”. “It’s never ‘moving’, it has to be ‘deeply moving’,” says Willder.Publishers’ blurbs aren’t the only thing on book covers; they are also clogged with endorsements from fellow authors. According to Willder, “audiences say they’re mistrustful” of these. There’s a sense that they are favours for friends – which may be justified. When it comes to quotes, “networking is crucial” confirms the commercial copywriter. “I’ll try to get two or three endorsements from my circles, or the author’s circles,” adds Gwyn Jones.Author endorsements are, in any event, more often aimed at booksellers than readers. Even though many books are now sold online, the visibility of books in shops remains crucial to their success. Although some names may offer more effective badging than others – certain authors “seem to pop up on every single book”, says Brett Wolstencroft, manager at independent chain Daunt Books. “Stephen King has endorsed so many people,” says the commercial copywriter. “Tony Parsons is another culprit.”Not all booksellers need to be persuaded, it should be said – some need to be paid. One experienced publicist I spoke to said: “To get books into supermarkets, you have to pay quite a lot of money. The general public thinks that those top 10s are earned positions and they are very much not earned positions. They’re paid for.” This practice used to be widespread. TG Jones, formerly WH Smith, also charged publishers for chart space,according to a 2022 BBC report, though the chain said that sales performance was also a factor. And in the time before James Daunt took over, Waterstones charged publishers to put their books on display tables. But now, one Waterstones bookseller tells me, “everything is down to individual booksellers”.Publishers send out early copies of books to booksellers, because if they read and like them, they can kickstart a book’s success. Books need advocates, and booksellers are among the finest. Wolstencroft tells me that “the public trust us [as booksellers] because they know we really have read these books, we really do like them, we’re not driven by the tricks of the publisher.”View image in fullscreenIllustration: Giacomo Gambineri/The GuardianBut what about the tricks of the bookseller? Three of the four window displays in Daunt’s Marylebone branch are each focused on one title. “People have a very limited attention span,” Wolstencroft says. “Give them a wall of different books and they’ll move on quite quickly.”Conversations with customers – hand-selling books – are crucial, because “they’re not just talking to one person, but to 30, 40 people around them in the shop. And the business of hearing a book recommended is incredibly powerful,” Wolstencroft adds. “Three or four people will come to the till in the next five minutes with that book.”In many bookshops, a surrogate for hand-selling books are the cards attached to shelves praising particular books – shelf talkers, as they’re known. The Waterstones bookseller tells me that these “go a long way if they read sincerely. If they’re short and just say ‘I love this book’ or ‘It really made me cry’, that will work almost 100% of the time. One that doesn’t feel emotional will never work.” Waterstones, however, has a “standard that there have to be three review cards per bay [of shelves], so sometimes you have to churn them out to fill the bay. And if nobody [in the shop] has read it, you just steal something off Goodreads.” Those cards, they admit, “are less successful”.“Enthusiasm is the thing that sells,” the bookseller tells me. “People often ask for recommendations and you’re supposed to go for the [Waterstones] book of the month, [but] I like to recommend things I actually want people to read.”Smaller independent bookshops can manage personal recommendations via tailored book subscription services. “I don’t really use the word subscription,” says David Headley, who runs Goldsboro Books in London and Brighton. “We call it a book club, with members rather than subscribers.”Goldsboro has four book clubs, each sending out a new work of fiction in an exclusive edition to its members every month, including clubs for fantasy (with 2,000 members) and a recently launched club for debut fiction, with almost 500 members. Numbers like these give Goldsboro’s clubs tremendous clout. Being chosen for one of them – Headley picks the books himself – “can get you into the top 10 bestsellers”, he tells me.How does he choose the books? “I go into publishers every six months and they pitch their books that are coming out.” But the final choice is Headley’s, and publishers don’t contribute to the cost. “We pay for everything, so if I buy 2,000 books, I have to sell them.”Headley is also a literary agent, and several of his own client authors have appeared as Goldsboro book club choices. How does that work? “Not every author gets that privilege,” he says. “I don’t ever take on a client and promise them that. But if I really love the book and think people should read it, then I’ll choose it.”What publishers are always chasing is the elusive word-of-mouth recommendation, an artificial version of a trusted friend pressing a favourite new book on you. That’s what can be provided by booksellers and, increasingly, online influencers, on platforms such as TikTok and YouTube. “Influencers are important because they talk to a community and they’re trusted by the community,” says Lee Dibble, digital marketing director at Pan Macmillan. “Jack Edwards [who has 1.6 million followers on YouTube and 1.2 million on Instagram] or Dua Lipa can create huge interest from nowhere,” adds Gwyn Jones. See, for example, how Edwardsput a rocket under Fyodor Dostoevskyin 2024, helping the obscure novella White Nights shift more than 100,000 copies.How do publishers persuade influencers to cover their books? “You might gather influencers round a restaurant table,” says Gwyn Jones. For books that publishers have spent a lot of money on, the process begins early. “Big dinners a year and a half ahead of publication,” a publicist tells me. “If it’s a debut they’ll invite [the debut author] alongside lots of established names to draw the [influencers] in.”“You’re trying to buy their favour,” says Gwyn Jones of the influencers. In some cases, the buying is literal: “There are some BookTokers who expect to get paid to review books,” says the publicist. “It feels like you’re breaking some sort of contract there.” It is not, they add, about securing a positive review. “It’s more that it’s so competitive, some people think they can charge just to cover your book.”This is separate from paid partnerships, where, as Dibble puts it, “they have to make it really clear they’ve been paid for that work” and “there might be a brief where there’s a couple of messages [the publisher] wants to get across, but it’s completely up to them how they talk about it”.It’s arguable, however, that any paid advert by an influencer muddies the waters of that crucial trust relationship with their community. “The whole thing of it being a common endeavour sort of dies the minute you start charging for your services,” says Gwyn Jones. Search Instagram or TikTok for “books” and “ad” and you’ll find numerous book influencers with text such as: “my fave author has a new book out and it is one of her best” or “this series felt like three arrows in the chest”. If they’re being paid to post this, how can their followers be sure it’s a sincerely held opinion?Publicists are the publisher’s frontline in seeking to secure attention for their books, but even this has changed in the digital age. “There’s an old adage where you have to see [the book] seven times before you buy it, so you’re trying to cover as many bases as you can,” the publicist tells me. As well as space in traditional media, this means social media (“a huge part” of publicity now) and new media. “If you can get an author on a really big podcast, that book can go to number one,” the publicist says. And “the big podcasts for books aren’t podcasts about books – The News Agents, Fearne Cotton’s Happy Place, or Davina McCall. You’re trying to pull out the lifestyle angles.”Some traditions persist: “I stand by the fact,” the publicist tells me, “that there is no such thing as bad publicity. When there was all the controversy over The Salt Path, sales actually went up.”There are areas that remain largely out of publishers’ control, such as Amazon. But they do have some techniques. Publishers now usually add subtitles to a book on Amazon (“For readers of Sally Rooney”) to try to draw stray web searches. They also tag books with keywords. But it only goes so far. “You won’t show up next to Richard Osman by mentioning him 100 times in the metadata,” Dibble says.If you’ve ever wondered why your favourite author is constantly urging you on social media to pre-order their new book, it’s because “the impact of Amazon rankings is huge”, the publicist tells me. “Preordering can have the biggest impact, and then it’s much easier to stay [in the charts] because it’s a snowball effect.” And where once search engine optimisation (SEO) was the big thing, now it’s GEO – generative engine optimisation, or “making sure our books are discoverable by chat bots”, Dibble says. So how do you court ChatGPT or Claude? It’s an evolving science, she says, but “you can format your content in particular ways that bots like, such as author Q&As or listicles”.Are prizes still important? “Definitely, absolutely,” says Philip Gwyn Jones. “You’ve got to make choices and prizes help people make choices.” It is, of course, not possible to sway prize juries, but there are other tools available. “You think about the kind of people who get put on prize juries and review regularly and you send the book to them,” says Gwyn Jones. You decide, as a publisher, which books to submit: “an exercise in diplomacy, as you can imagine … A publisher’s responsibility is to manage it in such a way that it doesn’t cause any outlandish hissy fits.”“Those meetings can get really heated,” agrees the publicist, who adds that another tool in their armoury is to “strategically publish books so they tie in with eligibility periods for book prizes”.But what came across time and again from the people I spoke to is how authenticity is key. “It’s not like Quaker Oats,” says one publicist. “You’ve got to be passionate.” “I would only pitch things that are genuinely good,” says another. “Trust is the important thing,” David Headley adds.All of these techniques can help to give a book a leg up, but nothing guarantees success even then. “We’re always quoting [screenwriter] William Goldman,” says Louise Willder. “‘Nobody knows anything.’” In the end, as readers and browsers, despite all the nudges and cajolery and the tricks of the trade, the final decision really is ours.

title: The best music of autumn 2026: Johnny Marr, Phoebe Bridgers, Rachel Chinouriri and more | Culture | The Guardian
description: Irish noisemongers Gilla Band, shadowy producers Two Shell and lovable band the Big Moon have new records, and there are tours from Bob Dylan and Kelela – plus the best of jazz, global and classical
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Irish noisemongers Gilla Band, shadowy producers Two Shell and lovable band the Big Moon have new records, and there are tours from Bob Dylan and Kelela – plus the best of jazz, global and classical
Content: Unbiddable … Kehlani and Noah Kahan.Composite: Guardian Design/Kaio Cesar/Patrick McCormackView image in fullscreenUnbiddable … Kehlani and Noah Kahan.Composite: Guardian Design/Kaio Cesar/Patrick McCormackAutumn arts preview 2026CultureThe best music of autumn 2026: Johnny Marr, Phoebe Bridgers, Rachel Chinouriri and moreIrish noisemongers Gilla Band, shadowy producers Two Shell and lovable band the Big Moon have new records, and there are tours from Bob Dylan and Kelela – plus the best of jazz, global and classical‘It’s easier when nobody’s watching’: inside the secretive and sublime freak-folk of @See all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations herePop picks byAlexis Petridis. Global and jazz picksAmmar KaliaandJohn Fordham. Classical picksFlora WillsonSat 29 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 04.44 EDTSharePop, rock and moreGilla Band – PugnelloIt’s tempting to say that Ireland’s Gilla Band have quietly become one of the most innovative alt-rock bands around, but there’s absolutely nothing quiet about their music, which owes as much to extreme avant garde electronics as it does to punk. The two singles thus far released from Pugnello display no letup in the intensity of their approach:Placeholdermight have been shoutier thanGiraffe, but both deal in thrillingly intense sonics.Released 25 SeptemberJohnny Marr – The Age of EverythingThe former Smiths guitarist’s fifth solo album arrives hot on the heels of his appearance atGorillaz’s lauded shows at Tottenham Hotspur’s ground. For a musician who once seemed an eternal sideman, Marr has made an impressive fist of his solo career: Top 10 albums, gigs bolstered by his willingness to sprinkle Smiths classics throughout. If the wheel is unlikely to be reinvented on The Age of Everything, he remains a rich and purposeful songwriter.Released 2 OctoberTwo Shell – Infinite NowTheLondon electronic duoclearly prize their anonymity, or at least their ability to wrongfoot their audience: they’ve sent decoys to interviews and to DJ for Boiler Room; their last album, a remix collection, appeared for sale online then vanished without trace or explanation. This is diverting, but it’s ultimately the music that matters – and the four tracks already available from Infinite Now are brightly hued pop-dance that’s also somehow deeply weird, even unsettling. It’s a unique and fascinating space.Released 16 OctoberView image in fullscreenEagerly awaited … Rachel Chinouriri.Photograph: Yana Van NuffelRachel Chinouriri – I Think I Spoke Too SoonThe Guardian recently called Chinouriri“every pop star’s favourite UK pop star”: Sabrina Carpenter, Gracie Abrams, Olivia Rodrigo, Florence + the Machine and Wolf Alice have all selected her as a support act, a testament not just to the fact that she’s one of the few high-profile Black British female artists in alt-rock, but to the quality of what she does. Her second album, more synth-focused than her guitar-heavy debut, is understandably eagerly awaited.Released 16 October‘It’s easier when nobody’s watching’: inside the secretive and sublime freak-folk of @Read moreJ ColeLike Kendrick Lamar, J Cole is a 21st-century rapper deeply rooted – both stylistically and thematically – in the genre’s past. He audibly prizes technical virtuosity as both a lyricist and MC and his most recent releases have been steeped in hip-hop history; he even promoted this year’s The Fall-Off by touring the US in a Honda Civic, selling CDs from the boot. Rumours abound that it is to be his last album: he’s worth catching live now, on the off-chance they’re right.Tour begins 19 October,O2 Arena, LondonEzra FurmanFurman’s most recent album, Goodbye Small Head, set unflinching self-examination to music that sounded like heartland US rock in the process of falling to pieces: a set of fantastic songs bolstered by a hint of chaos. A similar raucousness attends her live shows: she’s a sharp, funny, self-deprecating and genuinely charismatic presence, as anyone who’s heard her too-infrequent presence as a guest presenter on BBC Radio 6 Music can attest.Tour begins 20 October,Cottiers theatre, GlasgowView image in fullscreen‘Scrappily exuberant’ … The Big Moon.The Big Moon – ForeverLondon indie quartet the Big Moon are not a band that deals much in flash: their following is based on really good songs, and possibly the sense that they’re growing up alongside their audience. Debut albumLove in the 4th Dimensionwas a scrappily exuberant celebration of youth; almost a decade later, the first single from Forever,Gravity, deals with picking up your child from nursery. It is, typically, excellent.Released 30 OctoberKelelaKelela set up camp in the far left field of R&B long ago. It’s 13 years since her debut mixtape Cut 4 Me, long enough for her to become an inspiration to a new generation of artists: there’s something telling about the fact that her recent album New Avatar featured acollaboration with PinkPantheress. Its sound is as unique and out-there as ever: jazz, shoegaze, goth-rock, funk, neo-soul and electronica are all part of its exciting stew.Tour begins 4 November,O2 Academy Brixton, LondonNoah KahanBy far the most likable and gifted of the current crop of sad-boy acoustic troubadours – his autumn-hued music sounds like it has substantially more dirt under its fingernails than that of his peers – Kahan has neatly sidestepped the problem of having a huge hit that could, theoretically, overshadow everything else he does.Stick Seasonmay have racked up nearly two billion streams on Spotify, but his recent albumThe Great Dividehas remained stubbornly lodged around the Top 10 since release.Tour begins 5 November,OVO Hydro, GlasgowBob DylanYou might have thought Dylan’s2024 shows at the Royal Albert Hallcarried a sense of farewell about them – an octogenarian artist adding a distinctly elegiac air to his renditions of It’s All Over Now, Baby Blue and Watching the River Flow. But it would appear that was a misinterpretation: two years on, the never-ending tour is still in full swing, and this particular leg of it takes in afive-night residency at the Royal Festival Hall.Tour begins 25 November,BIC, BournemouthView image in fullscreenHotly anticipated … Phoebe Bridgers.Photograph: Frank OckenfelsPhoebe BridgersPhoebe Bridgers’ return as a solo artist – six years after her wildly acclaimed albumPunisher– is understandably hotly anticipated: in the interim, her indie supergroupBoygeniuswon three Grammys, and she’s guested with everyone from post-punk band Shame to SZA. Her new album,Lost Weekend, has proved worth the wait: another set of heart-rending songs, haunted by the death of her father among other things, this time given a striking electronic makeover.Tour begins 26 November,Co-op Live, ManchesterEsDeeKidNever let it be said that pop is predictable: before the arrival of EsDeeKid, who would have thought that a white rapper with a scouse accent wouldbreak the US, not a country much given to importing hip-hop artists from overseas? But his mixtape Rebel made the US Top 30; propelled by a deeply unexpected remix featuring actor Timothée Chalamet, so did the single4 Raws. It would seem like a novelty but for the fact that EsDeeKid is really good at what he does, turning his accent to advantage as he rips through tales of snotty hedonism.Tour begins 3 December,Ovo Arena Wembley, LondonHorsegiirLAs any fan of the musical Gypsy will tell you, You Gotta Get a Gimmick – and Berlin-based DJ/singer-songwriterHorsegiirL’s is more striking than most: she performs wearing a horse head mask, refuses to reveal her real identity and refers to her fans as “farmies”. It sounds stupid – itisstupid – but her debut album Nature Is Healing is genuinely great: electropop, hyperpop and a dash of new age pastiche to silence the neigh-sayers. And, one assumes, her live show is pretty visually diverting.4 December,O2 Academy Brixton, LondonView image in fullscreenSilencing the neigh-sayers … HorsegiirL.Photograph: Alex LockettMane character energy: part-nag pop provocateur HorsegiirL on burnout, eco tunes and pompous idiot DJsRead moreKehlaniBy any metric, Kehlani has enjoyed an intriguing career: an attempt at TV talent show fame with the band PopLyfe; a period reduced to shoplifting to support themself; reinvention as an acclaimed R&B star, hugely commercially successful and impressively unbiddable. The intro to their recent eponymous album announced they had “no fear, no filter and no apologies”. What they do have is killer tunes in abundance.Tour begins 8 December,O2 Arena, LondonSex Pistols feat Frank CarterIt could – and possibly should – have been a disaster: replacing the most unique and iconic frontman in punk history is no small ask. And yet, the gigs the Sex Pistols have played with Carter on vocals have been rapturously received: perhaps because the former Gallows singer makes no attempt to imitate Johnny Rotten’s characteristic vocal style; perhaps because the songs from Never Mind the Bollocks are so good, they can handle reinterpretation.Tour begins 9 December,Edinburgh Corn ExchangeGlobalSoumik Datta – Melodies in Slow MotionSoumik Datta, maestro of Indian classical stringed instrument the sarod, releases his nature-inspired latest album, Melodies in Slow Motion. Developed during an eight-month journey across India where Datta compiled field recordings and workshopped music in local arts spaces, the resulting album mimics the frenzied dance of honeybees through polyrhythmic percussion on Waggle Dance, as well as featuring whispering field recordings on Mangroves and intricately overlaid sarod melodies on the classical harmonics of Fireflies. A masterclass in folk fusion.Released 21 OctoberAmmar KaliaManchester Collective –ConstellationsView image in fullscreenComposer Nwando Ebizie and percussionist Sidiki Dembélé in Constellations.Photograph: Mike SkeltonThis genre-spanning tour from theManchester Collectivestring ensemble features guest performances and new works from west African griot percussionist Sidiki Dembélé and British folk violinist Rakhi Singh. An interpretation of Henry Purcell’s 17th-century baroque score for the comedic play The Old Bachelor is also programmed alongside the premiere of an Afrofuturist opera by composer Nwando Ebizie that seeks to draw the rhythmic connections between west Africa, the Caribbean and the Americas.AKTour 2-10 OctoberJazzEFG London jazz festivalThe biggest event in the UK jazz calendar for more than three decades, the EFG London jazz festival returns for 10 days in November running A-list and new-talent gigs across the city. American vocal starsLizz Wrightand Melody Gardot, Cuban piano firebrandRoberto Fonseca, global-jazz trumpeterIbrahim Maaloufand east London new-talent spotters Church of Sound are on a huge bill – while cross-genre vocal gala Jazz Voice returns as the festival’s ever-popular opener.Various venues, London, 13-22 NovemberJohn FordhamBranford Marsalis and Dianne Reeves – Dedicated to YouMarking 100 years since the birth of boundary-breaking saxophonistJohn Coltrane, saxophonistBranford Marsalisand singer Dianne Reeves pay tribute to the jazz master by tackling one of his most popular works, the 1963 vocal duet album John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman. Supplanting Hartman’s resonant baritone for Reeves’s tender melodics and Coltrane’s supple lines for a more lively energy, Dedicated to You manages to find new ground in this decades-old selection of standards.Released 18 SeptemberAKClassicalLammermuir festivalView image in fullscreenPianist Jeremy Denk performs six Mozart concertos at the festival.Photograph: Robin MitchellFeaturing more than 450 artists in almost a fortnight of performances, this ever-ambitious rural festival spans opera, chamber music, song, folk music, choral works and orchestral favourites. Highlights this year include a residency from acclaimed US pianist Jeremy Denk, who performs six Mozart piano concertos across three concerts with the Royal Northern Sinfonia – and an unprecedented opportunity to hear 100 tuba players in the UK premiere of Anthony Braxton’s Composition No 19.Venues across East Lothian, 8-20 SeptemberPygmalion and Raphaël Pichon perform MozartThe French period-performance outfit acclaimed for its fresh, fiercely creative interpretations of centuries-old repertory returns to London in its 20th anniversary year. The choir and orchestra are joined by soloists including celebrated French soprano Sabine Devieilhe and must-see British baritone Huw Montague-Rendall for a programme focused on the vital musical legacy of the Baroque era. Mozart’s Great Mass in C Major takes centre-stage, alongside choral works by Bruckner, Mendelssohn and Schubert.Barbican Hall, London, 9 NovemberPerle Noire: Meditations for JoséphineView image in fullscreenJulia Bullock as Josephine Baker in Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine.Photograph: Ruth WalzHow best to celebrate the boundary-smashing 20th-century artist and activistJosephine Baker? In a performance that refuses to be pigeonholed, of course. Directed by Peter Sellars and featuring Grammy-winning US soprano Julia Bullock as Baker, this event – part-opera, part-song cycle, with nods to jazz, spirituals and music hall – sees Baker’s songs reimagined by composer and multi-instrumentalistTyshawn Sorey, with spoken interludes from the genre-bending poetClaudia Rankine.Barbican Hall, London, 20 OctoberBritten’s War RequiemCommissioned for the reconsecration of Coventry Cathedral, which had been badly bombed in 1940, Britten’s response to the second world war was premiered by soloists from the UK, Germany and Russia – across the conflict’s divide. In this performance marking 50 years since the pacifist composer’s death, Russian soprano Irina Lungu, British tenor Andrew Staples and German baritone Christian Gerhaher star alongside the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra and vast choral forces. Kazuki Yamada conducts.Coventry Cathedral, Coventry, 11 NovemberKaija Saariaho’s Adriana MaterView image in fullscreenThe Finnish composer Kaija Saariaho, who died in 2023.Photograph: Emmi Korhonen/Lehtikuva/AFP/Getty ImagesThree years since her death, this 2006 opera by the great Finnish composer receives its first full staging in the UK. Drawing on Saariaho’s experiences of motherhood and librettistAmin Maalouf’s work as a war correspondent, the opera is performed by English National Opera in a new English translation and is the first collaboration between ENO’s artistic director Annilese Miskimmon and incoming music director André de Ridder.Coliseum, London, 28 November-12 December

title: ‘It’s easier when nobody’s watching’: inside the secretive and sublime freak-folk of @ | Music | The Guardian
description: Their un-Googlable, very online name is the antithesis of this earthy duo’s sublime art-folk. Like their emotionally ambiguous music, the pair don’t give up their mysteries easily
Author: Quinn Moreland
Headline: Their un-Googlable, very online name is the antithesis of this earthy duo’s sublime art-folk. Like their emotionally ambiguous music, the pair don’t give up their mysteries easily
Content: Victoria Rose and Stone Rosenberg, AKA @.Photograph: Ingmar ChenView image in fullscreenVictoria Rose and Stone Rosenberg, AKA @.Photograph: Ingmar ChenAutumn arts preview 2026MusicInterview‘It’s easier when nobody’s watching’: inside the secretive and sublime freak-folk of @Quinn MorelandTheir un-Googlable, very online name is the antithesis of this earthy duo’s sublime art-folk. Like their emotionally ambiguous music, the pair don’t give up their mysteries easilyThe best music of autumn 2026: Johnny Marr, Phoebe Bridgers, Rachel Chinouriri and moreSee all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations hereSat 29 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVictoria Rose arrives at Philadelphia’s 30th St Station and apologises for the sticky streaks covering her car’s interior. She’s a beekeeper, and it’s just propolis, a resinous sealant for gaps in the hive. Her bandmate, Stone Filipczak, is riding shotgun, and her protective gear occupies the rear passenger seat. We’re heading to one of their favourite spots, an Ethiopian restaurant that doubles as a venue. The dining room quickly gets boisterous – a challenge for our interview given that Filipczak and Rose are relatively soft speakers, and not wildly keen to divulge specifics about the music they make as @. Like Rose’s bees, they’re a secretive and self-sustaining pair.As you might guess, @ is pronounced “at”. It’s a tough Google. The name, Filipczak explains, came from “a vision of an @ sign on a kick drum head”. Not that they have any need for one: @’s art-folk is rooted in acoustic guitar, woodwinds and vocal harmonies that furrow and frolic. Their fantastic second album, Autosmile, is their first with the venerated indie label 4AD. (The name is a reference to amemeshowing a dopey sunflower: “When you and gang faded and auto smile gets turn on …”)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ingmar ChenRose offers a concise summary of Autosmile’s themes: “Turmoil, processing and acceptance.” They don’t always know the context behind each other’s songs, either. “We’re close enough friends that we can infer,” Filipczak says. “It’s better if we give each other a little bit of space and don’t crawl up each other’s asses around every lyric.” It’s an album open to the possibility that darkness can always be tinged with light or levity.Punish My Mind is about the ouroboros of discipline and pleasure, but comes down on the side of play thanks to a recurring sample of a shrieking primate.The duo met while living in Boston, where both had moved to attend college, though Filipczak quickly dropped out. Each was active in the city’s DIY scene: Rose was making solo acoustic music asBrittle Brian, while Filipczak hailed from noise and experimental scenes. They were introduced through mutual friends. “We went to the Harvard Museum of Natural History to look at the taxidermied animals,” Rose recalls of their first hang. “I was a little nervous to talk to you because you werereallylooking at everything,” she tells Filipczak.He had run there, wearing leggings covered in lightning bolts. “It’s so to my taste,” he says. “Dead animals and stuff – that’s the type of museum that would hold my interest, looking at actual, real things.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caity ArthurThey fell out of touch when Filipczak returned to his native Baltimore in 2017. He remained there during lockdown, passing the days skateboarding and recording music. Rose was still in Boston, working at a farm with plenty of time to spare. They reconnected and began sharing works-in-progress material. Rose wondered if Filipczak could add some soft drums to one of her songs. The song became Star Game, and the start of the long-distance collaboration behind their beguiling 2021 debut, Mind Palace Music.“Messing around” led them to a gently strange, freak-fried folk sound evoking Animal Collective’s 2005 EP with Vashti Bunyan, the music of Linda Perhacs or maybe Zelda’s Ocarina of Time set in the Shire. The record had become a sleeper favourite among indie fans by the time @ played their first show in 2022. Representatives from the Washington DC indie label Carpark were in attendance, and reissued Mind Palace Music the next year. “We were like: ‘All right, I guess this is a band now’,” says Filipczak.Both bandmates lived in Philadelphia while making Autosmile, but they still wrote and recorded separately from home. “Various people tried to ply us with studio time,” Filipczak says. “It didn’t work.” Their setups are simple, and each appreciates the time, space and privacy. “It’s easier to get something to where you want it to be when nobody’s watching you,” Rose says, “and that includes Stone.” The pair convened at Filipczak’s to add final touches, and local peersNina Ryserand Garrett Burke (Gloorp) contributed to several songs.While their 2024 EP, Are You There God? It’s Me, @ was proggy and processed,Autosmile is an acoustic guitar record in the vein of their debut. It’s enchanting, unassuming yet hypnotic in the vein of Jessica Pratt’s early releases. The compositions are expansive and unfurl with greater intention. Case in point: the nearly seven-minute-long title track, a tender ballad built around the duo’s intertwined vocal melodies and guitar playing. The emotional terrain is candid, yet ambiguous: “I don’t know how I belong to you but I do somehow / I don’t know how I came to stand up to you but I have no doubt.”Amid so much diaristic songwriting elsewhere,@ want to leave room for interpretation. “That’s kind of what folk songs are, something that can travel from person to person and be played by many different individuals,” Filipczak says. “If the song starts out in a hyper-individualistic place, it’s not really going to be able to make that jump.” The conceptual hive mind can get a bad rap as an echo chamber of groupthink, but @ tap into the idea that, like bees building their home, collective creation can lead to something greater than the sum of its parts.Autosmile is released via 4AD on 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicAutumn arts preview 2026Folk musicPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Adele Parks: ‘If I could ​edit my pas​t, I’d be fitter younger – I​ would have been hotter’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The author on the habit she can’t control, the writer she’s never read, and the true love of her life (it’s not her husband)
Author: Rosanna Greenstreet
Headline: The author on the habit she can’t control, the writer she’s never read, and the true love of her life (it’s not her husband)
Content: Adele Parks: ‘Sex is important because it’s about connection.’Photograph: Dave Bennet/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAdele Parks: ‘Sex is important because it’s about connection.’Photograph: Dave Bennet/Getty ImagesThe Q&ALife and styleInterviewAdele Parks: ‘If I could ​edit my pas​t, I’d be fitter younger – I​ would have been hotter’Rosanna GreenstreetThe author on the habit she can’t control, the writer she’s never read, and the true love of her life (it’s not her husband)Sat 29 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBorn in North Yorkshire, Adele Parks, 57, studied English at the University of Leicester then worked in advertising. In 2000, she published her debut novel, Playing Away, and has since written a book every year. Her latest is Eyes on You. Her work has been translated into 31 languages and in 2022 she was awarded the MBE for services to literature. She is an ambassador for charities promoting literacy including the National Literacy Trust, which is collaborating with the Department for Education on the National Year of Reading 2026. Parks is married with a son, and lives in Surrey.What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?Speaking negatively to myself.What is the trait you most deplore in others?Laziness.What was your most embarrassing moment?When I concentrate, I put my thumb in my mouth. I once did it during a really important meeting when asked a question I didn’t know the answer to. When I left the meeting my friend said: “What did you put your thumb in your mouth for?” I didn’t know I’d done it.Describe yourself in three wordsEnthusiastic, resilient, empathetic.What would your superpower be?Teleportation – but with clothes. I don’t want to turn up anywhere naked.What makes you unhappy?Hopelessness – when people have stopped believing they can improve or a situation can improve.If you could bring something extinct back to life, what would you choose?My last cat, Lilac, to meet the new cats.Stockard Channing: ‘I cried at the election of Joe Biden, thinking we were out of the woods. Wrong!’Read moreWho would play you in the film of your life?Reese Witherspoon.Who is your celebrity crush?Taylor Swift, because her lyrics are so thought-provoking.Which book are you ashamed not to have read?I’ve never read any Salman Rushdie.What was the last lieyou told?When people tell me about their book ideas, I never say: “Look, don’t bother – it’s never going to get published.” I go: “Go for it – you never know.”What is your guiltiest pleasure?Staying at home and playing Scrabble.To whom would youlike to say sorry, and why?When I was in my 20s, I had an uncle who took his own life. I would like a second chance to say: “Hang in there.” My parents were living abroad, and me and my sister were just too young to notice the flags.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat or who is the greatest love of your life?Jim [Parks’s husband] will just have to deal with this, but words are the love of my life. I have Jim because of words, I have my life because of words.What does love feel like?A mix – safety to be yourself, acceptance, a feeling of peace and reliance, but also challenge, whether that’s intellectual or emotional.If you could edit your past, what would you change?I would become fitter younger. Because I would have been hotter younger!What single thing would improve the quality of your life?A sushi chef in my kitchen.What do you consider your greatest achievement?How much my son loves me, particularly considering I’ve had a huge career.What keeps you awake at night?Plots.Would you rather have more sex, money or fame?I really like sex and I think it’s so important because it’s about connection. I’m going with sex.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Q&AfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Underground Monk Show review – hysterical visions enrobed in mystery | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Four clowns stir up a strange stew of ideas about faith in this playful and highly physical comedy
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Four clowns stir up a strange stew of ideas about faith in this playful and highly physical comedy
Content: Giddy spirit … Claire Woolner, Max Baumgarten, D Marcucci and John Norris in Underground Monk Show.Photograph: Jennifer Forward-HayterView image in fullscreenGiddy spirit … Claire Woolner, Max Baumgarten, D Marcucci and John Norris in Underground Monk Show.Photograph: Jennifer Forward-HayterEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewUnderground Monk Show review – hysterical visions enrobed in mysteryAssembly George Square Gardens, EdinburghFour clowns stir up a strange stew of ideas about faith in this playful and highly physical comedyChris WiegandSat 29 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Anyone ever been born before?” That’s a rare bid for relatable crowd work in this buzzy, bizarre hour bya bunch of cowled Los Angeles clowns-cum-monks, nominated forEdinburgh’s best comedy newcomer award. We witness the birth of one, umbilical cord held by the others, with a “goo goo ga ga – G’day!” greeting gurgled by D Marcucci as the mercurial newborn.But everyone on stage seems to be discovering their body for the first time. John Norris is half-fascinated, half-frightened, on removing his robe’s hood, to realise he has a bushy moustache. Claire Woolner and Max Baumgarten are not just finding their voices but simply getting used to having a tongue in their mouths.In a show co-directed by Norris and Corey Podell, this pack of monks nervously shuffles among us clutching each other as well as a bowl of water. A lanyard is torn from an audience member and thrown in with a satanic sizzle. They appear bound by a secret code that they may not quite remember. All fingers and thumbs with the bowl, their ritual devolves into a game of rock, paper, scissors with some tricksy lighting. When they dunk themselves, the bowl becomes a mystical portal for each monk’s interlinking vision.View image in fullscreenConnection and alienation … Underground Monk Show.Photograph: Jennifer Forward-HayterRather than plunge in, I spent the first few minutes sceptical, wary of self-indulgence as the quartet endlessly fretted. But with each passing chime that rings out, the show becomes a richly weird stew of ideas – about connection, alienation, the limits of language – expressed through masterly movement.Clown Show review – after 250 years, the American dream explodes over one anarchic nightRead moreThe dynamic between each individual and the rest of the ensemble is carefully choreographed even outside routines such as a ball in a nonsense kingdom, a slow duet with an audience member soundtracked to Adele or the Bob Fosse-esque routine that meets Marcucci’s birth.The foursome are testing faith too – not just in an irresistible repeated gag where they don’t fully understand how to do a trust fall. It’s one of those shows that retains the giddy spirit of an easy-to-imagine devising process. Twisted and twisty until a flurry of final reveals, this monkish mischief also leaves lots to contemplate.AtAssembly George Square Gardens, Edinburgh, until 30 August.
