title: Charli xcx, Reading Festival review – Pretentious? Just a bit. But Nietzsche would have loved it | Charli xcx | The Guardian
description: There’s not much time to dig into her deep catalogue of future-facing pop, but she satisfies the hardcore
Author: Chal Ravens
Headline: There’s not much time to dig into her deep catalogue of future-facing pop, but she satisfies the hardcore
Content: Charli xcx performing on the the Grid stage during the Reading Festival.Photograph: Henry Redcliffe/PAView image in fullscreenCharli xcx performing on the the Grid stage during the Reading Festival.Photograph: Henry Redcliffe/PACharli xcxReviewCharli xcx, Reading Festival review – Pretentious? Just a bit. But Nietzsche would have loved itReading FestivalThere’s not much time to dig into her deep catalogue of future-facing pop, but she satisfies the hardcoreChal RavensSat 29 Aug 2026 04.23 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 21.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Time itself is a circle,” as the rock’n’roll philosopher Nietzsche once said, accurately foreshadowing Charli xcx’s only UK festival appearance this summer. Like her performance on Glastonbury’s Other Stage last year – a pyrotechnic farewell to the puke-green reign of Brat – Charli’s Reading and Leeds appearance is a not-quite-headline slot that also follows a rowdy set from grime don Skepta.Yet in the past 14 months, everything else in Charli’s pop factory has undergone a hard reset. She’s released two albums – a grandiose, gothic soundtrack to Emerald Fennell’s adaptation of Wuthering Heights, and last month’s high-concept Music, Fashion, Film, an album of raw, glitching micro-rock, with guitars shredded into Tetris-like pieces, and fitted with lacerating lyrics about shopping, egotism and mortality. She’s also launched an acting career, thrown a big fat celebrity wedding and, somewhere along the way, found time to rehearse her biggest, most vertiginous show to date.View image in fullscreenCharli xcx performs during her only UK festival appearance this summer.Photograph: Henry RedcliffeMost of the new album gets an airing, starting with mission statement single Rock Music – a hard pivot away from Brat’s all-night rave energy and an ode to Charli’s on-stage urge to self-destruct: “I’m really banging my head / I’m really hurting my neck / The nerve damage is real.” Backed by a live band (with guitar, bass and drums played by the kind of underfed, skinny-trousered men who ruled these stages circa 2006) Charli rattles through Yeah, her pocket-sized take on Song 2, and shopaholic reckoning Card Declined, during which she’s joined by a huge cast of dancer-slash-models prowling a three-storey scaffolding set.Her rotation of outfits is another daring homage to the late ‘00s – glittery blazer over push-up bra and fishnets; ripped T-shirt dress with low-slung belt – and the mood board is tightly curated, with video screens stuck on the same monochrome palette as every outfit and image from this era, including the album’s black-and-white cover, featuring three totemic males of music, fashion and film: John Cale (whose disembodied voice heralds a tense rendition of their claustrophobic duet, House), Marc Jacobs and Martin Scorsese. Pretentious? Just a bit. But Nietzsche, I reckon, would have got on board with it – Charli’s current pop era is basically a cosmic battle between her ego and her vulnerabilities, all watched over by serious Big Dick Energy.View image in fullscreenBacked by a live band, most of her new album gets an airing.Photograph: Henry RedcliffeCharli’s crowd are less debauched than her “365 party girl” reputation suggests, but they save their energy for a speed run of Brat’s biggest hits, including Von Dutch and girly smut fest Guess, where knickers fall from the sky like elasticated manna. There’s not much time to dig into her deep catalogue of future-facing pop, but she satisfies the hardcore – like the young man next to me who saw the Brat tour 24 times – with Track 10, a shirt-tearing favourite from 2017’s Pop 2.The end of the show circles back to new songs, including the hilariously arch “B side” Playboy Bunny, sung on one note like a coquettish Joey Ramone: “All my music sounds the same / Well, that’s because I made it”. There’s a set from Fontaines D.C. still to come, but Charli makes it tricky for the headliners to follow her closing flourish on Nothing Lasts Forever, a morbid reflection on “the crushing highs and lows of ego”, which fades out with director David Cronenberg’s voice on a loop, reminding us of the fate of even the greatest artists – “They are dead, they are gone / Nothing lasts for ever” – as Charli and her dancers stand rigid, staring into the distance. No stage banter, no compromise – just an absolute commitment to the bit.Explore more on these topicsCharli xcxReading and Leeds festivalMusic festivalsFestivalslive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Trials of Magnus Coffinkey review – time stands still at 3.43am in fringe fairytale | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Angele and Malcolm Galea’s two-hander cycles through grief and sorrow as a broken-hearted hero is trapped in purgatory
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Angele and Malcolm Galea’s two-hander cycles through grief and sorrow as a broken-hearted hero is trapped in purgatory
Content: Emotional pull … Becky Camilleri and Joseph Zammit in The Trials of Magnus Coffinkey.Photograph: Harry ElletsonView image in fullscreenEmotional pull … Becky Camilleri and Joseph Zammit in The Trials of Magnus Coffinkey.Photograph: Harry ElletsonEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewThe Trials of Magnus Coffinkey review – time stands still at 3.43am in fringe fairytaleSummerhall, EdinburghAngele and Malcolm Galea’s two-hander cycles through grief and sorrow as a broken-hearted hero is trapped in purgatoryMark FisherSat 29 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA fairytale plunges the reader into a dilemma then resolves it. But what if the happy ending never arrives? Will the tale just circle around into a netherworld, never finding a conclusion?That is the prospect in this two-hander by Malta’s Angele and Malcolm Galea, a couple whose experience of pregnancy loss finds expression in a thwarted fairytale – the kind of tale, perhaps, they might have read to their daughter.In Philip Leone-Ganado’s production, starring Becky Camilleri and Joseph Zammit, the writers envisage a picture-book landscape of archetypes and autumn leaves. Here, Magnus Coffinkey, a man who makes a living fixing bells, climbs a tower to complete the most difficult job of his career, one made harder by ominous gargoyles and bats.At 3.43am, he and the bell come crashing down, a symbol of a child lost seven months into a pregnancy. There is no coming back from this, or so it would seem: no relief from the loss, no escape from the emptiness, only a debilitating grief. Duly, Magnus ends up in a purgatory known as the “gloom”, his heart broken, with only guilt, pain and sorrow ahead. Among his visitors is Harmony who, like an unborn child, is “not dead and yet not living”.As the rhyming narrator of this faltering tale, Camilleri interrupts. She cannot see a way out for her characters, only a depressive cycle of broken hearts. Her fairytale will not resolve. It takes time, a sympathetic therapist and a “safe space for dialogue” to make an ending possible.Camilleri is a sharp and physically lively actor, bringing levity and perspective to a tale of gothic inertia. But the play is slow to reveal its purpose and, when it does, dwells on emotions that are more sad than dramatic.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026FairytalesTheatreEdinburgh festivalSummerhallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Fourth time lucky as Chris Cantrill’s spoof whodunnit wins Edinburgh comedy award 2026 | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Nominated in three previous years, the rambunctious standup – one half of The Delightful Sausage – wins the prize for his show Rewilding while Marty Gleeson is named best newcomer for Dog Ear
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Nominated in three previous years, the rambunctious standup – one half of The Delightful Sausage – wins the prize for his show Rewilding while Marty Gleeson is named best newcomer for Dog Ear
Content: Palpable mainstream potential … Chris Cantrill.Photograph: Jack KirbyView image in fullscreenPalpable mainstream potential … Chris Cantrill.Photograph: Jack KirbyEdinburgh festival 2026Fourth time lucky as Chris Cantrill’s spoof whodunnit wins Edinburgh comedy award 2026Nominated in three previous years, the rambunctious standup – one half of The Delightful Sausage – wins the prize for his show Rewilding while Marty Gleeson is named best newcomerBrian LoganSat 29 Aug 2026 08.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 08.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe annual Edinburgh comedy award has been won by the standup Chris Cantrill, two years after his comedy partner Amy Gledhill – in the raucous northern double actThe Delightful Sausage– won the same prize.Cantrill, 42 and from Bradford, received the so-called “Oscar of live comedy” for a show,Rewilding, about his new life in rural Northumberland, where an act of vandalism shocks the local community – and a spoof whodunnit ensues. It builds on the foundations laid in 2024 byEasily Swayed, which documented his move to the countryside and secured what was then Cantrill’s third nomination (but first as a solo act) for the award.Like Gledhill, Cantrill is an uproarious, fun-loving and relatable act with palpable mainstream potential, and his victory comes against the grain ofan awards shortlistthat (in both the best show and best newcomer categories) trended leftfield. The oddballs are represented among this year’s winners by Marty Gleeson, who has received the best newcomer gong withher show Dog Ear. This eccentric set is inspired by Gleeson’s experiences at art school in her native Limerick, and – with its live bodhrán accompaniment and setpiece that requires shaking the hand of every single audience member – marches entirely to the beat of its own drum.View image in fullscreenMarching to the beat of her own drum … Marty Gleeson.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianFor my money, I didn’t have either winner down as frontrunner for the prize, which is famously a star-maker in British comedy. Previous winners of the main award, initiated in 1981, include Steve Coogan, Frank Skinner and Bridget Christie, and of the best newcomer gong (introduced in 1992) Harry Hill and Sarah Millican. I had the Mexican-American comicLara Ricoteand the London-based, Chinese-born standupLi Jin Haoas the acts most likely on this year’s list, and still marvel that the buzziest comedy shows on the fringe (byElf Lyons, the sketch groupCrybabiesandthe Australian clown Conk) weren’t even nominated.But I’m delighted to see Cantrill’s rambunctious comedy rewarded, after years of delivering big laughs to fringe audiences. And I’m excited by Gleeson’s arrival on the scene, and to see what she’ll do next. This year’s panel prize, meanwhile, which rewards initiatives that best sum up “the spirit of the fringe”, was won byOne Joke, a new event asking “how many comedians can tell one joke each, in an hour?” Produced by Liebenspiel, compered by Jonathan Oldfield, and headlined by the comic Lorna Rose Treen, it featured contributions by 60 comedians, and raised money for charity.Magicians and margarine: 10 of the funniest jokes from the Edinburgh fringe 2026Read moreThe organisers of the Edinburgh comedy award (formerly known as the Perrier), theatre producerNica Burnsand its new executive director Emma Brünjes, said that “in Chris and Marty we have two outstanding winners: both are exceptional comedians, writers and performers who have crafted wonderful shows”. The winners were selected from more than 550 eligible shows at a festival claiming, yet again, to be bigger than ever, with just over 4,200 registered shows across 299 venues. Whether the attendances were bigger than – or as big as – ever remains to be seen. (The sense on the ground was: perhaps not.) As winner of the best show prize, Cantrill walks off with £10,000; best newcomer Gleeson wins £5,000. title: I avoided restaurants after a disastrous job as a waitress. Then I watched The Bear … | The Bear | The Guardian
description: Working in a high-end restaurant was stressful and scarring. It took an accidental encounter with the TV show to help me heal – and change my attitude towards work
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Working in a high-end restaurant was stressful and scarring. It took an accidental encounter with the TV show to help me heal – and change my attitude towards work
Content: Illustration: Martin O'Neill/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Martin O'Neill/The GuardianMy cultural awakeningThe BearI avoided restaurants after a disastrous job as a waitress. Then I watched The Bear …Working in a high-end restaurant was stressful and scarring. It took an accidental encounter with the TV show to help me heal – and change my attitude towards workMolly WilsonSat 29 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEight years ago, I was working as a waitress in a fine dining restaurant in the Cotswolds. The expertly crafted atmosphere had dim mood lighting, ambient music and a farm-to-table menu. I hated it.The other waiters could charm guests into purchasing expensive bottles, but I just gaped gormlessly when I struggled to recall the wine pairings. My brown leather brogues gave me blisters as I’d hobble to the kitchen to admit I’d forgotten an order in the middle of a busy dinner service. The chefs would shout and shake the ticket in my face.A year into my job, while serving an influencer, I attempted to remove her plate of oysters, but my sweaty palms slipped as I lifted the dish and I accidentally sloshed the water into her lap. She yelped and jumped up. Guests turned and stared as I stood frozen, my face burning. I blurted out an apology and ran off, leaving another waiter to placate her while I sobbed in the kitchen. I knew then that it was time to give up.When I went to university two years later, I hated restaurant work so much that I lived frugally on my student loan to avoid having to do the same again. On first dates, I insisted on drinks at the pub just so I wouldn’t have to sit in another formal restaurant. Waitressing had made me feel hopeless and stupid, and I became apathetic towards all work. If every job would be as bad as that one, the prospect of doing any work after university filled me with dread.Years later, when I overheard my boyfriend watchingThe Bear, it awoke some kind of terrified, sleeper-agent response. He was watching the first series’ acclaimed, mostly one-shot episode, Review, in which the kitchen descends into chaos over the course of 18 relentless minutes. The sound of kitchen doors slamming, frustrated screams and the constant whirring of a ticket machine all took me straight back to my worst days as a waitress.double quotation markLooking back, my experiences seemed funny, not as traumatic as they’d felt at the timeI refused to watch the show at first, expecting to feel the same panic I’d experienced at my old restaurant. What’s worse is that the protagonist, Carmy, played by Jeremy Allen White, bears a strange resemblance to my old head chef – he has the same white T-shirt, curly hair and stony-faced expression.Eventually, however, I couldn’t control my curiosity. It only took a couple of episodes before I began to appreciate the honest and comedic way The Bear presents those high-anxiety moments. Looking back, my experiences seemed funny, not as traumatic as they’d felt at the time. I even felt pride explaining restaurant terminology like “turns” and “covers” to my boyfriend.However, it was the second series episode Forks that fully defrosted my feelings towards hospitality. In it, Richie, the vulgar and abrasive assistant manager, begrudgingly visits a high-end restaurant to learn how to be a maître-d’.At first, Richie disparages the fact that he is delegated the menial task of polishing forks. Yet slowly putting effort into that small chore teaches him the importance of respecting the staff, guests, and himself. When finally given the chance to try his hand at waiting tables, he has an epiphany that serving others gives him satisfaction and purpose.Looking back, I realised that my restaurant’s standards were so high because every small flourish could make someone’s day. To feel that same pride and purpose, I knew I needed to stop treating all work like a chore.Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt convinced me to give up on my fashion industry dreamsRead moreThat image of Richie, suited up with renewed vigour, stayed with me after graduating, when I started working as a writer. Through rejection or long hours to meet deadlines, I still put in effort for whoever it could serve once published. And I’ve since enjoyed eating at my old restaurant and made a point of being extra kind to the waiter.Far from making me feel panic all over again, The Bear actually helped me appreciate my time working in hospitality – and also changed my attitude towards work. I now feel grateful for enduring those mortifying moments. After all – the worst shifts became the best stories.Share your cultural awakeningsYou can tell us how a cultural moment has prompted you to make a major life change by filling in the form below or emailing us on cultural.awakening@theguardian.com.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: The showgirl sisterhood: five former variety stars look back at their wild careers – in pictures | Stage | The Guardian
description: The ‘Golden girls of Eastbourne’ first crossed paths more than 50 years ago. They recall flammable feather head-dresses, wardrobe malfunctions and topping the bill over the Beatles
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: The ‘Golden girls of Eastbourne’ first crossed paths more than 50 years ago. They recall flammable feather head-dresses, wardrobe malfunctions and topping the bill over the Beatles
Content: Jacquie Toye now and in the UK’s first production of ChicagoComposite: courtesy of Jacquie Toye/David Pickens/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenJacquie Toye now and in the UK’s first production of ChicagoComposite: courtesy of Jacquie Toye/David Pickens/Guardian DesignStageThe showgirl sisterhood: five former variety stars look back at their wild careers – in picturesThe ‘Golden girls of Eastbourne’ first crossed paths more than 50 years ago. They recall flammable feather head-dresses, wardrobe malfunctions and topping the bill over the BeatlesWords:Kate Lloyd. Photographs: David PickensSat 29 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTShareIhear the Golden Girls of Eastbourne before I see them – hooting laughter leaking out of a house in the East Sussex seaside town. Inside, I find five energetic women in their 80s and 90s, sitting in a knick-knack-filled living room and talking over one another like teenagers.“None of us stripped, did we?”“Ohnooo. We didn’t have rotating tassels!”Friends for more than half a century, the women met in rehearsals and aftershow parties while working as dancers, singers and comedy stooges in the 1960s and 70s. Their careers took them from cruise ships and panto to British seaside theatres, where they performed in sequin dresses, high-cut leotards and huge feather headdresses, sharing bills with the biggest stars of the day.Over the decades, Eastbourne became one of the places where they made their names. In later life, they have gathered here again – this time not for work, but for friendship. It was this sisterhood that caught the eye of photographer David Pickens. A retired circus performer, he was once part of a double act with one of the group’s sons. “I was hearing stories of his mother and her friends and how they were locally known affectionately as the Golden Girls and I thought, that would make a great story,” he says. “They’ve got amazing life stories, amazing camaraderie. What I really admired was the fact they were all women in a very male-dominated world, and then all those men have gone now, and they’re the last people standing.”He decided to photograph them at the town’s Royal Hippodrome – a Victorian theatre where all the women performed when they were younger.“It’s a beautiful theatre,” says former dancer and dance teacher Jenny Lawrenson, 83. Petite, with the voice of Mary Poppins and the impeccable posture of a lifelong ballet dancer, she says she remembers it better for another reason – its tilted stage: “You’re dancing uphill!”“I’ve got something to tell you from the Hippodrome,” says Beryl Plummer, a gentle 90-year-old with lilac hair, red-framed glasses and a passion for cat-inspired crockery. My host today, she ferries out cups of tea and homemade rock cakes as we chat. She and her late husband Tommy were a smash-hit double act: he played the xylophone and the drums while she tap-danced alongside him. They were a mainstay of variety shows – multi-act performances that could span magicians to musicians, animal acts to a man known for balancing a cartwheel on his head.“I was coming to the end of the act with my tap dancing, and I had on a halterneck, which dropped down.” She leans forward. “I had nothing underneath. The press were in that night.” She chuckles. “The newspaper cutting said: ‘… and she never missed a beat’.”“You told me you never stripped!” someone shouts.double quotation markWe did one number with big feathers on our heads. One girl shimmied into a candle. Her feathers caught fireView image in fullscreenGolden Girls (from left) Jenny Lawrenson, Vicki Goodwin, Beryl Plummer, Jacquie Toye and Jan LyntonThe Plummers were so popular they once topped a bill ahead of the Beatles. “They were just normal boys, but you could not hear anything they sang because of all the screaming,” says Plummer.Another time, they were booked to support Cliff Richard, but the show was called off early after performers including comedian and singer Des O’Connor were pelted with eggs and potatoes. “An announcement was made to say: ‘Give the acts a chance!’”Plummer isn’t the only one with stories like these. Everyone here today worked with some of the biggest names of the time.Vicki Goodwin, 85, was a dancer and singer who appeared in shows including Dad’s Army, and performed with her second husband, comedianKen Goodwin. Jacquie Toye, an 83-year-old former comedy stooge for Ken Dodd – and committed heckler this afternoon – had a West End career that included playing Velma Kelly in the UK’s first production of Chicago. But rather than show off about their greatest hits, the former showgirls prefer to laugh about all the things that went wrong.Goodwin remembers being found by Bruce Forsyth after breaking her arm. “I fell down a flight of stairs outside his dressing room.” Toye recalls tripping over a plug while rushing for a curtain call, turning off the electricity in a theatre. “I had to apologise to everyone!”“I worked in a club in Cairo,” says Jan Lynton, 82, a former showgirl, whose performances took her from Japan to Egypt. Her chin-length bob is as sharp as her punchlines. “We did the number with big feathers on our heads, shimmying back and forth. The girl opposite me shimmied back and went into a candle. When she came up, her feathers were on fire. She didn’t know.” Her friends gasp. “Somebody threw a jug of water over her!”The women say that a shared sense of humour has helped them to bond over the years. Back in the day it was how they’d deal with the less glamorous side of show business. The digs for performers were often ropey. They talk about rooms in Glasgow with black mould and places in London with no hot water. Lawrenson remembers doing a season in Cardiff with her dance partner, Robert Marlowe, and looking for accommodation. “The landlord took us into the bathroom and there was a chipped, brown rusty bath. And he said: ‘And do you know, [comedian] Gladys Morgan had a bath here!’ My God!”double quotation markAn agent chased me around a table once. He was horribleView image in fullscreenBeing a young woman in the industry came with its own challenges: bottoms being pinched, stagehands getting their mates backstage to ogle, producers dangling dubious invitations. “You just took it in your stride,” says Lynton. “An agent chased me around a table once. He was horrible.”The groups’ lives diverged eventually. Lawrenson was only in the business for five years before leaving to settle down with her husband. She moved from Bournemouth to East Sussex in 2005 after his death, and after the loss of one of her twin daughters, too. Plummer and her husband kept threatening to retire, but never quite did it until 2016, settling in Eastbourne. Lynton became a choreographer, only retiring in 2022, while Goodwin moved to Spain and then Llandudno with Ken, until his death from Alzheimer’s in 2012.“We’ve all been through the mill one way or another,” says Toye. “We’ve all had tragedy in our lives.” She lost her husband. Sisterhood becomes of utmost importance in your later years, they all agree.“I rely on all my lovely friends here, and if I need them, they will come to me,” says Plummer. “Oh no we won’t!” heckles Toye. Still, when Plummer had a serious operation in 2019, Toye took her to hospital and brought her home several weeks later, decorating her house with welcome home balloons. She also stayed with Lynton when she experienced a period of memory loss.double quotation markTo be honest – and we all feel the same – I sometimes say, ‘There was this old person.’ And I think, ‘No, I’m old’View image in fullscreen“The group is inclined to drop things for you if you need it,” says Lynton. “We’re there for each other, and even if you’re not there physically, you can talk on the phone.” Goodwin calls Lynton most nights, and Plummer every evening.“It’s nothing really, after this length of time,” she says. Then she jokes: “I like to know she’s not lying on the floor in the kitchen.”But the Golden Girls are not just a support network. They have approached retirement with the same vim they brought to their careers. Their days are filled with lunches, showbiz-themed talks at local hotels and whatever else they can find to keep busy. Toye has a hospital radio show. Lawrenson runs an exercise class. Tomorrow, they’re going to a “gentleman friend’s” tower-block flat to watch an airshow. “He calls it Ladies’ Day at the tower,” I’m told as they all howl.Lynton says she doesn’t feel her age. “I have to be honest – and we all feel the same – I sometimes say of others, ‘There was this old person.’ And I think, ‘No,I’mold.’ But they just seem a lot older, because of their mentality.” She recently bought some coasters that say “Growing old disgracefully”, she tells me. It’s how she intends to see out her later years. “Age is a number,” she says.“What’s the secret to that attitude?”“Gin and tonic,” says Toye. And the laughter starts again.Jacquie ToyeView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThis is the CambridgeTheatrein the West End. I’m playing Velma in the first UK production of Chicago. Every night there was a buzz.I also worked with Morecambe and Wise in pantomime at the Alexandra Theatre, Birmingham, playing a boy. There was suddenly a lot of laughter. Eric had poured a big back of crisps down the back of my jacket then slapped me on the back. I couldn’t get the crisps out!Jan LyntonView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThis is me at Birmingham Hippodrome. I was playing the Genie of the Ring with ventriloquist Keith Harris. It was a production that had been at the London Palladium.When you did a summer season or panto, the cast became like a new family. And as you were going to different places, you’d meet up with people you’d worked with before.Beryl PlummerView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenI was a dancer at Butlin’s, where I met my husband. We started a double act, Tommy Wallis and Beryl. It was a hit from the start. This was taken during the summer season at the Cliffs Pavilion in Southend-on-Sea in 1969.Variety shows often had strange acts. There was a chap who used to have a cartwheel on his head, and somebody had an act with chimps, that used to pinch the girls’ bottoms.Jenny LawrensonView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThese photos were taken to promote my dancing act with Robert Marlowe. We performed on the first Queen Mary and Queen Elizabeth cruises going to New York. There was huge first class accommodation, then cabin class was smaller, and then tourist had a very low ceiling. I heard one dancing act lost her wig when it got caught on the sprinkler. She left it up there.Vicki GoodwinView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenI was 16 when I came back from the hairdresser blond, and my mother said: ‘My God, you’d better not let your father see that.’ And I’ve been blond ever since.I reckon I knew I wanted to perform from when I was 12. There were queues for auditions – 400 people for one part. When seasons would finish, we all went out and got jobs. We were never out of work.

title: Laurie Anderson’s next manuscript to be locked away for 88 years in Future Library | Future Library | The Guardian
description: Grammy award-winning American artist selected as 13th person to submit written work to Oslo-based project
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Grammy award-winning American artist selected as 13th person to submit written work to Oslo-based project
Content: Laurie Anderson credits her mother for her love of books.Photograph: Wolfgang TillmansView image in fullscreenLaurie Anderson credits her mother for her love of books.Photograph: Wolfgang TillmansFuture LibraryLaurie Anderson’s next manuscript to be locked away for 88 years in Future LibraryGrammy award-winning American artist selected as 13th person to submit written work to Oslo-based projectNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentSat 29 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe next manuscript by the American artistLaurie Andersonwill remain unseen for 88 years, as she becomes the 13th figure to contribute to the Future Library project.Anderson joins Margaret Atwood, Han Kang, Ocean Vuong and other prominent authors who have written secret manuscripts, which have been locked away until 2114.The texts are stored in a specially designed silent room in the Deichman Bjørvika building at the public library in Oslo. At the end of the project, the full anthology of texts will be printed using paper made from trees from theFuture Libraryforest in Nordmarka, in northern Oslo, where 1,000 spruce trees were planted by Katie Paterson, the artist behind the project, in 2014.Anderson is a writer, director, composer, visual artist, musician and vocalist whose work spans art, theatre, experimental music and technology.She has created numerous multimedia stage performances and published 10 books, as well as being nominated for six Grammy Awards, winning once and receiving a lifetime achievement award in 2024. Her visual art has been exhibited globally at institutions including the Hirshhorn Museum in Washington DC and Moderna Museet in Stockholm.Anderson’s manuscript for the project may be a text, a score, a story, a set of instructions or “something for which we do not yet have a name”, Paterson said.View image in fullscreenLaurie Anderson performs in Amsterdam in 1982.Photograph: Rob Verhorst/RedfernsAnderson said: “I absolutely loved the idea of theFuture Libraryas soon as I learned about it. I’ve always been in love with books, libraries and forests. When I was a kid we lived next to a large park filled with maple, elm and oak trees. At the far corner of the park was an enormous red oak tree and up the street and just around the bend, there was the library, a rustic fieldstone building filled with comfortable pillows and many thousands of books.“‘You better check with grandfather tree today if you have the time,’ my mother would say some mornings. In a house where candy of all kinds was forbidden, we knew what that meant: there would be chocolate bars and chocolate mints up in the fork of the red oak, just low enough for us to hoist ourselves up and grab them. It also meant that we’d have extra incentive that day to get to the library.”Anderson called her mother a “brilliant and unhappy woman”. She said she should have been a chief executive of a large corporation but instead had eight children. “She loved books and somehow made it a project to get up early in the morning, walk through the park and hide chocolate bars in a tree. She taught us to love books, magic and old trees.“I’m hoping to be able to write something useful about love for the people who will read this in 2114. My favourite books are the ones in which I can hear someone’s voice, which is why I’ll try my best to make myself clear to the people who come across these books in the next century.”The Future Library Trust said it had selected Anderson for her “singular ability to speak across time, creating work that is profoundly human, radically imaginative and alive to futures we cannot yet foresee”.Paterson added: “Laurie Anderson has spent a lifetime sending signals into the unknown. For decades, she has explored how we tell stories, how we remember, and how we imagine what is yet to come. Moving freely between language, music, visual art, technology and performance, her work travels between the intimate and the planetary, love and loss, politics and poetry, with humour, tenderness and wonder.”Other writers to have contributed to the project include David Mitchell, Sjón, Elif Shafak, Karl Ove Knausgård, Tsitsi Dangarembga, Judith Schalansky, Valeria Luiselli, Tommy Orange and, most recently, Amitav Ghosh.In June 2022, the City of Oslo signed an agreement that ensures the forest will remain in the hands of the Future Library Trust for the duration of the project.Explore more on these topicsFuture LibraryLaurie AndersonNorwayEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Blind date: ‘She’s one of the easiest people to talk to that I’ve ever met’ | Dating | The Guardian
description: Mike, 37, a scientific editor, meets Caterina, 35, a teacher
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mike, 37, a scientific editor, meets Caterina, 35, a teacher
Content:
Composite: Antonio Olmos & Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenComposite: Antonio Olmos & Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianBlind dateDatingBlind date: ‘She’s one of the easiest people to talk to that I’ve ever met’Mike, 37, a scientific editor, meets Caterina, 35, a teacherSat 29 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenMike on CaterinaWhat were you hoping for?Good company, nice food and an interesting evening with someone new. I got everything I hoped for.First impressions?Warm, confident and easy to talk to.What did you talk about?The joys of being an aunt/uncle. Freelance life. Jury duty as a newly minted British citizen.Most awkward moment?None that I recall, so either the evening went smoothly or the malbec did its job.Good table manners?If there were any faux pas, I was too busy enjoying the conversation to notice.Best thing about Caterina?She’s genuinely one of the easiest people to talk to that I’ve ever met.Would you introduce Caterina to your friends?Without hesitation.Describe Caterina in three wordsWarm, kind, elegant.Q&AFancy a blind date?ShowBlind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two 
strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans 
to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we 
take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the
 UK) and online attheguardian.comevery Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you canread all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We
 ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of
 person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions 
cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.Can I choose who I match with?No,
 it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, 
preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely 
to be.Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.How should I answer?Honestly
 but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that
 Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.How to applyEmailblind.date@theguardian.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.What do you think Caterina made of you?Hopefully polite, easy company and good for a chat. Perhaps a lack of shared passions meant the spark wasn’t there, but the conversation never ran dry.Did you go on somewhere?We were the last two in the restaurant, so we went for a stroll around London until midnight, when I had to dash for the last train back to Cambridge.And … did you kiss?Sorry to disappoint: just a farewell hug.If you could change one thing about the evening, what would it be?I’d have liked a bit more time before that last train forced the evening to end.Marks out of 10?9.5. Hard to fault a thoroughly enjoyable evening just because it wasn’t heading toward romance.Would you meet again?We may meet for a coffee when I’m in London, and there’s an open invitation for a guided tour of Cambridge.View image in fullscreenMike and Caterina on their date.View image in fullscreenCaterina on MikeWhat were you hoping for?To meet someone special.First impressions?Nice smile and face; a bit nervous or shy.What did you talk about?Favourite cuisine. Past and future travels. Harry Potter. Even politics.Most awkward moment?I felt I was leading the conversation most of the time, asking questions.Good table manners?Very nice: he would pour water in my glass whenever it was empty.Best thing about Mike?You can tell he’s someone who loves putting care into what he does and what he says – a rare find these days.Would you introduce Mike to your friends?Not sure – my friendship group has a lot of energy.Describe Mike in three wordsOrganised, thorough, kind.Blind date: ‘I asked him to compliment my outfit and he said he didn’t really like it’Read moreWhat do you think Mike made of you?Not sure. Maybe that I’m a weird woman who eats fast and laughs loudly!Did you go on somewhere?We had a walk around Soho/Covent Garden – I felt he deserved a bit of tourism, coming from Cambridge.And … did you kiss?No, just a hug.If you could change one thing about the evening, what would it be?Nothing major – maybe just a slightly quieter spot to chat.Marks out of 10?7.5.Would you meet again?As friends. I would like to grab a coffee together.Mike and Caterina ate atTagine & Grillat theSun and 13 Cantons,London W1. Fancy a blind date? title: Flipping marvellous: Yotam Ottolenghi on the joy of simple breakfasts – plus six exclusive recipes | Breakfast | The Guardian
description: Weekend mornings are for family – and whoever happens to be over. Forget fussing and focus on just one big lovely thing for the middle of the table. Here’s how
Author: Yotam Ottolenghi
Headline: Weekend mornings are for family – and whoever happens to be over. Forget fussing and focus on just one big lovely thing for the middle of the table. Here’s how
Content: Yotam wears Tekla sleepwear. Grooming: Carol Morley at Carol Hayes.Photograph: Pål Hansen/The GuardianView image in fullscreenYotam wears Tekla sleepwear. Grooming: Carol Morley at Carol Hayes.Photograph: Pål Hansen/The GuardianYotam Ottolenghi recipesBreakfastFlipping marvellous: Yotam Ottolenghi on the joy of simple breakfasts – plus six exclusive recipesWeekend mornings are for family – and whoever happens to be over. Forget fussing and focus on just one big lovely thing for the middle of the table. Here’s howYotam OttolenghiSat 29 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFamily life has had a bigger impact on how I cook at home than almost anything else. There’s a lot of pasta on the menu these days, and potato wedges with different sauces. A lot of meatballs. And a great manypancakes– more than I would have ever predicted before I had kids.My weekend pancakes – which made their way into my bookSimple Too– are supposed to be a batch-cooking exercise: lots made on Sunday, then reheated through the week, in the toaster or a dry pan on the stove, so breakfast is more or less solved until Friday. That’s the theory. In practice, all 22 pancakes the recipe makes are gone by Sunday lunch – eaten by the boys, their friends, or whoever happens to be over for breakfast.double quotation markI love having friends over and what I want is something so they can help themselvesBut my kitchen on a weekend morning doesn’t only answer to my kids, even though that’s their indisputable assumption. I love having friends over for brunch, and what I actually want, most weeks, is one big thing in the middle of the table – generously for everyone. So they can help themselves and I’m not the only one standing after everyone else has sat down.Like the butter beans with Urfa chilli butter, with toast, bacon and semi-hard-boiled eggs. Or a big tray of bakedza’atartomatoes and mascarpone, with some sausages and sourdough. Or a big pan ofmenemen(Turkish scrambled eggs) with a leaf salad and a few slices of avocado.I feed a lot of people – with the things I really want to eat and without too much fuss: that’s the idea. Here are some of the breakfasts and brunches in Simple Too – for you, your hungry family and all your breakfast guests.MenemenView image in fullscreenFood styling: Alice Wood.Photograph: Jonathan LovekinMenemenis a Turkish breakfast dish: scrambled eggs, spices, tomatoes. Simple! It’s the most comforting of all ways to start – or end – the day. The key is to add the eggs off the heat, so that they cook gently in the residual warmth of the pan. Serve with buttered toast or a leafy salad with slices of avocado.Prep5 minsCook15 minsServes24 eggs3 tbsp olive oil1 onion,finely chopped (160g)3 garlic cloves,crushed1 tsp cumin seeds½ tsp Aleppo chilli flakes½ tsp ground cinnamon½ tbsp tomato paste300g cherry tomatoes,halved1 tbsp double cream5g coriander leaves,roughly choppedFine sea saltBright and breezy: Yotam Ottolenghi on simple summer entertainingRead morePut the eggs into a bowl with half a teaspoon of salt. Lightly beat, just to break up the yolks, and set aside.Put the oil into a medium frying pan on a medium-high heat. Add the onion and garlic and cook for five minutes, stirring a few times, until softened and starting to colour. Add the spices, tomato paste and an eighth of a teaspoon of salt and cook for two minutes, until fragrant. Add the tomatoes and 60ml of water, then cook, uncovered, for 10 minutes until the tomatoes have broken down. Squish them with the back of a spoon if they need a bit of help.Remove from the heat and swirl in the eggs, using a wooden spoon or spatula and moving the pan gently until just set. Spoon over the cream, sprinkle over the coriander and serve straight from the pan.Coconut greens with Scotch bonnet and eggsView image in fullscreenFood styling: Alice Wood.Photograph: Jonathan LovekinThis recipe is inspired by the Trinidadian bhaji, which Milli Taylor, my test kitchen colleague, first discovered through her friend, the chef and food writer Shivi Ramoutar. Traditionally, these braised greens are served alongside rice and dal as a main meal, but we think they are equally delicious with the addition of eggs for breakfast. Play around with whatever greens are in season. Chard is great – just make sure you chop the stems and add them before the leaves, at the same time as the onions.Prep5 minsCook25 minsServes43 tbsp olive oil1 small onion,thinly sliced (150g)2 tsp cumin seeds,lightly crushed1 Scotch bonnet pepper (or regular red chilli),pierced a few times with a knife4 garlic cloves,crushed400g baby spinach leaves400ml tin of coconut milk6 eggsFine sea salt and black pepperHeat the oil in a large saute pan on a medium-high heat. Add the onion and three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt and cook for about eight minutes, stirring often, until softened and golden. Add the cumin, Scotch bonnet, garlic and lots of pepper and cook for another minute. Add the spinach, in two or three batches, and cook for about three minutes until wilted. Add the coconut milk, bring to a simmer and cook for 10 minutes, until the sauce has thickened and reduced slightly.Use a spoon to make six wells in the mixture and crack one egg into each. Sprinkle the eggs with salt and pepper, cover, and cook for a further four to five minutes, until the whites are set but the yolks are still runny. Serve straight from the pan.Getting aheadIf you want to get everything ready in advance, the dish can be prepared up to the point just before the eggs are cracked in.Weekend pancakes with date butter syrupView image in fullscreenFood styling: Alice Wood.Photograph: Jonathan LovekinThis is a much-loved recipe used in our London delis. Once made, these fluffy pancakes keep well in the fridge for up to three days (or longer in the freezer), ready to be reheated in the toaster or in a dry pan on the stove. That’s why we suggest making a pretty big batch at the weekend to eat throughout the week.Prep10 minsCook25 mins total(2–3 minutes per batch)MakesAbout 22 pancakesFor the pancakes350ml buttermilk3 eggs,2 whole, 1 white70g unsalted butter,melted1 tsp vanilla bean paste or extract250g plain flour40g caster sugar2 tsp baking powder½ tsp bicarbonate of sodavegetable oil,for fryingFine sea saltFor the date butter syrup75g date molasses75g unsalted butter,cut into small cubesIn a jug, whisk together the buttermilk, whole eggs, egg white, melted butter and vanilla. If you don’t have buttermilk, make your own by adding 25ml of lemon juice or white wine vinegar to 325ml of whole milk and setting aside for 15 minutes to curdle.Whisk together the dry ingredients and three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt in a large bowl. Make a well in the centre and pour in the egg mixture. Whisk until just combined – do not over-mix: a few small lumps here and there are fine – then set aside for five minutes to thicken.Meanwhile, put the date molasses, an eighth of a teaspoon of salt and 2 tablespoons of water into a small saucepan on a medium heat. Bring to a simmer and whisk in the butter, a couple of pieces at a time, until emulsified. Keep warm.Place a large non-stick frying pan on a medium heat. Once hot, brush with oil and drop 3–4 large tablespoonfuls of batter, evenly spaced apart, into the pan. Cook for two to three minutes, until the batter has risen and you can see small bubbles on the surface. Flip the pancakes and cook for another 30–60 seconds, until springy to the touch. Transfer to a wire rack (or keep warm in a low oven) and continue with the remaining batter. Serve with the date butter syrup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBaked za’atar tomatoes and mascarponeView image in fullscreenFood styling: Alice Wood.Photograph: Jonathan LovekinThese are inspired by Simon Hopkinson’s creamed tomatoes on toast, from his classic cookbookRoast Chicken and Other Stories. Use any ripe tomatoes: this is a great opportunity to use up whatever you happen to have lying around – all shapes and sizes are welcome. They are best served hot.Prep5 minsCook25 minsServes6300g mascarpone50ml double cream3 garlic cloves,1 crushed, 2 thinly sliced2 tsp cornflour600g ripe tomatoes,halved, quartered or thickly sliced (depending on size)1 tbsp za’atar1½ tbsp olive oil1 tsp thyme leavesFine sea salt and black pepperPreheat the oven to 220C (200C fan/425F/gas 7).Mix together the mascarpone, cream, crushed garlic, cornflour and a quarter of a teaspoon of salt in a large, round baking dish (26-28cm). Smooth the surface and arrange the tomatoes on top, cut side up. Season with a quarter of a teaspoon of salt and plenty of pepper, and scatter over the za’atar and sliced garlic. Drizzle with 1 tablespoon of oil and bake for about 25 minutes, until the tomatoes are tender and the cream is golden and bubbling round the edges. Leave to rest for five minutes.Serve with the remaining half a tablespoon of oil and some thyme sprinkled on top.Everyday granolaView image in fullscreenFood styling: Alice Wood.Photograph: Jonathan LovekinWe get spoiled in the test kitchen whenever my co-author Verena Lochmuller brings in one of her weekend “projects”. In fact, we’ve come to rely on them on a Monday morning. This granola came about this way. For the sake of simplicity, Verena had to trim down the ingredient list. That was somewhat painful, but you are more than welcome to start adding your favourites back in. Just take your pick from almonds, pecans, walnuts, ground cinnamon or ginger, or any dried fruit, stirred through once cooled. This granola is good for every occasion, even spooned over ice-cream. Make a big batch. It keeps for at least six weeks in an airtight container.Prep5 minsCook1 hr 15 minsMakesAbout 800g275g jumbo rolled oats150g blanched hazelnuts25g sesame seeds50g pumpkin seeds50g sunflower seeds110ml olive oil85g demerara sugar85ml maple syrup3 tbsp tahini1–2 very ripe bananas,finely mashed(150g)2 tsp vanilla bean paste or extractFine sea saltPreheat the oven to 160C (140C fan)/325F/gas 3.Combine the oats, nuts, seeds and half a teaspoon of salt in a large bowl.Put the oil, sugar and maple syrup into a small saucepan on a medium-low heat. Cook for about five minutes, whisking occasionally, until the sugar has melted (the oil might be separated on top, but that’s OK). Whisk in the tahini, banana and vanilla until combined, then pour over the oat mixture. Stir well and spread out on a large parchment-lined baking tray. Bake for about 1 hour and 10 minutes, stirring every 15 to 20 minutes, until browned and starting to crisp up. Leave to cool completely.Crisp up further before transferring to a jar or airtight container.Butter beans with Urfa chilli butterView image in fullscreenFood styling: Alice Wood.Photograph: Jonathan LovekinThis dish is for all the butter addicts – the word even appears twice in the title. The beans become so creamy and buttery that you’ll want to spoon them straight on to toast with nothing else.Prep5 minsCook15 minsServes450g unsalted butter1 tsp Urfa chilli flakes1 preserved lemon,seeds removed, finely chopped (20g)2 tsp lemon juice1 onion,thinly sliced (160g)2 garlic cloves,crushed1 tbsp biber salçasi (Turkish red pepper paste),mild or hot (or tomato paste with a pinch each of sugar and dried chilli flakes)1 tsp ground cumin1 tbsp double cream700g jar of butter beans,with the liquid, or 2 x 400g tinsFlaked sea saltPut 30g of butter into a small saucepan and place over a high heat. Cook, swirling the pan occasionally, for two to three minutes, until nutty and deeply brown. Take off the heat, carefully add the chilli flakes, preserved lemon and lemon juice, and set aside.For the beans, add the remaining 20g of butter to a large frying pan and place over a medium-high heat. When hot, add the onion and fry for about seven minutes, stirring occasionally, until starting to caramelise. Lower the heat to medium, add the garlic,biber salçasiand cumin, and cook for one minute. Add the cream, beans (including the liquid) and 60ml of water. Cook for about five minutes, until the liquid has thickened and lightly coats the beans.Drizzle over the Urfa butter, add a pinch of flaked sea salt and serve straight from the pan.Note on the ingredientsThe rest of the jar ofbiber salçasican be used in any recipe that calls for regular tomato paste – it adds a little more depth and flavour. Keep the jar in the fridge once opened.Ottolenghi Simple Too by Yotam Ottolenghi and Verena Lochmuller is published by Ebury (£30). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
