title: Remaking the biscuit: from Doritos to digestives, why the UK’s snacks are being ‘reformulated’ | Food | The Guardian
description: Healthy eating rules are forcing brands to recook their recipes. Are consumers noticing the difference?
Author: Sarah Marsh
Headline: Healthy eating rules are forcing brands to recook their recipes. Are consumers noticing the difference?
Content: The RSSL lab testing the break of a biscuit.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe RSSL lab testing the break of a biscuit.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianFoodRemaking the biscuit: from Doritos to digestives, why the UK’s snacks are being ‘reformulated’Healthy eating rules are forcing brands to recook their recipes. Are consumers noticing the difference?Sarah MarshConsumer affairs correspondentSat 29 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBite into a Ritz cracker today and you’re eating 80% less saturated fat than you would have been just a few years ago. The biscuit looks and snaps the same, and tastes close enough that most buyers have no idea they’re eating a new recipe.One of the biggest changes was swapping palm oil for sunflower oil, but there was much more to it than that. The reformulation took years to perfect in a laboratory, where scientists tested everything from density to how the cracker responds to heat, moisture and packaging.Everything you need to know about sugar – from how much you should consume, to some of its 50 disguisesRead moreIt’s a story playing out across an entire industry. From Doritos to digestives, Britain’s best-loved snacks have been re-engineered, gram by gram, to meet stricter government rules on foods high in fat, sugar and salt. BelVita’s soft bakes range, including its bestselling choc chip and choc hazelnut flavours, has been reformulated to fall outside the “less healthy” category, with sodium cut by 56%.Since January 2026, paid-for advertising of high-fat, salt and sugar (HFSS) products was banned online entirely. Now the industry faces a fresh problem: the government is reviewing the formula that decides which foods count as “less healthy” in the first place.Foodcompanies warn the changes could undo years of work overnight – the Food and Drink Federation estimates 80% of reformulated products could fail under the new model, particularly on sugar.Where the recipes get rewrittenEarlier this month at the Reading Scientific Services Ltd (RSSL) – the lab where, for many of Britain’s snack foods, recipes go to get rebuilt – that tension is being discussed. Mondelēz International, the global food and beverage giant behind Oreo and Ritz, has invested £40m since 2020 in reformulation work.The UK is now the company’s largest research and development hub anywhere in the world, with more than 750 scientists and engineers working across nutrition and product innovation at Bournville consumer research centre and RSSL.View image in fullscreenThe RSSL kitchen and lab in Reading, where many of Britain’s snack foods are tested.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianThe government is proposing a tougher Nutrient Profiling Model (NPM), including stricter thresholds for free sugars and greater weighting for fibre. The changes could mean some products that manufacturers have already changed to reduce sugar are classified as “less healthy”, potentially bringing them within advertising and promotion restrictions.Jacinta George, managing director at RSSL, says the current nutrient profiling model, drawn up in 2018, counts “free sugars” against a product’s score but there’s no settled definition of what that term actually means.“The inclusion of free sugars in the 2018 NPM model is incredibly challenging for manufacturers, as there is no universally agreed definition of what a free sugar is,” George says. “There is also no standardised laboratory method for distinguishing between intrinsic and free sugars.”Swapping out sugar isn’t as simple as removing it, either. “Sugar does more than sweeten – it provides texture, bulk and preservation,” George says. “Sweeteners provide sweetness but not these other qualities, meaning additional bulking agents or functional ingredients may be needed. This can increase processing, and potentially conflict with consumer demand for simpler formulations.”The science of taking a cracker apartReformulation at RSSL runs through several disciplines in sequence. Kerry Tanner, a group leader on the product development team, works on ingredients first – often starting with sauces and cooking bases, where salt reduction is a frequent target. “If we’re trying to reduce the score, we might be working on a sauce, and we’re trying to reduce the salt,” she says. “We used a natural alternative to salt that has a lower sodium content.” Because sauces already carry complex layers of flavour, she adds, a modest cut often goes unnoticed by the consumer. RSSL also draws on a network of culinary chefs, who work alongside the product developers on new formulations.Next comes texture – the domain of specialist Emma Nelson, whose job is making sure a reformulated product still behaves the way people expect. Complaints, she notes, can come down to something as small as how quickly a biscuit softens in tea. Every reformulated product goes through stability testing, checking shelf life and structural performance under different conditions once ingredients change. The team frequently turns to 3D printing to build physical models of a product’s internal structure, allowing them to take it apart and reassemble it to study how it holds together.Downstairs, an industrial CT scanner takes that analysis further. As colleague George Middleton explains, the machine fires X-rays through a sample; denser materials absorb more energy, and thousands of rotating scans are stitched together into a full 3D dataset of the product’s internal structure. BelVita went through the same process during its own reformulation.The problem with chocolateNot every attempt to reimagine a snack succeeds and chocolate bars have proven the hardest category of all. When Mondelēz launched Cadbury Dairy Milk with 30%less sugar shoppers didn’t buy it.The product, along with Cadbury Dairy Milk Fruitier and Nuttier, was pulled from shelves after poor sales.View image in fullscreenSome Cadbury Dairy Milk products with 30% less sugar were pulled from the shelves after poor sales.Photograph: Carolyn Jenkins/AlamySo the company has shifted its strategy, leaning on portion control instead of ingredient substitution. Freddo, Curly Wurly and Chomp – thebars most likely to end up in a child’s hand– are kept under 100 kcal. Multipacks stay under 200 kcal per product, and single bars under 250. Chocolate brings its own added constraint too: to legally carry the name, a product has to contain a minimum amount of cacao, which limits how far any recipe can be pushed.The looming challengeFor all the lab hours and investment, the industry’s biggest worry isn’t scientific – it’s regulatory uncertainty. Kate Halliwell of the Food and Drink Federation says companies need a stable target to aim at, because reformulation is a slow process. “It’s from signing off investment – you’re probably looking at a couple of years to get something actually through and into market,” she says.That’s what makes a shifting NPM formula so alarming to manufacturers, particularly paired with the ban on HFSS advertising. “I think companies can’t really see how they can do it,” Halliwell says. “If you’re going to invest to make a healthier product, but at the end of it you can’t promote or advertise it, then it’s unlikely that it will actually succeed on shelf. People won’t know to choose it or try it. And they’re more likely to fail. That’s a really big concern for companies.”But others disagree. Sonia Pombo, head of research and impact at Action on Salt & Sugar, says the “goalposts” cannot be fixed “forever”. She added that the current Nutrient Profiling Model is “more than 20 years old, and the updated model better reflects the latest evidence”.She said the industry “has known that changes to the model were being considered for many years, having first been consulted on it in 2018, so this should come as no surprise.”Pombo said reformulation and a lowering of sugar should be celebrated but “where unnecessary levels remain, further reductions should be encouraged.” She added: “Protecting past reformulation efforts cannot take precedence over continuing to improve the nutritional quality of the food we eat.”Explore more on these topicsFoodHealthConsumer affairsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meera Sodha’s recipe for spicy mozzarella, green bean and edamame salad | Vegetables | The Guardian
description: An enticing, slightly spicy, east/west fusion stacked with vigour and colour
Author: Meera Sodha
Headline: An enticing, slightly spicy, east/west fusion stacked with vigour and colour
Content: Meera Sodha’s spicy mozzarella, green bean and edamame salad.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.View image in fullscreenMeera Sodha’s spicy mozzarella, green bean and edamame salad.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.Meera Sodha recipesVegetablesMeera Sodha’s recipe for spicy mozzarella, green bean and edamame saladAn enticing, slightly spicy, east/west fusion stacked with vigour and colourMeera SodhaSat 29 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne thing I learned during the recent hot weather is that I don’t have enough “substantial but quick salads” in my locker. A salad one could call lunch (or a light dinner when served with other bits). On rotation in my “throw-together” category is myno-cook chickpea, tomato and cucumber salad, to which I’m also going to add my favouritesummer vegetable, bulgur and pesto salad, which isn’t quite an assembly job, but near-enough and a family favourite. To that line-up, I’m happy to introduce this gently spicy, green beauty.Spicy mozzarella, green bean and edamame saladMy recipe tester, Hannah, and I disagree on how much mozzarella a person can eat. I like a whole ball to myself, she prefers a half-ball. Adjust as you see fit.Prep10 minCook20 minServes21 tbsp rapeseed oil250g green beans, topped150g frozen edamame beans, defrosted100g frozen petit pois, defrosted2½ tbsp toasted sesame oil3 garlic cloves, peeled and minced1 tbsp sambal oelek1 tbsp light soy sauce½ tbsp light agave syrup½ tsp brown or red miso15g fresh mint, leaves picked and chopped2125g mozzarella ballsPut the rapeseed oil in a wide frying pan on a medium to high heat. Test the heat with a wooden spoon – when it’s hot enough, bubbles should form around the bottom of the spoon. Add the green beans to the pan, spacing them out, and leave for two minutes. Turn the beans, leave for another two minutes, then turn again and cook for a further two minutes, until blistered or blackened in places. Transfer the beans to a large bowl, then add the edamame beans and petit pois to the same bowl.To make the dressing, put the sesame oil in the same pan on a low to medium heat and, when it’s hot, add the garlic and stir for a minute. Add the sambal oelek, light soy sauce, agave and miso, stir well, cook for up to a minute, then take off the heat.Pour the dressing into the bean bowl, mix well to coat, then fold in the chopped mint.To serve, use tongs (or two forks) to lift the greens on to a platter, leaving behind the dressing. Tear open the mozzarella, arrange on top, then pour any remaining dressing over the cheese and salad.Explore more on these topicsVegetablesMeera Sodha recipesFoodSaladCheeseMain courseStarterHerbs and spicesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Households could save up to £173 a year by switching to fixed energy deal | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: Moving tariffs will cushion the blow from the October price cap rise and the increase widely predicted for January
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Moving tariffs will cushion the blow from the October price cap rise and the increase widely predicted for January
Content: Gas and electricity prices will rise by 4% from 1 October under the new cap.Photograph: Alamy/PAView image in fullscreenGas and electricity prices will rise by 4% from 1 October under the new cap.Photograph: Alamy/PAEnergy billsHouseholds could save up to £173 a year by switching to fixed energy dealMoving tariffs will cushion the blow from the October price cap rise and the increase widely predicted for JanuaryRupert JonesSat 29 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith higher energy bills looming and warnings of worse to come in the new year, many households could save up to £173 a year by switching to a fixed deal.Millions of households in Great Britain will facethe highest energy charges in three yearsafter it was announced that the government’s price cap will rise again in October. This will be the second increase in three months.However, moving to a fixed tariff would enable people to avoid this increase and one that has been widely predicted for January. These tariffs offer a set standing charge and unit costs for a certain period; often one or two years.No more UK energy bills support likely before price cap riseRead moreGas and electricity prices will rise by 4% from 1 October under the new cap, after climbing 13% at the start of July. This will take the rate for 22 million households on default tariffs to the equivalent of £1,723 a year, based on typical gas and electricity usage, and will kick in just as many people will probably be turning the heating back on.However, even the energy regulator for Great Britain,Ofgem, has gone into Martin Lewis mode, extolling the money-saving benefits offered by a fixed tariff.“Savings are available by choosing a fixed tariff, which are available at £100 or more below the October price cap,” it says.View image in fullscreenSwitching deals is one way to trim your energy bills, but Ofgem says the best way to keep bills under control is to cut your energy use wherever possible.Photograph: Alamy/PAAbout 11m homes (35% of the total) are already on fixed tariffs and will not be affected by the rise announced this week. They will be protected from price increases until their current deal comes to an end.Price comparison websites say many households could save decent sums by switching to one of the cheapest fixed energy tariffs on the market.Doing a quick check using one of these sites will show you what is available for your household based on your personal usage.At the time of writing there were plenty of fixed energy deals available that beat the new October figure, “offering households certainty over what they’ll pay through the coldest months, regardless of what happens to wholesale prices”, says Uswitch.com.The cheapest is a fixed tariff from Fuse Energy priced at £1,550 a year for a typical-usage home – which is £173 below the October cap figure, and £113 below the current cap. This deal is available in various forms: there is one that lasts for 14 months – Fuse Energy August 2026 Fixed (14m) V1 – being offered by Uswitch and Confused.com, as well as Fuse Energy itself.Meanwhile, MoneySuperMarket offers a version of it that is fixed for 18 months, called Fuse Energy August 2026 Fixed (18m) V10.There are several other fixed deals available from suppliers including Co-op Energy, Octopus Energy, E.ON Next and Ecotricity that offer people typical savings (versus the October price cap) of more than £100 a year. Some of these deals are exclusive to one or more comparison sites but in many cases you can get them direct from the supplier.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAbout 11m households are already on fixed tariffsPhotograph: David J Green/AlamyThe advice to consider switching to a fixed tariff has been given extra weight by the prediction that the pain is only going to get worse.According to analysts at Cornwall Insight, bills are forecast to rise by a further 9% in January, just when temperatures may be at their lowest. If that happens, the typical household bill will climb by £149 to about £1,872 a year. However, the January 2027 figure will not be confirmed until November, and a lot could happen between now and then.Before you switch, you will need to check how long remains on your contract and whether there are any exit fees, says Gareth Kloet at Go.Compare.October’s cap would have been even higher if the government had not announced atemporary VAT cuton domestic electricity. This will reduce the tax from 5% to zero between 1 October this year and 31 March 2027, resulting in a £45 a year saving for a typical household (this has been reflected in the new cap).The VAT cut will benefit those currently on fixed tariffs as well as those whose bills are pegged to the price cap – the discount will be automatically applied to people’s accounts by suppliers.Many suppliers offer tariffs with cheaper electricity to smart meter customers for power consumed outside of peak times, says Ofgem, so it is worth asking about those.Because the price cap is based on typical usage, aside from shopping around for a better deal, the best way to keep bills under control is to cut your energy use wherever possible.You may want to check to see if you qualify for help, says Sarah Coles at the investment platform AJ Bell. Initiatives include thewarm home discount scheme, which will reopen in October and is a one-off £150 discount off your electricity bill.Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsEnergy industryOfgemConsumer affairsHousehold billsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It gives Shein’: how did polyester become the world’s most-hated material? | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Due to its ubiquity in fast fashion, gen Z are pushing back against the synthetic material and using it as an insult
Author: Hannah Marriott
Headline: Due to its ubiquity in fast fashion, gen Z are pushing back against the synthetic material and using it as an insult
Content: ‘I think the hatred towards polyester is more indicative of everyone being dissatisfied with the choices available to them,’ says Ione Gamble, editor of Polyester zine.Photograph: luanateutzi/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘I think the hatred towards polyester is more indicative of everyone being dissatisfied with the choices available to them,’ says Ione Gamble, editor of Polyester zine.Photograph: luanateutzi/Getty Images/iStockphotoFashion‘It gives Shein’: how did polyester become the world’s most-hated material?Due to its ubiquity in fast fashion, gen Z are pushing back against the synthetic material and using it as an insultHannah MarriottSat 29 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2015, Kate Moss called an easyJet pilot a “basic bitch” and a catchy new insult meaning obvious and uncoolhit the mainstream. Had it happened in 2026, Moss might have used the word “polyester”,reportedlygen Z’s new favorite diss, levied at cheap-looking videos on TikTok, and sometimes at other users’ taste.But its use as a figurative insult also echoes a literal backlash against polyester, now the most-produced synthetic fibre on the planet.Young people are pushing back against polyester, many of them expressing concern about cheap-looking garments, sweaty-feeling fabrics and concern about what wearing polyester may be doing to their health (though the science is still developing, studies suggest that the dyes, flame retardant and “sweat-wicking” chemicals frequently used on synthetic fabricscan leach into sweaty skin, a particular concern for workout clothes.)In gyms, the pilates princess aesthetic with its synthetic matching sets is waning while 1990s-style exercise gear is becoming fashionable once more as manylionize exercise garments displaying visible sweat– think Sylvester Stallone in Rocky, or John Travolta being sweatily hypnotized by Jamie Lee Curtis’s rocking pelvis in the 1985 movie Perfect.View image in fullscreenJamie Lee Curtis in James Bridges’ Perfect (1985).Photograph: Columbia Pictures/AllstarSome of the pushback centres around polyester’s impact on the planet. Derived from fossil fuels, it does not biodegrade, and sheds microplastics when washed. Many anti-polyester influencers, however, talk about giving up the fabric in the same way they might talk about giving up sugar, sharing content with hashtags such as #naturalfibers, #antipolyester and #nontoxicclothing while posting videos of large shopping hauls of cotton and linen from Zara.There is a Maha element too. The USDA recently launched a Plant Not Plastic initiative, attempting to revitalize American cotton, stating that US farmers have been “crushed by rising costs, unfair foreign competition, and a flood of cheap synthetic products” for too long. RFK Jr shared campaign imagery – featuring blue jean-wearing, horse-riding outdoorsy types – in May, along with the strapline: “Real Americans wear cotton.”Before you throw out all the synthetic fabrics in your closet, read thisRead moreMuch online backlash is about fakeness, a perception that fashion brands are catfishing their customers by selling good-looking garments online that look and feel nasty in real life, as was illustrated by a recent furore over a capsule collection inspired by Gap’s much-loved 1990s Happy Stripe sweaters. Part of its higher-end Gap Studio range, the garments, which that cost up to $128 sold out quickly online. But the backlash came when shoppers received their packages. Many had assumed the items were knitted, but instead, they featured a printed photograph of a knit thatone TikTokuser described as “fake knitting! It just looks horrible!” And with the fabric being 80% polyester and 20% elastane, she continued, you would be “literally wrapped in a sheet of plastic” during “one of the hottest summers on record”.“GivesSheinunfortunately,” said another customer, in reference to the Chinese ultra-fast fashion company which is, indeed, very cheap and very polyester; looking at the fabric content of the first 10 dresses served to me on their site, nine were polyester.Though Shein’s appeal may be waning – it was valued at $100bn in 2022 but is now preparing tolist on the Hong Kong stock exchangefor a quarter of that, $27bn – that decline seems to have less to do with any lack of demand for cheap clothes produced dubiously, and more to do with the rise of similar “polyester” (gen Z meaning intended) offerings at Temu, Amazon and other Shein-esque challenger brands, as well as its struggle to keep prices quite as low owing to Donald Trump’s trade policies.One byproduct of Shein’s recent ubiquity, however, is that it has made other fast fashion brands – the kind that charge, say, $79.90 for a dress, as opposed to Shein’s absurd $9.22 – look mid-market in the eyes of young customers. Some gen Z – usually defined as those born between 1997 and 2012 (the oldest of them will turn 30 next year) – are vocal about expecting better than Shein when paying higher than Shein prices. And one of the ways they judge whether an item’s quality is higher is by checking whether it contains polyester.View image in fullscreenA 1975 Playboy magazine advert features a double-knit polyester set.Photograph: Patti McConville/AlamyGen Z may think they invented the use of “polyester” as an insult, but the word has potent previous form as a cultural diss. At Studio 54 in the late 1970s, for example, when the nightclub was the center of contemporary fashion and music culture, there was an anti-polyester policy.“We didn’t want people with polyester shirts,” co-founder Ian Schrager remembered a 2018 documentary. His business partner, Steve Rubell associated it with “bridge-and-tunnel people” – meaning suburbanites sporting “the chains, the polyester shirts, the hairy chests”, he said. Their presence, Rubell said, would “kill the night”.Polyester was already omnipresent in fashion, having found favor with American households in the 1950s, when it was heralded as a labor-saving miracle: the fashion equivalent of a TV dinner. It was easy to clean, didn’t require ironing because it did not wrinkle, was attractive to designers because it can be moulded, dyed and made to ape properties of other, more expensive, fabrics. It was intrinsic to the aesthetic of the 1960s for its ability to absorb bright dyes; it was infused with Lycra around the same time women abandoned their girdles.View image in fullscreenTab Hunter and Divine in John Waters’ Polyester (1981).Photograph: New Line/AllstarIn many ways it was perfect for the 1970s disco era of hot lights and dancing – but that era exposed its disadvantages too. Stories of polyester wrap dresses catching on fire on the Studio 54 dancefloor (or so Randy Jones, the Village People’s original cowboy, told the Wall Street Journal in 2008) and there was much talk of overheating. Gloria Gaynor said that polyester “was gross. It was horrible. It was just so cheesy,” and that she had to leave her polyester jacket open on stage to let in some air while she performed. John Travolta’s famous Saturday Night Fever white polyester suit, chosen, according to the movie’s costume designer, because it looked like something a working-class kid could afford, was so sweat-soaked he had to keep rotating between two identical suits,giving the other time to dry.Polyester’s status as a byword for sweaty naffness was cemented with the 1981 release of John Waters’ cult hit movie of the same name, which was a satire of suburban life, featuring a polyester-clad loutish husband and a set dressed with “the ugliest polyester furniture we could find”, as Waters put it.Though its image has been less than aspirational for decades, polyester has only grown more commonplace since.Its versatility means that it has always been part of high catwalk style – Lanvin’s Alber Elbaz put posh polyester frocks for thousands of dollars on the catwalk in the mid-aughts, and you can buy a luxe 11% elastane and 89% recycledpolyester shirt from Pradatoday if you have a spare $3,000 – though the real boom has been in cheap clothing.View image in fullscreenA polyester-silk combine in Dimitrovgrad, Bulgaria, 1980.Photograph: Brandstaetter Images/Getty ImagesIt first overtook cotton in popularity in 2000,according to one analysis, and it has mushroomed ever since. In 2024, a report found thatfashion’s overall carbon footprint had risen, for the first time since 2019, fueled by a rise in polyester use, which was up from 71m to 78m tonnes in one year, owing to the boom of ultra-rapid fashion.In reality, polyester use is so entrenched that the viral backlash is only going so far. H&M told the Guardian its polyester use has been fairly static over recent years (it uses 56% cotton and 23% recycled polyester) – though its use of recycled materials had risen and was at 100% recycled for polyester (which is better for the environment, as it is not made from virgin fossil fuels, thoughhow much better has been debated).Edited, a retail intelligence platform, analysed the new polyester offerings on the websites of Nike, Urban Outfitters and Zara at this time during the past three years. It found that polyester use was down by about 3% overall at Nike, but at Urban Outfitters, polyester was up 1% year on year. There was a similar story at Zara, which had risen 1.9%. (Meanwhile, recycled polyester was down 2.6% at Urban Outfitters and 0.5% at Zara, respectively.) The findings, said Edited senior retail analyst Krista Corrigan, showed that “mass-market fashion remains structurally reliant on polyester to maintain margins”. What is changing is the way “brands are actively highlighting natural fibres in product titles to appeal to material-conscious shoppers” with product names using the word “cotton” up 28% at Zara and 30% up at Urban Outfitters year on year, Corrigan said.That shift suggests that the appetite for natural fibres is driving some customers to shop differently – a big reason the direct-to-consumer brand Quince, which was recently valued at $10.1bn, has flourished. Its entire USP is about fabric (its meta description on Google says it offers “luxury products like Mongolian Cashmere, Italian Leather, Turkish Cotton and Washable Silk to everyone at radically low prices”), which gives it an aura of sustainability, compared with, say, Shein, even if the Good on You directory of ethical fashion classifies it as “not good enough” because, while it uses “some lower-impact materials including organic cotton”, it does not release enough information about its environmental and labour policies.View image in fullscreenIone Gamble, the editor of Polyester zine, in her London flat in 2022.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The ObserverThe realities of ethical clothing production and use are far more complex than avoiding polyester. Choosing cotton and wool, for instance, may feel more natural, but they often have huge environmental impacts too, including astonishing water use.Ione Gamble, founding editor-in-chief of the influential zine Polyester and author ofThe Polyester Book of (Bad) Taste, chose the word when she launched in 2014, partly in tribute to Waters partly from a desire to “rebut ideas about ‘good taste’”, she said. “I wanted to create a publication that celebrated the things we consider to be in bad taste while also interrogating the sociopolitical implications of why some things are labelled as tasteful and others as trashy.”While she thinks criticisms of polyester are valid, she points how tempting and easy it is for people to parrot a line without fully understanding the nuance. “By all means I’m anti-mass-produced, cheaply made clothes but I think the hatred towards polyester is more indicative of everyone being dissatisfied with the choices available to them, rather than a full understanding of polyester itself.”Explore more on these topicsFashionYoung peopleFashion industrySheinRetail industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A slow travel success story in Slovenia’s secret valley | Slovenia holidays | The Guardian
description: Tourism is only just taking hold in Vipava, but the locals are determined to do it right, by putting community first and preserving what makes it special
Author: Ailsa Sheldon
Headline: Tourism is only just taking hold in Vipava, but the locals are determined to do it right, by putting community first and preserving what makes it special
Content: Vipava is a landscape shaped by a strong wind, theburja, which creates the perfect terrain for dry winesView image in fullscreenVipava is a landscape shaped by a strong wind, theburja, which creates the perfect terrain for dry winesSlovenia holidaysA slow travel success story in Slovenia’s secret valleyTourism is only just taking hold in Vipava, but the locals are determined to do it right, by putting community first and preserving what makes it specialAilsa SheldonSat 29 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe drive to Pedrovo is vertiginous, and each hairpin bend has me sending a silent prayer that we won’t meet a tractor coming the other way. When we near it, we abandon the car and continue on foot to the hamlet, a scattering of red-roofed, whitewashed houses high on the steep karst hillside. The air is warm and dry, scented with wild sage.We follow a hand-painted sign to Čilčevi Farmstead. Descending stone steps to a lush garden, we find a shaded table set with fresh cheeses produced at the farm’s own dairy. Below, the valley stretches in both directions, a wide flat plain hemmed in by steep mountain slopes, with the Vipava River winding lazily through fields and vineyards.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian GraphicsIf the Vipava valley gets a mention in a Slovenian guidebook, it’s usually as a wine region footnote. The area is an hour’s drive south-west of Ljubljana, meeting Italy at thecross-border city of Nova Gorica (called Gorizia on the Italian side). Most visitors skip it in favour of the Soča valley to the north, drawn to the turquoise river and opportunities for rafting on the rapids.Vipava is a landscape shaped by a strong wind, theburja, which barrels down from the Alps, keeping the red earth arid, the trees bent low, and creating the perfect terrain for dry wines and dried meats. Tourism has traditionally been less of a focus, but I’m here with my family to meet local entrepreneurs and producers, to learn how this valley is building a genuine visitor experience that works for the community.Part of the reason for the slow development of tourism has been the scarcity of accommodation, save a few nondescript business hotels and a handful of holiday cottages. One place that’s helping change that narrative isWellba, a boutique guesthouse in the village of Planina, where an old abandoned farmstead has been converted into self-catering apartments and guest rooms by a local couple, working with traditional craftspeople and salvaged materials.View image in fullscreenMarko and Tereza Kobal run the boutique Wellba hotel in PlaninaMarko and Tereza Kobal grew up on this hillside and then worked in Ljubljana before deciding to return to build a family business, striving to create the kind of place they seek out when travelling. “People who travel want to experience something that is just the way it is, without embellishment, pretence, exaggeration – somewhere authentic,” says Marko. We enter Wellba through a traditional “black kitchen”, its walls darkened by generations of wood smoke. “When we came here the building needed work but it had a real soul. We want the building to stand for another 300 years, so we took the renovation slowly and carefully.”Our light, spacious accommodation wears its history lightly, with plenty of space for playing card games and reading books on the balcony, with views of the neighbouring farmyard and the valley beyond. Next door, another tumble-down farm building will be converted and opened in 2027. The couple are also working on a boutique hotel in Vipava town in the valley below. The dream is for their children to run Wellba one day, forging their futures in this valley.Across Vipava, similar small projects are emerging: small, family-run and developing slowly and thoughtfully. Tom Ločniškar and Borut Kokalj beganČilčevi Farmsteadduring the pandemic, having moved to Pedrovo and become interested in farming. “We started to keep animals. Now we have 150, which is too many animals for just a hobby,” laughs Tom.View image in fullscreenFresh cheeses at the Čilčevi Farmstead dairy in Pedrovo.Photograph: Ailsa Sheldon/The GuardianHe recalls the mad panic to source equipment before the lockdowns began. The pandemic also brought him his first customers, people who were out walking and keen to support local businesses. Tom and Borut keep local Istrska sheep and Drežnica goats, which graze on dry karst grasslands, changing pastures across this hillside every four days. Having tasted fresh cheese straight from the chill of the dairy, including creamy goat’s cheese with fenugreek and buttery mature sheep’s cheese, we walk uphill to meet the goats.Tom says that in the early 1900s around 1,000 people lived in Pedrovo, but by the 1970s the permanent population had fallen to just two, and remained that low until the 1990s. “The village was almost abandoned because people moved to the cities,” he says. “It was the same in a lot of hill villages: life was hard and tractors didn’t work on steep slopes.” Today the population has risen to 20, with second homeowners roughly doubling that number in the holidays.double quotation markDishes are served family style and there’s plenty of time for stories, with wine straight from the barrels in the cellarElsewhere in the village, I meet Alenka and Mark Smerajc, who were one of the first families to return, raising three children and running a business here. Today they have two smallholiday cottagesin what were farm outbuildings and run a relaxed courtyard restaurant for guests, opening to the public at weekends and for holidays. “People wanted food,” shrugs Alenka, as her teenage children help bring out beautiful plates of handmade pasta with local cheese and wild herbs from the kitchen.“In Vipava valley there was no tourism, so we got to decide how to build it,” says Jani Peljhan. That means GPS-guided cycling tours along roads too small to merit signposts, and experimenting with “wine trains”, carrying visitors from Nova Gorica to the vineyards with local winemakers on board to lead tasting sessions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJani’s company,Wajdušna, also offers hiking and paragliding, both gaining in popularity here. He meets us at Wellba with some e-bikes and we pedal through Ajdovščina to spot Roman ruins, and up to Vipavski Križ, famed for being one of the smallest towns in Slovenia, before zigzagging back up the other side of the valley through vineyards. The warmth of the afternoon and the steep hillsides makes me appreciate the “sport” mode on the bikes.View image in fullscreenThe region’s many narrow lanes are perfect for cycling trips.Photograph: Nejc BoleIn other regions, wine tourism often means visitor centres and branded experiences. In Vipava it still means sitting in someone’s kitchen. AtVina Lisjakin Zalošče, I eat at a little restaurant run by two brothers. “We opened the restaurant to show the wine,” says Peter Lisjak. “It’s all from our farm.” We eat generous platters of house dried meat, aged mountain cheeses, a fennel frittata and slow-cooked celeriac steaks with celery pesto and spinach. Dishes are served family style and there’s plenty of time for stories, with samples of delicious wine straight from the barrels in the cellar.From Wellba, we walk across the village toFerjančič vineyard,where seventh generation winemaker Matic Ferjančič talks us through his wines. His father developed the vineyard, going from five to 50,000 plants. “We work hard in the vineyard to make it easy in the cellar,” he says. As we chat, Matic keeps an ear to the baby monitor for the eighth generation sleeping upstairs.Although many of my favourite restaurant experiences are the simple ones, Vipava valley cuisine can reach loftier heights. One night we smarten up the best we can and follow a winding road uphill to Zemono Manor, to eat atGostilna Pri Lojzetu. Chef Tomaž Kavčič is known as a Slovenian slow food pioneer, and has earned a Michelin star for his playful dishes and proud use of local ingredients.Summer on the Slovenian RivieraRead moreWe eat delicate Vipava river trout with fermented apricots from the previous summer, and langoustine bisque from the coast. Traditional dishes such asjota, a sauerkraut and potato stew, are honoured on the menu, their humble roots celebrated not hidden. There are some theatrics, like a juniper plant producing flavoured vapour to complement a sorbet, but the restaurant atmosphere is friendly and relaxed. The server chats with my young stepson about his preferences, and brings him a generous bowl of gnocchi. It’s Kavčič’s night off so he sits with friends and a bottle of wine at the back of the restaurant, coming round all the tables frequently to chat.Vipava may not remain overlooked for ever. But talking to the people building businesses here, there is little appetite for becoming the next famous wine destination. What they seem to want instead is something rarer and more interesting: tourism that helps a place thrive without changing what made it worth visiting in the first place.The trip was provided byVipava Valley Tourismandthe Slovenian Tourist Board.Wellba Planinahas doubles from £97Explore more on these topicsSlovenia holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tim Dowling: my TV contract has run out – and so has my patience | Family | The Guardian
description: I need to buy a smart television big enough to read ransom notes – and I’m taking no prisoners
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: I need to buy a smart television big enough to read ransom notes – and I’m taking no prisoners
Content: Composite: Selman HosgorView image in fullscreenComposite: Selman HosgorThe Tim Dowling columnFamilyTim Dowling: my TV contract has run out – and so has my patienceI need to buy a smart television big enough to read ransom notes – and I’m taking no prisonersTim DowlingSat 29 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 12.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFourteen years ago, I received a text from my eldest son claiming he’d just found the TV face down on the sitting room floor, destroyed. I didn’t entirely buy his theory about the dogs being responsible – I discovered a football lying suspiciously near the crime scene – but it was a problem I needed to solve before my wife returned from a business trip.That was the last time I bought a new television. It still works, but it’s small by today’s standards, to the extent that it’s impossible to read the contents of a ransom note held by a detective in a drama. As TVs have expanded, the ransom notes have got smaller; I often have to pause the programme, get up and put my nose to the screen.On a Monday afternoon I come in from my office shed to find the middle one typing furiously on his laptop, with my wife looking on.“Show Dad,” she says.“What?” I say.“Your broadband and TV package is ending,” he says.“Yeah, I think I got an email,” I say.double quotation markThe middle one begins extricating us from our present deal, progressing from chatbot to chat human to chat human’s supervisor“Next month your bill goes up by like, 50%,” he says. He turns his screen to show me. He wants me to be shocked by the new number, but I’m too busy being shocked by the old number.“How long have I been paying that?” I say.“Two years,” he says.“Can I cancel the contract?” I say.“The contract is over,” he says.“You have to explain it very slowly to him,” my wife says.The middle one says we can renew the contract for the same price, or threaten to quit and hope they make us a better offer. “Or,” he says, “you can switch to broadband only, buy a smart TV like everyone else and save 70 quid a month.”“A new TV?” I say. “Will it be big enough to read ransom notes?”“I don’t know what that means,” he says.Armed with our new project, we all repair to the living room. The middle one begins the tiresome process of extricating us from our present deal, progressing from chatbot to chat human to chat human’s supervisor. My wife starts looking at televisions. I take a tape measure to the alcove between the chimney breast and the wall, where our present TV resides.“Here’s a nice one,” my wife says. “Highly recommended, 50 inches.”“Fifty inches?” I say, extending the tape measure. “Far too big.”“Not that way,” says the middle one, looking up. “It’s 50 inches diagonally.”“What use is that to me?” I say. “I’m measuring across!”“All tellies are measured diagonally,” he says.“Still?” I say.“What do you mean, still?” he says.double quotation mark‘I’m afraid your father’s gone mad,’ my wife says. On the contrary, I’m the only sane one leftHere’s what I mean: the first cathode ray tube TV screens were round, so the size of the display was naturally expressed as the diameter. When the round screen was masked in a rectangular box, the diameter was also the diagonal. And the convention persisted for decades because, from a marketing standpoint, it made screens sound bigger than they were.Tim Dowling: my working holiday just isn’t workingRead more“But now it’s like, TVs are huge – who cares?” I say.“Measuring diagonally is childish.”“I’m afraid your father’s gone mad,” my wife says.“On the contrary,” I say. “I’m the only sane one left.”To demonstrate my sanity, I use a  plank from the garden to mark off the exact horizontal capacity of the alcove at TV height: 1,113mm. Then, looking up the listed dimensions of various 50in tellies, I note that they actually vary in total width by up to 8mm.“Why do we care about 8mm?” my wife says.“Because,” I say, “as my research shows, 40% of the most highly recommended 50in TVs will not fit in that gap.”“You must be very pleased,” she says, leaving the room. The middle one, I notice, has already gone.“I am pleased,” I say, to no one.The pall I’ve managed to cast over the whole project persists even after our new broadband-only contract arrives by email. It still hasn’t lifted the next afternoon when, all alone, I unbox our new TV and slide it gently into place, with barely a millimetre to spare either side.I plug it in and follow the setup process. Then, after double-checking to make sure no one is home, I scroll through the guide in search of a programme in which someone is kidnapped for ransom.Explore more on these topicsFamilyThe Tim Dowling columnfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The angle of the dog, the hat and the tattoo on her foot all come together’: Trace Meek’s best phone picture | Photography | The Guardian
description: A family day in a Florida back yard was the setting for a summertime memory it would be impossible to recreate
Author: Grace Holliday
Headline: A family day in a Florida back yard was the setting for a summertime memory it would be impossible to recreate
Content: Summer Fun, 2024, shot on iPhone 14 Pro. Photograph: Trace Meek/mobilephotoawards.comView image in fullscreenSummer Fun, 2024, shot on iPhone 14 Pro. Photograph: Trace Meek/mobilephotoawards.comSmart shotPhotography‘The angle of the dog, the hat and the tattoo on her foot all come together’: Trace Meek’s best phone pictureA family day in a Florida back yard was the setting for a summertime memory it would be impossible to recreateGrace HollidaySat 29 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrace Meek is abundantly proud of his Florida back yard. For the last 10 years, he and his wife, Lauren, have worked diligently on it. “It’s our happy place,” he says. “We live in Belleair Bluffs, and I’ve watched my son and daughter grow up playing in the dirt under our giant oak trees, swinging on the tree swing, riding their bikes and scooters on the circular path, and swimming in our pool. It’s big, with a really deep end and three water fountains that shoot over the top. We like to have a last jump into the pool before bed and, best of all, there are no iPads or TVs.”‘You can feel the warmth of the sun’: Bertram Greenhough’s best phone pictureRead moreThe family had friends visiting for 4 July celebrations when Meek took this photo on his phone. There were six adults, six children and two dogs present. Harvey, a braque français, is pictured here on Lauren’s lap.“Harvey was four at the time. He loves to swim, and had been jumping in the pool all day, but eventually tired and climbed on to Lauren’s lap to rest,” Meek says.Re-enacting the shot would be almost impossible, he adds, but “that’s the cool part. The angle of the dog, the hat and the cup, the tattoo on her foot, along with the vibrant colours of the raft – it all comes together. I love how the water creates shapes, too. You have to really study the image to see what it’s about.”Lauren’s face being covered by her hat lends an air of mysteriousness that Meek also enjoys. “You can put yourself in her place and be immersed in a wonderful summertime memory; a moment when you were truly content.”Explore more on these topicsPhotographySmart shotArtS-TownfeaturesShareReuse this content
