title: ‘The butcher may be gone, but to many he is a hero’: victims condemn glorification of Mladić | Ratko Mladić | The Guardian
description: Architect of Srebrenica genocide is dead but those scarred by his atrocities say his ideology is still shockingly pervasive
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: Architect of Srebrenica genocide is dead but those scarred by his atrocities say his ideology is still shockingly pervasive
Content: Džemil Hodžić (right) was 12 when his 16-year-old brother Amel (left) was killed by a sniper while playing tennis in Sarajevo in 1995.Photograph: Family handoutView image in fullscreenDžemil Hodžić (right) was 12 when his 16-year-old brother Amel (left) was killed by a sniper while playing tennis in Sarajevo in 1995.Photograph: Family handoutRatko Mladić‘The butcher may be gone, but to many he is a hero’: victims condemn glorification of MladićArchitect of Srebrenica genocide is dead but those scarred by his atrocities say his ideology is still shockingly pervasiveKim WillsherSat 29 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 09.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo most of the world, he was and will always be the “Butcher of Bosnia”, a grim epithet but one that still fails to fully convey the evil and horror inflicted on its people by Gen Ratko Mladić, whodied in prison on Thursday.As commander of the Bosnian Serb forces, Mladić was responsible for the killing of an estimated 100,000 men, women and children during the savage breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s. He was most notoriously the architect of ethnic cleansing and thegenocide at Srebrenicain which at least 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were slaughtered.Today, 31 years after the Dayton agreement ended the Bosnian conflict and the 1,425-day siege of Sarajevo – the longest in modern warfare – Mladić is dead, but his legacy still divides the Balkans.Džemil Hodžićwas 12 when his brother Amel, 16, was killed by a sniper while playing tennis in Sarajevo in May 1995. “As kids, Mladić was a kind of horror creature. Everyone knew him and his name. We were very well aware that he was responsible for our situation and the suffering we were going through,” Hodžić, now 43 and founder of theSniper Alley photo projectin Sarajevo, told the Guardian.View image in fullscreenDžemil and his father at Amel’s grave after his funeral.Photograph: Family handout“Perhaps we were too young to comprehend everything, but children living through the Sarajevo siege knew the shootings by snipers, the shelling of our schools, the killing of our friends and family … all of that was down to him.”Zoran Kusovac, a Croatian journalist and geopolitical analyst who reported from the Balkan wars, met Mladić several times, once on a mountain plateau overlooking Sarajevo where Bosnian Serb forces surrounding the city had installed heavy artillery. During the siege of the Bosnian capital they killed more than 11,000 people, including 2,000 children, in a terrifying daily campaign of shelling, bombing and sniping.How the ‘Hanging Woman’ revealed truth of Bosnia’s mass killerRead more“We were up on the mountain overlooking the city and Mladić said to me: ‘Look, I have Sarajevo in the palm of my hand. I can either destroy it or take it whenever I want,’” Kusovac said.“He was a bully and nobody, not even his superiors, had the guts to tell him he was wrong. He also kept meticulous notes of what he did … he wrote everything down with the absolute confidence of a man who believed he would never be held responsible for it.”As well as those killed in Bosnia in the 1992-95 conflict, 20,000-50,000 women and girls were raped and 2.7 million people were displaced.Srebrenica is remembered as one of the mostshameful failuresof the international community. The Bosnian town, its mainly Muslim population swollen by refugees, was declared a UN “safe haven” and residents were ordered to hand over all weapons to international peacekeepers.View image in fullscreenA memorial cemetery near Srebrenica, in eastern Bosnia.Photograph: Andrej Isaković/AFP/Getty ImagesThe UN then abandoned Srebrenica to a bloody fate. The image of Mladić ruffling the hair of a child in the enclave shortly before marching all men and boys away to be killed, is particularly chilling.To many Serbians, however, Mladić was a hero: a man who believed in a mythical “Greater Serbia” but was traduced in an international campaign against Serbs who felt – and still feel – misunderstood and victimised.On Thursday, the Serbian government in Belgrade once again defied international condemnation as it announced that Mladić, who died serving a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity, would be buried with “all the military and state honours to which he is entitled”. He was either 83 or 84 when he died, according to differing official and family accounts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe ultranationalist politician Vojislav Šešelj told journalists: “Mladić fought against those villains [at The Hague] for a long time; they expected his death two or three years ago, but he did not give up.” Milorad Dodik, the Bosnian Serb separatist leader, added: “Mladić was respected by the Serbian people. As a commander he stood to defend Serbs.”View image in fullscreenSupporters of Mladić in Novi Sad, Serbia, on Thursday.Photograph: ReutersA statement from the office of the UN secretary general, António Guterres, cautioned those in power to “refrain from denying the seriousness of the crimes”, particularly the denial of the Srebrenica genocide or glorifying of war crimes.Emir Suljagić, the director of the Srebrenica Memorial, who was one of only a handful of males to escape the town, said Mladić’s death did not change historical facts or erase the consequences of genocide. “The people he sent to their deaths never had the chance to grow old. That is the only fact about his death that matters to me,” Suljagić told the Bosnian newspaper Dnevni Avaz.“Now the hardest part of the job remains: not to let the truth, responsibility and memory die with him. Mladić’s death is another moment in which we must decide what we will remember and, more importantly, what we will not allow to be erased.”Suljagić has repeatedly pointed out that Mladić did not act alone. “When are we going to deal with the people who did his bidding? Everyone knows who they are, the Bosnian judiciary knows who they are,” hetold the Observer in 2021. “These guys are mass murderers, they are knee-deep in blood and they are walking about as free men. It means that Bosnian people still don’t feel entirely safe – and who can blame them?”Dr Waqar Azmi, of the Remembering Srebrenica group,wrote on X: “His legacy is not one of heroism, but of shame: a dark reminder of the depths of human cruelty.”Hodžić added: “Sadly, there are people who consider Mladić a hero and celebrate his life and his atrocities. The butcher may be gone, but unfortunately his legacy is still there … many share his ideology and views that the job is not yet finished because we are still here … still fighting genocide denial and the relativisation of his crimes.“His ideas and ideals are not dead and we are witnessing this on a daily basis. It is the glorification of a monster.”Explore more on these topicsRatko MladićSrebrenica massacreBosnia and HerzegovinaSerbiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Was it a mistake for 99 Colombian guerrillas to lay down their arms? | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Fighters in legal limbo after accepting ‘total peace’ plan of Petro government just days before hardliner Abelardo De la Espriella took over
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Fighters in legal limbo after accepting ‘total peace’ plan of Petro government just days before hardliner Abelardo De la Espriella took over
Content: Tattoo of a former combatant now in a designated zone in Colombia under the ‘total peace’ plan.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTattoo of a former combatant now in a designated zone in Colombia under the ‘total peace’ plan.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianColombiaWas it a mistake for 99 Colombian guerrillas to lay down their arms?Fighters in legal limbo after accepting ‘total peace’ plan of Petro government just days before hardliner Abelardo De la Espriella took overDaniela Díaz in Valle del Guamuez andTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroSat 29 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 10.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn mid-June, 99 guerrilla fighters were flown by helicopter to a small settlement in a rural area of southernColombiawhere they lined up and, one by one, handed their weapons to government officials: rifles, pistols, machine guns and grenade launchers.They also stripped off their heavy tactical vests, field packs and camouflage uniforms, which were each piled into a bonfire to mark the beginning of a new life away from an armed conflict that has claimed nearly half a million lives in the last six decades.That was precisely what the former president Gustavo Petro’s “total peace” plan had sought to achieve: negotiating with and disarming all of Colombia’s criminal groups, which are estimated to have nearly 30,000 members.But the group of just 99 people was the only one to disarm, and did so just three days before the presidential runoff, which waswon by the far-rightmillionaire lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella, who had campaigned on a promiseto end “total peace” and return to a full-on strategy of jailing or killing criminals.Now, several weeks after the new president took office – and amid efforts to deal with the aftermath of the7.4-magnitude earthquake, as his government hasalready begunthe promised airstrikes against criminal groups – the 99 do not know what will happen to them.“We’re in limbo,” said Natalia Bríñez, 29, one of 13 women among the group staying in the temporary location zone, or ZUT by its Spanish initials, a government-controlled zone where, under surveillance and unable to leave, they were supposed to make the transition to civilian life over the following months.View image in fullscreenNatalia Briñez, a former guerrilla fighter, is one of 13 women in the ZUT.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianThe former guerrillas are housed in beige brick buildings decorated with drawings they painted themselves, including doves of peace, with a communal dining hall where three meals a day are served. No weapons are allowed inside and soldiers guard the ZUT from a perimeter less than a mile away.One former combatant built a makeshift gym with weights made from metal pipes and tins filled with cement and sand, and there is an improvised football pitch, but most of them spend their days on their phones.De la Espriella has repeatedly said his government will no longer negotiate peace agreements and has yet to announce what he intends to do regarding the people at the ZUT. The president has not responded to requests for comment.In theory, any arrest warrants against the group are suspended, and they remain under state protection until 25 December, when Petro’s decree establishing the ZUT expires. But De la Espriella could revoke the decree at any time.Armando Novoa, the former government official who led peace negotiations with the group, said “the worst-case scenario would be for the new government to close the ZUT, launch a military operation and try to capture or kill them. That would be a crime against humanity, because these people are unarmed.”Between 2 and 4 August, days before De la Espriella’s inauguration, Novoa led journalists including the Guardian through the ZUT. The Office of the High Commissioner for Peace, where he worked, has since been absorbed into the newly created National Security Commission – a move expected to result in more than 200 job losses – and Novoa has resigned.For now, at least, the ZUT remains in operation and has a small library run by Bríñez, who has a phoenix tattoo on her left shoulder as a symbol of her rebirth away from the armed conflict.View image in fullscreenNo weapons are allowed inside the ZUT and soldiers guard it from a perimeter less than a mile away.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The Guardian“The hardest thing for me has been being away from my children,” said Bríñez, who has a seven-year-old daughter and a 10-year-old son and speaks to them on video calls, but will only be able to see them in person once her “transition” is complete, a process that includes vocational training and psychosocial support.They were also supposed to receive financial support of about £425 a month, which had not yet been paid. In the meantime, some of them were planning to start achicken-rearing business.The 99 made up a small part of a group of about 1,000 combatants calledCommandos of the Frontier– most of whom remain armed – and are part of the National Coordinator of the Bolivarian Army (CNEB), a former dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) with about 2,500 members which controls the border with Ecuador.The Petro administration said negotiations were also under way with other members of the CNEB, who published anopen letteraddressed to De la Espriella saying they were willing to continue talks with him. It is not known whether the president responded.View image in fullscreenOne of the works of graffiti in the ZUT painted by the former guerrillas.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianThe CNEB’s chief “peace negotiator”, Geovany Andrés Rojas, known as “Araña” (Spider), had been in custody since February under a US extradition request for drug trafficking, which Petro had delayed. Last Wednesday, De la Espriellaorderedextradition.Although such groups emerged in the 1960s as leftwing rebels fighting government abuses and seeking revolution – followed soon afterwards byfar-right paramilitary groups– ideology has long since been overtaken for most of them by economic interests, above all drug trafficking (Colombia is the world’s largest producer of cocaine) and illegal mining.“Here in the ZUT, the vast majority were not in the group because of any ideological commitment, but for economic reasons,” said Novoa. “It even surprised us that most of them simply called the group ‘the company’.”Petro repeatedly tried to negotiate peace agreements with larger groups. The armed factions took advantage of temporary ceasefires to continue expanding, a process that had already begun before he took office. They also clashed among themselves for control of territory and illicit economies, which many security experts say contributed to a rise in homicides, kidnappings and massacres.“Total peace” was an attempt to address what thelandmark 2016 peace dealbetween the government and the Farc failed to resolve, as other armed groups and Farc dissidents remained active.Petro’s administrationfailed to reduce violence, which instead reached its worst levels in a decade, and to reach the disarmament stage with any of the gangs, apart from the 99 former combatants – who handed over their weapons only on the eve of an election thatevery poll indicatedthe government-backed candidate would lose.“They [the government] told us: ‘If this works, you’re opening the door for other groups and will set an example,’” said Bríñez.Some security experts saw the agreementas rushed.View image in fullscreenFormer guerrillas in the ZUT have little to do and spend much of their time looking at their phones.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The Guardian“It was a somewhat irresponsible decision,” said Paula Tobo, a senior researcher at the thinktank Ideas for Peace Foundation, which published anextensive reporton why Total Peace failed.Tobo said the 99 were now in a “legal limbo” because their protection rested on decrees that could be revoked and there is no legal framework for their transition to civilian life. All of the Petro administration’s proposals to regulate surrenders failed in Congress and, under current law, anyone who has committed crimes such as kidnapping or drug trafficking is not eligible for amnesty.“It’s positive that these people wanted to lay down their arms, but it really wasn’t the right time for the government to take that decision … The previous administration clearly put them at risk of this government suddenly deciding to abolish the ZUT and arrest them,” said Tobo.View image in fullscreenA wristband with the logo of the armed group to which Adrián, 19, belonged.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianThe group wrote a letter to De la Espriella reaffirming its “irreversible decision to commit to peace” and inviting him to visit the ZUT. At the time of publication it had received no response.The youngest member of the group, a 19-year-old who asked to be identified only as Adrián, said they wanted “to have a home, a family”.However, he knows what he will do if things do not go according to plan. “Honestly, I’d take up arms again, because we’re keeping our side of the bargain and the government should do the same, shouldn’t it?” he said.Daniela Díaz travelled to Valle del Guamuez at the invitation of the Colombian government’s former Office of the High Commissioner for Peace.Explore more on these topicsColombiaFarcAmericasDrugs tradefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Search continues as number missing in Nepal-Tibet floods rises to 2,478 – as it happened | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Chinese rescue team reaches all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex to find ‘nothing but ruins’
Author: Adam Fulton
Headline: Chinese rescue team reaches all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex to find ‘nothing but ruins’
Content: 21.54 EDTDeath toll now stands at 579 in Nepal, seven in TibetNepal’s official death toll from Wednesday’s flash flood now stands at 579 people, whileChinasays seven people have died in Tibet, the state Xinhua news agency reported early Saturday.Chinese authorities said also they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists and 499 Chinese residents fromTibet.In India, authorities said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing fromNepal, believed to be flood victims.Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among those missing on the border, as many were on a pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash.Sivaranjani Muthunathan was travelling by bus with 56 others to the Chinese border when they became stuck in what they thought was a traffic jam.“Then there was fog, smoke, something that seemed to suddenly engulf us,” Muthunathan, 46, told Agence France-Presse on Friday, showing a phone video she recorded of a torrent surging towards her. Around them, vehicles were swept away or buried under mud.Relatives check the lists of missing people following the flash floods in Nepal, outside a hospital in Kathmandu on Friday.Photograph: Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty ImagesShareUpdated at22.45 EDT

title: August reveals Australians’ big appetite for weight-loss drugs, love for ‘dupe’ brands and an accelerating EV uptake | Australian economy | The Guardian
description: August reporting season shows how consumers are responding to cost of living pressures and how retailers are responding
Author: Jonathan Barrett
Headline: August reporting season shows how consumers are responding to cost of living pressures and how retailers are responding
Content: High petrol and diesel prices are causing Australians to turn to electric vehicles, with almost a third of new car sales in July being an EV.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenHigh petrol and diesel prices are causing Australians to turn to electric vehicles, with almost a third of new car sales in July being an EV.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPAustralian economyExplainerAugust reveals Australians’ big appetite for weight-loss drugs, love for ‘dupe’ brands and an accelerating EV uptakeReporting season shows how consumers are responding to cost of living pressures and how retailers are respondingFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJonathan BarrettBusiness editorSat 29 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 21.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralians are buying less pizza but moreweight-loss drugs. They love “dupes” but don’t enjoy writing letters.Here are five key takeaways from the August reporting season that show what consumers are buying as cost of living pressures reignite, and how retailers are responding.1.Anko everywhereKmart’s home brand, Anko, started out with a strategy of mimicking popular items, like Birkenstocks and Skims, at a fraction of the price.The “dupe” strategy that won over the masses is expanding, and going upmarket.The Wesfarmers-owned Kmart Group, which includes Target, generated $11.7bn in sales last financial year, underpinned by Anko, according to its annual results.Anko has moved into furniture and is pitching itself as a rival to Ikea through its new K home store. Meanwhile, there are now six Anko-branded stores in the Philippines run via a joint venture, and further global expansion on the horizon.The biggest strategy change in recent months has been what the retailer describes as “one-up and two-up” price tier categories, whereby Anko offers an entry-level product and a couple of higher quality – and higher priced – options to entice those who like more stylish dupes.2.Pizza vouchersDomino’s Pizza has long been popular for budget-conscious families and penniless teenagers, with value deals aplenty.That has started to change, with the pizza chain reducing its level of discounting, in a move designed to improve profitability for franchisees and investors.While revenue dropped more than 11% from its Australian and New Zealand operations over the past 12 months, it believes the new model will help its franchisees operate more sustainable businesses.Domino’s is Australia’s fourth biggest fast food chain by store numbers, after Subway, McDonald’s and KFC, data from analytics company GapMaps shows.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailBut the pizza chain is in a tricky place given it is trying to reduce discounting at the same time as cost-of-living pressures reignite.It is hoping its new tie-up with Coca-Cola, replacing Pepsi from September, may pay dividends as customers respond to a new and expanded drinks menu.3.Weight boomSigma Healthcare-owned Chemist Warehouse is cashing in on weight loss drugs in unexpected ways, as sales of appetite-altering GLP-1 drugs grow.Sigma’s chief executive, Vikesh Ramsunder, told analysts after the company’s earnings result that customers who buy GLP-1 drugs, like Ozempic, are also putting other products such as protein powders into their shopping baskets because rapid weight loss can also lead to muscle loss.Interestingly, those taking weight-loss drugs are also buying more beauty products.“It’s really about the fact that we’re selling products linked to individuals who are taking these medicines that they probably feel better, so they buy more kinds of beauty products and more healthcare-related vitamins and supplements,” Ramsunder told analysts.All up, the shopping basket size of a GLP-1 customer is 40% larger than those not buying weight-loss products, according to Chemist Warehouse data.4.Electric salesTheelectrification of Australia’s car industryis in full swing, accelerated by high petrol prices caused by the Iran conflict.Eagers Automotive, operator of the largest network of car dealerships in Australia, noted in its financial results that once a driver steps away from a full combustion engine, they rarely go back.“The one thing we have observed is that the transition from a fully combustion engine car to a full electric vehicle – and that transition might include a hybrid vehicle, a plug-in hybrid vehicle, and ultimately a full battery electric vehicle – is a one-way street,” the Eagers chief executive, Keith Thornton, told analysts.Almost one in three new vehicles sold in Australia during July was electric, with combined battery-electric and plug-in hybrid sales reaching a record 32% of new car sales, according to the Electric Vehicle Council.EV sales are now running about triple the volume from a year ago.5.Snail mailThe government-owned Australia Post reported a pre-tax loss of $108m for last financial year, as rising delivery costs and the existential decline of letter sending weighs on its finances.Letter volumes are now at 1930s levels, when Australia’s population was about one-quarter the current size. Today, most letters are sent by businesses and government agencies.The problem for the postal service is that the cost of maintaining a national delivery system is getting more expensive at the same time as letters are phasing out, with volumes falling a further 15% during the last year alone.To partially offset costs, Australia Post is increasing the price of a basic stamp by 15c to $1.85 on 1 September.Stamp price increases have been extreme – it cost 70c just over a decade ago to send a regular letter – raising questions over how much longer snail mail will exist.Explore more on these topicsAustralian economyBusinessDomino's PizzaFood & drink industryElectric vehiclesConsumer spendingexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Statins can safely cut risk of heart attacks or strokes in healthy people aged over 70, world-first clinical trial shows | Health | The Guardian
description: Australian-led trial finds low risk of side effects from common cholesterol-lowering medication for otherwise healthy older people
Author: Melissa Davey
Headline: Australian-led trial finds low risk of side effects from common cholesterol-lowering medication for otherwise healthy older people
Content: New research shows taking statins can reduce the risk of people aged over 70 suffering heart attacks or strokes.Photograph: Carol Heesen/AlamyView image in fullscreenNew research shows taking statins can reduce the risk of people aged over 70 suffering heart attacks or strokes.Photograph: Carol Heesen/AlamyHealthStatins can safely cut risk of heart attacks or strokes in healthy people aged over 70, world-first clinical trial showsAustralian-led trial finds low risk of side effects from common cholesterol-lowering medication for otherwise healthy older peopleMelissa DaveyMedical editorSat 29 Aug 2026 02.25 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 21.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaking a common cholesterol-lowering medication can reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke for people aged over 70, with a low risk of serious side effects, a world-first clinical trial led by Australian researchers has found.Statins are already commonly prescribed to people under the age of 75 who meet certain risk criteria, such as having diabetes and high cholesterol, to prevent them from having a major heart event such as a heart attack, stroke, or from requiring heart surgery.Statins helping people with obesity match those of healthy weight on key metrics, study findsRead morePeople who have already had a major heart event are also commonly prescribed the drugs, regardless of their age.What doctors did not know was whether it was safe to prescribe a daily statin to people aged 70 and over who were healthy overall, having never experienced a heart attack, stroke or heart surgery, and whether doing so could prevent these cardiac events.A co-author of the study, Adjunct Prof Mark Nelson with the Monash University school of public health and preventive medicine, said it was an important piece of missing information, because the biggest risk of major heart-related events “is increasing age”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“Our society is ageing, and therefore the burden of disease is increasing, making it important to improve our ability to prevent disease in this group,” he said. “So we needed the evidence for this group to see if prescribing statins as a prevention measure works.”But Nelson said older adults were often overlooked in early statin research because 40 years ago, heart disease was most common in middle-aged populations especially if they smoked, leading public health efforts to focus on preventing premature deaths in that group. Elderly populations may also be sick and on other medications, making trialling drugs risky, he said.To address the gap, Monash researchers analysed the cardiovascular outcomes of almost 10,000 study participants over the age of 70 who were given either a daily statin or a placebo, in a scientifically-robust type of study known as a randomised control trial. The participants were enrolled with the help of almost 3,400 GPs across Australia.Most statin side-effects not caused by the drugs, study findsRead moreThe researchers excluded people who had a condition that might make taking a statin unsafe, if they were not living independently, or if they already needed the drug because they had suffered a heart attack.The decade-long study found the medication decreased the risk of a first major cardiovascular event by 30% for those aged over 70.In real terms, this means one major cardiac event such as a heart attack, stroke, or heart surgery could be prevented for every 37 older adults treated with daily statins over almost six years.Prof James Chong, a cardiologist at Sydney’s Westmead hospital, said if the research “leads to increased statin use globally, the absolute reduction of (heart-related) events can be significant”.“One of the major changes that may result, in my opinion, is more elderly patients having confidence to take long term statins,” he said.“However, one thing we have to keep in mind is it was an almost exclusively white population with the mean age around 75 years of age, so the results may not be as generalisable globally without further supporting evidence.”The findingswere published in the New England Journal of Medicineon Saturday and presented concurrently at the European Society of Cardiology Congress in Germany.Lead researcher on the paper, Adjunct Prof Sophia Zoungas, said: “What we hope to see, now that we have provided such strong evidence, are updated treatment guidelines to help clinicians make use of this new finding.”Older patients should have a conversation with their GP about whether statins are appropriate to help them stay healthy, the researchers said.Prof Tom Marwick, a cardiologist at Hobart’s Royal hospital, said there had been a lot of misinformation about statins increasing the risk of dementia, making some older people reluctant to take the drugs.A benefit of the Monash study was that the findings “really close the book on that, in large numbers,” he said. The study found no statistically significant difference in dementia rates among those who received a statin and those who did not.Marwick described it as a “well done, really important trial”.But he said the study also found patients were reluctant to adhere to therapy, with more than 15% of patients in the trial discontinuing their medication.Marwick said “a slight disappointment” in the findings was that although major heart events were reduced, the disability-free survival was the same among the participants whether they took the statin or the placebo.In other words, taking the medication didn’t extend life or its quality.“We can reduce cardiovascular events, but the health burdens of ageing are less amenable,” he said.Explore more on these topicsHealthHeart diseasenewsShareReuse this content

title: Royal Navy spent three days tracking Russian vessels in UK waters | Military | The Guardian
description: Three vessels and a helicopter deployed to monitor four ships travelling through the North Sea to the Channel
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Three vessels and a helicopter deployed to monitor four ships travelling through the North Sea to the Channel
Content: The destroyer HMS Duncan, pictured in Portsmouth Harbour, was one of three Royal Navy vessels deployed to monitor Russian ships.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe destroyer HMS Duncan, pictured in Portsmouth Harbour, was one of three Royal Navy vessels deployed to monitor Russian ships.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/ReutersMilitaryRoyal Navy spent three days tracking Russian vessels in UK watersThree vessels and a helicopter deployed to monitor four ships travelling through the North Sea to the ChannelGeraldine McKelvieSat 29 Aug 2026 11.06 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 09.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheRoyal Navyspent three days tracking Russian vessels as they passed through UK waters, it has emerged.The “intense” 72-hour operation took place last week, with radars used to monitor four ships that made their way from the North Sea through to the Channel.The fleet was surveilled by HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn, with a Merlin helicopter providing support, officials said.The Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko was observed escorting the cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta, which are under sanctions, towards Dover.In response, Russia deployed its own military resources, including the Neustrashimy frigate, to guard the shipment. Gen Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord, said there was “no room for complacency” as shadow fleet vessels continued to pose “an unacceptable risk” to UK security.“Alongside our allies, this approach is forcing Moscow to divert Russian warships away from their core purpose,” he said. “That is because Russia knows we stand ready to act again, should it be required.”The Royal Navy recently warned ofincreasing Russian activity in UK waters. In July, it spent 21 days monitoring ships from Moscow, an increase of 25% compared with the previous year. Officials say they have repeatedly observed warships in the Dover strait and the North Sea.In June, the Royal Marinesseized the Russian tanker Smyrtos, the first time British troops have directly boarded a shadow fleet vessel, one of more than 500 that have been sanctioned by the UK.The Kremlin hasthreatened the UKafter Andy Burnham visited Kyiv this week in his first overseas trip as prime minister. During the trip, Burnham said the UK would provide Ukraine with military support, including blueprints for components of long-range Scalp missiles.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlthough western officials have tried to play down the prospect of direct conflict between Russia and Nato, the Kremlin has accused the UK and its allies of “playing with fire” in relation to their continued support for Ukraine.Andrei Fedorov, a former Russian foreign minister, said he could not “100% exclude” the possibility of “semi-military” action against Britain in retaliation, raising the prospect of an attack on British drone factories from “unknown sources”.Explore more on these topicsMilitaryRoyal NavyRussiaUK security and counter-terrorismEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian drone strike on Kyiv warehouse storing weapons kills at least 37  | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian prosecutors open investigation into why munitions were stored so close to residential buildings
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Ukrainian prosecutors open investigation into why munitions were stored so close to residential buildings
Content: Emergency service workers respond to a Russian strike on a warehouse in the town of Myla, near Bucha, in the Kyiv oblast.Photograph: Aleksandr Gusev/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEmergency service workers respond to a Russian strike on a warehouse in the town of Myla, near Bucha, in the Kyiv oblast.Photograph: Aleksandr Gusev/Sopa Images/ShutterstockUkraineRussian drone strike on Kyiv warehouse storing weapons kills at least 37Ukrainian prosecutors open investigation into why munitions were stored so close to residential buildingsDonna FergusonSat 29 Aug 2026 09.34 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 07.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 37 people have been killed after a Russian drone struck a warehouse near Kyiv’s western suburbs that was storing “explosive objects”.The attack damaged at least 50 residential buildings, including a care home for elderly and disabled people, and sparked a huge fire and explosions in the Bucha district of the Kyiv region. The regional governor, Tymur Tkachenko, said a further 42 people, including four children, had been injured in the strike.More than 370 people have been evacuated from the area and the evacuation process was continuing, the Ukrainian president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said. In a statement, he said a warehouse in the town of Myla had been struck, “followed by a detonation”.The warehouse was a depot owned by the Ukrainian military and stored shells, drones and other munitions, he said in a video address. “The first impact was on a place where ammunition was being stored that absolutely should not have been there – a depot of the defence forces. [There was] detonation of shells, mines, other munitions and drones on a significant scale,” Zelenskyy said.Criminal proceedings had been opened on charges of official negligence, he added.“There are regulations in place; ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas.”He said one of the people killed was the head of the Dmytrivka community, Taras Didych, who died while rescuing others.View image in fullscreenSmoke and flames rise from the warehouse after the strike in the Bucha district of the Kyiv region.Photograph: Libkos/GettyUkrainian prosecutors said they had opened an investigation into the legality of the “storage of explosive objects and materials”.The Ukrainian prime minister, Serhii Koretskyi, expressed regret that mistakes had not been learned from aprevious deadly strike on a munitions depot in Vyshneve, near Kyiv, in July.An investigation into that incident, in which 22 people were killed and fires tore through nearby homes, revealed serious failings on the part of a state-owned company, which did not comply with regulations on the proximity of residential buildings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA man walks past destroyed houses after the Russian strike in Bucha.Photograph: Libkos/Getty“Unfortunately, we can already see that the terrible tragedy in Vyshneve did not become a lesson,” Koretskyi said. “In the fifth year of a full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes is criminal negligence. And all those guilty, without exception, must be severely punished so that such situations do not happen again.”In a statement, Russia’s ministry of defence said it had hit a warehouse in Myla storing components and launch boosters for long-range drones. It said it had also attacked the ports of Mykolaiv and Izmail, as well as a logistics centre and warehouse facilities storing parts for Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles in the Kyiv region.Elsewhere, Russian attacks across Ukraine’s southern Kherson region killed two people and wounded 27 more on Saturday, including a child, a local official said.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeVolodymyr ZelenskyynewsShareReuse this content

title: Laurie Anderson’s next manuscript to be locked away for 88 years in Future Library | Future Library | The Guardian
description: Grammy award-winning American artist selected as 13th person to submit written work to Oslo-based project
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Grammy award-winning American artist selected as 13th person to submit written work to Oslo-based project
Content: Laurie Anderson credits her mother for her love of books.Photograph: Wolfgang TillmansView image in fullscreenLaurie Anderson credits her mother for her love of books.Photograph: Wolfgang TillmansFuture LibraryLaurie Anderson’s next manuscript to be locked away for 88 years in Future LibraryGrammy award-winning American artist selected as 13th person to submit written work to Oslo-based projectNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentSat 29 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe next manuscript by the American artistLaurie Andersonwill remain unseen for 88 years, as she becomes the 13th figure to contribute to the Future Library project.Anderson joins Margaret Atwood, Han Kang, Ocean Vuong and other prominent authors who have written secret manuscripts, which have been locked away until 2114.The texts are stored in a specially designed silent room in the Deichman Bjørvika building at the public library in Oslo. At the end of the project, the full anthology of texts will be printed using paper made from trees from theFuture Libraryforest in Nordmarka, in northern Oslo, where 1,000 spruce trees were planted by Katie Paterson, the artist behind the project, in 2014.Anderson is a writer, director, composer, visual artist, musician and vocalist whose work spans art, theatre, experimental music and technology.She has created numerous multimedia stage performances and published 10 books, as well as being nominated for six Grammy Awards, winning once and receiving a lifetime achievement award in 2024. Her visual art has been exhibited globally at institutions including the Hirshhorn Museum in Washington DC and Moderna Museet in Stockholm.Anderson’s manuscript for the project may be a text, a score, a story, a set of instructions or “something for which we do not yet have a name”, Paterson said.View image in fullscreenLaurie Anderson performs in Amsterdam in 1982.Photograph: Rob Verhorst/RedfernsAnderson said: “I absolutely loved the idea of theFuture Libraryas soon as I learned about it. I’ve always been in love with books, libraries and forests. When I was a kid we lived next to a large park filled with maple, elm and oak trees. At the far corner of the park was an enormous red oak tree and up the street and just around the bend, there was the library, a rustic fieldstone building filled with comfortable pillows and many thousands of books.“‘You better check with grandfather tree today if you have the time,’ my mother would say some mornings. In a house where candy of all kinds was forbidden, we knew what that meant: there would be chocolate bars and chocolate mints up in the fork of the red oak, just low enough for us to hoist ourselves up and grab them. It also meant that we’d have extra incentive that day to get to the library.”Anderson called her mother a “brilliant and unhappy woman”. She said she should have been a chief executive of a large corporation but instead had eight children. “She loved books and somehow made it a project to get up early in the morning, walk through the park and hide chocolate bars in a tree. She taught us to love books, magic and old trees.“I’m hoping to be able to write something useful about love for the people who will read this in 2114. My favourite books are the ones in which I can hear someone’s voice, which is why I’ll try my best to make myself clear to the people who come across these books in the next century.”The Future Library Trust said it had selected Anderson for her “singular ability to speak across time, creating work that is profoundly human, radically imaginative and alive to futures we cannot yet foresee”.Paterson added: “Laurie Anderson has spent a lifetime sending signals into the unknown. For decades, she has explored how we tell stories, how we remember, and how we imagine what is yet to come. Moving freely between language, music, visual art, technology and performance, her work travels between the intimate and the planetary, love and loss, politics and poetry, with humour, tenderness and wonder.”Other writers to have contributed to the project include David Mitchell, Sjón, Elif Shafak, Karl Ove Knausgård, Tsitsi Dangarembga, Judith Schalansky, Valeria Luiselli, Tommy Orange and, most recently, Amitav Ghosh.In June 2022, the City of Oslo signed an agreement that ensures the forest will remain in the hands of the Future Library Trust for the duration of the project.Explore more on these topicsFuture LibraryLaurie AndersonNorwayEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Winter panic’: EU gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years | Gas | The Guardian
description: As one of Europe’s biggest consumers of gas the UK may be particularly exposed to heightened price volatility
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: As one of Europe’s biggest consumers of gas the UK may be particularly exposed to heightened price volatility
Content: An LNG (liquefied natural gas) tanker from the US arrives at the Isle of Grain, Kent, last year. The UK relies on imports of gas via pipelines from Europe or tankers from the US and Middle East.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/GettyView image in fullscreenAn LNG (liquefied natural gas) tanker from the US arrives at the Isle of Grain, Kent, last year. The UK relies on imports of gas via pipelines from Europe or tankers from the US and Middle East.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/GettyGas‘Winter panic’: EU gas stores at their lowest level in 13 yearsAs one of Europe’s biggest consumers of gas the UK may be particularly exposed to heightened price volatilityJillian AmbroseSat 29 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEurope is on course to enter the cooler months with gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years, which has triggered “winter panic” among energy traders, experts have warned.The EU’s gas stocks were 63% full in the last week of August, well below the 80% average for late August over recent years and among the lowest levels ever recorded for this time of year.At the current sluggish rate of gas storage injections, the EU is likely to enter the winter heating season with gas stocks about a fifth below the five-year average, and at their lowest level since 2013, according to Greg Molnar, a gas analyst and professor.“Low storage levels are naturally increasing the risk of heightened winter price volatility,” he said, which could be made worse by “cold spells or slow wind patterns” increasing gas usage over the winter.The UK may be particularly exposed to market volatility, because it is one of the biggest gas consumers in Europe but has some of the lowest levels of domestic gas storage capacity.Typically, the UK relies on imports of gas via pipeline from Europe or tankers from the US and the Middle East. Chris O’Shea, chief executive of the British Gas ownerCentrica, said this week the UK had “almost no gas in storage” for the coming winter.The EU’s gas stores have struggled to rise towards a watered-down target of 80% full by the start of winter, since the US-Israel war on Iran triggered severe disruption to exports of oil and gas from the Gulf region.graphA cold end to last winter, and higher-than-usual gas power generation during Europe’s heatwaves this summer, have also contributed to the bloc’s depleted gas stores. In a typical year, owners of storage facilities fill them up during the summer when both demand and prices are lower.Europe’s gas market prices have “stayed relatively calm” this summer in the hope that the strait of Hormuz would be reopened and winter stocks could be rebuilt. However, “no one expects it to happen any time soon”, according to Bjarne Schieldrop, chief analyst commodities at the Nordic banking group SEB.“As a result, the European natural gas market has run into a bit of a winter panic over the past week,” Schieldrop added.Although Europe is not expected to experience physical shortages of gas this winter, traders expect higher prices.Benchmark gas price has climbed to three-year highs above €68 per megawatt-hour (MWh) in recent weeks, more than double the price at the start of the year. Prices have risen sharply on the growing expectation that market traders in the EU will need to compete with Asian buyers to secure cargoes of liquefied natural gas as temperatures begin to cool.Without a return of gas exports from the Middle East, Europe’s benchmark price “would likely need to move above €100/MWh” to attract enough shipments of gas to meet winter demand, according to analysts at Goldman Sachs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGas supply concerns are particularly acute in western Europe, where storage levels are well below those in countries such as Italy and Poland, which have managed to top up their gas stores to over 80% full.In Germany, which has Europe’s largest gas storage capacity, facilities are about half-full, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe. Storage levels in Belgium and the Netherlands, which connect directly to the UK gas market via gas pipelines, stand at 51% and 45%.The UK’s reliance on global gas importsis expected to deepenas declining gas production from the UK’s North Sea sector accelerates, and Norwegian output begins to fall from 2030.The government is considering plans to provide direct financial support to safeguard domestic gas infrastructure, after an official consultation found that homes and businessesrisk running out of gas within the next decade, despite its growing clean energy sources.This could include offering financial support to the owners of gas storage facilities and pipeline operators, to make it economically viable to upgrade and maintain them in the decades ahead.The UK energy regulator, Ofgem, said this week that typical gas and electricity bills willrise by 4%from October under its quarterly cap, afterclimbing 13%at the start of July, to take account of global energy market price rises caused by the war on Iran.Explore more on these topicsGasEnergy industryEuropean UnionCentricaCommoditiesEuropeEnergy billsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ireland will be united, says Gordon Brown | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: Former PM believes Northern Ireland will leave UK in the long term – but remains opposed to Scottish independence
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Former PM believes Northern Ireland will leave UK in the long term – but remains opposed to Scottish independence
Content: Gordon Brown said a united Ireland would be ‘a long process where people have got to come together and find a way of agreeing’.Photograph: Victoria Jones/PAView image in fullscreenGordon Brown said a united Ireland would be ‘a long process where people have got to come together and find a way of agreeing’.Photograph: Victoria Jones/PANorthern IrelandIreland will be united, says Gordon BrownFormer PM believes Northern Ireland will leave UK in the long term – but remains opposed to Scottish independence‘I don’t want to be a backseat driver’: Gordon Brown on Burnham, billionaires – and his vision for a better BritainPeter WalkerandCharlotte EdwardesSat 29 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 04.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former prime ministerGordon Brownhas said it is inevitable that Ireland will become united at some point in the future, in a wide-ranging interview with the Guardian.While he added that any union would necessarily be “a long process” and based on mutual agreement, Brown’s comments are notable both because of his vehement opposition to Scottish independence, but also because of his involvement in government in efforts to bring peace toNorthern Ireland.He was Tony Blair’s chancellor when the Good Friday peace agreement was signed in 1998. In 2010, he was prime minister when justice and policing powerswere devolvedto Northern Ireland’s power-sharing government, another major step for reconciliation.But,speaking to the Guardian’s Saturday magazine, Brown argued that Northern Ireland had a potentially different position with regards to the rest of the UK than, for example, Scotland.Asked about continued pressure for Scottish independence, Brown said: “Scotland’s got to find a way of living in cooperation with other countries, and independence would not be the right way forward. We’re geographically, economically, socially, culturally linked to the rest of the United Kingdom, whether it’s Wales, England or parts of Ireland.”Questioned about whether the geographical link of NorthernIrelandwith the Republic of Ireland meant uniting the two made sense, he replied: “Yes. Well, of course, in the long term, Ireland will be united.”Such a process would be, he added, “a long process where people have got to come together and find a way of agreeing. Basically, that is the issue: whether people can actually agree.”Elsewhere in the interview, coinciding with the publication of Brown’s new book,The Future Starts With Us, he said he did not want “to be a backseat driver” in terms of telling Andy Burnham – who served in his cabinet – what to do.He nonetheless made the case for continued oil and gas drilling in the North Sea, one of the most politically sensitive decisions facing Burnham in the coming months, notably over the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields, consultations on which have now closed.Brown argued that decisions over the North Sea had been incorrectly portrayed as a binary choice between fossil fuels and renewables, when in fact it was a question of helping a transition towards the latter.He said: “I think you can support renewables as the future for British energy and support the development of the North Sea to use some of the existing oil and gas.“And in fact, the way to use the North Sea for hydrogen, for wind – it could be floating wind– and for carbon capture and storage, which are three energy products that could come out of the North Sea, the way to make that happen is to keep the infrastructure and skills that you have in the development of the North Sea for oil and gas.“In other words, the transition to renewables in the North Sea should come from keeping the infrastructure and skills that we have in the first instance for oil and gas, and gradually moving them across to doing wind, hydrogen, and carbon capture.”This transition, he argued, could be managed via a “European consortium” also involving Norway, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and Denmark.But more widely, Brown said, environmental policies had “got to be seen as a benefit and not just a cost”.He added: “It’s quite important that renewable costs are coming down all the time. So, 20 years ago it would’ve been cheaper to produce coal and oil and gas, but now of course you have the advantages of solar power and wind power and everything else. So, investing in the environment is potentially a money-saving thing.”Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandIrelandGordon BrownEuropeGood Friday agreementScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Palestinian woman and NBC News team reportedly attacked in West Bank | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Matt Bradley and crew assaulted while interviewing woman who said settlers had driven family out of home
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Matt Bradley and crew assaulted while interviewing woman who said settlers had driven family out of home
Content: Matt Bradley of NBC News in the West Bank on 13 August.Photograph: mattmcbradley/NBC NewsView image in fullscreenMatt Bradley of NBC News in the West Bank on 13 August.Photograph: mattmcbradley/NBC NewsWest BankPalestinian woman and NBC News team reportedly attacked in West BankMatt Bradley and crew assaulted while interviewing woman who said settlers had driven family out of homeEdward HelmoreSat 29 Aug 2026 17.55 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 17.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Palestinian woman and an NBC News team are reported to have been attacked and injured by masked Israeli settlers in the Israeli-occupiedWest Bankon Saturday, amid worsening confrontations in the area.Benjamin Netanyahu said he condemned the violence committed “by a handful of rioters”.The attack occurred when four members of the news team wereinterviewingAida Ahmed Abdullah and her family in the Palestinian town of Jalud, near Nablus.Abdullah told the outlet that they had been driven out of their home by settlers, and the team was walking down a hill toward the house.A car with Israeli license plates reversed up the hill toward them. At least four men with their faces covered leapt from the vehicle, hitting them with sticks and throwing rocks.“They jumped out, beat us, then jumped back in the car,” saidNBCNews correspondent Matt Bradley. Bradley was hit twice in the arm and treated at a nearby clinic.Abdullah, 51, was taken for medical care by the Red Crescent. Her injuries were not life-threatening. Three other members of the news team were also injured and treated.“Suddenly a car came to us,” said producer Lawahez Jabari. “The settlers had sticks, I saw a gun, but they didn’t use the gun.”Camera operator Khaldoon Eid said the team had not expected to be attacked in a village.Several violent incidents in the area were reported on Saturday. Palestinian workers were pepper-sprayed in nearby Qusra by masked Israeli settlers.Israeli security forces told the outlet they had received reports that “violent clashes had occurred, including stone-hurling toward Palestinians and additional civilians”.They said “security forces identified dozens of rioters who had barricaded themselves inside a Palestinian home while Palestinian residents were inside”, the statement said.“The security forces who arrived at the scene initially operated to remove the rioters from the home and separate the groups, in order to protect the residents inside. In addition, the security forces confiscated vehicles belonging to the Israeli rioters that were suspected of having been used to reach the area,” the statement said.“IDF soldiers and Israel Border Police forces continue to operate in the areas of Qusra and Jalud to prevent further disturbances and restore order in the area,” it added.Earlier this month, a group of settlers began blocking supplies from entering Palestinian houses on the outskirts of the village near Nablus, trapping residents inside and drawing strong criticism from the US ambassador.Israeli forces continue to operate in the area while settlers still roam the surrounding hills.Netanyahu, whose government has been accused of turning a blind eye to the settler attacks, condemned the “criminal acts of violence” and blamed “a handful of rioters who violate the law, cause enormous injustice to the law-abiding settler public, hinder the IDF in fulfilling its missions and harm Israel’s standing in the world”.According to the United Nations’ office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs, Israeli forces or settlers killed 76 Palestinians in the West Bank in the year to 24 July. Three Israelis were killed over the same period.Explore more on these topicsWest BankNBCIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Nepal-Tibet floods: Nepal calls for technical support for rescue efforts as number of missing rises to nearly 3,000 – as it happened | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian

Author: Wendy Frew
Headline: This blog is now closed.
Content: 09.33 EDTNepal government calls for specialised assistance from neighbouring countries to aid rescue effortsThe Nepalese government has requested “specific and specialised assistance” from neighbouring countries to aid search and rescue efforts.This includes assistance with opening tunnels where people are trapped, technologies that can help locate people alive in affected areas, rapid forensic and DNA analysis, and mortuary facilities for the proper storage of bodies, Nepal’s ministry of foreign affairs said in a statement.It added: “An 11-member specialised technical reconnaissance team for tunnel rescue fromIndiahas been mobilised and a tunnel rescue team from China is expected to arrive very soon.”ShareUpdated at09.55 EDT

title: Daughter traces mother and aunt’s last known location in Nepal through TikTok video  | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Tulshi Patel says Hemangini Jitendra Patel and aunt, Hema Sunil Amin, were last seen at Friendship Bridge on Nepal-China border
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Tulshi Patel says Hemangini Jitendra Patel and aunt, Hema Sunil Amin, were last seen at Friendship Bridge on Nepal-China border
Content: Sisters Hema Sunil Amin, left, and Hemangini Jitendra Patel are unaccounted for after the flooding in Nepal.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenSisters Hema Sunil Amin, left, and Hemangini Jitendra Patel are unaccounted for after the flooding in Nepal.Photograph: BBCNepal-Tibet flood disasterDaughter traces mother and aunt’s last known location in Nepal through TikTok videoTulshi Patel says mother Hemangini Jitendra Patel and aunt Hema Sunil Amin were last seen at Friendship Bridge on Nepal-China borderNepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updatesSammy GecsoylerSat 29 Aug 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 13.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe daughter of a woman missing inNepalhas told how she traced her mother’s location through a TikTok video posted hours before the devastating flash flood hit.The catastrophic flash floods thathit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and sweeping away entire villages, have killed at least 675 people, while more than3,000 remain missing.Among the missing are 33 British nationals, including a 13-year-old, NHS workers and a priest. A team from the UK will arrive in the Nepali capital, Kathmandu, on Saturday.Tulshi Patel’s mother, Hemangini Jitendra Patel, and her aunt, Hema Sunil Amin, set off on a pilgrimage in which they had planned to travel intoTibet, but the pair have not been contactable since the flash floods hit.In an interview with LBC’s Matt Frei, Patel said the two women had been talking about the trip since the start of the year and the journey had been “on their bucket list”.She said she had last spoken to her mother and aunt on Monday, had received a photo of them on Tuesday, and their last known location had come from a GPS signal from the tour group at a place called Friendship Bridge at the Nepal-China border.View image in fullscreenThe Chinese immigration centre on the Tibet border. The green Friendship Bridge which crosses the river between Tibet and Nepal was swept away in the floods.Photograph: Armand Terruli/Guardian CommunityPatel, a pharmacist from Milton Keynes, said: “We did our own deep-dive research and we found a TikTok video that verified and showed my mum and auntie and three other people from the tour at the border waiting to cross, I guess, that the local Nepali tour guide had made.”Of the video, Patel said: “It was Wednesday morning, just before 6am, Nepal time.“They were supposed to have crossed the border on Tuesday, but I guess due to weather conditions, or whichever it was, they got delayed and unfortunately crossed over on Wednesday.”The flood is believed to have occurred after amagnitude 5.2 seismic eventnear the border between Nepal and China on Wednesday at 8.37am local time, according to the US Geological Survey.Patel said her mother and aunt had been in good health and had prepared well for the trip. “They’d gone on walks regularly, they were looking forward to it. This is all they wanted,” she said.“Their positive viewpoints, health, mental health was great and they were very strong and positive about everything.“This was something that they were both looking forward to. They’d been talking about this from the beginning of the year. It was something that was on their bucket list that they really wanted to do.”Neetu Goyal Tiwari.Photograph: FacebookPatel said she had messaged the two women “in the hopes that maybe we’ll see a tick to say they’ve seen it or read it” and had attempted to contact the tour guide. “We’ve messaged the tour guide in case he has a signal because he’ll have a local Sim as well.“Every day we’re calling via WhatsApp … We’ve not given up, but, from our end, all we can do is research, but we just need kind of eyes and ears there from our side to basically get them out. Get all of them out and safe.”Patel said the family had considered travelling to Nepal to join search efforts but had decided against this as they did not know how close they could get to the region in order to help.View image in fullscreenLeena Bector.Photograph: FacebookSome of those missing were visiting Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists. Neetu Goyal Tiwari, 51, was on her “dream” trip to complete a pilgrimage when the flash floods hit.The family have been desperately phoning contacts in Nepal in an attempt to find her, though they increasingly believe her to still be in China. As many of the family members are based in India, it is difficult for them to obtain visas to search for her. Her brother, Naresh Goyal, said Neetu’s husband and daughter remained in the UK for now.“We’re not sure what the next second holds and what we should do from our end, because we’re trying to reach everyone we can,” he said. “She was a very fun-loving woman [and] really had a great heart. I really hope she comes back soon.”Other families of those missing have travelled to the affected region from the UK. Leena Bector, 53, from Slough, was among 27 travellers who are unaccounted for.Her husband, Bhupesh Bector, told the Times he was booking the next flight to Kathmandu after the Home Office had failed to confirm whether Leena was on its missing persons list.He said: “Even if they find her today or tomorrow, I need to be there. She must be in trauma.”Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetSouth and central AsiaNatural disastersnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Their whole village has disappeared’: frantic hunt for survivors in Kathmandu hospital | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Family members pin photos of Nepal’s missing to hospital wall as people try not to give up hope on loved ones
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Family members pin photos of Nepal’s missing to hospital wall as people try not to give up hope on loved ones
Content: People search posters of those missing in Nepal floodNepal-Tibet flood disaster‘Their whole village has disappeared’: frantic hunt for survivors in Kathmandu hospitalFamily members pin photos of Nepal’s missing to hospital wall as people try not to give up hope on loved onesNepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updatesHannah Ellis-PetersenandGaurav Pokharelin KathmanduSat 29 Aug 2026 10.11 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 10.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePosters of missing people line the wall of the hospital, the glue still fresh beneath. A schoolgirl smiling in her uniform; a beaming, chubby-cheeked baby; a couple smiling on their wedding day; a young man, hands on hips, atop a mountain peak; a young girl with flowing hair, peaking out from behind a door.These faces are just a fraction of the thousands who have not been seen since deadly flash floods coursed through the Himalayas and wiped away entire villages. By Saturday morning, the toll of the missing had risen to almost 3,000, in both Nepal andTibet.View image in fullscreenRelatives search through lists of people reported missing outside the hospital in Kathmandu.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianSo far,Nepalhas recovered 675 bodies, but many remote areas have only been accessed by army helicopters on the hunt for survivors. Rescuers said it was too difficult to assess how many more people might be buried beneath the mud.The task of identifying the dead is also gargantuan.In the Nepali city of Chitwan, the morgues have been overrun by the sheer number of bodies and a makeshift building has been set up to house the dead.Some of the bodies were carried so far down the river by the force of the floods, they were recovered in neighbouring India.2:02Timeline of how deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – explainerAt Tribhuvan University teaching hospital in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, desperate relatives gathered in the hope of news. Four days on since the disaster struck, people continued to crowd round the police desk to register the names of missing family members. Hundreds of the injured are recovering in the hospital’s wards and people were frantically checking lists of patients, desperate to find a sign that their loved ones were still alive.View image in fullscreenRelatives look through the lists of missing flood victims at the teaching hospital.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianIn the absence of information and with affected areas almost completely cut off, many families have resorted to making posters to appeal for information. Yavraj Lama said his sister, her husband and their two children were missing after their village of Jaydada, in Rusawa district, had been entirely washed away.His eyes filled with tears as he glued a photo of one-year-old Sijan Tawang, a baby in the arms of his mother, to the hospital wall. A picture of 12-year-old Sahil, his brother, hung next to it.“We are numb, we don’t have words to say how sad and distraught we are,” said Lama. “Our main focus is trying to find baby Sijan. He was so sweet and innocent; it’s impossible for us to think he is not with us any more.“But their whole village has disappeared,” he added, “so we have no hope left that any of them survived.”View image in fullscreenMonita Nepali, right, whose husband is missing, is comforted at the hospital in Kathmandu.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianMonita Nepali, 22, howled in grief as a poster of her missing husband, Vishal Nepali, 30, was pinned to the hospital wall. They had married six months ago and his work as a driver regularly took him to the border between Nepal and Tibet. She had spoken to her husband an hour before the floods hit when he was out for a morning walk in Rusawa. He had promised to call her that evening, but his phone has been ever off since.“I don’t want to live on the face of this earth without him,” she said. Four days may have passed, Nepali said, but she had not stopped believing in her husband’s return. “I feel it in my heart he will come back.”10:11‘Erased before their eyes’: desperate rescue efforts continue after Nepal-Tibet floods - The LatestFor some families, the scale of the loss was too hard to comprehend. Tulmaya Tamang, 36, came to the hospital bearing posters of some of her 12 family members, including her five-month-old niece, who lived in a village in Rusawa and have not been seen since the floods.“Our family is under tremendous stress,” she said. “So many are gone, and those of us who are left behind are struggling.”As hopes for their survival faded, Tamang said they were now just hoping the bodies could be retrieved. “If we had the bodies, then at least we could have peace,” she said. “Otherwise, the family will never stop wondering and this pain will go on for a very long time.”At least 900 of those still missing were working on the vast hydropower projects along the Trishuli River corridor, high up in the Himalayas, which were decimated by the floods and mudslides. Many of the workers were low-paid labourers, including at least 63 from India.View image in fullscreenA Nepali soldier rescues a survivor from a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa district, Nepal.Photograph: Nepal Army Handout/EPAOn Friday, dramatic footage showed Nepali soldiers pulling several survivors out through a thick wall of mud from a tunnel in the Trishuli-1 hydropower project. The Nepali army said they believed at least another 100 people were still trapped inside the tunnels, as well as dozens more stuck underground in the Trishuli-3 hydropower plant.Among those missing was 24-year-old Sujan Nepali, who had just finished his night shift at the hydropower project and was asleep in bed when the wall of water came gushing down the valley. At the hospital trauma centre in Nepal, his sister, Sushisha Maluwar, had returned anxiously every day to check if his name was listed.“We haven’t lost hope,” she said. “We are writing down his name at the hospitals and putting up his photographs everywhere, hoping that we might find him somewhere. Maybe he has already been rescued. Maybe he had managed to escape and survive.”Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetFloodingSouth and central AsiaNatural disastersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Far-right media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos deported by ICE from US to UK | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Ex-Breitbart editor has vocally supported immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residency
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Ex-Breitbart editor has vocally supported immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residency
Content: Milo Yiannopoulos in New York City on 21 February 2017.Photograph: Drew Angerer/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMilo Yiannopoulos in New York City on 21 February 2017.Photograph: Drew Angerer/Getty ImagesUS immigrationFar-right media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos deported by ICE from US to UKEx-Breitbart editor has vocally supported immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residencyEdward HelmoreSat 29 Aug 2026 13.08 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFar-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US after beingdetainedon Thursday by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in New Orleans in connection with what the agency said was expired authorization to be in the country and a deportation order.Yiannopoulos’s deportation to the UK occurred on Friday, said a statement on Saturday from a spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE.A DHS spokesperson on Friday said that Yiannopoulos, 41, had been arrested by ICE on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans international airport. The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019 through New York City but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.The spokesperson said that Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”.The spokesperson added: “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”Yiannopoulos – who has previously been a vocal supporter of ICE and immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residency – was believed to have been arrested while heading to a concert by rapper Ye, formerly Kanye West.West performed at New Orleans’s Caesars Superdome on Friday. In 2022, Yiannopoulosworked onWest’s short-lived 2024 White House campaign, and his social media account suggests he was working for a company of the rapper.Yiannopoulos, aformer editor of the conservative media outlet Breitbart News, previously servedas an internfor the former US congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene. He eventually became locked into a feud with fellow far-right commentator Laura Loomer, a Trump administration ally who claimed on Friday that she had reported Yiannopoulos to ICE over his immigration status.At the peak of his influence, Yiannopoulos was offered a speaking slot at the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, in 2017 after he had been supportive of Donald Trump during his run for his first presidency.He fell out of favor in conservative circles after the publication of a video inwhich he condoned sexual relationswith boys as young as 13.Yiannopoulos claimed that his experiences as a victim of teenage sexual abuse gave him license to comment on the subject. He soon resigned as a senior editor atBreitbart.Yiannopoulos was also banned from Twitter, now called X, in 2016 for directing racist and misogynistic tweets against a Black actor in a Ghostbusters remake. His accountwas reinstated to the platform in 2022after it was acquired and renamed by multibillionaire Elon Musk.A little more than a year before his detention by ICE, a social mediapostfrom Yiannopoulos called on immigration checkpoints to be set up at California “supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersection and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally”.He had also sarcasticallyaskedwhether it was impolite for one “to masturbate” in public rather than in private “if you are going about your business and find yourself observing an ICE raid” amid the mass deportation campaign that Trump has pursued throughout his second presidency.Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationFar right (US)ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)BreitbartUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: James Cleverly resigns from shadow cabinet to run for mayor of London | James Cleverly | The Guardian
description: Shadow minister for housing, communities and local government to resign with immediate effect
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Shadow minister for housing, communities and local government to resign with immediate effect
Content: Cleverly has held the posts of both home and foreign secretary for the Conservatives.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCleverly has held the posts of both home and foreign secretary for the Conservatives.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianJames CleverlyJames Cleverly resigns from shadow cabinet to run for mayor of LondonShadow minister for housing, communities and local government to resign with immediate effectSammy GecsoylerSat 29 Aug 2026 12.24 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 11.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJames Cleverly has resigned from the shadow cabinet to run for mayor of London.The Tory heavyweight, who was once home and foreign secretary and is shadow minister for housing, communities and local government, told the Sunday Times he will resign with immediate effect.The MP for Braintree, who lost his bid to lead theConservativesto Kemi Badenoch, is considered a more moderate voice in a party that has lurched to the right. On breaking the news to Badenoch, Cleverly told the Sunday Times: “She took it very well. Kemi has been very gracious.”He added: “Our route to getting Kemi in No 10 has got to be through success inLondon,” he said. “It’s a business city, entrepreneurialism, arts, culture. I don’t buy the lazy idea that London is a Labour city. It represents the philosophical heart of the Conservative party.”Cleverly’s resignation comes in advance of the Conservative party conference in October, where he is expected to make his case to party members.According to the Sunday Times, sources close to Badenoch said she was “gutted” about the news but added that she “is delighted that someone of his calibre wants to put himself forward to be Conservative nominee for mayor of London”.Cleverly had kind words for Badenoch. “Frankly, Kemi is doing really well now. She’s getting great cut-through. It took longer than any of us would have liked, but she’s getting it,” he said.Sadiq Khan is halfway through his third term as mayor. He has not stated whether he will run for a fourth term in the contest to be held in May 2028.
