Susan Hall was the Tory candidate in 2024 but lost to Khan, who was declared the winner with 43.8% of the vote.If Khan does step down, the Labour MP for Brent Central and Brent South, Dawn Butler, is expected to throw her hat in the ring, having previously revealed her desire for the job.Cleverly is the most senior Tory politician to run for mayor of London in recent times. Making his bid, he said Khan was “asleep at the wheel” and accused him of using the role as a stepping stone for a higher-profile position.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Sadiq has been trying to get out of that job for quite a while. He went in with the intention of doing what Boris [Johnson] did, using it as a high-profile platform to get him his next big job in government. There has been lots of posturing, very little delivery. Lots of picking rows with the president of America, less focus on bringing down street crime. It wouldn’t surprise me if he bows out for 2028. He’s lost the passion for the job.”Days before Keir Starmer stood down as prime minister, he handed Khan a peerage, potentially opening the door to him joining Andy Burnham’s cabinet in future. However, while Burnham and Khan have worked closely together over the years and have a shared understanding of the challenges of devolution, it is understood Khan has told the former Manchester mayor that he has no wish to be a minister in his government.Explore more on these topicsJames CleverlyConservativesLondonMayoral electionsLocal governmentLocal politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sarah Ferguson to return to UK after relocating amid Epstein revelations | Sarah Ferguson | The Guardian
description: Former Duchess of York moved to Swiss chalet during fallout over her friendship with convicted child sex offender
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Former Duchess of York moved to Swiss chalet during fallout over her friendship with convicted child sex offender
Content: Ferguson used to live with her ex-husband, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, at his former home Royal Lodge in Windsor until he was forced to vacate the premises.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PAView image in fullscreenFerguson used to live with her ex-husband, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, at his former home Royal Lodge in Windsor until he was forced to vacate the premises.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PASarah FergusonSarah Ferguson to return to UK after relocating amid Epstein revelationsFormer Duchess of York moved to Swiss chalet during fallout over her friendship with convicted child sex offenderSammy GecsoylerSat 29 Aug 2026 10.32 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 08.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSarah Ferguson will return to the UK after relocating to a Swiss chalet amid the fallout over the friendship between her and her ex-husband,Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, and the convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, according to reports.The pair werestripped of their royal titlesin October over the scandal of their relationship with Epstein. According to the Sun, the former Duchess of York, 66, is renting a six-bedroom gated property in the home counties.Ferguson used to live with Mountbatten-Windsor at Royal Lodge in Windsor until he was forced to vacate the premises and move to Marsh Farm on King Charles’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk.She could “imminently” move into a new home, which has three bathrooms and a “granny annexe”, according to the Sun.It is believed Ferguson has been spending time out of the public eye at a Swiss chalet in Verbier since leaving Royal Lodge, and her belongings were collected from Andrew’s home in Sandringham this week, the newspaper added.Her expected return comes just days after the Duke and Duchess of Sussex arrived back in the UK with their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. The family are expected to enjoy an “extended stay” in Britain, with the children enrolled at school and due to start next week.There is clearly trouble ahead for Harry and Meghan on their return to the UK. Here are five ways to avert it | Stephen BatesRead moreFerguson has faced calls to speak to US authorities about Epstein after last year’s release of millions of documents associated with him shed fresh light on their relationship. One email exchange suggested Ferguson had taken her daughters to see Epstein in the US days after he was released from prison for child sex crimes.A year after his conviction for child sex crimes, Ferguson thanked Epstein for being the “brother” she had “always wished for” in an email.Last September, the Mail on Sunday published emails from 2011, in whichFerguson privately described Epstein as her “supreme friend”and apologised for “letting him down”, despite having publicly called her association with him “a gigantic error of judgment”.The messages were sent less than two months after she had insisted she would “never have anything to do with [Epstein] again”, amid pressure over the ties she and Mountbatten-Windsor had maintained with him – including a £15,000 payment Epstein made to help settle Ferguson’s debts.Epstein has been the downfall of Mountbatten-Windsor, who was stripped of his titles by the King because of “serious lapses of judgment” over his friendship with the late child sex offender and allegations of sexual assault against him by one of Epstein’s victims,Virginia Giuffre.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFerguson lost her courtesy royal divorcee title and reverted to her original name, and also lost the freedom of the city of York after councillors voted unanimously to remove the honour over her links to Epstein. She and Mountbatten-Windsor were given the honour as a wedding present from York in 1987 during a visit to the city.The former duchess has published more than 50 books – largely children’s titles – but after the Epstein revelations, thousands of copies of her latest children’s book were withdrawn from sale and “pulped”.Earlier this year, Ferguson’s international charity, Sarah’s Trust, announced its closure “for the foreseeable future”. Seven charities, including the Teenage Cancer Trust and children’s hospice, have alsocut ties and revoked Ferguson’s patronagedue to her links with Epstein.Six companies linked to Ferguson – S Phoenix Events, Fergie’s Farm, La Luna Investments, Solamoon Ltd, Philanthrapreneur Ltd and Planet Partners Productions Ltd – were wound down in February after more damaging revelations came to light with the release of the Epstein files.Explore more on these topicsSarah FergusonMonarchyAndrew Mountbatten-WindsorJeffrey EpsteinnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cells for arrested offenders may run out without early prison release, says Labour | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Bridget Phillipson says government would not have to consider releasing prisoners early if Tories had created more capacity
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Bridget Phillipson says government would not have to consider releasing prisoners early if Tories had created more capacity
Content: Bridget Phillipson said police could end up in a position where they had nowhere to send someone arrested for serious offences.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster Editorial/AlamyView image in fullscreenBridget Phillipson said police could end up in a position where they had nowhere to send someone arrested for serious offences.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster Editorial/AlamyPrisons and probationCells for arrested offenders may run out without early prison release, says LabourBridget Phillipson says government would not have to consider releasing prisoners early if Tories had created more capacityKevin RawlinsonSat 29 Aug 2026 09.25 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 11.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCells to hold newly arrested people could run out without the early prison release scheme, a minister has said.Bridget Phillipson defended the plan to address the prison capacity crisis in England and Wales by releasing thousands of prisoners early, which has been criticised bydomestic abuse charities, bereaved families and probation officers among others.“We have faced some really difficult and unpalatable choices because of the huge crisis that was left behind in the prisons estate,” the women and equalities minister told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Saturday.She insisted the “most serious offenders” would not be released early under the scheme, details of which would be set out during the week.“But the reality of what we are confronting is that, if allowed to go unchecked, we could end up in a position where someone who was arrested for very serious offences, for example, offences related to violence against a woman, and we wouldn’t have anywhere to send that individual. That was the full scale of the real crisis we face.”Andy Burnham has been facing pressure to balance the competing aims of creating space in prisons and avoiding causing further upset to victims of serious crime. Under the scheme, a sentence would not be ended early but the portion of it served in custody would be shortened. The remainder would be served in the community, a principle that already exists in most sentences.On Friday, families of those affected by homicide called for those convicted of any form of manslaughter to be excluded from the scheme. In a letter to the justice secretary, Alex Norris, they said they felt victims were “being asked to bear the consequences of the prison capacity crisis”.Signatories included Emma Webber, whose son Barnaby was stabbed to death in Nottingham in 2023 and whose killer, Valdo Calocane, wasconvicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility. Another was Diana Parkes, whose daughterJoanna Simpson was killed by her estranged husband, Robert Brown, in 2010. Brown was also convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility.Phillipson said she had the “utmost respect and sympathy for the victims and their families” and blamed the previous Conservative government for allowing the prison capacity problem to fester. “We didn’t create enough prison capacity in the years that they were in government so that we don’t have to be even considering these kinds of options, which – in an ideal world – we would not be having to consider.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn January, the government announced a set of measures, which came into force in March, that were designed to stave off a looming crisis this summer. Sources indicated, however, that these measures were never thought to be enough to avert further crises. They pointed to the Sentencing Act, which introduces wholesale changes to sentencing, as the government’s plan to fix the issue once and for all.Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceEnglandWalesBridget PhillipsonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fourth time lucky as Chris Cantrill’s spoof whodunnit wins Edinburgh comedy award 2026 | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Nominated in three previous years, the rambunctious standup – one half of The Delightful Sausage – wins the prize for his show Rewilding while Marty Gleeson is named best newcomer for Dog Ear
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Nominated in three previous years, the rambunctious standup – one half of The Delightful Sausage – wins the prize for his show Rewilding while Marty Gleeson is named best newcomer for Dog Ear
Content: Palpable mainstream potential … Chris Cantrill.Photograph: Jack KirbyView image in fullscreenPalpable mainstream potential … Chris Cantrill.Photograph: Jack KirbyEdinburgh festival 2026Fourth time lucky as Chris Cantrill’s spoof whodunnit wins Edinburgh comedy award 2026Nominated in three previous years, the rambunctious standup – one half of The Delightful Sausage – wins the prize for his show Rewilding while Marty Gleeson is named best newcomerBrian LoganSat 29 Aug 2026 08.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 08.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe annual Edinburgh comedy award has been won by the standup Chris Cantrill, two years after his comedy partner Amy Gledhill – in the raucous northern double actThe Delightful Sausage– won the same prize.Cantrill, 42 and from Bradford, received the so-called “Oscar of live comedy” for a show,Rewilding, about his new life in rural Northumberland, where an act of vandalism shocks the local community – and a spoof whodunnit ensues. It builds on the foundations laid in 2024 byEasily Swayed, which documented his move to the countryside and secured what was then Cantrill’s third nomination (but first as a solo act) for the award.Like Gledhill, Cantrill is an uproarious, fun-loving and relatable act with palpable mainstream potential, and his victory comes against the grain ofan awards shortlistthat (in both the best show and best newcomer categories) trended leftfield. The oddballs are represented among this year’s winners by Marty Gleeson, who has received the best newcomer gong withher show Dog Ear. This eccentric set is inspired by Gleeson’s experiences at art school in her native Limerick, and – with its live bodhrán accompaniment and setpiece that requires shaking the hand of every single audience member – marches entirely to the beat of its own drum.View image in fullscreenMarching to the beat of her own drum … Marty Gleeson.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianFor my money, I didn’t have either winner down as frontrunner for the prize, which is famously a star-maker in British comedy. Previous winners of the main award, initiated in 1981, include Steve Coogan, Frank Skinner and Bridget Christie, and of the best newcomer gong (introduced in 1992) Harry Hill and Sarah Millican. I had the Mexican-American comicLara Ricoteand the London-based, Chinese-born standupLi Jin Haoas the acts most likely on this year’s list, and still marvel that the buzziest comedy shows on the fringe (byElf Lyons, the sketch groupCrybabiesandthe Australian clown Conk) weren’t even nominated.But I’m delighted to see Cantrill’s rambunctious comedy rewarded, after years of delivering big laughs to fringe audiences. And I’m excited by Gleeson’s arrival on the scene, and to see what she’ll do next. This year’s panel prize, meanwhile, which rewards initiatives that best sum up “the spirit of the fringe”, was won byOne Joke, a new event asking “how many comedians can tell one joke each, in an hour?” Produced by Liebenspiel, compered by Jonathan Oldfield, and headlined by the comic Lorna Rose Treen, it featured contributions by 60 comedians, and raised money for charity.Magicians and margarine: 10 of the funniest jokes from the Edinburgh fringe 2026Read moreThe organisers of the Edinburgh comedy award (formerly known as the Perrier), theatre producerNica Burnsand its new executive director Emma Brünjes, said that “in Chris and Marty we have two outstanding winners: both are exceptional comedians, writers and performers who have crafted wonderful shows”. The winners were selected from more than 550 eligible shows at a festival claiming, yet again, to be bigger than ever, with just over 4,200 registered shows across 299 venues. Whether the attendances were bigger than – or as big as – ever remains to be seen. (The sense on the ground was: perhaps not.) As winner of the best show prize, Cantrill walks off with £10,000; best newcomer Gleeson wins £5,000. BBC Radio 4 will tonight broadcast a special showcase featuring nominees for the two awards.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Awards and prizesFestivalsScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fire in California’s Big Sur region doubles in size overnight, forcing evacuations | California wildfires | The Guardian
description: Plaskett fire has swept through more than 5,900 acres in Monterey county and remains un-contained, says Cal Fire
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Plaskett fire has swept through more than 5,900 acres in Monterey county and remains un-contained, says Cal Fire
Content: A firefighter moves an injured animal as the Plaskett fire burns towards Highway 1 on Friday, in Big Sur, California.Photograph: Ethan Swope/APView image in fullscreenA firefighter moves an injured animal as the Plaskett fire burns towards Highway 1 on Friday, in Big Sur, California.Photograph: Ethan Swope/APCalifornia wildfiresFire in California’s Big Sur region doubles in size overnight, forcing evacuationsPlaskett fire has swept through more than 5,900 acres in Monterey county and remains un-contained, says Cal FireUwa Ede-OsifoSat 29 Aug 2026 19.51 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 19.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA fire in California’s Big Sur region doubled in size overnight, forcing the evacuation of nearby residents, in a coastal region where firefighters have battled another blaze for weeks.The Plaskett fire, which sparked on Tuesday, had swept through more than 5,900 acres (2,400 hectares) in Monterey county as of Friday, and remained un-contained, according to Cal Fire. Its cause is under investigation.View image in fullscreenFirefighters watch as the Plaskett fire burns toward Highway 1 on Friday.Photograph: Ethan Swope/APFire authorities have deployed helicopters and air tankers to suppress the flames with targeted water drops, but the remote area’s steep terrain and scarce roads have hindered ground crews’ ability to access the fire.Meanwhile, to the north, the Timber fire continues to burn through more than 24,000 acres (9,700 acres), as authorities have it under 21% containment. The blaze broke past certain containment lines. Smoke from the fire and cloud cover prevented officials from mapping the fire’s expansion overnight.View image in fullscreenSage Harvey tosses a rope off the roof of his house as the Plaskett fire approaches on Friday in Big Sur, California.Photograph: Ethan Swope/APBoth fires have prompted partial closures of Highway 1, whose Big Sur stretch offers a scenic route between Los Angeles and San Francisco.Explore more on these topicsCalifornia wildfiresCaliforniaWildfiresWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tennessee governor says he backs airport name change to honor Dolly Parton | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: Bill Lee says he favors proposal to rename Nashville’s international airport after legendary country singer
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Bill Lee says he favors proposal to rename Nashville’s international airport after legendary country singer
Content: A mural of Dolly Parton in East Nashville, Tennessee, on Friday.Photograph: Justin Renfroe/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA mural of Dolly Parton in East Nashville, Tennessee, on Friday.Photograph: Justin Renfroe/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockDolly PartonTennessee governor says he backs airport name change to honor Dolly PartonBill Lee says he favors proposal to rename Nashville’s international airport after legendary country singerEdward HelmoreSat 29 Aug 2026 15.57 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBill Lee, the Tennessee governor, on Friday said he favored a proposal to rename Nashville’s international airport after legendary country singerDolly Parton, who died three days earlier at age 80.In a statement, Lee said he and the managers of the airport in Tennessee’s capital city – where Parton resided – wanted to create “a lasting tribute to her indelible legacy and the generations of people she inspired”. He said he had spoken previously to the 11-time Grammy winner and her team, who were “touched by the idea”.“Dolly Parton’s extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state,” Lee said, noting that Nashville airport is where Tennessee welcomes the world.He added: “It is fitting thatNashvilleInternational Airport would bear the name of our state’s favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly’s music, generosity, faith, and kindness.”The proposal was scheduled to be addressed at a meeting of the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority (MNAA) on 17 September. A statement from Doug Kreulen, MNAA president, said the Nashville airport shared Parton’s understanding that “dignity, kindness and opportunity should never be defined by where you come from or your socioeconomic status”.“Whether you are boarding a private aircraft or taking your first flight, you deserve to be welcomed, respected and served with the same level of care,” he remarked.Partonhad requested a private funeral for immediate family, and there is not going to be any public memorial. She will be buried beside her husband, Carl Dean, at Nashville’s Woodlawn memorial park and mausoleum.The singertold Entertainment Weeklyin 2014 that she expected Whitney Houston’s rendition of I Will Always Love You to be part of her service. Parton also said she wanted an old gospel hymn, If We Never Meet Again, which was her father’s favorite.In a video statement announcing her death on Tuesday, Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver, her longtime head of security, remarked: “Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because, after a life wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest.”Lee discussed the proposal to rename Nashville’s airport after a plane tugging a banner urging the name change buzzed over theTennesseestate capitol on Friday. A petition was also launched, and it has since gained more than 150,000 signatures.“Everybody is looking for a way to honor Dolly and her legacy,” petition organizer Dan Diontold the Tennessean. “Our airport is so important, and there’s symbolism in flying into Parton Airport. With Dolly’s message of love, acceptance, music, kindness, humor and all these things, people feel that she is representative of what Tennessee truly is.”If it comes to be, renaming Nashville airport will be at least the second airport in a matter of months to make a switch. Palm Beach airport was recently renamed for Donald Trump, withmixed reactionsfrom travelers and locals about naming the facility after the president.Freddie O’Connell, the Nashville mayor, hinted that the proposed name change is only the start of metropolitan tributes in the city. He said the 9 to 5 and Jolene singer had been in the process of developing a hotel and museum called SongTeller “that she called her love letter to Nashville”.“Now it’s our turn to share a love letter to Dolly – by renaming Nashville International Airport to Dolly Parton International Airport in Nashville,” O’Connell told the Tennessean.He also said the city was “working closely” with Parton’s team and family “on appropriate public recognition”.Explore more on these topicsDolly PartonNashvilleTennesseeAirline industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: LAPD releases footage of death of man whom police handcuffed and beat | Los Angeles | The Guardian
description: Jose Carlos Hoyoz-Munoz was arrested after a family altercation and handcuffed for ‘combative’ behavior
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Jose Carlos Hoyoz-Munoz was arrested after a family altercation and handcuffed for ‘combative’ behavior
Content: Los Angeles’s mayor, Karen Bass, called for an independent evaluation into officer-involved deaths.Photograph: Damian Dovarganes/APView image in fullscreenLos Angeles’s mayor, Karen Bass, called for an independent evaluation into officer-involved deaths.Photograph: Damian Dovarganes/APLos AngelesLAPD releases footage of death of man whom police handcuffed and beatJose Carlos Hoyoz-Munoz was arrested after a family altercation and restrained for ‘combative’ behaviorUwa Ede-OsifoSat 29 Aug 2026 15.52 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 18.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA cadre of Los Angeles police officers beat and restrained a handcuffed man in July, minutes before he was found dead in a jail cell, according to newly releasedbody-cam footage.On 15 July, Jose Carlos Hoyoz-Munoz, 58, was found unconscious in his cell at the Van Nuys regional jail. At the time, the LAPD said two use-of-force incidents had occurred, without specifying the nature. In the video released on Friday, the department said three use-of-force incidents occurred.Body-cam footage showed Hoyoz-Munoz flapping what appeared to be a piece of cloth against the window in his holding cell. Several officers entered the cell and pinned him to the ground. The department described the restraint as being spurred by Hoyoz-Munoz’s “combative” behavior as they sought to fingerprint him.The officers placed him in a harnessed chair, which they used to transport him to the booking stalls, the video shows. Police used the weight of their bodies to restrain him again, citing resistance. The department said Hoyoz-Munoz also spat at officers, after which they put a spit hood over his face.Hoyoz-Munoz was escorted back to his cell. He was still handcuffed with the spit hood partly covering his face and his pants sagging down to his ankles, exposing his backside.After Hoyoz-Munoz climbed on top of a toilet, officers again entered the cell. They moved him to the cell bed, piling on top of him as he was positioned face down.The department said officers conducted wellness checks for 20 minutes afterward, when he appeared to exhibit signs of life.Later, an officer saw that Hoyoz-Munoz was not moving. He was found unconscious and not breathing when they checked on him.Hoyoz-Munoz was arrested on 13 July, when police received a call about a suspected assault with a deadly weapon. Hoyoz-Munoz allegedly injured his mother and another relative with a knife.Upon arrival at the scene, an officer encountered Hoyoz-Munoz’s mother with a laceration on her arm.“He has lost his mind. He’s gone crazy,” she said in Spanish.Another family member had a wound on his arm.After an hours-long standoff with law enforcement, during which Swat agents deployed teargas, an agitated Hoyoz-Munoz was located in the residence, kneeling before a piano as he touched the keys and spoke of religion.Los Angeles police also released video showing the death of 33-year-old Alejandro Luis Garcia, whom officers fatally shot. Garcia had allegedly shattered car windows with a baseball bat.Los Angeles’s mayor,Karen Bass, described both videos as difficult to watch in a Friday statement. She called for an independent evaluation into officer-involved deaths concerning people experiencing mental health crises.“People who experience behavioral or mental health crises often do not receive the proper care they desperately need. Without it, they can deteriorate into behavior that can result in severe injury or death,” the mayor said.“We must rigorously examine whether our policies, training, tactics, supervision and accountability systems are sufficient.”Explore more on these topicsLos AngelesUS policingMental healthKaren BassCaliforniaWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Artemis II astronauts receive nation's highest space honor for their successful moonshot | Artemis II | The Guardian
description: Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen receive Congressional Space Medal of Honor
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen receive Congressional Space Medal of Honor
Content: From left, Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, Jeremy Hansen and Donald Trump at the Johnson Space Center in Houston on Friday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFrom left, Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, Jeremy Hansen and Donald Trump at the Johnson Space Center in Houston on Friday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesArtemis IIArtemis II astronauts receive nation's highest space honor for their successful moonshotReid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen receive Congressional Space Medal of HonorAssociated PressSat 29 Aug 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 18.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheArtemis IIastronauts who flew around the moon in April received the US’s highest space honor on Friday.Donald Trumppresented the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the three Americans and one Canadian whose lunar flyby for the US space agency Nasa set a new distance record for humanity.Nasa’s administrator, Jared Isaacman, and other dignitaries took part in the packed ceremony atHouston’s Johnson Space Center, home to mission control. The president used the occasion to announce the creation of a US space academy for the nation’s space force as well as Nasa and the commercial space community.Nasa space telescope set to launch after surviving Trump budget cutsRead more“Space is the hot thing,” Trump told the crowd, adding that the academy’s location had yet to be determined.Cmdr Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen, a Canadian, became the first astronauts to travel to the moon in more than half a century, coming within 4,067 miles (6,545km) while test-driving Nasa’s new Orion capsule. They were the first to launch onboard Nasa’s new moon rocket, a 30-story behemoth that had soared only once before from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center.While they didn’t stop at the moon, the four set the stage for next year’s Artemis III docking rehearsal in orbit around Earth. Artemis IV’s moon landing by two astronauts, near the lunar south pole, could follow as soon as 2028.Trump said Americans will land back on the moon before his second presidency ends. Mars is next – “very shortly”, he said.The president called the newest recipients “four intrepid space heroes”. He pointed out that they did not do it alone, thanking all who contributed to the Artemis II mission.“There are no finer humans we could have sent as our ambassadors to the stars,” Isaacman added.Wiseman and his crew are in good company, with only 30 astronauts receiving the prestigious honor before them. Many of the recipients were honored posthumously following their spaceflight-related deaths.Apollo 11 commander Neil Armstrong – whose phrase “that’s one step for man, one giant leap for mankind” gripped the world when he became the first person to walk on the moon on 20 July 1969 – was the first to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor.President Jimmy Carter awarded six of these medals in 1978, which also went to Alan Shepard, the first American in space; John Glenn, the first American in orbit; and Apollo 8 commander Frank Borman, whose 1968 mission marked humanity’s first lunar voyage.The most recent recipients were Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken, the first astronauts to launch aboard a SpaceX rocket. Coming nine years after the space shuttle program’s close, their 2020 test flight to the International Space Station restored the US’s ability to launch crews from home soil. Joe Biden awarded them the medals in 2023, during the third year of his presidency.Dozens of astronauts participated in the ceremony, including Apollo 17 moonwalker Harrison Schmitt, who is now 91 – and the four men assigned to Nasa’s upcoming Artemis III mission.Schmitt noted that his mission – Apollo’s last moonshot – was the most productive lunar exploration yet.“Soon to be surpassed by Artemis,” he said of active astronauts standing behind him.Nasa plans a sustainable moon base staffed by astronauts and robots near the lunar south pole, where permanently shadowed craters are thought to hold tons of frozen water that could be turned into rocket fuel and drinking water. China is eyeing the same region.“The second space race has begun,” Nasa’s deputy administrator, Matthew Anderson, said.As the two-hour ceremony came to a close, the Artemis II astronauts presented Trump with his own blue flight jacket complete with space patches, which they had promised him while visiting him in the Oval Office after their mission.The president then hustled over to mission control to call the three US astronauts onboard the International Space Station. He informed them of the new US space academy, then briefly handed the phone to two of their spouses for a quick hello.Explore more on these topicsArtemis IIDonald TrumpThe moonSpaceHoustonTexasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers says he saw Bin Laden’s body with his ‘own eyes’. He did not | Michigan | The Guardian
description: Ex-House intel committee chair, now running against Abdul El-Sayed, instead saw photo of Osama bin Laden’s body
Author: Robert Mackey
Headline: Ex-House intel committee chair, now running against Abdul El-Sayed, instead saw photo of Osama bin Laden’s body
Content: Mike Rogers speaks during a campaign event on 20 August 2026 in Detroit.Photograph: Paul Sancya/APView image in fullscreenMike Rogers speaks during a campaign event on 20 August 2026 in Detroit.Photograph: Paul Sancya/APMichiganMichigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers says he saw Bin Laden’s body with his ‘own eyes’. He did notEx-House intel committee chair, now running against Abdul El-Sayed, instead saw photo of Osama bin Laden’s bodyRobert MackeySat 29 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a recent fundraising email, the Republican candidate forMichigan’s open US Senate seat, former congressman Mike Rogers, appeared to mislead supporters about his past by suggesting that he had played an active role in the killing ofOsama bin Laden, the leader of al-Qaida who was shot and killed in an American military raid on his compound in Pakistan in 2011.“When I served as a US army officer and an FBI special agent, I swore a sacred oath to defend the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic,” Rogers wrote, according toa screenshot of the emailshared online by Azi Paybarah, a former Washington Post reporter now with Straight Arrow News. “I dedicated my life to keeping our families safe – working in the shadows, hunting down terrorists, and standing on the frontlines of our national security.”He then added, in a section of the email highlighted in bold type: “I saw the dead body ofOsama bin Ladenwith my own eyes, knowing that together, we had delivered justice for America.”Democrats ignored the uncommitted movement for Gaza in 2024. Now, it’s winning electionsRead moreRogers, however, was not in Abbottabad, Pakistan, on 1 May 2011, when Bin Laden was shot and killed – nor was hein the White House Situation Room, where then president Barack Obama and senior administration officials at the time, including Joe Biden and Hillary Clinton, followed the raid in real time.Instead, as Rogerstold reporters the next day, andrecounts in a campaign video, he was at home in Washington DC – where, as the chair of the House intelligence committee at the time, he was informed about the raid in a phone call from Obama’s CIA director, Leon Panetta.While the Rogers campaign did not respond to requests to explain what the former congressman meant by his claim, Paybarah, who first reported the fundraising email sent by Rogers on Sunday, suggested that Rogers must have been referring to the fact that he was one of a select few US officials to have seen a photograph of Bin Laden’s dead body.Rogers said – days after the raid – thatthe photograph he’d seenmade it clear that Bin Laden was dead. But he said hesupported Obama’s decisionto not make the graphic images of the raid public.“The risks of release outweigh the benefits,” Rogers said in a statement at the time. “Conspiracy theorists around the world will just claim the photos are doctored anyway, and there is a real risk that releasing the photos will only serve to inflame public opinion in the Middle East.”In the years since, though, Rogers has frequently referred to his role as a congressman who helped provide funds for US intelligence agencies in vague terms that seemed to exaggerate his role.Since Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim doctor and former public health official, became his opponent in the Senate race, Rogers has repeatedly cited his own role in the US war on Islamist terrorism in his campaign statements.“Abdul doesn’t represent a vision for the future. He’s leading a movement grounded in ideological fanaticism,”Rogers saidthe night that El-Sayed won the Democratic nomination. “I spent years hunting terrorists and bringing Osama bin Laden to justice. Never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11.”A New York Times factcheckpointed outthat the second part of Rogers’s “incendiary statement” was false: it was not El-Sayed, but one of his supporters, the Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who once said that the US deserved 9/11, before retracting and apologizing for that statement seven years before he endorsed El-Sayed.For his part, El-Sayed has clearly denounced the 9/11 attacks for years. In a recollection of that day written in 2021,El-Sayed wrote:“I watched terrorists with names like mine attack my country in the name of my faith. Three thousand of my fellow Americans were killed in the craven terrorist attacks in New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania. The attack devastated me.”Explore more on these topicsMichiganUS SenateOsama bin LadenUS midterm elections 2026RepublicansUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘If it’s made in the US, I don’t buy it’: Canadians on boycotting Trump’s America | International trade | The Guardian
description: Avoiding US goods and services – from tech to whisky to air travel – has forced many to find a new way of living
Author: Jane Clinton
Headline: Avoiding US goods and services – from tech to whisky to air travel – has forced many to find a new way of living
Content: A sign in a liquor shop in Vancouver, British Columbia promotes native Canadian alcohol.Photograph: Chris Helgren/ReutersView image in fullscreenA sign in a liquor shop in Vancouver, British Columbia promotes native Canadian alcohol.Photograph: Chris Helgren/ReutersInternational trade‘If it’s made in the US, I don’t buy it’: Canadians on boycotting Trump’s AmericaAvoiding US goods and services – from tech to whisky to air travel – has forced many to find a new way of livingJane ClintonSat 29 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor William McDonald, 38, a diesel mechanic from Thunder Bay, Ontario, “Canadian is always the first choice,” even if it means his weekly bills are higher.“As soon as Trump started putting those tariffs on in February [last year], I started boycotting US goods,” he said. “Avoiding American products has driven my costs up, and I’m still happy to do it.“I used to drink US beer, but now I drink Canadian beer, and that costs me an extra C$1,000 (£531/US$720) a year. Likewise, groceries cost about C$50 more a week, but you work that extra hour to pay for it.”McDonald likened Donald Trump’s behaviour towardsCanadaas “a lot like the schoolyard bully yelling and stomping their feet when they don’t get the cowering reaction they expect”.View image in fullscreenA shop poster in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada.Photograph: Artur Widak/NurPhoto/Rex/ShutterstockThis week the US imposed 50% tariffs on US$20bn (£15bn) of Canadian goods, and Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, hasvowed to match them “dollar for dollar”after the collapse of trade talks between the two countries last weekend. Donald Trump retaliated on Thursday by ordering the federal government torename Lake Ontario to Lake America.Such actions have added fuel toa widespread boycott of US products and services by Canadiansthat began early last year in response to the president’s trade war andthreats to annex his northern neighbour.More than 3,500 people from across Canada shared with the Guardian via an online callout how they have made changes to their lives in response to the US administration’s political and economic stance. Many expressed deep anger and sadness, but remained resolute that this was now a new way of living.View image in fullscreenA ‘Made in Canada’ sign at a liquor store in Victoria, British Columbia, Canada.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesBuying only Canadian groceries, including fresh produce, and boycotting travel south of the border featured heavily among the responses. Respondents have stopped paying for US technology; streaming services provided by Netflix, AmazonPrime, AppleTV and Disney+; petrol; vehicles such as Teslas; and whiskies including Jack Daniel’s. Social media sites including X, Facebook and Instagram were also being avoided.In July, an Angus Reid survey found40% of grocery shoppers were actively checking where products came from, and most of those avoiding US products where possible.double quotation markI think you need to be in Canada to understand how deep the animosity to the US isDenise, WinnipegThe ABUS (Anything but US) or ABUSA (Anywhere but USA) acronyms and “Elbows Up!” slogan – a hockey term for offering a stiff defence – began appearing in Canada last year.“I think you need to be in Canada to understand how deep the animosity to the US is … even across the political spectrum,” said Denise from Winnipeg, Manitoba.“‘Elbows up’ is a real thing. We don’t fly US airlines, we stay in locally owned hotels, we won’t even connect in a US airport … we’ve moved investments to Canadian companies, and we actively avoid USA products, produce and groceries. It can be pretty inconvenient to do the research and read signs and labels, and often more costly, but BDS [boycott, divestment, sanction] is the only tool ordinary people have to stand up for our values.”View image in fullscreenElizabeth started growing her own vegetables to avoid buying American.Photograph: Elizabeth/Guardian CommunityElizabeth Lorenz, 68, a retired teacher who lives in Nanaimo, British Columbia,said she would change a recipe to work around a lack of certain ingredients.“I read labels on packaged food, and if it’s made in the US, I don’t buy it,” she said. “Annie’s Pasta is an example of a product I no longer purchase.“Grocery stores are increasingly offering more produce from Mexico, Peru, Guatemala, Chile and South Africa. Although this means the transportation of this produce has contributed to more environmental degradation than if I were to buy American produce, my outrage at America’s greed and corruption trumps (apologies for the pun) my environmental concerns.”She has planted yams and sweet potatoes in her garden “since only American-grown yams and sweet potatoes are available”, she said.Jane, 54, a teacher, was one of many who believed the relationship between the US and Canada had been badly damaged, perhaps beyond repair.“I definitely will not support America economically while this administration is in power and, to be honest, I may not ever again,” she said.“The relationship, in my eyes, has been permanently tarnished.”View image in fullscreenA liquor shop in Winnipeg announces its rejection of American produce.Photograph: Ed White/ReutersJane has been buying only Canadian groceries and alcohol for more than a year and has also stopped travelling to the US, opting for a longer journey to see sports in Canada.“I have been vacationing in Mexico and the Dominican Republic and Europe instead,” said Jane, who lives in Camlachie, Ontario. “I used to go to Detroit for sporting events or concerts and would pick up gas and groceries before returning to Canada. For more than a year, I have been driving four hours to Toronto for those events that I normally would drive only an hour to in the US.”She said at first making the changes to non-US goods was “quite challenging” but she uses apps and online forums which direct her to Canadian options.Among the many US products Jane has replaced with Canadian equivalents are Heinz Tomato Ketchup, Kraft Cheese and Charmin toilet paper. She uses the apps CanMade – Canadian Made, Buy Beaver and O SCANada: Buy Canadian. She also uses the websitemadeinca.ca.“Grocery shopping is now easier as stickers are used to indicate place of origin,” she said. “Checking origin of product information has become second nature to me now.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJames Buchan has swapped out all his US tech.Photograph: James/Guardian Communitydouble quotation markI’ve sold all my Apple productsJames Buchan, HalifaxThe same is true of James Buchan, 36, who works in IT, lives in Halifax, Nova Scotia and describes himself as “a habitual label reader”.“All Procter & Gamble and Colgate products have been replaced by Attitude and Lavo products from Quebec,” he said.“Canadian produce is quite easy to get hold of, and we can get food from Mexico, but ready-made meals are more difficult to find, as the US has it on lock. So making the change could be more difficult for some.”He also did a clearout of his tech. “I sold all my Apple products: a year-old MacBook, iPhone, AirTags and AirPods, and replaced them with alternatives,” he said. “Tech was the easiest – I do not miss my iPhone or Mac at all.”He switched his email providers to European-based ones and has done the same for his mapping applications, language-learning apps and calendar. He also left Facebook, Reddit, Instagram and WhatsApp.Kurt, 61, a retired engineer who lives in Calgary, Alberta, said his whiskey-tasting group “spent a small fortune” annually on American whiskies – in the region of US$10,000.“Since‘Liberation Day’and the first round of tariffs, we decided one way of expressing our distaste is not to buy American whiskies,” he said. “So since then we’ve spent US$0.00. Amazingly, we just stumbled on a whole new batch of Canadian equivalents. We didn’t realise the range and quality of stuff available locally. So we’ve got no intention of ever going back.”He is also now a “vigorous” label checker, but added this was not always straightforward, citing the US company Kraft, which has a Canadian operation, employs Canadians, and “uses Canadian materials and ingredients when they can”.“It actually pains me to buy a product that, yes, it’s made here in Canada, but we know their revenues are going back to the company in the States,” he said.View image in fullscreenA billboard in Mississauga, Ontario, Canada promotes Canadian-made pet food.Photograph: Xinhua/Rex/ShutterstockHis wife also no longer drinks California wine, and despite being “frequent visitors for 30-plus years” to the US, Kurt said they have not been there since January 2025.Many who got in touch with the Guardian felt that trust had been broken irrevocably with their US neighbour.double quotation markI won’t go back to buying US products, even if the regime changesSarika, Vancouver“I won’t go back to buying US products, even if the regime changes, because the US is unreliable and untrustworthy,” said Sarika, 61, an academic who lives in Vancouver.“It’s a shame, as many of us in the border regions have friends across the border, and we don’t want to see their businesses and towns suffer, but perhaps Americans will now get a little more involved in voting for and enabling a more fair and just government and trade system.”Vikram, 51, who works at a finance firm and lives in Toronto, said he refused to travel to the US even though he has family there. They visit him instead. He also avoids US products and is now boycotting Amazon.He reflected the sentiment of many who found the turn of events lamentable.“I find it quite sad that Canadians are forced to do this as a protest against these ridiculous threats to our sovereignty, but I’m not sure how else to react,” he said. “We cannot go back to looking at our relationship with the US as it was before, because things have changed. We need to shift focus for our own protection and to maintain our sovereignty and control over our economy.”Kurt, however, sounded a quiet note of optimism.“We’re going to look back, and we’re going to say, you know what, it was painful, and it was a shock, especially to have your best friend turn on you, but it was the best thing that could ever happen to us,” he said. “Canada will be stronger and healthier after all this is over.”William also took some solace from how he feels things have changed in Canada.“After years of internal division in our country, it’s nice to finally see something bind us together again,” he said. “I guess sometimes it just takes a mutual enemy to find one’s resolve.”Explore more on these topicsInternational tradeCanadaUS economyAmericasEconomicsGlobal economyTrump administrationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Inept, incompetent, craven’: Scott Bessent struggles to clean up the president’s mess | US economy | The Guardian
description: There’s little optimism about treasury secretary’s ability to handle Trump’s tariffs, Iran sanctions and colossal US debt
Author: David Smith
Headline: There’s little optimism about treasury secretary’s ability to handle Trump’s tariffs, Iran sanctions and colossal US debt
Content: Scott Bessent speaks at a news conference on 24 August 2026 in Washington.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenScott Bessent speaks at a news conference on 24 August 2026 in Washington.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APUS economy‘Inept, incompetent, craven’: Scott Bessent struggles to clean up the president’s messThere’s little optimism about treasury secretary’s ability to handle Trump’s tariffs, Iran sanctions and colossal US debtDavid Smithin WashingtonSat 29 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHistory remembersGen Dwight Eisenhower, the supreme commander of the allied forces in Europe during the second world war, for his role in the D-day invasion of Normandy. Whether Scott Bessent will achieve similar posterity as the face of the “economic D-day” inIranremains to be seen.The US treasury secretary, already trying to manage a $40tn national debt pile, this week took charge ofDonald Trump’s effort toreverse-engineerhis war of choice. Whereas the US would typically take on an adversary with diplomacy, sanctions and military force, in that order, the US president started with a six-month bombing campaign and now hopes that economic isolation can finish the job.The effort shines a harsh spotlight on Bessent, a billionaire hedge fund manager and former Democratic donor who the president likes to say is “central casting” but critics warn is dangerously out of his depth. The coming months could reveal whether Bessent serves as a constraint on Trump’s worst impulses – or, in fact, enables them beneath a veneer of respectability.“He is, bar none, the worst treasury secretary in the history of the United States,” saidSteve Schmidt, a former political strategist for President George W Bush and the John McCain presidential campaign. “Because the first treasury secretary was a true genius, the distance between Alexander Hamilton and Bessent in evolutionary scale is the difference between a flea and a human being. He is inept, he is incompetent, he is dishonest, he is smug, he is craven.”The treasury bond mess: is this the demise of the US as a safe haven?Read moreScott Kenneth Homer Bessent is an unlikely avatar of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement. Born in South Carolina, he made his way to Yale and graduated in 1984. Openly gay, in 2015 he told theYale Alumni magazine: “If you had told me in 1984, when we graduated, and people were dying of Aids, that 30 years later I’d be legally married and we would have two children via surrogacy, I wouldn’t have believed you.”Bessent went on to play an influential role in the liberal philanthropist George Soros’s London investment operations, including his famous 1992 bet against the pound, which generated huge profits on“Black Wednesday”, when the pound was delinked from European currencies.He also donated to various Democratic causes in the early 2000s,notably Al Gore’s presidential run, but eventually drifted toward the Republican fold, transforming into an adviser and intellectual defender of Trump’s economic nationalism. He championed spending cuts while vigorously advocating for the extension of the tax cuts approved by Congress in Trump’s first term.Still, in a cabinet of questionable qualifications, there were hopes that Bessent – an advocate for deficit reduction and deregulation – would prove a moderating influence on Trump. Last year the Senate confirmed him as treasury secretary by a vote of 68 to 29, with those in favourincluding some Democratsand independents. Bessent was hailed as thefirst openly gay treasury secretaryin US history.double quotation markBessent is in the unenviable position of trying to make Trump’s whimsical preferences become realityLarry Jacobs of the Center for the Study of Politics and GovernanceIt has been far from smooth sailing. With the national debt ticking past $40tn, the bond markets have begun to rebel. Yields on long-dated treasury bonds have soared to heights not seen in nearly 20 years, dramatically escalating the cost of servicing the nation’s debt. Earlier this month, Bessent carried out the first joint intervention in the Japanese yen in 15 years to support currency stability.Then, last week, he surprised global investors by announcing that the treasury would double the size of its quarterly buybacks of longer-dated bonds – boosting the repurchases of 10-to-30-year securities to at least $4bn per operation. Bessent claimed that his objective was to support liquidity in a thinly traded August market.The market intervention achieved its goal, but only fleetingly. Yields dropped briefly before retracing nearly all of those losses by the end of the week. The core problem remained: Bessent has not identified the funding source for the buybacks, leading analysts to assume he will tap the Treasury General Account (TGA) at the Federal Reserve.Perceptions of Bessent’s competence were shaken by the move. Charlie McElligott, a cross-asset strategist at Nomura, told the Financial Times newspaper that it was a “band-aid on a bullet hole” and would “not be enough to placate market forces”.Bill Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, summed it up: “The long bond buyback was perceived as somewhat farcical by the financial community, and when he went on to opine that we could grow our way out of the debt, I’m sure he knows better than that. I don’t think he’s thrown away his reputation but as headlines in the past 24 hours have been indicating, Wall Street, like Queen Victoria, is not amused.”Then there wasIran. With a six month-bombing campaign having failed to break Tehran’s will, and the US running low on the defensive weapons it would need to repel a counterattack, Trump handed Bessent the unenviable task of finding another way. The upshot was “Operation Economic Outcast”, designed to isolate Iran from the global financial system.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGalston observed: “The president has decided on a strategy of maximum economic pressure. Bessent has no choice but to devise the best plan possible. Now, it does matter what he’s telling the president behind the scenes.”At a press conference on Monday, Bessent’s rhetoric about “economic asphyxiation” was sweeping, but the reality was far more tentative: a series of warnings rather than the immediate imposition of secondary sanctions on Iran’s major trading partners.If Bessent were to enforce secondary sanctions fully, he would have to target major Chinese state-owned banks. This could spark a catastrophic trade war between the world’s two biggest economies, shattering the fragile trade truce that Trump has spent the last year trying to maintain. “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” the secretary reasoned.But to observers the lack of concrete penalties suggested a bluff.Larry Jacobs, director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota, said: “His effort on the economic D-day appears to have been mostly rhetorical, not breaking any major new ground. At its core, what Bessent announced is an attempt to create an out for Donald Trump from the war he created and the mess that has resulted.”He added: “Bessent is in the unenviable position of trying to make Trump’s whimsical preferences become reality and is repeatedly failing or making the situation worse.”Meanwhile the president continues to be fixated on tariffs, which he often describes as his “favourite word”. Trumpannounced 50% tariffson $20bn worth of Canadian goods over the weekend, after talks between the countries broke down. Canada retaliated by imposing retaliatory tariffs on $20bn worth of American goods including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment.There is little evidence that Bessent disapproves, or has sought to rein Trump in. Although he wrote an investor letter in 2024 arguing that tariffs were inflationary, Bessentsaid last year: “I’ve evolved on this. The president has been right.” He has alsodescribed tariffsas “a useful tool for achieving the president’s foreign policy objectives”, claiming that Hamilton was their original proponent.Such remarks suggest that the former Democratic supporter now feels the zeal of the convert, and has become a true believer in Trump. Jacobs is not so sure. “We shouldn’t dismiss the possibility that it’s the attraction to power,” he said. “He’s got vast wealth but he’s now got a global standing that he’s never enjoyed before. But now that he is into the thick of a job you can see how ill prepared he is for a complicated situation with an out-of-control president.”The price to pay, however, could be Bessent’s reputation.Kurt Bardella, a political commentator and former congressional aide, commented: “Bessent has zero credibility on the global stage and appears in over his head. On interest rates, the national debt, inflation, tariffs, he has mismanaged expectation and appears to be more preoccupied with being a yes-man to Trump than actually protecting the full faith and credit of the United States. At this point, the United States would be better off with an AI-bot running the treasury department than this blowhard.”Explore more on these topicsUS economyTrump tariffsCanadaIranDonald TrumpTrump administrationBondsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Winter panic’: EU gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years | Gas | The Guardian
description: As one of Europe’s biggest consumers of gas the UK may be particularly exposed to heightened price volatility
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: As one of Europe’s biggest consumers of gas the UK may be particularly exposed to heightened price volatility
Content: An LNG (liquefied natural gas) tanker from the US arrives at the Isle of Grain, Kent, last year. The UK relies on imports of gas via pipelines from Europe or tankers from the US and Middle East.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/GettyView image in fullscreenAn LNG (liquefied natural gas) tanker from the US arrives at the Isle of Grain, Kent, last year. The UK relies on imports of gas via pipelines from Europe or tankers from the US and Middle East.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/GettyGas‘Winter panic’: EU gas stores at their lowest level in 13 yearsAs one of Europe’s biggest consumers of gas the UK may be particularly exposed to heightened price volatilityJillian AmbroseSat 29 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEurope is on course to enter the cooler months with gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years, which has triggered “winter panic” among energy traders, experts have warned.The EU’s gas stocks were 63% full in the last week of August, well below the 80% average for late August over recent years and among the lowest levels ever recorded for this time of year.At the current sluggish rate of gas storage injections, the EU is likely to enter the winter heating season with gas stocks about a fifth below the five-year average, and at their lowest level since 2013, according to Greg Molnar, a gas analyst and professor.“Low storage levels are naturally increasing the risk of heightened winter price volatility,” he said, which could be made worse by “cold spells or slow wind patterns” increasing gas usage over the winter.The UK may be particularly exposed to market volatility, because it is one of the biggest gas consumers in Europe but has some of the lowest levels of domestic gas storage capacity.Typically, the UK relies on imports of gas via pipeline from Europe or tankers from the US and the Middle East. Chris O’Shea, chief executive of the British Gas ownerCentrica, said this week the UK had “almost no gas in storage” for the coming winter.The EU’s gas stores have struggled to rise towards a watered-down target of 80% full by the start of winter, since the US-Israel war on Iran triggered severe disruption to exports of oil and gas from the Gulf region.graphA cold end to last winter, and higher-than-usual gas power generation during Europe’s heatwaves this summer, have also contributed to the bloc’s depleted gas stores. In a typical year, owners of storage facilities fill them up during the summer when both demand and prices are lower.Europe’s gas market prices have “stayed relatively calm” this summer in the hope that the strait of Hormuz would be reopened and winter stocks could be rebuilt. However, “no one expects it to happen any time soon”, according to Bjarne Schieldrop, chief analyst commodities at the Nordic banking group SEB.“As a result, the European natural gas market has run into a bit of a winter panic over the past week,” Schieldrop added.Although Europe is not expected to experience physical shortages of gas this winter, traders expect higher prices.Benchmark gas price has climbed to three-year highs above €68 per megawatt-hour (MWh) in recent weeks, more than double the price at the start of the year. Prices have risen sharply on the growing expectation that market traders in the EU will need to compete with Asian buyers to secure cargoes of liquefied natural gas as temperatures begin to cool.Without a return of gas exports from the Middle East, Europe’s benchmark price “would likely need to move above €100/MWh” to attract enough shipments of gas to meet winter demand, according to analysts at Goldman Sachs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGas supply concerns are particularly acute in western Europe, where storage levels are well below those in countries such as Italy and Poland, which have managed to top up their gas stores to over 80% full.In Germany, which has Europe’s largest gas storage capacity, facilities are about half-full, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe. Storage levels in Belgium and the Netherlands, which connect directly to the UK gas market via gas pipelines, stand at 51% and 45%.The UK’s reliance on global gas importsis expected to deepenas declining gas production from the UK’s North Sea sector accelerates, and Norwegian output begins to fall from 2030.The government is considering plans to provide direct financial support to safeguard domestic gas infrastructure, after an official consultation found that homes and businessesrisk running out of gas within the next decade, despite its growing clean energy sources.This could include offering financial support to the owners of gas storage facilities and pipeline operators, to make it economically viable to upgrade and maintain them in the decades ahead.The UK energy regulator, Ofgem, said this week that typical gas and electricity bills willrise by 4%from October under its quarterly cap, afterclimbing 13%at the start of July, to take account of global energy market price rises caused by the war on Iran.Explore more on these topicsGasEnergy industryEuropean UnionCentricaCommoditiesEuropeEnergy billsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lavish spending fails to fix Tottenham’s big issue – the lack of a soul or spine | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: It might be too early to push the panic button after the 2-0 defeat by Newcastle but Roberto De Zerbi faces a huge task if he is to turn Spurs around
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: It might be too early to push the panic button after the 2-0 defeat by Newcastle but Roberto De Zerbi faces a huge task if he is to turn Spurs around
Content: A dejected Roberto De Zerbi trudges across the pitch after Tottenham’s 2-0 defeat against Newcastle.Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA dejected Roberto De Zerbi trudges across the pitch after Tottenham’s 2-0 defeat against Newcastle.Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty ImagesTottenham HotspurAnalysisLavish spending fails to fix Tottenham’s big issue – the lack of a soul or spineJonathan Liewat Tottenham Hotspur StadiumIt might be too early to push the panic button but Roberto De Zerbi faces a huge task if he is to turn Spurs aroundSat 29 Aug 2026 16.33 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 16.53 EDTShareTime for Tottenham to start panicking? This is, of course, a subtle trick question. Tottenham is one of those clubs that never actually stops panicking. They panic when they concede and they panic when they score. They panic when they have the ball and they panic when someone else does. They have a coach inRoberto De Zerbiwhose face evokes a state of permanent alarm, the expression of a man perpetually having a toilet door opened on him. One year they even managed to panic their way to the Europa League. For the ever-rattled Spurs fan, this club is less a treasured devotion and more a lifelong haunting, broken up by occasional panic substitutions.Elanga and Wissa strike as Newcastle extend Spurs’ miserable start to seasonRead moreYou could intuit that sense of encrusted resignation pretty much from the moment Anthony Elanga’s improvised shot kissed the post and trickled over the line to give Newcastle the lead. Since beating Aston Villa 4-1 in late 2024, Tottenham have gone behind 44 times in all competitions and come back to win precisely zero of them. There is something innate and endemic here, a chronic case of Long Tottenham for which – despite the new coach, the new leadership structure and more than a third of a billion pounds in transfer fees – there remains no proven cure. Yoane Wissa’s clincher was of zero surprise to anyone.And so welcome back to the temple of pain, the Theatre of Everyone Else’s Dreams, a stadium that fittingly still has no naming rights because pretty much every visiting side gets to own the place. Over the past 12 months, Aston Villa have won the same number of domestic fixtures atTottenham HotspurStadium (two) as Tottenham. Unai Emery’s men may well get the chance to retake their lead here in three weeks’ time. In the meantime it was Newcastle, with one clean sheet in their last 18 matches, who feasted on Tottenham’s neuroses, stayed tight and stayed patient, waited for the train that always arrives.Perhaps as Matthias Jaissle’s team climbed all over the duels and the second balls there was also a certain reassuring symbolism here: a lesson in the enduring value of culture over commerce. Newcastle have lost half a team but kept their soul; Tottenham have bought half a team and are still searching for theirs. There were inevitable boos for Sandro Tonali, who was actually fine: one of those rare Tottenham players who actually treasures the ball and wants to do interesting things with it. Alongside him Mateus Fernandes was restless, classy, excellent. Omar Marmoush on his debut looked fit and sharp. But of course the individuals were never the problem here.View image in fullscreenSandro Tonali tussles with Anthony Elanga.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAThe problem was the little things: the lost headers, the fractional pauses on the ball that kill momentum, the rushed shots, the extra touches, the tackles not quite committed to, the barely perceptible signs of a deep-rooted softness. Take Elanga’s goal, which sprang from an unpressed Nico González long ball, a poorly challenged Amar Dedic header, a cool turn and finish. Three very simple things in a row, at least two of which should probably have been prevented. No screaming howler or smoking gun here. Just a run of lost battles, a sum of marginal flaws, a team that for all its moments of promise and competence has not yet been welded together into a coherent whole.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBiggest problem for Spurs is finding right mentality, says Roberto De ZerbiRead moreHow De Zerbi fixes this is anyone’s guess. It feels increasingly clear that for all the new blood there is still a kind of generational trauma here, perhaps dating back to the injury crisis of 2024-25, when a threadbare squad was pushed beyond the boundaries of wellness and sanity. For the veterans of that campaign, your Archie Grays and Micky van de Vens, your Destiny Udogies and Rodrigo Bentancurs, you occasionally glimpse that accumulated tension in the 50-50 tackles and big physical clashes, the sense of players still not quite trusting their bodies. And oppositions really do pick up on this stuff. Right now there is a clear blueprint for beating Tottenham: compete, do the simple things well, and eventually bully them into playing your game.How much worse does this get before it gets better? Are Spurs fans ultimately in for another season of discontent and disgruntlement, of taking an unhealthy interest in the latest score from the Coventry Building Society Arena? The instinct here is still to be patient and wait for the required chemistry to develop. But what if two defeats become four, or six? What if it’s November and the top scorer is still somehow Richarlison with two? How does a club so medicinally addicted to panic possibly avoid it?Quietly, there is now some ridiculous creative talent at this club. The signings of Marmoush and Sávio, the new-look midfield, the return of Mohammed Kudus and Dominic Solanke, the prospect of James Maddison and Dejan Kulusevski and Xavi Simons to come. A World Cup finalist in Marcos Senesi sitting unused on the bench. It feels inconceivable that Tottenham could be in relegation trouble again. But as with so many clubs before them, Tottenham are discovering that buying new footballers is the easy part. Growing a spine will take considerably longer.Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurNewcastle UnitedRoberto De ZerbianalysisShareReuse this content

title: William Jewell running back MicahJo Barnett dies after medical emergency during game | College football | The Guardian
description: William Jewell running back suffered a medical emergency during Saturday’s season opener against Fort Lewis College and was later pronounced dead
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: William Jewell running back suffered a medical emergency during Saturday’s season opener against Fort Lewis College and was later pronounced dead
Content: William Jewell College running back MicahJo Barnett died after suffering a medical emergency on the sideline during the Cardinals’ season opener on Saturday.Photograph: David Madison/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWilliam Jewell College running back MicahJo Barnett died after suffering a medical emergency on the sideline during the Cardinals’ season opener on Saturday.Photograph: David Madison/Getty ImagesCollege footballWilliam Jewell running back MicahJo Barnett dies after medical emergency during gameJunior taken to hospital after first-quarter emergencyDivision II season opener suspended and later canceledSchool plans vigil for Barnett and his familyAgenciesSat 29 Aug 2026 19.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWilliam Jewell College running back MicahJo Barnett had a medical emergency on the sideline during ⁠the school’s season opener on Saturday. and the school later announced his death.Barnett, a junior, ⁠reportedly experienced seizure-like ⁠symptoms during ​the first quarter of the Division II contest against Fort Lewis College. The game was played ⁠on William Jewell’s campus in Liberty, Missouri, about 20 miles northeast of Kansas City.North Carolina defeat Texas Christian as college football kicks off season in Dublin – in picturesRead moreBarnett experienced the emergency at ⁠approximately 12.20pm local time. Paramedics from the Liberty Fire Department ​took him to a ‌local hospital, where he was ‌pronounced dead.The game was suspended after the medical episode and ‌subsequently canceled.“William Jewell College and the Liberty, Missouri, community mourn the passing of MicahJo Barnett, junior business administration major and member of Jewell Cardinal Football team and former Liberty North Eagle,” the school wrote on its website. “Our thoughts and prayers are ‌with MicahJo’s family, our students, the Cardinal Football family, and the rest of our community during this time ​of loss.“Officials planned a vigil Saturday night on the school’s quad to honor Barnett and his family.Barnett rushed six times for 29 yards during the game, which included a one-yard touchdown run at ⁠the 5:15 mark of the first quarter for the ​game’s lone score. The ​game was halted with ​4:32 left in the first.Barnett, an academic all-conference ​honoree in ‌2025, was beginning ​his third season ​with the Cardinals. He rushed for 366 yards and four touchdowns in five games last season before sustaining a season-ending injury. In 2024, he rushed for 91 yards and two scores in eight games.Explore more on these topicsCollege footballCollege sportsUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Filip Hrgovic stuns Britain’s Moses Itauma to claim IBF world heavyweight title | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Moses Itauma’s hopes of becoming the second-youngest world heavyweight champion lay in ruins as Filip Hrgovic rallied to stop him in the ninth round
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: Moses Itauma’s hopes of becoming the second-youngest world heavyweight champion lay in ruins as Filip Hrgovic rallied to stop him in the ninth round
Content: Filip Hrgovic gets on top of Moses Itauma.Photograph: Richard Pelham/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFilip Hrgovic gets on top of Moses Itauma.Photograph: Richard Pelham/Getty ImagesBoxingFilip Hrgovic stuns Britain’s Moses Itauma to claim IBF world heavyweight title21-year-old Itauma stopped after ninth-round rally34-year-old Hrgovic is first Croat to win such a titleDonald McRaeat the O2 ArenaSat 29 Aug 2026 19.40 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 20.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMoses Itauma’s hopes of becoming the second-youngest world heavyweight champion in history lay in ruins after the extraordinarily tough and resilient Filip Hrgovic stopped him in the ninth round of their IBF title fight. Yet, until the latter stages of round eight, the sheer speed and dextrous power of the Briton had dominated the contest, with the Croat being dropped in the second and caught again and again by jolting combinations.The fight changed course when Itauma’s stamina suddenly dipped and he began to weave in woozy fatigue as Hrgovic fought back with granite-like determination. Itauma could not withstand the dark storm rolling over him in the ninth and he sank back against the ropes as Hrgovic opened up with renewed conviction. Just as the referee stepped in to stop the fight, Ben Davison, Itauma’s trainer, also sent a white towel sailing sadly over the listing ropes to save his man from a knockout.Filip Hrgović completes astonishing comeback to stun Moses Itauma and win IBF title – live reactionRead moreThe shocking twist was too much for the 21-year-old and he left the ring on a stretcher, apparently having injured his knee. But the damage was done by the remarkable fightback from his opponent, who made his own significant slice of boxing history. The admirable Hrgovic is the first world heavyweight champion from Croatia – a country that has no real boxing heritage.The shock result was also a sobering reminder that, for all Itauma’s obvious skill, a heavyweight tyro is always vulnerable to a world-class opponent who simply refuses to surrender. Itauma’s inexperience also cost him badly for, rather than boxing with more care and staying out of trouble from the eighth round onwards, he allowed himself to be caught up in a slugfest.Before the late dramatics, Itauma walked with calm solemnity to the ring, seemingly unmoved by the fact that the crammed and partisan crowd had begun singing his name in raucous harmony even before he left his dressing room.View image in fullscreenMoses Itauma lands a punch on Filip Hrgovic early in their fight.Photograph: Richard Pelham/Getty ImagesFighting out of a southpaw stance, Itauma landed the first meaningful punch, a sweeping right hand. Moving with menacing intent Itauma clipped Hrgovic with fast and cuffing blows. His speed was striking as he backed up the bigger man with a shuddering right cross which nailed and shook up Hrgovic.Itauma missed with a scything left early in the second but Hrgovic walked almost immediately on to a jolting short right hook which dropped him to the canvas for a count of eight. Hrgovic fought back near the end of the round only for Itauma to produce another blistering combination.A sharp left snapped back Hrgovic’s head at the start of the third, as sweat glistened on the faces and torsos of both men. Itauma switched to the body, sinking a cruel blow to Hrgovic’s gut, but the Croat refused to wilt. His vociferous supporters at ringside began screaming their support as he had a measure of success for the first time in the fight to prove that his ambition remained undimmed.Itauma began to grimace occasionally as the pace of the fight began to leave its mark. A beautiful short left snaked through Hrgovic’s defence in the fifth but the older man marched forward with stoic determination. Itauma was starting to breathe heavily and he had to use a glove to slip his black gum shield back into his mouth. It was the first real sign of distress in Itauma’s previously impassive expression. But at the bell a spiteful uppercut rocked back Hrgovic’s head on the plinth of his massive neck.The cut about Hrgovic’s right eye began to seep with a tickle of blood. But just before the bell Hrgovic landed some heavy shots. Itauma absorbed them and fired back as the fight really caught fire.Itauma had never boxed more than six rounds before and he entered uncharted territory in the seventh.
