But he again forced Hrgovic on to the back foot and landed some deft combinations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe referee raises his hand to stop the fight as Moses Itauma’s team throw the towel in.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersHrgovic ate one meaty blow after another in the eighth round but was resolute as ever. Itauma looked desperately weary as Hrgovic, unbelievably, rallied again. He would soon overwhelm the exhausted youngster and finish a remarkable resurgence.Throughout an intriguing fight week, the 34-year-old Hrgovic had tried to unsettle his complex rival by suggesting that becoming a world heavyweight champion at such a young age would be “bad for his soul”. Itauma, who is so suspicious of fame, engaged fully with those doubts about his readiness for sporting celebrity. It was almost as if the callow prodigy was uncertain, deep down, whether his world title shot had arrived too early.Hrgovic was always going to provide an acid test of Itauma’s much lauded credentials. The experienced Croat had lost only one previous bout in his nine years as a professional. It had been expected that he would not match Itauma’s deft footwork, fast hands, clarity of thinking and the kind of power that is impressive because it arrives from such dizzying and unexpected angles.But Itauma, instead, was rendered helpless by Hrgovic’s superior stamina and bludgeoning will and self-belief. “Let me tell you something,” Hrgovic said afterwards. “It was not me tonight. It was Jesus Christ in me. Holy Spirit. Father, Son and the Holy Spirit. It was not me. I was losing every round. I was outboxed. And I don’t know from where I got energy in that ninth round. And it was really not my strength. It was the Holy Spirit.”He then turned his attention to his fallen opponent. “He’s an amazing fighter,” Hrgovic said of Itauma. “I want to thank him for accepting this fight, to give me a chance to become a new superstar in the heavyweight division. I’m the present and he’s definitely the future.”Itauma is obviously more than young enough to come back from such crushing disappointment but it is Hrgovic who will celebrate victory in the weeks and months to come. The new world champion administered a chastening lesson in the harsh and unforgiving realities of heavyweight boxing.Explore more on these topicsBoxingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Novak Djokovic feels ‘as best as I can be’ before tilt at 25th grand slam title in New York | Novak Djokovic | The Guardian
description: Novak Djokovic said he was as prepared as he could be for the US Open as he attempts to take advantage of the wide-open men’s draw
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Novak Djokovic said he was as prepared as he could be for the US Open as he attempts to take advantage of the wide-open men’s draw
Content: Novak Djokovic has his eyes on grand slam No 25 as he prepares for the US Open.Photograph: Frank Franklin II/APView image in fullscreenNovak Djokovic has his eyes on grand slam No 25 as he prepares for the US Open.Photograph: Frank Franklin II/APNovak DjokovicNovak Djokovic feels ‘as best as I can be’ before tilt at 25th grand slam title in New YorkSerb hopes to take advantage of wide-open men’s drawElena Rybakina has eyes on No 1 world rankingTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsSat 29 Aug 2026 18.58 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNovak Djokovic said he was as prepared as he could be for the US Open as he attempts to take advantage of the wide-open men’s draw and battle for a potential 25th grand slam title.Djokovic arrived in New York having competed only once after his semi-final run at Wimbledon,losing in his opening match of the Cincinnati Opento Thiago Agustín Tirante while struggling with the humidity. However, he now sees the silver lining in that defeat, which he believes gave him the time to make sure he was in optimal shape for the US Open. “I don’t like early losses anywhere, to be honest, but it gave me time to be prepared for US Open in a most adequate way,” he said. “I had almost a few weeks, actually two weeks, to really train and get my body and mind into the right state, prepared for what’s coming up.‘Why would you want to retire me?’: Novak Djokovic is still driven by doubtRead more“So it remains to be seen. If you ask me if I’m prepared, I feel like I am as best as I can be, but it’s different training and then getting out on the Arthur Ashe Stadium and playing best-of-five.”Over the course of the past two years, nobody other than Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner has been as consistent at the grand slams as Djokovic, who has reached the semi-finals or better in six of his last seven such tournaments. However, Sinner and Alcaraz account for five of those defeats, along with a retirement loss at the Australian Open last year.With Sinner absent because of injury and Alcaraz competing for the first time since being sidelined for four and a half months by a right wrist problem, the field is wide open. Had this scenario unfolded 12 months ago, Djokovic would have been the clear favourite at the start of the tournament, but a year is a very long time at 39 years old and despite how high his level remains, each tournament brings more physical problems for the Serb to manage.Meanwhile, Elena Rybakina declared herself healthy for the US Open as she recovers from a foot injury. She is aiming to take advantage of a golden opportunity to claim the No 1 ranking for the first time. “I didn’t play for exactly a week, and we consulted with different doctors. I have been doing the recovery. Slowly started to go on the court. Just a lot of gym,” she said.View image in fullscreenElena Rybakina had to retire from the Cincinnati Open with a foot injury but has declared herself fit for Flushing Meadows.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty Images“It wasn’t easy, because we didn’t know exactly how the foot was gonna react, since it was very painful for me to go and serve in that match in Cincinnati, because I wanted to try once more. Then for a couple of days, it was painful to even walk. Afterwards we managed to do everything possible for it to get better, and I’m glad how the process is going for now.”Rybakina, the second seed and Australian Open champion, begins the tournament at No 1 in the live rankings and she can be overtaken only if Aryna Sabalenka, who has been No 1 for 97 consecutive weeks, Coco Gauff or Jessica Pegula win the title and Rybakina fails to reach the semi-finals.After a difficult period during the summer, Rybakina found her form again during the North American hard-court swing, reaching the final in the Canadian Open before moving into the last eight of the Cincinnati Open. However, she was forced to retire early in her quarter-final against Swiatek last week by a foot injury.“I don’t check the rankings [for] the point situation, but from the media mostly I know where I should get, how the others should play. It’s all the different scenarios,” she said. “But for me, especially now when I had this injury last week, I feel like the most important thing is to just try to stay healthy, play one match at a time, because this is not the last tournament of the year. Of course it’s a grand slam, and you want to do well. But you have plenty of opportunities after if you’re healthy and you keep on playing. I’m trying not to think about it at all, and just play one match at a time.”Explore more on these topicsNovak DjokovicUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Utterly baffled’: the 17-year-old girl who struck out Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig | Baseball | The Guardian
description: In a 1931 exhibition, Jackie Mitchell silenced the greats back-to-back. It sparked still-ongoing debates over legitimacy and opportunities for women in baseball
Author: Tom Dart
Headline: In a 1931 exhibition, Jackie Mitchell silenced the greats back-to-back. It sparked still-ongoing debates over legitimacy and opportunities for women in baseball
Content: Lou Gehrig and Babe Ruth look on as Jackie Mitchell, one of the first women to play professional baseball, practices her form.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenLou Gehrig and Babe Ruth look on as Jackie Mitchell, one of the first women to play professional baseball, practices her form.Photograph: APBaseball‘Utterly baffled’: the 17-year-old girl who struck out Babe Ruth and Lou GehrigIn a 1931 exhibition, Jackie Mitchell silenced the greats back-to-back. It sparked still-ongoing debates over legitimacy and opportunities for women in baseballTom DartSat 29 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Sultan of Swat sounded exasperated. “I don’t know what things are coming to,” Babe Ruth sighed during spring training in 1931.“I don’t know what’s going to happen if they begin to let women in baseball,” heelaboratedto reporters. “Of course, they will never make good. Why? Because they are too delicate. It would kill them to play ball everyday.”The next day, Ruth and Lou Gehrig were struck out back-to-back by a 17-year-old girl.‘I felt like Babe Ruth’: baseball’s 3ft 7in pinch-hitter, 75 years onRead moreMaking their way home from preseason in Florida, theNew York Yankeeshad stopped off in Tennessee for an exhibition game against the minor-league Chattanooga Lookouts. The Lookouts handed a debut to a promising young pitcher with precise control, a quirky side-arm delivery and a vicious sinker. Her name was Jackie Mitchell.The strikeouts of two all-time greats sparked still-ongoing debates over the legitimacy of Mitchell’s achievement and the general lack of opportunities for female players.Mitchell was summoned from the bullpen in the first inning. In front of a 4,000-strong crowd, Ruth, an Associated Press reporter wrote at the time, came to the plate with “a wry smile playing at the corners of his mouth”. A New York Times writer implied that it was all theater: “The Babe performed his role very ably. He swung hard at two pitches then demanded that Umpire Owens inspect the ball, just as batters do when utterly baffled by a pitcher’s delivery.”View image in fullscreenLou Gehrig, Jackie Mitchell, Joe Engel and Babe Ruth pose before the Yankees played the Chattanooga Lookouts in a 1931 exhibition.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyRuth struck out looking and was said to have hurled his bat while somehow “registering disgust with his shoulder and chin”. Gehrig then struck out after “three hefty swings”. Mitchell came out of the game after walking the next batter, Tony Lazzeri, and the Yankees went on to win 14-4.Asked in a postgame press conference if the strikeouts were genuine, Mitchell was reported to have “retorted with a gaze of utter scorn and a contemptuous silence”. As Lapham’s Quarterlynoted, Ruth and Gehrig enigmatically kept mum on the matter.There is cause to be suspicious. The occasion had been scheduled for April Fool’s Day, though it was postponed by a day because of bad weather. And the Lookouts were run by a tireless promoter and showman known as the Barnum of the Bush Leagues. A former Major LeagueBaseballpitcher and scout, Joe Engel became president of the Lookouts in 1929 and opened a new ballpark - Engel Stadium - the following year.Desperate for publicity as he sought to boost attendance during the Great Depression, Engel made the Lookouts theSavannah Bananasof their era.He famously traded his shortstop, “Binky” Jones, for a turkey “because the turkey washaving a better year”. He then served the bird to critical sportswriters, offering them a free lunch and telling them, “You’ve been giving me the bird, so now have one on me.”So Mitchell’s signing was undoubtedly an exploitative publicity stunt, but that does not necessarily mean that the strikeouts were staged. (Though Engel did have an affinity for hoaxes: he would later pretend to carry out a phone call with Adolf Hitler at home plate for the entertainment of a wartime crowd.)One explanation promulgated at the time by male sportswriters waschivalry: it would have been ungentlemanly to have humiliated the kid by launching the ball into the stratosphere. “Babe Gallantly Strikes Out For Benefit Of Girl Hurler,” read one headline. But that explanation does not take into account professional pride. While being struck out by a girl might have appealed to the media-savvy Ruth’s sense of fun, Gehrig was a more earnest character. And Mitchell clearly had talent.View image in fullscreenJackie Mitchell learned the basics of baseball from her father.Photograph: Everett Collection Historical/AlamyBorn in Chattanooga on 29 August 1913, the 5ft 8in lefty was a gifted all-round athlete who learned baseball basics from her father and played for Engel’s all-female team (somewhat inevitably named the Engelettes). The story goes that she was taught to throw her signature “drop” pitch by a neighbor in Memphis - “Dazzy” Vance, a Hall of Famer who led the National League in strikeouts for seven seasons in a row.The 36-year-old Ruth would go on to smack 46 home runs in the 1931 regular season with 162 runs batted in; Gehrig, who turned 28 that summer, also hit 46 homers, with an American League-record 185 RBI. Mitchell, though, did not feature for the Lookouts again - at least not until she was invited to throw a ceremonial first pitch in 1982.Kenesaw Mountain Landis, a federal judge and commissioner of baseball, was reported to have voided her contract on the basis that professional baseball was too physical for women and for their own safety they should stick to playing recreationally among themselves. While reports of Landis’s verdict have not been definitively confirmed, Mitchell herself thought it was the case. “I believe I could qualify and might be signed by a major league team and might someday get to play in a World Series if Judge Landis hadn’t ruled against my playing in major league ball,” she told the St Louis Post-Dispatch in 1933.Capitalizing on her fame, she played in exhibitions and, curiously, for theHouse of David– a barnstorming outfit that was a side hustle for a Michigan religious cult that forbade male members from cutting their hair. She retired in 1937 and went to work for her father, an optician.Organized women’s baseball in the US had started in 1866 when Vassar College in New York state, then an all-female institution, founded a team, the Resolutes. The first known female professional teams, the Blondes and the Brunettes, started play in Illinois in 1875, but they were essentiallytheatrical troupesperforming a novelty act and their rosters were stuffed with actresses, according to the author and historian Debra Shattuck.View image in fullscreenJackie Mitchell speaks to her teammates on the House of David barnstorming team.Photograph: Anonymous/APBarnstormingBloomer Girls- so called because of their baggy trousers - were common in baseball from the 1890s andLizzie Arlington, the first woman to take part in a professional minor-league men’s game, pitched a scoreless ninth inning (two hits, no runs) in 1898 for the Reading Coal Heavers in an Atlantic League win over the Allentown Peanuts in front of a thousand-strong crowd.This long history did not dissuade sexist newspapers from treating Mitchell as a novelty act. “The curves won’t all be on the ball when pretty Jackie Mitchell … takes the mound,” one preview declared. “It might be supposed that having adopted the exciting and strenuous profession of baseball, Miss Mitchell has abandoned the usual feminine arts, but the contrary is true. She can sew and make a dress, she cooks with skill and success and even plays the piano,” anotherreportobserved.Three years after Mitchell’s moment in the spotlight, the celebrated multi-sport athleteBabe Didrikson Zahariaspitchedtwo scoreless innings for the New Orleans Pelicans against the Cleveland Indians in a spring training game, days after pitching one inning for the Philadelphia Athletics against the Brooklyn Dodgers (giving up a walk and no hits) and for the St Louis Cardinals against the Boston Red Sox (conceding three runs on four hits). One of three women to play in the Negro Leagues, and the only pitcher, 5ft3inMamie “Peanut” Johnson, compiled a 33-8 record for the Indianapolis Clowns between 1953 and 1955.When shortstopEleanor Englesigned for the struggling minor-league Harrisburg Senators in 1952 it was the kindling for a media firestorm. Acting with the support of MLB commissioner Ford Frick, the boss of the minor leagues, George Trautman, cancelled her contract shortly before her scheduled debut, forcing her to change out of her uniform and watch the game from the press box. Trautman issued a statement asserting that “such travesties” would not be tolerated and clubs attempting to sign women in the future would be “subject to severe penalties”.In 1993 the Chicago White Sox made history by selecting a female player, pitcher Carey Schueler - the daughter of Ron Schueler, a former major league pitcher and a White Sox executive at the time - in the 43rd round of the MLB draft. She did not sign and instead played college basketball. Four years later,Ila Borderspitched for the St Paul Saints and went on to appear in 52 minor league games for four professional clubs over four seasons.Whether Ruth and Gehrig struck out intentionally in 1931 remains an enduring mystery, though the self-assured Mitchell herself had no doubt: “Why, hell, they were trying, damn right,” shetold a reportershortly before her death in 1987. “Hell, better hitters than them couldn’t hit me. Why should they’ve been any different?”Explore more on these topicsBaseballUS sportsNew York YankeesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lando Norris agrees new deal until at least 2030 with ‘second family’ McLaren | Lando Norris | The Guardian
description: Lando Norris has said he would like to see out his career with McLaren after the defending F1 world champion signed a new multi-year deal
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lando Norris has said he would like to see out his career with McLaren after the defending F1 world champion signed a new multi-year deal
Content: Lando Norris has said McLaren ‘feel like my second family in some ways’.Photograph: Jens Mommens/Momenol Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLando Norris has said McLaren ‘feel like my second family in some ways’.Photograph: Jens Mommens/Momenol Images/ShutterstockLando NorrisLando Norris agrees new deal until at least 2030 with ‘second family’ McLarenNorris: ‘I want my whole career to be with McLaren’F1 title holder says other teams have approached himGiles RichardsSat 29 Aug 2026 05.26 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 05.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLando Norris has said he would like to see out his career with McLaren, as the defending Formula One world champion announced he has agreed a multi-year deal until at least 2030 with the team he described as like “a second family”.The 26-year-old,who won his first F1 title last season, joined McLaren to make his debut in the sport in 2019. He has been with them ever since and his current contract was due to run until the end of this year. Norris emphasised that he had not countenanced leaving McLaren and had made no approaches toward other teams – although some had made advances towards him.Mercedes’ Wolff wary that Norris and Hamilton are genuine F1 title contendersRead more“It really was the easiest decision I’ve had to make in my career so far,” Norris said. “I’ll be very, very happy at the end of my career to say thatMcLarenis the only team I’ve been with. I kind of want my whole career to be with McLaren, because I’m happy here and I don’t want to change.The British driver added: “Even when we go through a harder year, such as we’ve had so far this year, there’s no thought comes to my head of: ‘Was this the right decision or not?’”Norris joined McLaren as part of their young driver programme in 2017 and stepped up to the team two years later alongside Carlos Sainz. McLaren were still undergoing a rebuilding process after an extended period of underperforming. He took his first podium at the Austrian Grand Prix in 2020 during difficult years for McLaren.Under the leadership of the chief executive, Zak Brown, and, more recently, the team principal, Andrea Stella, McLaren have returned to the front of the grid. Norris tookhis first GP win in 2024 in Miamiand the team went on to claim the constructors’ championship that year. Last year, with Norris winning the title, McLaren took the drivers’ and constructors’ double. He has taken 13 wins for the team and, with 163 grands prix raced, he is their longest-serving driver.This season, the team have struggled somewhat under the new regulations but with comprehensive upgrades to their car are once more in the mix, as Norris’s victories in the last two racesat Zandvoortandthe Hungaroringhave demonstrated.Norris made the announcement at a friends and families day held at the McLaren Technology Centre in Woking, where the team also confirmed he was to be presented with one of the MCL39 cars he drove to the title in 2025 as part of the deal. Norris emphasised it was the environment at McLaren that played a central role in him sticking with them.“I always want to be where I’m happy first and foremost, closely followed by the fact I want to be where I believe there’s always going to be good results,” he said. “I still believe through the harder periods that what we achieved over the last few years was possible, and obviously all of that came true.”View image in fullscreenLando Norris signed his new deal after two successive race victories, most recently at the Dutch Grand Prix.Photograph: Xavi Bonilla/DPPI/Shutterstock“People is the most important thing for me. Of course the leaders – but every individual. I’ve built very good relationships with so many people here over the years. People that work here every day, to the mechanics, to the engineers. It just very much feels like my home. They just feel like my second family in some ways.”No details of how much Norris will be earning were released, but he did concede it was not as much as Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen have been reported as making in their recent contracts. Hamilton’s deal with Ferrari is thought to be worth $60m (£44.3m) a year. Verstappen’s new contract with Red Bull,announced at the Dutch GP last weekend, prompted speculation it was worth as much as $100m a year.“It’s certainly not close to the level of Lewis or Max,” Norris said. “It shouldn’t be because I’ve not achieved as much as they have in their career. In a way, I believe it should be, because I believe I can fight against them whenever I need to and I can do a better job whenever I need to. So I guess I have the two opinions on it.”Last year Norris’s teammate Oscar Piastri also agreed to a multi-year contract extension with McLaren.Stella said: “Lando is an exceptional driver, someone who combines outstanding natural speed with maturity, consistency and a strong commitment to McLaren, but above all, he is a special human being who is valued by everyone in the team. This extension gives us important continuity and reinforces our confidence in the direction we are taking together.”Explore more on these topicsLando NorrisMcLarenFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man posed as 49ers player to scam women out of $1.3m, FBI says | NFL | The Guardian
description: Federal authorities say Daejon Love posed as a San Francisco 49ers player and used sham romances and investments to defraud women of $1.3m
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Federal authorities say Daejon Love posed as a San Francisco 49ers player and used sham romances and investments to defraud women of $1.3m
Content: The FBI arrested Daejon Love, 35, and Taylor Jamie Chan, 18, in Boise, Idaho, on 24 August over an alleged $1.3m romance and investment scam.Photograph: Kevin Carter/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe FBI arrested Daejon Love, 35, and Taylor Jamie Chan, 18, in Boise, Idaho, on 24 August over an alleged $1.3m romance and investment scam.Photograph: Kevin Carter/Getty ImagesNFLMan posed as 49ers player to scam women out of $1.3m, FBI saysAuthorities say 26 women targeted across four statesSuspect allegedly used dating apps, fake investmentsFBI believes there may be ‘many more victims’AgenciesFri 28 Aug 2026 22.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFederal authorities claim a man posed as aSan Francisco 49ersplayer and scammed more than ⁠two dozen women out of about $1.3m.TheFBIarrested Daejon Love, 35, and his alleged accomplice ⁠Taylor Jamie Chan, 18, on ⁠24 August in Boise, Idaho. They were charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and wire fraud, according ⁠to the US attorney’s office in the District of Oregon. The men remain in federal custody in Boise.MLB suspends Dominican prospect after age-fraud plot involving fake graveRead moreIn a scheme ⁠that began in February 2022 and spanned more than four years ​until the 24 August arrests, authorities ‌say Love created ‌fictitious personas to meet women on dating apps, presenting himself as a ‌player for the Niners. To support that claim, he posted photos on social media wearing official team gear and posing with luxury vehicles.The pair allegedly created fictitious investment opportunities to defraud 26 victims in California, Idaho, Washington and Oregon. The FBI believes there are “many more victims” out ‌there.“Love convinced many of the victims they were in sincere romantic relationships, that he was a sophisticated investor, and ​that Chan was his investment adviser who helped Love grow a fortune worth tens of millions of dollars,” the US attorney’s office said in a statement.“Love had romantic relationships with many of the victims and told them ⁠he wanted to build wealth and a future together. Love ​advertised nonexistent investment vehicles ​and claimed these investments would ​generate massive returns for both him and his victims.“None of ​the alleged ‌victims interviewed said ​they received ​any return on their investments, or repayments for loans made to Love and Chan.The US attorney’s office said Love would block communications with the women after they ran out of funds to invest or asked too many questions.Explore more on these topicsNFLSan Francisco 49ersUS sportsFBIShareReuse this content

title: Liverpool’s Andoni Iraola angered by substitution delay before Forest penalty | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Andoni Iraola revealed his frustration after being unable to make substitutions before Nottingham Forest were awarded a penalty at Liverpool
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Andoni Iraola revealed his frustration after being unable to make substitutions before Nottingham Forest were awarded a penalty at Liverpool
Content: Liverpool’s Andoni Iraola looks on as the substitutes Rio Ngumoha, Ryan Gravenberch and Kostas Tsimikas wait to come on.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenLiverpool’s Andoni Iraola looks on as the substitutes Rio Ngumoha, Ryan Gravenberch and Kostas Tsimikas wait to come on.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPALiverpoolLiverpool’s Andoni Iraola angered by substitution delay before Forest penaltyFourth official appeared to struggle with electronic boards‘I wanted to make those substitutions about three minutes before’Andy Hunterat AnfieldSat 29 Aug 2026 11.55 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 15.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndoni Iraola bemoaned a poor first-half display plus a broken electronic board forLiverpool’s disappointing 2-2 draw with Nottingham Forestin the first home game of his Anfield reign. Forest led twice, but were denied a third successive Premier League win at Liverpool by Víctor Muñoz’s emphatic 82nd-minute equaliser.The visitors’ second goal, from a penalty converted by Morgan Gibbs-White, stemmed from a throw-in taken quickly by Liam Delap while Iraola was attempting to make a triple substitution.Iraola’s Liverpool start slow again but Muñoz strike denies Nottingham ForestRead moreHe was prevented from doing so because the fourth official was unable to flash up the substitutes’ numbers due to a malfunctioning electronic board. “I cannot explain because I don’t have an explanation,” said the exasperatedLiverpoolhead coach.“I wanted to make those substitutions about three minutes before. It was two, three, four times the ball had gone out. He [the fourth official] was having some problems with the board. The penalty wouldn’t have happened if I had made the subs.“I had complained the previous time. The supporters were shouting and they were aware of the situation. I’ll leave you to decide whether it was a penalty or not.”Despite his annoyance over the buildup to Forest’s penalty, Iraola conceded that Liverpool created their own problems for the second week in succession with a sluggish start.He said: “The first half was poor, it was not good enough. We haven’t controlled the game and after we improved a lot in the second half. We were much more intense, quicker on the ball and had more urgency, but it hasn’t been enough to win the game and we have to blame the first half.“I am frustrated because we want to win, especially at home. It’s not a good result. We have come back from two results where we were losing and I like what we have done in the second half, but we haven’t been able to complete the comeback.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“In the first half we were too passive without the ball. Afterwards we improved this and intensity gives you the chance to win duels and attack quicker and better. But in the first half there was a lack of intensity and we had issues with throw-ins today.”Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolAndoni IraolaNottingham ForestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Carrick dismisses ‘lazy’ Manchester United criticism and defends Fernandes’ leadership | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick has said it was ‘lazy and easy’ to say everything was wrong with Manchester United after the opening-day defeat at Hull
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Michael Carrick has said it was ‘lazy and easy’ to say everything was wrong with Manchester United after the opening-day defeat at Hull
Content: Bruno Fernandes captained Manchester United to their first loss to a promoted team on the opening day of the season.Photograph: Greig Cowie/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBruno Fernandes captained Manchester United to their first loss to a promoted team on the opening day of the season.Photograph: Greig Cowie/ShutterstockManchester UnitedCarrick dismisses ‘lazy’ Manchester United criticism and defends Fernandes’ leadershipManager says opening-day defeat just ‘one game’United to be without Carlos Baleba against IpswichJamie JacksonSat 29 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 17.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick has said it was “lazy and easy” to say everything was wrong withManchester Unitedafter the opening-day defeat at Hull.United lost 2-0 in a tame displayand the manager was asked whether his captain, Bruno Fernandes, and Youri Tielemans, Belgium’s captain, had shown the leadership that might have affected the performance and result.Plight of Pogba, Sancho and others is cautionary tale for any Carrick rebuildRead more“It’s one game,” Carrick said. “I think there’s enough leadership in our dressing room that we’ll have it throughout the season. Just because we lose a game doesn’t just mean leadership [is the reason]. I got ‘passion’ thrown at me after the game; it’s not just that. You lose two set plays like we did [for the goals], it changes the game.”Carrick was asked what the reason was for the performance. “You’ve watched football a long time, right? Teams lose games and win games, and it’s not just because you try or you don’t try. There’s all sorts of different reasons. I don’t have to give you the total reason, because we know what we’re trying to improve on.”The 45-year-old was pressed to offer one factor why the defeat occurred. “I think it’s so easy and lazy to just … a team loses a game, everything’s wrong: this is wrong, this is wrong, not trying enough, not enough passion,” Carrick said. “It’s like the obvious answer. So, there’s a lot that goes into a game of football that can take [the result away] from [you].“We’ve probably played like that and won games, and everyone goes: ‘What a great team, what a great coach, what a great load of players’ – when we find a way to win 1-0. So, from my perspective, when you’re analysing it, it’s not the feeling [that the inverse is true]. We’ve got to dig deeper than that and understand the details of it. And we don’t get carried away when we win certain games because we know it’s not been perfect.”United host Ipswich on Sunday without Carlos Baleba, who signed on Tuesday for£70m from Brightonbut has an ankle injury that may rule him out for three or more weeks. This means the midfielder may not make his debut until Tottenham’s visit on 10 October, after the international break.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnited have admired the Cameroon international since last summer so Carrick was asked why the 22-year-old was signed so late in the window. He said: “It’s not always straightforward, and things have got to drop. So we’ve been patient. We wanted to get the right players in, that fit the group, that will take us forward, and Carlos is definitely one of them.”Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickPremier LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: No country for old men: Premier League grind is why managers are getting younger | Premier League | The Guardian
description: The boss in the dugout is typically no longer an ageing former player – most are in their 40s on an exhausting treadmill
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: The boss in the dugout is typically no longer an ageing former player – most are in their 40s on an exhausting treadmill
Content: Unai Emery (left) and David Moyes (right) are part of the old guard in the Premier League with most managers, including Matthias Jaissle (centre left) and Fabian Hürzeler, significantly younger.Composite: Guardian Pictures; PA; Action Images/Reuters; Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUnai Emery (left) and David Moyes (right) are part of the old guard in the Premier League with most managers, including Matthias Jaissle (centre left) and Fabian Hürzeler, significantly younger.Composite: Guardian Pictures; PA; Action Images/Reuters; Getty ImagesInside footballPremier LeagueNo country for old men: Premier League grind is why managers are getting youngerJonathan WilsonThe boss in the dugout is typically no longer an ageing former player – most are in their 40s on an exhausting treadmillSat 29 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 16.57 EDTShareOne of the problems with getting older is that you’re never quite sure whether it’s you or them. Is the world really changing, or is it just you, struggling to adapt? There’s a milestone in life, probably as you’re contemplating university or a first job, when you realise you’re watching a footballer who is younger than you. Then, 15-20 years later, you realise you’re watching a manager who is younger than you. And 15-20 years after that, especially if you’re watching the modernPremier League, you realise that almost every manager is younger than you.At which you do two things: give thanks for David Moyes; and check to see whether it’s actually happening, or whether this is just the football equivalent of the policemen-getting-younger cliche.Managerial turnover means we need new ways to predict Premier League fixturesRead moreIt turns out it is true. Managers used to be ashen-faced men with nicotine-grey hair dressed in the sports jackets of grim experience. They spoke with a rasping melancholy of the depths of human fallibility and of fates that were not to be trusted. Now they’re trim, sprightly figures in T-shirts, convinced that analytics can explain the world.There are fewer Premier League managers now aged 50 or over than at any point in the past 20 years: only four, and two of those have only just made it over the threshold. Moyes is 63 (three months younger than José Mourinho, which, like Aberdeen being further west than Bristol, is a fact both true and too counterintuitive to be worth believing). Then there is Unai Emery at 54, Oliver Glasner at 52 and Régis Le Bris at 50. Most Premier League managers are in their 40s, with the youngest two Matthias Jaissle, 38, and Fabian Hürzeler, 33.A chart showing the age ranges of Premier League managers at the start of seasons over the past 30 yearsThis is not coincidence; rather it seems the result of two interconnected trends. Even at the turn of the century, when Mourinho was starting out, it was unusual for a manager not to have played the game to at least a reasonable level, which meant they were starting their managerial careers in their mid-thirties. That’s still the route many take – Andoni Iraola, Michael Carrick, Gary O’Neil or Álvaro Arbeloa, for instance.View image in fullscreenAndoni Iraola’s first appointment as head coach was at AEK Larnaca in 2018, aged 35.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APBut there’s also a recognition, to use Arrigo Sacchi’s phrase, that a jockey does not need first to have been a horse. Coaching is regarded as a job in its own right, requiring a very different skillset to playing. Hürzeler came through the youth systems at Bayern Munich, Hoffenheim and 1860 Munich but, aged 22, in part because of an ankle injury, decided to focus on coaching.Jaissle was a member of the Hoffenheim side that soared through the divisions to win promotion to the Bundesliga before knee and achilles tendon injuries ended his playing career at 26. The early switch into coaching seems particularly common in Germany: Thomas Tuchel and Julian Nagelsmann have similar stories.That greater receptiveness to career coaches explains the wave of younger managers. But there are also fewer older coaches.In part it may be coincidence: an experienced generation – Sam Allardyce, Tony Pulis and Alan Pardew – grew old together. That the process occurred just as many of their tactical characteristics – low blocks, direct play, a focus on set pieces – re-entered the mainstream may not simply be irony. The old must be cast out before it is reinvented as new; the modish cannot be represented by a 60-something football man.But it’s also because modern management is exhausting. At Ipswich, Kieran McKenna would have his coaches present their plans to him for the day at 6am, altering anything he felt wasn’t quite right. That plan would be sent to the staff at the training ground to set up all the various pitches and drills. McKenna would then go to check everything was laid out properly. It was all extraordinarily detailed; everything was marked out, down to where players should stand when they weren’t directly involved and where water bottles would be placed.During sessions, McKenna would walk between each unit, stepping in to offer advice and make amendments. After sessions, coaches would watch them back and report to McKenna on what could be improved before planning the next day’s drills to be presented at 6am the following morning.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKieran McKenna’s relentless coaching at Ipswich was exhausting so it was no surprise he needed a break following their third promotion in five years.Photograph: Cat Goryn/Action Images/ReutersDuring 11 v 11 practice games, McKenna would be the only one who coached. Over his five years at Ipswich, no drill was ever repeated in exactly the same form; repetition and possible staleness were to be avoided at all costs. Little wonder that after a third promotion in five seasons at the club, he felt exhausted, in need of a break rather than taking on an uneven fight in an ungrateful Premier League that could only sap his reserves further.Brian Clough would take holidays during the season. He would turn up only infrequently at training. His input was sharp, erratic, impressionistic. Four decades on, a top-level manager is running a team of coaches and analysts that probably outnumbers the players with whom he has direct contact.He cannot simply ignore the board until he needs money for a signing but has to manage up to whatever structure of sporting directors exists above him. He often will have little autonomy, althoughthe success of Mikel Arteta, who has a more traditional role and seems to micromanage everything at Arsenal, may change that. And he is liable to be sacked after a month of poor form. The pressure is enormous, the margin for error minute.That perhaps explains why so many top managers are nowdrifting into international football. Management, it’s commonly said, is a drug, but perhaps that fix is more palatable when it is delivered in five doses spread over a season, plus a major tournament every other year, rather than in the relentless drudgery of the club game. Carlo Ancelotti took his break from the club game at 66, Jürgen Klopp at 56, Tuchel at 50. None have demonstrated any great desire to return to the remorselessness of the league.The Premier League may be the greatest stage in management. It may be where the best salaries are paid. It may be where every manager wishes to test himself. But it is an exhausting and capricious world that requires extraordinary reserves of energy, physical and mental. It is no theatre for old men.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueInside footballcommentShareReuse this content

title: Transfer roundup: Moyes wants to keep Armstrong while Forest agree Muñoz deal | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: David Moyes said Everton could not afford to lose their best players after fans made clear their displeasure at the possible transfer of Harrison Armstrong
Author: John Brewin
Headline: David Moyes said Everton could not afford to lose their best players after fans made clear their displeasure at the possible transfer of Harrison Armstrong
Content: Harrison Armstrong was especially influential in the first half for Everton at Bournemouth.Photograph: Graham Hunt/ProSports/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHarrison Armstrong was especially influential in the first half for Everton at Bournemouth.Photograph: Graham Hunt/ProSports/ShutterstockTransfer windowTransfer roundup: Moyes wants to keep Armstrong while Forest agree Muñoz deal‘I don’t think we can afford to lose any players,’ says MoyesForest’s Armstrong bid said to be £40m; Palace agree £22m feeJohn Brewinat the Vitality Stadium andBen FisherSat 29 Aug 2026 14.14 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 16.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe sale of the 19-year-old Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest would be a “club decision” for Everton, according to David Moyes. After his team’s1-1 draw at Bournemouth, in which Armstrong played the full 90 minutes, Moyes said he would prefer to keep a player for whom a reported £40m offer has been made.“I know there’s been an offer, I don’t really think there’s much else I’ve got to say about it,” Moyes said, initially refusing to be drawn. “It’s not really a question for just now, it’ll be a club decision.”James Tarkowski pounces at the death as Everton deny Bournemouth winRead moreMoyes has previously suggested his discomfort with a lack of business this summer, suggesting his squad was not big enough. His stance was unaltered here on Saturday. “I have said we could do with strengthening and hopefully we can do that. We have a good basis. Let’s hope we can build on it.“I don’t think we can afford to lose any players, certainly not our better ones. The club dictates a lot of that and we will see how the next few days go.”TravellingEvertonfans sang that the club would have a “riot on your hands” should Armstrong be sold. Moyes, when asked about the supporters’ reaction, said: “I’d say the manager’s an Evertonian.”He continued: “You always have to consider supporters. Supporters aren’t always wrong. But then there’s also times where I’ve fortunately had people at clubs who are really powerful and make difficult decisions.“I’d bring into that Bryan Gray, who was at Preston North End, and also Sir Philip Carter, who was at Everton when I first came in. Not always decisions are popular, and sometimes they have to do it for different reasons. It’s like managers have to make decisions on players … but there’s sometimes bigger decisions to be made and the club will, I’m sure, make what they think is the right one.”On the performance of Armstrong, the teenager lining up in midfield in a game where James Tarkowski’s injury-time goal was required to rescue a point, Moyes said: “Harrison played really well, he did a lot of good work. He ran out of legs a little bit later in the game, but it’s amazing the effort he puts in and he was probably more of an influence in the first half than he was in the second half.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDaniel Muñoz, meanwhile, will have a medical in the next few days afterNottingham Forestagreed a deal worth an initial £22m with Crystal Palace for the Colombia defender. The 30-year-old moved to Selhurst Park in 2024 under Oliver Glasner, who moved to the City Ground from Palace this summer.Muñoz sat through Friday’s 4-1 home defeat by Manchester City on the bench as talks between the clubs continued. He had played in Pierre Sage’s first game in charge of Palace, the 2-0 defeat at Everton.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowEvertonDavid MoyesCrystal PalaceNottingham ForestnewsShareReuse this content

title: European football: Elversberg stun Leverkusen in dream Bundesliga debut | European club football | The Guardian
description: Elversberg, from a town of just 13,000 people, stunned Bayer Leverkusen with a 3-2 victory, while in Italy Juventus beat Parma 2-0
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Elversberg, from a town of just 13,000 people, stunned Bayer Leverkusen with a 3-2 victory, while in Italy Juventus beat Parma 2-0
Content: David Mokwa laps up the adulation of the crowd after scoring Elversberg’s third goal at home to Bayer Leverkusen.Photograph: Thilo Schmülgen/ReutersView image in fullscreenDavid Mokwa laps up the adulation of the crowd after scoring Elversberg’s third goal at home to Bayer Leverkusen.Photograph: Thilo Schmülgen/ReutersEuropean club footballEuropean football: Elversberg stun Leverkusen in dream Bundesliga debutTeam from town of 13,000 shock 2024 championsJuventus 2-0 Parma; Sevilla 1-3 Atlético MadridReuters and Agence France-PresseSat 29 Aug 2026 17.46 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 14.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Bundesliga newcomersElversbergbegan their first top-flight campaign in style, stunningBayer Leverkusenwith an impressive 3-2 home victory on Saturday.Lukas Petkov and Cole Campbell scored within 60 seconds of each other to put Elversberg 2-0 up before the 10-minute mark. David Mokwa added another early in the second half in front of 9,307 delirious fans.Patrik Schick and Christian Kofane pulled late goals back, but it was not enough to prevent a famous victory for Elversberg, as they embarrassed a team who won the title in 2024 without losing a game.José Mourinho claims Kylian Mbappé should win Ballon d’Or ahead of PSG and Spain starsRead moreThe town of Elversberg has a population of just 13,000, making it the smallest settlement to have ever hosted aBundesligaside. Their ground, the Ursapharm-Arena, has a reduced capacity while upgrades are made to meet the German top flight’s stadium criteria.“It’s an indescribable day,” the Elversberg captain, Lukas Pinckert, told Sky. “We worked hard to earn the right to play in this league. The victory is deserved. I am incredibly proud of the team.”Leverkusen looked disorganised and lacked energy until late on, showing new coach Carles Martínez Novell that he has work to do. The Spaniard took over from Kasper Hjulmand in the summer after leaving his previous role at Ligue 1 side Toulouse.RB Leipzigcruised to a 3-0 home win overBorussia Mönchengladbach, with the former Chelsea and France forward Christopher Nkunku setting up a goal on his return to the club.Ridle Baku’s first-half goal came against the run of play for Leipzig but the hosts took control when Antonio Nusa produced a stunning finish early in the second half. Nkunku came on midway through the second half and set up a goal for the former Gladbach forward Rocco Reitz just two minutes later.View image in fullscreenAntonio Nusa’s shot flies beyond Moritz Nicolas at the Red Bull Arena.Photograph: Ronny Hartmann/AFP/Getty ImagesUnion Berlincame from 3-1 down to draw 3-3 withEintracht Frankfurt, cancelling out Younes Ebnoutalib’s hat-trick for the visitors. Union’s Tim Skarke scored in the third minute of stoppage time to level for the hosts.TheColognesubstitute Thijs Dallinga scored two goals and young winger Said El Mala scored a dazzling solo effort as the hosts came from behind twice to beatHoffenheim3-2. Elsewhere,Mainzplayed out a scoreless draw at home to promotedPaderborn.Juventussaw offParma2-0 to make it back-to-back wins at the start of the Serie A season, whileFiorentina’s celebrations of the club’s 100th anniversary were spoilt by a 3-0 home defeat by promotedFrosinone.Juve had to work hard for their three points, needing second-half goals from the substitutes Nicolás González and Teun Koopmeiners to secure the victory.The close-season signings Randal Kolo Muani and Jhon Lucumi both started, while 18-year-old Bosnian Kerim Alajbegovic had an impact after coming off the bench to make his debut.In Florence, club legends, including Gabriel Batistuta and Claudio Ranieri, were in attendance, only to see Fiorentina fail to bounce back from their 4-0 thrashing at Roma last weekend in their opener. Antonio Raimondo netted twice for the visitors, with Gabriele Bracaglia also on the scoresheet.In Ligue 1, winger Gessime Yassine struck twice asStrasbourgcame ⁠from behind to beatLens2-1 at home, ending the visitors’ ⁠strong start to ⁠the ​season. Lens took the lead when Jeyland Mitchell felled Abdallah Sima in the box, and captain Florian Thauvin stepped up to confidently rattle home the spot-kick in the 38th minute.Strasbourg came out firing in the second half, equalising ​through a deflected Yassine strike after three minutes. The hosts had a goal ruled out for offside in the 56th minute, but grabbed a deserved late winner when Sebastian Nanasi ​crossed for ‌Yassine to volley home.AtléticoMadridput the noise of the Julián Alvarez transfer saga behind them with a convincing 3-1 victory atSevillato move top of the early La Liga table. Diego Simeone’s men have taken seven points from their first three matches of the league season.Atleti have repeatedly ruled out a move to Barcelona for Alvarez, who has also been heavily linked with Arsenal. The Argentina international was left out of the matchday squad in Seville, having been booed by his own fans last weekend in a 2-2 home draw with Villarreal.The two forwards who started in his absence combined to great effect to give Atlético a fourth-minute lead. Lee Kang-in, a summer signing from Paris Saint-Germain, played an excellent pass in behind for Álex Baena to rifle a low shot into the net.View image in fullscreenÁlex Baena scores Atlético Madrid’s third goal at Sevilla.Photograph: Fran Santiago/Getty ImagesTheRojiblancosdoubled their advantage in the 26th minute, as Ademola Lookman planted a clever shot inside Odysseas Vlachodimos’s near post.Atlético were three goals in front just seven minutes later as Spanish World Cup winner Baena scored his second. He drove a shot into the bottom corner from outside the box after being teed up by Marcos Llorente.Sevilla improved in the second half and pulled one back through Miguel Sierra’s volley, but never looked like mounting a comeback.Real Betismissed the chance to extend their perfect start, and briefly go top of La Liga, as they slumped to a 5-2 defeat atLevante. Dela broke the deadlock for the hosts with a glancing header, but centre-half Marc Bartra levelled quickly with a powerful strike from the edge of the penalty area.Levante reclaimed the lead in first-half stoppage time, Enzo Bardeli lobbing Betis goalkeeper Álvaro Valles from long distance – only for Rodrigo Riquelme to equalise again from a corner before the break. Roger Brugué struck twice in the second half to putLevantein charge and a late Jon Ander Olasagasti header sealed the win.Real Sociedadgot their first points of the season with a 2-1 home win overEspanyol.Explore more on these topicsEuropean club footballBundesligaSV ElversbergRB LeipzigStrasbourgLensBorussia MönchengladbachnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hull maintain flying start as Liam Millar’s winner ruins Coventry’s day | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Coventry’s first home Premier League game for 25 years ended in a 1-0 defeat after Liam Millar kept up Hull’s 100% start
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Coventry’s first home Premier League game for 25 years ended in a 1-0 defeat after Liam Millar kept up Hull’s 100% start
Content: Liam Millar’s first Premier League goal is a vital one for Hull at Coventry.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenLiam Millar’s first Premier League goal is a vital one for Hull at Coventry.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersPremier LeagueHull maintain flying start as Liam Millar’s winner ruins Coventry’s dayBen Fisherat the Coventry Building Society ArenaSat 29 Aug 2026 12.11 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 16.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePerhaps last Saturday’s triumph was not a one-off. Hull backed upa shock victory against Manchester Unitedby maintaining their 100% start to the Premier League and condemning Coventry to successive defeats. “We’re gonna win the league,” was the glorious chant raining down from the Hull support after Liam Millar’s 82nd-minute strike.The goal was a sucker punch for Coventry, who were pushing for a winner and looked set to claim at least their first point of the season. Frank Lampard, arms folded, was unmoved as the away end rejoiced.James Tarkowski pounces at the death as Everton deny Bournemouth winRead moreHe and Coventry may wonder where their first point – and, indeed, their first goal – will come from. Next is a daunting trip to Manchester City, before they host Brighton, who began the season witha 4-0 trouncing of Aston Villa. Hull, as they did last season, are exceeding all expectations.Was losing to another promoted team, one who finished 22 points behind them last season, a mental blow? “It depends how much you want it to be,” Lampard said. “There are 36 games left; we’re two games in. It depends how you react to a defeat.”For Coventry, as their owner and chair, Doug King, said beforehand, a firstPremier Leaguefor more than 25 years was a historic day for the city. “I know how much it means to all of us,” he said, this also their first top-flight game in this stadium.The buzz before kick-off was palpable, none more so than when King – wearing an elephant brooch on his suit, the animal that adorns Coventry’s badge and the city’s coat of arms – joined Coventry supporters in singing along to The Enemy’s We’ll Live and Die in These Towns, the club’s adopted prematch anthem. The pyrotechnics left a haze drifting across the pitch as things got under way.At full time, it was down to Millar and Sergej Jakirovic, albeit after a little persuading, to conduct the Hull celebrations. “It gives us big confidence as a team, individuals, for me as well, because I don’t have experience at this level,” said Hull’s head coach. “We have a lot of work to do, we need to keep our feet on the ground and stay humble. We know our target: 38, 41 points? We will see.”View image in fullscreenLiam Millar slots the ball away in the 82nd minute to win Hull the game.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersBoth teams lacked quality, but Coventry were undeniably the more threatening side. Taiwo Awoniyi, on his full league debut for the club, sent a weak header at Konstantinos Tzolakis and later forced the Hull goalkeeper into a smart right-hand save after Loum Tchaouna’s cross skidded off the head of Nobel Mendy. Lampard cycled through substitutions, the arrival of Gustavo Hamer, something of a hero in these parts, lifting the home crowd, but they struggled to work Tzolakis.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIraola’s Liverpool start slowly again but Muñoz strike denies Nottingham ForestRead moreMillar, who arrived on the hour, had wasted Hull’s best opening with 74 minutes on the clock, Jakirovic wearing a look of disgust after the Canada winger ignored an unmarked Mohamed Belloumi to his right and sent his shot bobbling wide after a clever first-time pass by Oli McBurnie released Millar behind Bobby Thomas. Until then, their only shot on target was Mendy’s speculative shot from 30 yards.But Millar made amends, coolly slotting past Carl Rushworth to cap a devastating counterattack. Victor Torp’s attempted cross from the left boomeranged off Lucas Gourna-Douath and into midfield, where Belloumi overpowered Tatsuhiro Sakamoto and sent Millar streaming into the opposition half with a sumptuous outside-of-the-boot pass.“I think Millar was a bit disappointed with the first chance but then showed massive bollocks to score the second,” McBurnie said. “As a striker, it’s not the one you want when you’ve just missed a chance: you’ve got to run 40 yards and then think about your shot. You’ve got too much time to think.”Twelve months ago, Hull were reeling from back-to-back defeats against Blackburn and Bristol City and adapting to life under a transfer embargo. They made up for lost time this summer with Mohamed Ali-Cho, who made his debut late on here, and another forward, Ilyas Ansah, a £20m buy from Union Berlin, their 12th and 13th arrivals of the window respectively.“We knew this was going to be a really tough game, in some ways even tougher than last week,” McBurnie said. “Considering we’re ‘the worst team in Premier League history’, it’s not a bad start from the boys.”Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueCoventry CityHull Citymatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Amin Nabizada sparkles for Watford as draw puts pressure on West Ham’s Nuno | Championship | The Guardian
description: West Ham remain winless in the Championship after a 1-1 draw at Watford with Mattie Pollock’s own goal cancelling out Amin Nabizada’s opener
Author: Ben Bloom
Headline: West Ham remain winless in the Championship after a 1-1 draw at Watford with Mattie Pollock’s own goal cancelling out Amin Nabizada’s opener
Content: Amin Nabizada races away in delight after opening the scoring for Watford.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenAmin Nabizada races away in delight after opening the scoring for Watford.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAChampionshipAmin Nabizada sparkles for Watford as draw puts pressure on West Ham’s NunoBen Bloomat Vicarage RoadSat 29 Aug 2026 12.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 14.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen a club is an established part of English football’s upper echelons, plays its home games inside a 68,000-seater stadium, and promptly breaks the Championship transfer recordfollowing relegation from the top flight, there are expectations that naturally follow. By all accounts, West Ham were supposed to breeze through what is only meant to be a brief dalliance with a second-tier existence. To be winless three league matches into the season was inconceivable.If the travelling contingent’s boos after this draw atWatfordwere fleeting, their subsequent burst of “you’re getting sacked in the morning” directed at their team’s manager left no ambiguity. No matter how embryonic this campaign is, the repeated impotency is already unacceptable, and now Nuno Espírito Santo is in the firing line.Championship roundup: Wolves and Swansea extend unbeaten starts in styleRead moreA 46-gameChampionshipseason is long and there remains abundant time to turn things around. But when you suggest that spending £22m on Arne Engels is with a view to him playing in the Premier League – as Nuno did earlier this summer – you leave yourself little wriggle room when things do not follow the expectedly smooth course.“We are a big club, we are favourites to go up,” said Nuno. “We have three games, we have two points. Who is happy? But me? I believe. I trust my boys. I work very hard with them. We are building a team. Things will change. I am positive.“The fans are the most important part of our club and I respect them so much. I understand everything. I just ask again to keep believing, keep trusting us, keep going and we will try to reverse it. The win must come, hopefully on Tuesday [against fellow relegated side Wolves]. We need it.”That this draw – which followed another against Burnley and defeat to Charlton – came against a Watford team openly treading water only emphasised West Ham’s struggles.A side that only finished 16th last season has barely strengthened in the intervening months, with the lack of depth leaving new manager Alessio Dionisi no choice but to alter training sessions to cope with having so few first-team players at his disposal. A bench that included two goalkeepers sent a silent message to those tasked with providing Watford reinforcements in the closing days of the transfer window.Yet after what was anticipated to be a horror start to the campaign – with fixturesagainst promotion favourites Southampton, Wrexham and West Ham – Dionisi’s side are unbeaten. The Italian admitted he did not know of Amin Nabizada before arriving in Hertfordshire, but few Championship followers are now unaware of the 19-year-old academy product’s unbridled talent now.View image in fullscreenNuno Espírito Santo is confident West Ham will quickly find their feet in the Championship.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAThe English-born Afghanistan international had never started a senior game prior to this season, but has been ever present in Dionisi’s side so far this campaign, frequently providing Watford’s most potent attacking threat. His second goal in three appearances put the hosts ahead when a neat stepover created sufficient space on the left side of the penalty area, and he delicately curled the ball over Mads Hermansen and into the top corner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor all that West Ham’s vigour rose as the match wore on, they ended it with just a solitary shot on target. A hefty dose of fortune was required for their equaliser, which arrived eight minutes after Nabizada’s opener. Watford’s culprit was Kévin Keben, who attempted to shepherd the ball out of play on his own goalline, only for Valentín Castellanos to nick it off him and prod across goal where it deflected off the unfortunate Mattie Pollock and into the Watford net.As Jarrod Bowen increasingly exerted his influence on proceedings, so Watford dropped deeper and West Ham enjoyed the type of territorial dominance expected of a side with vast Premier League experience and an England international in their ranks. But it counted for little, with Watford coming closest to a winner when Iker Bravo’s shot deflected over following a rapid counterattack.“We will gel, we will click and we are positive that, with the quality we have, we are going to do it,” insisted Nuno. If West Ham’s travelling fans are to be believed, time might be in short supply.Explore more on these topicsChampionshipWatfordWest Ham Unitedmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 9: Liverpool | Liverpool FC Women | The Guardian
description: Liverpool will hope Germany striker Vivien Endemann and Japanese youngster Mao Itamura can help get them off to a better start than they had last season
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Liverpool will hope Germany striker Vivien Endemann and Japanese youngster Mao Itamura can help get them off to a better start than they had last season
Content: Mao Itamura was named Eredivisie player of the year last season before moving to Liverpool. Photograph: Andrew Powell/Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesLiverpool will hope Germany striker Vivien Endemann and Japanese youngster Mao Itamura can help get them off to a better start than they had last seasonByTom GarrySat 29 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:8th (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:11thProspectsAfter a disappointing 2025-26 campaign, there is renewed positivity at Liverpool. A strong summer transfer window, coupled with encouraging results in pre-season, suggests they will significantly improve on their 11th-place finish, continuing the good run they had in the second half of last season.Gareth Taylor did not take charge until quite late last summer and the squad needed something of a rebuild. This time around, the former Manchester City head coach has been able to spend a full pre-season with his team. The managing director, Andy O’Boyle, has also had three transfer windows since starting his job to try to evolve the squad. The arrival of Germany forward Vivien Endemann, from Wolfsburg, is a very promising signing, while goalkeeper Khiara Keating has been reunited with Taylor, albeit she is not as experienced as Sweden’s Jennifer Falk. Falk was tremendous during a loan spell with Liverpool in the second half of last season, but opted not to make her stay permanent because she wanted to be closer to family.Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 8: EvertonRead moreThere were other notable losses, including the centre-back Gemma Bonner. Nonetheless, Liverpool appear to have a squad that is more than capable of staying up although they still look a long way off challenging for Europe and their budget is dwarfed by the big spenders.It took Liverpool until late January to record their first league win last season and this time around they will want to make an immediate impact. It should help that they begin away to promoted Charlton.Graphic showing where Liverpool finished in the past five seasonsOff-field pictureThe women’s team have never really benefited from the type of cash injections from their owners, Fenway Sports Group (FSG), that Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City’s women’s sides have from theirs. Liverpool have recorded an overall profit of more than £500,000 when the past eight seasons are combined and consistently break even. They also boast top-class facilities at their Melwood training base..The managerTaylor will want to see the team look more accustomed to his style of play. The 53-year-old has yet to win over the fanbase, but he does have a strong CV, winning the Women’s FA Cup and the League Cup with Manchester City in 2020 and 2022 respectively, and very nearly a league title, too. A former Wales international striker, Taylor represented a broad range of clubs, from Bristol Rovers to Nottingham Forest and Wrexham, with spells at Sheffield United and Manchester City in between.Star signingLiverpool were delighted that Endemann decided to make the switch from Wolfsburg. The 25-year-old had a good record in the Bundesliga, as well as 17 caps for Germany, whom she helped finish third at the 2024 Olympics. Endemann won a German Cup with Wolfsburg in 2024 and has Women’s Champions League experience, too.View image in fullscreenVivien Endemann will give Liverpool more threat in front of goal.Photograph: Nick Taylor/Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesStat attackLiverpool improved after a very slow start to the last campaign. They earned 11 points more in the second half of the season than in the first, the widest margin of improvement in the Women’s Super League. Doubling their tally from the second batch of 11 games would have given them 28 points, enough for sixth.Graphic showing points won in the first half and second half of the season by WSL teamsSet for a breakthroughThe 20-year-old Japan youth international Mao Itamura has been signed from Feyenoord. She was named as the Eredivisie player of the year last season and is a versatile forward with great dribbling skills. She should add a fresh and exciting dimension to Liverpool’s attack.What they say“We want to be in the first half of the table because we have really good players and I think we canshow what we are capable of. I believe in every single person in this team. We have good chances to have a great season. And we all have this good feeling; I can feel it in the training” – Liverpool and Switzerland forward Aurélie CsillagWhere are they playing their home games?Liverpool play the vast majority of their home matches at St Helens Stadium, which they share with the rugby league side. It has a modern feel and a capacity of about 18,000. They have announced they will be playing three times at Anfield this season; the first of those games being a derby against Everton in September.Explore more on these topicsWSL season previews 2026-27Liverpool FC WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Filip Hrgović completes astonishing comeback to stun Moses Itauma and win IBF title – as it happened | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Round-by-round report: Filip Hrgović stunned Moses Itauma for the vacant IBF heavyweight title in London. Bryan Armen Graham was watching
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: Round-by-round report: Filip Hrgović stunned Moses Itauma for the vacant IBF heavyweight title in London. Bryan Armen Graham was watching
Content: 18.41 EDTWhat an extraordinary turnaround at the O2.Itauma looked sensational early, his speed and power giving Hrgović all sorts of problems, and he dropped the Croatian in the second round. But Hrgović absorbed everything the 21-year-old threw at him and simply refused to go away.Then the fight turned. Itauma began to tire badly after the sixth and Hrgović’s experience, chin and persistence took over. By the ninth, Itauma was completely spent. Hrgović battered him around the ring until Ben Davison threw in the towel, completing a remarkable comeback.It is a stunning upset – and a historic one. Hrgovic becomes Croatia’s first world heavyweight champion, while Itauma suffers his first professional defeat after being anointed by so many as the division’s next king before he had even won a belt.Filip Hrgović celebrates after defeating Moses Itauma to win the IBF heavyweight title at the O2 Arena in London.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersShareUpdated at20.10 EDT

description: Tom Hooper scores decisive try in a messy game as Les Kiss earns biggest scalp of his early tenure
Author: Daniel Gallan

Content: 4h ago17.34 EDTMatch reportThat’ll do from me for tonight.Here is the report fromAngus Fontaine. Credit to the Wallabies for digging deep. Catch you next week.double quotation markThe Wallabies have landed a major blow in their redemption story under Les Kiss, defeating Argentina 27-21 in a thrilling showdown in San Salvador de Jujuy. The hard-fought victory gives Australia their first four-match winning streak since 2021 and means Kiss remains unbeaten in his three Tests in charge.That winning run has come against Italy and Japan, teams ranked No 11 and No 12 in the world.
