title: Biggest problem for Spurs is finding ‘right mentality’, says Roberto De Zerbi | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: Speaking after Tottenham’s 2-0 home defeat by Newcastle, Roberto De Zerbi also said Richarlison and Kevin Danso had asked for transfers
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Speaking after Tottenham’s 2-0 home defeat by Newcastle, Roberto De Zerbi also said Richarlison and Kevin Danso had asked for transfers
Content: Roberto De Zerbi hinted it would take time to find the right balance at Spurs after the 2-0 defeat by Newcastle.Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRoberto De Zerbi hinted it would take time to find the right balance at Spurs after the 2-0 defeat by Newcastle.Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty ImagesTottenham HotspurBiggest problem for Spurs is finding ‘right mentality’, says Roberto De ZerbiHead coach calls for patience after defeat by NewcastleRicharlison and Kevin Danso have asked for transfersPaul MacInnesat Tottenham Hotspur StadiumSat 29 Aug 2026 16.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 17.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRoberto De Zerbi has admitted his biggest challenge for his Tottenham team will be to find “the right mentality”, as they fell to a second consecutive defeat at the start of the Premier League season.Spurs were deservedly beatenby Matthias Jaissle’s Newcastle when they fell away in the second half of this match after dominating the first. De Zerbi said the outcome could have been much different, but called for patience both for his team and for his big-money signings, none more so than Sandro Tonali, who cost an initial £92.5m.Elanga and Wissa strike as Newcastle extend Spurs’ miserable start to seasonRead more“It’s the biggest problem, it’s the biggest challenge and the biggest target is to find the right mentality,” De Zerbi said after the match. “You can’t find the right mentality in the transfer market. Football is a magical thing, you can change a lot of players and you can find the balance immediately or you need more time. I want to achieve this target as soon as possible … but I am in no doubt that we will reach it.”De Zerbi said that Richarlison and Kevin Danso had asked to leave the club this week after Spurs completed further signings, bringing in Sávio and Omar Marmoush from Manchester City. “I love Danso and Richarlison, they are great guys but if they want to leave they have to bring the economic solution to the club and they can go and we find other players,” De Zerbi said.Of the players the club have bought, De Zerbi’s fellow Italian Tonali has been under keenest scrutiny, with former supporters at Newcastle booing his every touch and cheering when he was substituted shortly after Spurs conceded the opening goal. “Sandro is a crucial player that is not in the right, the best condition yet,” De Zerbi said. “But I love my players more today than if we had won. Because together we are rebuilding the club.”Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Jaissle, meanwhile, was able to celebrate the performance of the player signed in part to replace Tonali, Nico González. Another signing from Manchester City, the £50m defensive midfielder controlled the midfield in the second half and set up the opening goal with a 60-yard crossfield pass to the equally impressive Amar Dedic.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It was a great debut,” said the German, who has hit the ground running as the Newcastle head coach. “It’s not easy for a player who is just showing after a transfer, there is a human being behind that. I really, really think he did amazing and we look forward to seeing more from him. Right now everything is top, everything is great with the team, but we don’t follow that too much. It’s a moment to enjoy but we’re also smart enough to see it’s a long, long journey in front of us.”Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurRoberto De ZerbiNewcastle UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Tadej Pogacar requires surgery after crashing out of Vuelta a España | Tadej Pogacar | The Guardian
description: Leader ⁠Tadej ⁠Pogacar ​abandoned the Vuelta a España on ⁠Saturday after breaking his collarbone in a crash ⁠during stage ​eight
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Leader ⁠Tadej ⁠Pogacar ​abandoned the Vuelta a España on ⁠Saturday after breaking his collarbone in a crash ⁠during stage ​eight
Content: A giant screen at the Vuelta a España shows Tadej Pogacar entering an ambulance.Photograph: Josep Lago/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA giant screen at the Vuelta a España shows Tadej Pogacar entering an ambulance.Photograph: Josep Lago/AFP/Getty ImagesTadej PogacarTadej Pogacar requires surgery after crashing out of Vuelta a EspañaLeader abandons on stage eight with broken collarbonePogacar also suffers concussion and ‘stable’ neck fractureAgence France-PresseSat 29 Aug 2026 15.56 EDTFirst published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 11.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTadej Pogacar requires surgery on a broken collarbone sustained in a crash on stage eight of theVuelta a Españaon Saturday which forced him to abandon the race.The five-time Tour de France champion hit the tarmac with 31km remaining, ending his bid to complete a career clean sweep of the three grand tours.Pogacar had been leading by 3min 50sec a week into the race and was the overwhelming favourite for victory. Spaniard Enric Mas inherited the overall leader’s red jersey, a minute ahead of Primoz Roglic.“He is stable and, following a thorough medical assessment at hospital, Tadej has been diagnosed with a concussion, displaced left clavicle fracture, a stable C7 cervical fracture, and multiple abrasions,” said UAE Team Emirates-XRG’s medical director, Adrian Rotunno. “Fortunately, no other major injuries and no neurological fallout. He will require clavicle surgery which will be delayed due to concussion precautions. Tadej remains under the care of our medical team and we’ll provide further updates following the surgery.”Pogacar fell after brushing shoulders with another rider and losing control of his handlebars. With his entire team waiting as the peloton carried on without them, Pogacar tried to remount after a couple of minutes but cried out “no” and winced in pain when he touched his bike.He was then led to an ambulance as his teammates set off up the road towards the finish line at Xeraco, near Valencia.View image in fullscreenThe new overall race leader, Enric Mas, holds the red jersey after Tadej Pogacar’s withdrawal.Photograph: Josep Lago/AFP/Getty ImagesIt marks the first time the 27-year-old has failed to finish a grand tour.Mas (Movistar) took the ​red jersey after stage eight, becoming the first Spaniard to lead ​the Vuelta since ‌Jesus Herrada in 2018. ​Roglic (Red Bull-Bora Hansgrohe) moves up to ​second overall with Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM) 71 seconds back in third.At the podium, a sombre Mas accepted the red jersey ​but did not wear ‌it, holding it in ​front of him instead. “I hope he gets better quickly,” he said of Pogacar. “We’ve still got a few races left and I hope he’ll be in good shape for them.“skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn July, Pogacar joined a select group of five-time Tour de France winners in Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Induráin. He is the youngest rider to have won five Tours, more than a year younger than Merckx was in achieving the same feat, and is the first person to finish on the podium seven years running. He is also the only rider to have been on the podium in nine consecutive grand tours.Bryan Coquard (Cofidis) ⁠won the stage after several riders went down in ​another crash in ​the final kilometre. Mads ​Pedersen finished second while Jordi Meeus was third. The race continues on Sunday with a 187.5km mountainous ride from Villajoyosa to Alto de Aitana, before a rest day on Monday.Explore more on these topicsTadej PogacarVuelta a EspañaCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dan Lawrence hails ‘different mentality’ as he strives to make up for lost time | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: Dan Lawrence said he was ‘desperate’ to establish himself, after his unbeaten 50 helped England to a strong position against Pakistan at Lord’s
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: Dan Lawrence said he was ‘desperate’ to establish himself, after his unbeaten 50 helped England to a strong position against Pakistan at Lord’s
Content: Dan Lawrence hit his second 50 of the series against Pakistan on the third day at Lord’s.Photograph: Sam Mellish/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDan Lawrence hit his second 50 of the series against Pakistan on the third day at Lord’s.Photograph: Sam Mellish/Getty ImagesEngland v Pakistan 2026Dan Lawrence hails ‘different mentality’ as he strives to make up for lost timeEngland all-rounder ‘desperate’ to establish himselfLawrence hits second fifty of Pakistan series at Lord’sSimon Burntonat Lord'sSat 29 Aug 2026 15.27 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 15.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDan Lawrence said he was “desperate to establish myself in an England shirt” after taking some solid steps in the right direction on a rain-affected third day of the second Test against Pakistan.In a chill breeze and with frequent interruptions from the weather, the battle for England’s batting spots heated up in the continued absence of the injured Jacob Bethell. Emilio Gay’s hard-fought 31 was ended by a grubber before Lawrence scored his second half-century of the series – matching Jordan Cox on that metric – to put England in control, 177 for seven at stumps to stand 357 ahead.“I’ve really tried not to think about that,” Lawrence said about the contest for places, after finishing the day unbeaten on 50. “I’ve tried to just enjoy every day of being here and trying to contribute to the team. It’s pointless looking into the future. I’m just trying to give a good showing of myself and thankfully I think I have done.Lawrence stretches lead against Pakistan as weather delays England victory pushRead more“Thoughts creep into your head and I’m desperate along with all the other boys to establish myself in an England shirt. It’s just about trying to take every opportunity you get instead of feeling nervous about the occasion, just have fun and play the cricket that’s got me here this summer.”Lawrence’s last run in the team, three Tests against Sri Lanka in 2024, came as opener and without great effect, three single-digit scores and three in the thirties. “I got wrapped up in a lot of things and I was thinking about my position and what I needed to do to stay in the team, instead of just enjoying it and realising how lucky I am to play for England,” he said.“My mentality since coming back has been completely different. Hopefully, we get a good series win and then we’ll see what happens in the coming months and years.”As a middle-order batter by preference he does not covet Gay’s position as opener – “It has been great fun batting in a position that is a little bit closer to what I’m used to,” he said, after a third outing at No 6 – and certainly took no pleasure in the 26-year-old’s dismissal, trapped lbw by a Mohammad Abbas delivery that kept low. “He played beautifully last night, dug in really hard and fought for the team.“Hopefully that bit of bad luck he got, he gets all the good luck next week. He can take a lot of confidence in how he played.“To get off the mark I had a massive big whooshka and edged it over the slips. That could easily have been caught and I’d have looked really stupid.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOf the four occasions when Pakistan have scored more than 300 runs in the fourth innings to win a Test match, three came against Sri Lanka and only one score exceeded 350. On an awkward pitch and against in-form bowlers their task already seems extremely difficult.“As far as batting is concerned we can only hope,” said Mohammad Ali. “Until the last ball is bowled in cricket, or the last run is made, nothing is decided. Maybe if we can get them out quickly … Miracles do happen in cricket.”Explore more on these topicsEngland v Pakistan 2026England cricket teamPakistan cricket teamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Keep off the grass: British tennis players complain of marijuana smell at US Open | US Open tennis | The Guardian
description: Britain’s US Open hopefuls have noticed the smell of marijuana wafting over the courts at Flushing Meadows from a nearby public park
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Britain’s US Open hopefuls have noticed the smell of marijuana wafting over the courts at Flushing Meadows from a nearby public park
Content: The practice courts at the US Open venue in New York, where marijuana is legal for adults.Photograph: Lev Radin/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe practice courts at the US Open venue in New York, where marijuana is legal for adults.Photograph: Lev Radin/ShutterstockUS Open tennisKeep off the grass: British tennis players complain of marijuana smell at US OpenAroma wafts over courts from nearby Corona ParkKatie Boulter: ‘You smell it a lot. I’m not a huge fan’Press AssociationSat 29 Aug 2026 05.57 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 09.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s US Open hopefuls thought they had put the grass behind them when Wimbledon finished, but the smell of it is all around Flushing Meadows and they are not happy about it.Marijuana is legal for adults inNew Yorkand while smoking is not allowed on site, the aroma of weed wafts over some outside courts from the nearby Corona Park.Katie Boulter, the British No 1, said: “Yeah, I have experienced it. You go down to the practice courts and down in the park courts, you do smell it a lot. I’m not a huge fan of it. I know a lot of players have complained on some of the specific courts.View image in fullscreen‘I’m trying to focus and then it takes you out of the moment. You don’t need distractions,’ says Katie Boulter.Photograph: Seth Wenig/AP“I’ve played on one before and I did smell it during my match. It’s something that I wouldn’t like to smell in the middle of my match. I’m trying to focus and then obviously, it takes you out of the moment and you really don’t want to. You don’t need distractions. So I wasn’t a huge fan of it.”Fran Jones, the British No 3, said: “Last year I made a joke about that, in my first round, and I said to the guy: ‘Is this normal?’. Because I was on the stadium, and it’s next to the park. He’s like: ‘Yeah” and I was: ‘Well, no wonder I’m playing pretty well’. This year I’ll be like: ‘No, lock in, lock in!”Carlos Alcaraz believes ‘it is possible’ to win US Open despite long injury layoffRead moreHarriet Dart, who came through qualifying along with Jones, added: “I mean it’s New York. I feel like everywhere you walk around, it’s everywhere, no? It is what it is. Same for everyone.”The USTA said in a statement: “While we can’t control what takes place off the grounds of the USTA Billie Jean King NationalTennisCenter, we continue to be vigilant as we maintain this.”Fery sails into first ATP final against BuseArthur Fery has reached the first ATP Tour final of his career at the Winston-Salem Open after his semi-final opponent, James Duckworth, retired due to injury.Fery led 6-4, 1-2 when Duckworth withdrew because of an apparent right ​leg problem. Buse is one place above Fery in the world rankings at No 36, and is the 32nd seed at the US Open.Fery, who narrowly missed out on being seeded in New York, faces a tough opening test on his main-draw US Open debut against the world No 14, Lorenzo Musetti.ReutersExplore more on these topicsUS Open tennisUS Open Tennis 2026TennisUS sportsNew YorknewsShareReuse this content

title: The rebranding of ‘Lake America’ is Trump’s desperate attempt to distract us | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Ignore Iran, the Epstein files, and your wallet – not to mention Trump’s plummeting approval ratings
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Ignore Iran, the Epstein files, and your wallet – not to mention Trump’s plummeting approval ratings
Content: ‘As well as being a distraction, this pathetic maneuver is supposed to be a middle finger to Canada.’Photograph: Al Drago/Pool/Al Drago - Pool/CNP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘As well as being a distraction, this pathetic maneuver is supposed to be a middle finger to Canada.’Photograph: Al Drago/Pool/Al Drago - Pool/CNP/ShutterstockThe Week in PatriarchyDonald TrumpThe rebranding of ‘Lake America’ is Trump’s desperate attempt to distract usArwa MahdawiIgnore Iran, the Epstein files, and your wallet – not to mention Trump’s plummeting approval ratingsSat 29 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTShareDon’t mention the war! Or the economy, for that matter. Or the Epstein files. Or Natalie Harp. Or “affordability”, which, as Donald Trump recentlysaidat a rally, is a word that was “never used” by the media before he took office. Best not to talk about anything that affects ordinary people or embarrasses the president, really. Instead, let’s all rejoice in Trump’s latest triumph: renaming Lake Ontario, which is shared by Canada and the US, asLake America.On Thursday, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to America-fy the lake’s name on US maps and documents, which is an excellent use of time and resources. I suppose we can at least be thankful that the president, who is trying to slap his own name on everything fromairportsto theKennedy Center, didn’t decree that the body of water be called Lake Trump.This is not an isolated embarrassment: the Lake Ontario name change follows the president’srebrandingof the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America last year. “We have a gulf and we have a lake – now all we need is an ocean. Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific,” Trumptold reporters.Give it a few more months of the disastrous war in Iran and a bruised Trump may well make good on that threat: the man will do anything to distract from his failings.As well as being a distraction, this pathetic maneuver is supposed to be a middle finger to Canada. Trade negotiations between the US and Canada recentlycollapsed, with the Trump administration imposing a 50% tariff on some goods and the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, promising a “dollar for dollar” response. One suspects that Trump thinks Lake Ontario is named after the Canadian province it borders. Ergo he reckons a unilateral name change is a good way of showing the US’s northern neighbour who is boss.However, as Carney was forced topoint outon social media, the name Lake Ontario has been used for more than 400 years and comes from the Indigenous Wendat/Huron word Ontari’io, meaning: “The lake is beautiful, the lake is big.” It predates both the Confederation of Canada and the US Declaration of Independence.A US president ordering the name change of a Great Lake in order to antagonize one of its closest allies would have been headline news for weeks in a normal timeline. Now it’s just another Thursday. Still, this is more than a silly stunt that both Canada and the governor of New York have made clear they are going to ignore. It’s a glaring demonstration of just how desperate, isolated and out of ideas Trump is. His approval ratingshave hit a new low, sliding 14 points from 47% at the start of his second term to 33% now amid rising costs. The Iran war, which was sold as a “little excursion” that would only last a few weeks has hit thesix-month mark, and there isn’t a decent off-ramp in sight. And Canada isn’t the only former ally angry with Trump’s US; the country’s reputation hasplummetedglobally. A 36-country survey conducted by Pew earlier this year found overall ratings for the US are largelynegative; only seven countries rate the US positively, with Israel at the top of the list. Trump is weak and floundering: because he lacks the intellectual and diplomatic ability to reshape reality to his liking, he’s trying to rebrand it instead. But it doesn’t matter how many executive orders he signs; people will be calling Lake Ontario by its original name long after we can all stop calling Trump “president”.Florida ‘deputy of the year’ allegedly used Flock camera surveillance system to stalk exBrevard county’s 2025 deputy of the year has nowresignedfrom the sheriff’s office after an investigation found numerous examples of “egregious misconduct”, including images of him putting a gun in his ex-girlfriend’s mouth and a claim he used the Flock license plate readers to look up his ex-girlfriend. He also appeared to have posted a photo of himself sporting a Hitler-like moustache while performing a Nazi salute. (He denies that he used Flock to stalk his ex, and said the photo was merely a joke.) This is not a one-off: there arenumerous allegations involvinglaw enforcement officers using Flock to stalk people. Just this week a police officer in Kentucky was accused of using the Flock camera system to search for and track his exmore than 2,000 times.Tate brothers reportedly rented supercars to appear ‘uberwealthy’Theself-styledmisogynist Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan were arrested in the US in July as part of a UK police investigation into alleged sexual offences. Part of their lawyers’ strategy to fight extradition seems to be to paint them as posers who just pretended to be “uberwealthy” online in order to generate attention. “[T]he $2.1m Aston Martin and $5m and $7m Bugattis featured in Tristan’s videos were rented,” one legal submissionnotes. “The valuation of Andrew’s watch collection is based on a third-party enthusiast publication.”Women using HRT may be at lower risk of dementiaA studytracked183,450 postmenopausal women in the UK and found that those who had used hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for at least a year were 10% less likely to develop any form of dementia.Female-first music festivals are due for a resurgenceOlivia Rodrigo’s women-led Daisy Chain Fields Festival is taking place in California this Saturday, with net proceeds going to organizations like Planned Parenthood and the Center for Reproductive Rights. “[The festival] creates a necessary and refreshing culture of community, setting up women’s art to be received and valued in a less competitive and capitalist environment,” the pop artist Elitold the Guardian.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIsrael has killed at least 100 Palestinians in Gaza in the last two weeksThis is more than10 months intoa “ceasefire”. Still, that kill count is not enough for Itamar Ben-Gvir, the leader of Israel’s far-right Jewish Power (Otzma Yehudit) party and the minister of national security. “I think we should be doing 30 to 40 targeted assassinations per night,”Ben-Gvir recently saidon a podcast. “Not just those who pose an immediate threat. There are people there who don’t deserve to live … They are not even people.” Ben-Gvir went on to say that he thought Israel should occupy the entirety of Gaza. “I imagine settlements … throughout Gaza, and encouraging as much emigration as possible.” There has been a disturbing lack of outrage about these comments from the international community.A Texas judge has advice for people offended by drag shows“[T]he solution is relatively simple … just don’t go,” US district judge David Hittnerwrote in a rulingthat struck down a 2023 state law trying to restrict drag shows. Hittner ruled on the basis that the law was so vague that it was unconstitutional. As the New York Times noted in apiece last year: “Vagueness has become fundamental to the way Trump operates. It is not so much a legal strategy as a power dynamic.” People are more likely to self-police and comply in advance because they’re terrified they’ll get in trouble.Dolly Parton’s death united the US in griefIt’s not often that you’ll see Donald Trump and the Democratic Socialists of America pay homage to the same person. The Washington Postnotesthat Parton was “the only global figure that a majority of conservatives and liberals both supported in one Marchpoll– and by far – leaving the likes of Taylor Swift in the favorability dust”. RIP Dolly. As Robert Reichwrote in the Guardian, she was everything Trump is not: “Dolly Parton was a huge winner, bless her soul. Trump is the biggest loser on the planet.”Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpThe Week in PatriarchyTrump administrationCanadaAmericasUS politicsFloridaSurveillancecommentShareReuse this content

title: A $1.95m deposit and $10k a month: welcome to the for-profit world of Australian aged care where no one is a winner | Julianne Schultz | The Guardian
description: Like all the privatised care services, the business of aged care is about property, cheap labour and public money
Author: Julianne Schultz
Headline: Like all the privatised care services, the business of aged care is about property, cheap labour and public money
Content: ‘For the three-quarters of aged people on pensions, the new co-payments for non-clinical services are often beyond their means,’ writes Julianne Schultz.Photograph: Carly Earl/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘For the three-quarters of aged people on pensions, the new co-payments for non-clinical services are often beyond their means,’ writes Julianne Schultz.Photograph: Carly Earl/The GuardianOpinionAged careA $1.95m deposit and $10k a month: welcome to the for-profit world of Australian aged care where no one is a winnerJulianne SchultzLike all the privatised care services, the business of aged care is about property, cheap labour and public moneyFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSat 29 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 20.26 EDTShareYou know you have entered the parallel universe of residential aged care when you find yourself saying, “Just to clarify, the deposit for the room is $1.95m, and the charges will be about $10,000 a month?”“That’s correct,” the kindly sales agent replies.Sure, it’s Sydney’s eastern suburbs, but that is a lot of money for a 20 sq metre room – almost double the median price for a one-bedroom apartment in the same suburb.“In the brochure there are rooms for $1.25m, are they available?” you ask.“No, and when the current residents leave [die] they will be renovated, with new bathrooms.”“I guess that will make them more expensive?” you speculate.“Yes, they will be $1.65m.”A fifth of older Australians who contested automated decision on home support funding got more after human reviewRead moreEven with imported marble that seems excessive. Like all the privatised care services, the business of aged care is about property, cheap labour and public money.But when your loved one has been deteriorating in a hospital bed for eight months without any therapies, eating hospital food on plastic plates, with only a car park to walk around, you are desperate and say yes, hoping against hope that another option will emerge.In my case it did, and a few days later a 16 sq metre room with a big window in a well-run little centre became available. A mere $995,000 plus the day rate,the “hotelling fee”, non-clinical care contribution and special services charges.Welcome to the for-profit, highly regulated, severely rationed, underpaid, world of aged care – where no one is a winner, and the most frail and vulnerable and their carers are forced to navigate anextraordinarily complex system.There are endless online forms to complete, passwords to remember, physical certification to prove you are who you say you are, then more documents to sign, financial advisers to consult, medical specialists to listen to, occupational therapists to perform for, providers to negotiate with and an ever-changing group of service providers and staff.This time last year there were more than 2,000 older people in hospitals – “bed blockers” they were cruelly called – too frail to go home without more support, but with Buckley’s chance of finding a residential care bed, even if they could afford the now standard deposit of $750,000. Beds for the poorest and most needy wereeven scarcer.This year, despite the state health ministers winning extra money from Canberra, the“bed blockers”are understood to have almost doubled.The specialised facilities the frail elderly need cannot be conjured overnight. Last yearfew new bedsbecame available nationwide. The health minister, Mark Butler, says a new facility is needed every 72 hours to meet the 18,000 targetin three years.The new system of aged care, which was meant to address problems of the old model identified with heart-breaking detail by the royal commission into aged care, is not even a year old butalready broken.At least the Commonwealth Home Support Program, which costs 8% of the $40bn budget to assist 65% of aged care clients,will now continue until 2029.Hundreds of thousands of people are waiting for assessments and, when these assessments are completed with an algorithm that doesn’t allow for human oversight, they find themselveswaiting monthsfor a package to meet their needs and enable them to age at home. When the package is allocated theywait even longerfor a provider to deliver the services they need.If they can afford them.For the three-quarters of aged people on pensions, the new co-payments for non-clinical services are often beyond their means.That is, if they can find someone to do the work.Notes from a nursing home: ‘Our books told of who we were. The story of us. Then the movers came and asked what should go’Read moreIn the first two months of the new system, applications for financial hardship increased by 88%. “The way aged care reform is being implemented is causing harm … we have built inefficiency into the system by design,” the recently departed inspector general of aged care, Natalie Siegel-Brown,observed.She believes the system should be turned upside down to start with the outcomes we want, rather than the mechanics of funding and services: to put care first, help people stay at home and connected to their communities.This already occurs with theaged veterans’ care program.It has also worked in countries including Denmark, Japan and South Korea, where investment in individual home care is prioritised, reducing the need for much more expensive residential facilities. It would mean a system where the assessor is a human being, where the person delivering meals warms them and sits down and talks with the client as they eat, where assistive technology is delivered when it is needed, not after months of checking and vetting and another fall.All the ministerial platitudes in the world will not solve the problem. Action is needed, now, to keep people safely at home longer, before it becomes too hard,thousands of peopleand their carers needlessly suffer, and we all pay for it.Julianne Schultz is the author of The Idea of AustraliaExplore more on these topicsAged careOpinioncommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: The barbecue is fundamentally unenjoyable. Please, put a lid on it | Max Liu | The Guardian
description: Dress up the barbie however you like – it’s toxic, tiresome and, more to the point, malnourishing, says freelance writer Max Liu
Author: Max Liu
Headline: Dress up the barbie however you like – it’s toxic, tiresome and, more to the point, malnourishing, says freelance writer Max Liu
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onBarbecueThe hill I will die on: The barbecue is fundamentally unenjoyable. Please, put a lid on itMax LiuDress up the barbie however you like – it’s toxic, tiresome and, more to the point, malnourishingSat 29 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 09.44 EDTShare“If you’re invited to a barbecue, have your dinner before you go.” It is the wisest advice my dad has ever given me. Barbecues are one of life’s perennial disappointments. The romance of eating outside quickly degenerates into a recipe for mucky fingers, smelly clothes andmore mess than you bargained for, with grills that you can never get clean, uncomfortable seating that makes your back ache or, dafter still, eating while standing up. Worst of all is the true barbecue legacy – the nagging hunger that follows bitty dining, leaving you with the aggrieved sense that you missed a mealtime you’re never getting back.I grew up in Cornwall, where beach barbecues were a rite of passage. The flame under the sandy grill was blown out by the Atlantic wind, so these gatherings were impractical, unpredictable and interminable. One minute the sausages were raw and looked like they’d never be ready, the next they were hard and black and basically inedible. Rain frequently sent us scrambling to pack up and flee for shelter.Even when it doesn’t rain, and the scene is a suburban garden wheresomething that looks like it belongs in a gastropub kitchenhas been installed to char halloumi three times a year, I find myself wondering: “How is this fun?” Barbecues are terrible for socialising because the food trickles out, with kids served first (why, when they have the most energy?), so guests don’t eat at the same time and instead dine in silos, wondering if they’ll get home early enough to make pasta. As for drinks, they’re warm because ice buckets don’t work – they’re too small and the ice melts almost instantly in the kind of temperatures we’ve seen this summer – and nobody wants to dash back and forth to the fridge.The hill I will die on: Breakfast cereal is for babies – I eat salad in the mornings, like a grownup | Jacq KellyRead moreThe popularity of barbecues is inexplicable yet undeniable, with black smoke puffing from back gardens at the first sniff of a sunny day. When I broached my hatred with an Australian, she reacted as if I wanted to deprive her of her birthright. But just because people keep doing something doesn’t necessarily mean they actually enjoy it.Barbecues are antisocial in other, more important ways. I used to live above a man who liked to come home from work and barbecue steak on his patio, directly below my kitchen. I had to close every window to stop my whole flat stinking of beef. If you live in a densely populated area, it’s not particularly socially conscious to fill the air with meaty smog during hot weather, just so you can clog your arteries.Disposable barbecues, which have beenfactors in wildfiresduring this summer’s heatwaves, are the worst. This month, onecaused a forest fire in the North York Moors, while Dorset and Wiltshire fire and rescue recently told people togo to the pub instead. A spokesperson added: “I’d certainly challenge anybody to say whether they’ve ever had a good meal from a disposable barbecue.” An excellent point which, if we’re honest, applies to all variationsof barbecue.Max Liu is a freelance writerExplore more on these topicsBarbecueThe hill I will die onFoodcommentShareReuse this content

title: There is clearly trouble ahead for Harry and Meghan on their return to the UK. Here are five ways to avert it | Stephen Bates | The Guardian
description: With a sceptical public and hostility from a lot of the press, the Sussexes face quite a challenge. Still, they really could help themselves, says former Guardian royal correspondent Stephen Bates
Author: Stephen Bates
Headline: With a sceptical public and hostility from a lot of the press, the Sussexes face quite a challenge. Still, they really could help themselves, says former Guardian royal correspondent Stephen Bates
Content: ‘Harry and Meghan must face up to the fact they will always be newsorthy.’Photograph: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Harry and Meghan must face up to the fact they will always be newsorthy.’Photograph: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty ImagesOpinionPrince HarryThere is clearly trouble ahead for Harry and Meghan on their return to the UK. Here are five ways to avert itStephen BatesWith a sceptical public and hostility from a lot of the press, the Sussexes face quite a challenge. Still, they really could help themselvesSat 29 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 03.59 EDTShareThey’re back! Harry and Meghan’s quiet return to England this week,via Birmingham airport, was much anticipated but scarcely celebrated – no bunting or street parties.So far there are many questions but very few answers: not just “why return now?” and “why so suddenly?”, but also questions of security: who pays if not themselves, given that they are not working royals? And where will the money come from to keep them in the style to which they are accustomed?The bills are mounting: not justthe Daily Mail’s legal costsincurred by Harry’s ill-fated court action, but even the upkeep of their nine-bedroom Montecito mansion, which, with property taxes, mortgage and upkeep (including looking after their chickens), could costabout $80,000 (£60,000) a month. That’s to say nothing aboutthe house in Portugal. Meghan will have to get some pretty meaty and regularacting jobs– and fast.Maybe all will be well, they will readjust to British life and Britain will readjust to them, but on past experience this seems highly unlikely. Can they avert it? Here are five tips that might help.1. Find capable advisers.Not necessarily the pin-striped courtiers who serve at the palace and know a great deal but whom Harry hated, nor the subversives likeMark Bolland, the PR guru,who once advised Charles as prince and seems to have initiated rows with half the rest of the family. Young smart-alec briefers are not required, nor perhaps Americans who don’t have a feel for Britain and its generally pro-royalist population. There are considerable bridges to be rebuilt with the people who feel Harry and Meghan let them down, and especially with the rest of the royal family. The couple need careful guidance over how they should present themselves, when they should speak and what they should say – or not say. No moreinterviews with Oprah Winfreyslagging off the relatives. It makes a splash, but thereafter, it doesn’t exactly help.2. Make peace again with the family, especially William and Catherine.It may be difficult and arduous to restore trust, but they need to do that as quickly as possible. And no setting up a rival court: they must know by now the obligation to choose discreet friends wisely.View image in fullscreenOprah Winfrey chatting to the Sussexes during their 2021 TV interview.Photograph: Harpo Productions/Reuters3. Help out a bit.Not necessarily with the washing-up but with attendance at public events, visits and charities. Not by freeloading, the public hates that, but by generally doing good – not for a few minutes or a day or two between flips to California, but regularly and humbly.4. Breathe deeply and make nice with the media – and not just the networks that have previously been prepared to pay them mega money.Wiser members of the royal family face challenges too, but they know that they need the so-called dead tree media, including newspapers, for their popularity. A smile goes further than a snarl. Remember that you need them more than they need you – they have businesses to run, you have a public perception to shape via their products.If they stop reporting on the royals or all the coverage is negative, the institution’s days of crisis will never end.Think hard about what to communicate and what you try to keep secret. The “secret” – private –christening of Archiewas unnecessary as was William’s attemptto hide the name of a family dogfrom an avid press and public. The media will always ferret even more important things out – such as their new home and the children’s school (especially if, as reported,Harry wants to watch young Archie play rugby every Saturday) and a defensive, sneering approach gains nothing. It just makes ever-fragile media/royal relations even worse. Better to be as open as possible and broker an arrangement for the media to thereafter leave Archie and Lilibet alone – it has worked for William and Catherine’s children. Harry and Meghan must face up to the fact they will always be newsworthy and isn’t that partly what they want to publicise their ventures?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion5. Above all, smile, for God’s sake.Harry and Meghan are both in a very privileged position. People won’t like it if they appear to despise or patronise them, or to feel too sorry for themselves. They have the opportunity to be identified with the great cause of cheering people up. Cometh the hour … perhaps.Steve Bates is a former Guardian royal correspondentDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Sunsets, disasters, dinners: we now record them all with our phones. But what is that doing to our souls?  | Phoebe Greenwood | The Guardian
description: As a war correspondent, I worked with photographers who said the camera was a buffer between them and reality. It is much the same now as we snap and scroll, says journalist and author Phoebe Greenwood
Author: Phoebe Greenwood
Headline: As a war correspondent, I worked with photographers who said the camera was a buffer between them and reality. It is much the same now as we snap and scroll, says journalist and author Phoebe Greenwood
Content: A man takes a selfie in front of a smoking lava flow. But have phone cameras changed how we perceive danger?Photograph: Antonio Parrinello/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA man takes a selfie in front of a smoking lava flow. But have phone cameras changed how we perceive danger?Photograph: Antonio Parrinello/The GuardianOpinionSmartphonesSunsets, disasters, dinners: we now record them all with our phones. But what is that doing to our souls?Phoebe GreenwoodAs a war correspondent, I worked with photographers who said the camera was a buffer between them and reality. It is much the same now as we snap and scrollSat 29 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 03.09 EDTShareIwas sitting on a rooftop in Athens at sunset looking up at Filopappou hill.Athens in August is burning hot. Not so much hotter than London or Paris any more, but the sort of hot that makes it foolish to step out into sunlight before 6pm. Emerging from the air conditioning at dusk, I saw a dense line of silhouettes on the ridge above me. Almost every one of these shadows had its arm raised, holding a cameraphone towards the sunset.Of all the pretty hills in the Greek capital, Filopappou arguably has the best view. The Acropolis stands directly to its north. To its south, where I sat, the city sprawls out towards the sea and a dark horizon of islands – Aegina, Salamina, Agistri.Looking up, the wall of tourist photographers reminded me of something: war zones.I worked as a correspondent covering conflicts and disasters for the Guardian and other newspapers for more than a decade. Over time, every new disaster came to resemble the last: another catastrophic tableau of buildings and bodies with a dense ring of telephoto lenses pointed at it.Print reporters like me could stay at a distance from the gore and the horror because we could describe it. The photographers had to get as close as possible because they needed a clean shot.Later, when I asked them about their work over beers at the American Colony hotel bar or tea at Gaza’s now-destroyed Al Deira hotel – how could they do it? Spend their days gazing at suffering? – most said the same thing. The lens was a buffer, a sort of protective forcefield. They weren’t looking at the fatally injured child, they were looking at the image of one.View image in fullscreenTourists capture a sunset in Oia village on the Greek island of Santorini.Photograph: Dancar/ShutterstockThe illustrious war photographerDon McCullinwas wise to the danger in this distance. “I operate not as a photographer but as a human being,” he said in 1983, 16 years before the first cameraphone. “I try to balance what I photograph not as a photographer but as a person, a man, and photography has got nothing to do with it. It is just something I have learned, it is just a way of communicating.”Now it’s 2026 and almost every one of us – bar the kooks and the luddites – clutches a distancing device.I was late toInstagram, but it quickly became second nature. Now, when an attractive dish is put in front of me, an animal does something cute, a fight breaks out on a ferry, a helicopter lands to race some poor person to hospital, I pull out my phone and record it alongside everyone else.Like the people on the hill, most of us live our lives through lenses: camera first.And they aren’t always pointing outwards.Multi-billion-dollar industrieshave been built on people photographing themselves. Much has been written about the psychological perils of our narcissistic age, but increasingly, the danger is more than psychological.Earlier this month,five teenagers were killedin a car driving the wrong way down a motorway in Ireland. They crashed into another car carrying four members of a family, all of whom were seriously injured. It seems they died taking part in an online trend in which masked young men film themselves driving recklessly at high speed, baiting police into giving chase. The camera is not incidental to the danger: the danger is created for the camera.Forensic cyberpsychologistMary Aiken describes thisas “hybrid behaviour”: filming and driving simultaneously, with “one foot in the real world and one foot in cyberspace”. While the physical car accelerates down a motorway, part of the driver’s mind is watching the finished video, the audience, the likes from other picture-sharers around the globe.View image in fullscreenA lamplighter at work on Charles Bridge in Prague, Czech Republic, December 2024.Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPAThis could also explain thefatal selfiephenomenon.A study identified 332 selfie-related deathsbetween 2014 and 2021, most commonly caused by drowning, falling or some form of transport. These tragedies can’t all be blamed on vanity meeting the smartphone – people have always taken stupid risks – but phone cameras have changed how we perceive danger: a cliff edge becomes a backdrop, death is content.In Afghanistan in 2009,Associated Press photographer Julie Jacobsontook nine frames over two and a half minutes of 21-year-old US L/Cpl Joshua Bernard lying fatally wounded after a Taliban ambush as he was treated by his fellow marines. Jacobson didn’t help them, she photographed.The resulting image of Bernard’s dying face and horrific injuries provoked bitter debate. His family asked for it not to be published. The then US defence secretary, Robert Gates, called AP’s decision to release it “appalling”. The news agency argued that the photograph performed an essential public function: it forced people at home to see the reality of a war being fought in their name.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJacobson’s defence was that in the moment she couldn’t help him and she decided the most helpful thing she could do as a photographer was to document a painful truth.I suspect that for the average smartphone user, their cameras serve the opposite purpose. The world has become too difficult to look at directly.View image in fullscreenA man takes pictures of demolished houses in Hebron in the Israeli-occupied West Bank in 2023.Photograph: Mussa Issa Qawasma/ReutersEvery day, those same screens show us bombed homes in Gaza, burning forests everywhere, celebrities in psychological anguish, self-harming in front ofmillions of TikTok followers. After reels of influencers slurping “the best cacio e pepe ever”, we are shown executions, assaults, maimed and dying children. Phone users are exposed to more suffering than a human nervous system is built to absorb, and we keep scrolling.We’re addicted to our cameras because they have the magical capacity to turn much of what is frightening, painful or just intensely beautiful into something we can frame, edit, caption and share. They allow us to be present but absent.It’s this sort of moral confusion I tried to explore in my novel, Vulture. Its protagonist is a British correspondent in Gaza who finds that documenting other people’s suffering gives her not only purpose but somewhere to hide. Horror becomes a picture byline; every dead body a pull quote. Bearing witness becomes absolution.Not that we should, can or will stop recording. In Gaza,Palestinian journalistsfilming on their phones have provided an indispensable record of a war foreign reporters have largely been prevented from entering. There, picking up a camera is an act of extraordinary courage.“Photography for me is not looking, it’s feeling,” the greatMcCullin said, an approach that has produced some of the most affecting images ever taken in conflict zones.The rest of us may just have to work to remain human behind the lens; to remember to engage with reality once the image is posted.Phoebe Greenwood is a former Guardian correspondent, and the author of the novel VultureDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
