title: TV tonight: Nick Mohammed has a licence to thrill at the Proms | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: It’s a huge celebration of classic James Bond music! Plus: a fascinating look at what happened when Wham! went to China. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: It’s a huge celebration of classic James Bond music! Plus: a fascinating look at what happened when Wham! went to China. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Agent M … Nick Mohammed presents Celebrating James Bond at the Proms on BBC Two.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenAgent M … Nick Mohammed presents Celebrating James Bond at the Proms on BBC Two.Photograph: Mark AllanTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: Nick Mohammed has a licence to thrill at the PromsIt’s a huge celebration of classic James Bond music! Plus: a fascinating look at what happened when Wham! went to China. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Graeme Virtue,Phil Harrison,Jack SealeandSimon WardellSat 29 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCelebrating James Bond at the Proms7pm, BBC TwoShake up a martini for this one! The next 007 should be confirmed by the end of the year, but in the meantime it’s Nick Mohammed who has a licence to thrill with a night of Bond classics. You Only Live Twice, Nobody Does It Better and Diamonds Are Forever should all be on the bill, conducted by Daniel Bartholomew-Poyser with some top-secret guest singers.Hollie RichardsonAlan Carr’s Celebrity Picture Slam6.20pm, BBC OneSnaps, cackles and pop (stars): the zippy visual guess-’em-up gets a special charity edition featuring soap veterans (Charlie Brooks and Sue Cleaver), radio presenters (Richie Anderson and Jason Mohammed) and former chart-toppers (Kéllé Bryan and Lee Latchford-Evans). Which duo will prevail?Graeme VirtueSandi Toksvig’s Hidden Wonders7pm, Channel 4Surprisingly, Sandi Toksvig has never visited Hadrian’s Wall. She puts that right in this episode of the enjoyable archaeology series. While she’s in Northumberland, she ponders the lives of the soldiers guarding this outpost of the Roman empire and cleans a boot found in one of Vindolanda fort’s defensive ditches.Phil HarrisonGhosts US8.35pm, BBC ThreeIt may not be as adorable as the British original but, five seasons in, the US sitcom remake is still a vehicle for smart plots and quick gags. This week’s triple bill includes an unseasonal two-part Christmas special. Before that, the visit of an obsessive history podcaster causes undead jazz singer Alberta (Danielle Pinnock) to reveal more of her life story.Jack SealeWham! 10 Days in China9pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenHairy heights … Wham! 10 Days in China on BBC Two.Photograph: Martyn Goddard/© Andrew Ridgeley, Big Geoff Overseas Limited, Robobuild Limited t/a George Michael Entertainment. Photograph by Martyn GoddardIn both cultural and political terms, it’s hard to articulate exactly how much of an outlier George Michael and Andrew Ridgeley’s 1985 trip to China really was. This fun and fascinating film tells the inside story, putting the tour into its sometimes fraught cold war context while also offering a charming insight into the friendship between the duo.PHKabul9pm, BBC FourThese are the final episodes of this superb, albeit apocalyptically bleak series, and the consequences of the false promises made by the western allies are fully playing out on the ground. Gilles’ humanitarian efforts are facing Taliban hostility and American indifference. Meanwhile, Zahara looks to have escaped but soon faces an impossible choice. Harrowing.PHFilm choiceThe Whisper Man, out now, NetflixThis is the first novel by bestselling British crime writer Alex North to be made into a film but, with the Russo brothers producing, it surely won’t be the last. The eight-year-old son of widowed author Tom (Adam Scott) has been abducted, in a way reminiscent of serial killer the Whisper Man. However, the murderer was caught years ago by Tom’s estranged detective father Peter (Robert De Niro). So is a copycat at work or did Peter arrest the wrong person? Michelle Monaghan co-stars as a new cop on the case in a thriller by up-and-coming director James Ashcroft.Simon WardellBlack Panther, 8pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenOozing charisma … Chadwick Boseman in Black Panther on Channel 4.Photograph: Marvel/Disney/Kobal/REX/ShutterstockDespite being created in 1966, it took until 2018 for the Marvel comic character of Wakanda’s African king T’Challa to reach the big screen. Still, it was worth the wait, as director Ryan Coogler and star Chadwick Boseman delivered a Black superhero with charisma and complexity. The plot, revolving round a challenge for the throne, explores self-determination, colonialism and power politics with a sideline in Bond-style action – globetrotting to Korea, Q-like gadgetry courtesy of Letitia Wright’s Princess Shuri, and a helpful CIA agent (Martin Freeman).SWLee, 9pm, Sky AtlanticLee Miller’s life was one of many great adventures. And it’s her later career as a war photographer that director Ellen Kuras and star Kate Winslet focus on in their fierce film. Winslet – in a role she was born to play – is the magnetic, forthright Lee, a woman who won’t take no for an answer. When the second world war breaks out, she nabs a job taking pictures for Vogue, and gets herself front and centre for the London blitz, the liberation of Europe and, chillingly, the discovery of the Nazi death camps – snapping away in fury and shock at the inhumanity she sees.SWLive sportTest Cricket: England v Pakistan, 10.15am, Sky Sports CricketThe third day of the second Test from Lord’s.Premier League Football: Liverpool v Nottingham Forest, 11am, TNT Sports 1Tottenham v Newcastle is at 5pm on Sky Sports Main Event.Men’s Cycling: La Vuelta a España, 3.15pm, TNT Sports 1Stage eight from Puçol to Xeraco.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A slow travel success story in Slovenia’s secret valley | Slovenia holidays | The Guardian
description: Tourism is only just taking hold in Vipava, but the locals are determined to do it right, by putting community first and preserving what makes it special
Author: Ailsa Sheldon
Headline: Tourism is only just taking hold in Vipava, but the locals are determined to do it right, by putting community first and preserving what makes it special
Content: Vipava is a landscape shaped by a strong wind, theburja, which creates the perfect terrain for dry winesView image in fullscreenVipava is a landscape shaped by a strong wind, theburja, which creates the perfect terrain for dry winesSlovenia holidaysA slow travel success story in Slovenia’s secret valleyTourism is only just taking hold in Vipava, but the locals are determined to do it right, by putting community first and preserving what makes it specialAilsa SheldonSat 29 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe drive to Pedrovo is vertiginous, and each hairpin bend has me sending a silent prayer that we won’t meet a tractor coming the other way. When we near it, we abandon the car and continue on foot to the hamlet, a scattering of red-roofed, whitewashed houses high on the steep karst hillside. The air is warm and dry, scented with wild sage.We follow a hand-painted sign to Čilčevi Farmstead. Descending stone steps to a lush garden, we find a shaded table set with fresh cheeses produced at the farm’s own dairy. Below, the valley stretches in both directions, a wide flat plain hemmed in by steep mountain slopes, with the Vipava River winding lazily through fields and vineyards.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian GraphicsIf the Vipava valley gets a mention in a Slovenian guidebook, it’s usually as a wine region footnote. The area is an hour’s drive south-west of Ljubljana, meeting Italy at thecross-border city of Nova Gorica (called Gorizia on the Italian side). Most visitors skip it in favour of the Soča valley to the north, drawn to the turquoise river and opportunities for rafting on the rapids.Vipava is a landscape shaped by a strong wind, theburja, which barrels down from the Alps, keeping the red earth arid, the trees bent low, and creating the perfect terrain for dry wines and dried meats. Tourism has traditionally been less of a focus, but I’m here with my family to meet local entrepreneurs and producers, to learn how this valley is building a genuine visitor experience that works for the community.Part of the reason for the slow development of tourism has been the scarcity of accommodation, save a few nondescript business hotels and a handful of holiday cottages. One place that’s helping change that narrative isWellba, a boutique guesthouse in the village of Planina, where an old abandoned farmstead has been converted into self-catering apartments and guest rooms by a local couple, working with traditional craftspeople and salvaged materials.View image in fullscreenMarko and Tereza Kobal run the boutique Wellba hotel in PlaninaMarko and Tereza Kobal grew up on this hillside and then worked in Ljubljana before deciding to return to build a family business, striving to create the kind of place they seek out when travelling. “People who travel want to experience something that is just the way it is, without embellishment, pretence, exaggeration – somewhere authentic,” says Marko. We enter Wellba through a traditional “black kitchen”, its walls darkened by generations of wood smoke. “When we came here the building needed work but it had a real soul. We want the building to stand for another 300 years, so we took the renovation slowly and carefully.”Our light, spacious accommodation wears its history lightly, with plenty of space for playing card games and reading books on the balcony, with views of the neighbouring farmyard and the valley beyond. Next door, another tumble-down farm building will be converted and opened in 2027. The couple are also working on a boutique hotel in Vipava town in the valley below. The dream is for their children to run Wellba one day, forging their futures in this valley.Across Vipava, similar small projects are emerging: small, family-run and developing slowly and thoughtfully. Tom Ločniškar and Borut Kokalj beganČilčevi Farmsteadduring the pandemic, having moved to Pedrovo and become interested in farming. “We started to keep animals. Now we have 150, which is too many animals for just a hobby,” laughs Tom.View image in fullscreenFresh cheeses at the Čilčevi Farmstead dairy in Pedrovo.Photograph: Ailsa Sheldon/The GuardianHe recalls the mad panic to source equipment before the lockdowns began. The pandemic also brought him his first customers, people who were out walking and keen to support local businesses. Tom and Borut keep local Istrska sheep and Drežnica goats, which graze on dry karst grasslands, changing pastures across this hillside every four days. Having tasted fresh cheese straight from the chill of the dairy, including creamy goat’s cheese with fenugreek and buttery mature sheep’s cheese, we walk uphill to meet the goats.Tom says that in the early 1900s around 1,000 people lived in Pedrovo, but by the 1970s the permanent population had fallen to just two, and remained that low until the 1990s. “The village was almost abandoned because people moved to the cities,” he says. “It was the same in a lot of hill villages: life was hard and tractors didn’t work on steep slopes.” Today the population has risen to 20, with second homeowners roughly doubling that number in the holidays.double quotation markDishes are served family style and there’s plenty of time for stories, with wine straight from the barrels in the cellarElsewhere in the village, I meet Alenka and Mark Smerajc, who were one of the first families to return, raising three children and running a business here. Today they have two smallholiday cottagesin what were farm outbuildings and run a relaxed courtyard restaurant for guests, opening to the public at weekends and for holidays. “People wanted food,” shrugs Alenka, as her teenage children help bring out beautiful plates of handmade pasta with local cheese and wild herbs from the kitchen.“In Vipava valley there was no tourism, so we got to decide how to build it,” says Jani Peljhan. That means GPS-guided cycling tours along roads too small to merit signposts, and experimenting with “wine trains”, carrying visitors from Nova Gorica to the vineyards with local winemakers on board to lead tasting sessions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJani’s company,Wajdušna, also offers hiking and paragliding, both gaining in popularity here. He meets us at Wellba with some e-bikes and we pedal through Ajdovščina to spot Roman ruins, and up to Vipavski Križ, famed for being one of the smallest towns in Slovenia, before zigzagging back up the other side of the valley through vineyards. The warmth of the afternoon and the steep hillsides makes me appreciate the “sport” mode on the bikes.View image in fullscreenThe region’s many narrow lanes are perfect for cycling trips.Photograph: Nejc BoleIn other regions, wine tourism often means visitor centres and branded experiences. In Vipava it still means sitting in someone’s kitchen. AtVina Lisjakin Zalošče, I eat at a little restaurant run by two brothers. “We opened the restaurant to show the wine,” says Peter Lisjak. “It’s all from our farm.” We eat generous platters of house dried meat, aged mountain cheeses, a fennel frittata and slow-cooked celeriac steaks with celery pesto and spinach. Dishes are served family style and there’s plenty of time for stories, with samples of delicious wine straight from the barrels in the cellar.From Wellba, we walk across the village toFerjančič vineyard,where seventh generation winemaker Matic Ferjančič talks us through his wines. His father developed the vineyard, going from five to 50,000 plants. “We work hard in the vineyard to make it easy in the cellar,” he says. As we chat, Matic keeps an ear to the baby monitor for the eighth generation sleeping upstairs.Although many of my favourite restaurant experiences are the simple ones, Vipava valley cuisine can reach loftier heights. One night we smarten up the best we can and follow a winding road uphill to Zemono Manor, to eat atGostilna Pri Lojzetu. Chef Tomaž Kavčič is known as a Slovenian slow food pioneer, and has earned a Michelin star for his playful dishes and proud use of local ingredients.Summer on the Slovenian RivieraRead moreWe eat delicate Vipava river trout with fermented apricots from the previous summer, and langoustine bisque from the coast. Traditional dishes such asjota, a sauerkraut and potato stew, are honoured on the menu, their humble roots celebrated not hidden. There are some theatrics, like a juniper plant producing flavoured vapour to complement a sorbet, but the restaurant atmosphere is friendly and relaxed. The server chats with my young stepson about his preferences, and brings him a generous bowl of gnocchi. It’s Kavčič’s night off so he sits with friends and a bottle of wine at the back of the restaurant, coming round all the tables frequently to chat.Vipava may not remain overlooked for ever. But talking to the people building businesses here, there is little appetite for becoming the next famous wine destination. What they seem to want instead is something rarer and more interesting: tourism that helps a place thrive without changing what made it worth visiting in the first place.The trip was provided byVipava Valley Tourismandthe Slovenian Tourist Board.Wellba Planinahas doubles from £97Explore more on these topicsSlovenia holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Flipping marvellous: Yotam Ottolenghi on the joy of simple breakfasts – plus six exclusive recipes | Breakfast | The Guardian
description: Weekend mornings are for family – and whoever happens to be over. Forget fussing and focus on just one big lovely thing for the middle of the table. Here’s how
Author: Yotam Ottolenghi
Headline: Weekend mornings are for family – and whoever happens to be over. Forget fussing and focus on just one big lovely thing for the middle of the table. Here’s how
Content: Yotam wears Tekla sleepwear. Grooming: Carol Morley at Carol Hayes.Photograph: Pål Hansen/The GuardianView image in fullscreenYotam wears Tekla sleepwear. Grooming: Carol Morley at Carol Hayes.Photograph: Pål Hansen/The GuardianYotam Ottolenghi recipesBreakfastFlipping marvellous: Yotam Ottolenghi on the joy of simple breakfasts – plus six exclusive recipesWeekend mornings are for family – and whoever happens to be over. Forget fussing and focus on just one big lovely thing for the middle of the table. Here’s howYotam OttolenghiSat 29 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFamily life has had a bigger impact on how I cook at home than almost anything else. There’s a lot of pasta on the menu these days, and potato wedges with different sauces. A lot of meatballs. And a great manypancakes– more than I would have ever predicted before I had kids.My weekend pancakes – which made their way into my bookSimple Too– are supposed to be a batch-cooking exercise: lots made on Sunday, then reheated through the week, in the toaster or a dry pan on the stove, so breakfast is more or less solved until Friday. That’s the theory. In practice, all 22 pancakes the recipe makes are gone by Sunday lunch – eaten by the boys, their friends, or whoever happens to be over for breakfast.double quotation markI love having friends over and what I want is something so they can help themselvesBut my kitchen on a weekend morning doesn’t only answer to my kids, even though that’s their indisputable assumption. I love having friends over for brunch, and what I actually want, most weeks, is one big thing in the middle of the table – generously for everyone. So they can help themselves and I’m not the only one standing after everyone else has sat down.Like the butter beans with Urfa chilli butter, with toast, bacon and semi-hard-boiled eggs. Or a big tray of bakedza’atartomatoes and mascarpone, with some sausages and sourdough. Or a big pan ofmenemen(Turkish scrambled eggs) with a leaf salad and a few slices of avocado.I feed a lot of people – with the things I really want to eat and without too much fuss: that’s the idea. Here are some of the breakfasts and brunches in Simple Too – for you, your hungry family and all your breakfast guests.MenemenView image in fullscreenFood styling: Alice Wood.Photograph: Jonathan LovekinMenemenis a Turkish breakfast dish: scrambled eggs, spices, tomatoes. Simple! It’s the most comforting of all ways to start – or end – the day. The key is to add the eggs off the heat, so that they cook gently in the residual warmth of the pan. Serve with buttered toast or a leafy salad with slices of avocado.Prep5 minsCook15 minsServes24 eggs3 tbsp olive oil1 onion,finely chopped (160g)3 garlic cloves,crushed1 tsp cumin seeds½ tsp Aleppo chilli flakes½ tsp ground cinnamon½ tbsp tomato paste300g cherry tomatoes,halved1 tbsp double cream5g coriander leaves,roughly choppedFine sea saltBright and breezy: Yotam Ottolenghi on simple summer entertainingRead morePut the eggs into a bowl with half a teaspoon of salt. Lightly beat, just to break up the yolks, and set aside.Put the oil into a medium frying pan on a medium-high heat. Add the onion and garlic and cook for five minutes, stirring a few times, until softened and starting to colour. Add the spices, tomato paste and an eighth of a teaspoon of salt and cook for two minutes, until fragrant. Add the tomatoes and 60ml of water, then cook, uncovered, for 10 minutes until the tomatoes have broken down. Squish them with the back of a spoon if they need a bit of help.Remove from the heat and swirl in the eggs, using a wooden spoon or spatula and moving the pan gently until just set. Spoon over the cream, sprinkle over the coriander and serve straight from the pan.Coconut greens with Scotch bonnet and eggsView image in fullscreenFood styling: Alice Wood.Photograph: Jonathan LovekinThis recipe is inspired by the Trinidadian bhaji, which Milli Taylor, my test kitchen colleague, first discovered through her friend, the chef and food writer Shivi Ramoutar. Traditionally, these braised greens are served alongside rice and dal as a main meal, but we think they are equally delicious with the addition of eggs for breakfast. Play around with whatever greens are in season. Chard is great – just make sure you chop the stems and add them before the leaves, at the same time as the onions.Prep5 minsCook25 minsServes43 tbsp olive oil1 small onion,thinly sliced (150g)2 tsp cumin seeds,lightly crushed1 Scotch bonnet pepper (or regular red chilli),pierced a few times with a knife4 garlic cloves,crushed400g baby spinach leaves400ml tin of coconut milk6 eggsFine sea salt and black pepperHeat the oil in a large saute pan on a medium-high heat. Add the onion and three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt and cook for about eight minutes, stirring often, until softened and golden. Add the cumin, Scotch bonnet, garlic and lots of pepper and cook for another minute. Add the spinach, in two or three batches, and cook for about three minutes until wilted. Add the coconut milk, bring to a simmer and cook for 10 minutes, until the sauce has thickened and reduced slightly.Use a spoon to make six wells in the mixture and crack one egg into each. Sprinkle the eggs with salt and pepper, cover, and cook for a further four to five minutes, until the whites are set but the yolks are still runny. Serve straight from the pan.Getting aheadIf you want to get everything ready in advance, the dish can be prepared up to the point just before the eggs are cracked in.Weekend pancakes with date butter syrupView image in fullscreenFood styling: Alice Wood.Photograph: Jonathan LovekinThis is a much-loved recipe used in our London delis. Once made, these fluffy pancakes keep well in the fridge for up to three days (or longer in the freezer), ready to be reheated in the toaster or in a dry pan on the stove. That’s why we suggest making a pretty big batch at the weekend to eat throughout the week.Prep10 minsCook25 mins total(2–3 minutes per batch)MakesAbout 22 pancakesFor the pancakes350ml buttermilk3 eggs,2 whole, 1 white70g unsalted butter,melted1 tsp vanilla bean paste or extract250g plain flour40g caster sugar2 tsp baking powder½ tsp bicarbonate of sodavegetable oil,for fryingFine sea saltFor the date butter syrup75g date molasses75g unsalted butter,cut into small cubesIn a jug, whisk together the buttermilk, whole eggs, egg white, melted butter and vanilla. If you don’t have buttermilk, make your own by adding 25ml of lemon juice or white wine vinegar to 325ml of whole milk and setting aside for 15 minutes to curdle.Whisk together the dry ingredients and three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt in a large bowl. Make a well in the centre and pour in the egg mixture. Whisk until just combined – do not over-mix: a few small lumps here and there are fine – then set aside for five minutes to thicken.Meanwhile, put the date molasses, an eighth of a teaspoon of salt and 2 tablespoons of water into a small saucepan on a medium heat. Bring to a simmer and whisk in the butter, a couple of pieces at a time, until emulsified. Keep warm.Place a large non-stick frying pan on a medium heat. Once hot, brush with oil and drop 3–4 large tablespoonfuls of batter, evenly spaced apart, into the pan. Cook for two to three minutes, until the batter has risen and you can see small bubbles on the surface. Flip the pancakes and cook for another 30–60 seconds, until springy to the touch. Transfer to a wire rack (or keep warm in a low oven) and continue with the remaining batter. Serve with the date butter syrup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBaked za’atar tomatoes and mascarponeView image in fullscreenFood styling: Alice Wood.Photograph: Jonathan LovekinThese are inspired by Simon Hopkinson’s creamed tomatoes on toast, from his classic cookbookRoast Chicken and Other Stories. Use any ripe tomatoes: this is a great opportunity to use up whatever you happen to have lying around – all shapes and sizes are welcome. They are best served hot.Prep5 minsCook25 minsServes6300g mascarpone50ml double cream3 garlic cloves,1 crushed, 2 thinly sliced2 tsp cornflour600g ripe tomatoes,halved, quartered or thickly sliced (depending on size)1 tbsp za’atar1½ tbsp olive oil1 tsp thyme leavesFine sea salt and black pepperPreheat the oven to 220C (200C fan/425F/gas 7).Mix together the mascarpone, cream, crushed garlic, cornflour and a quarter of a teaspoon of salt in a large, round baking dish (26-28cm). Smooth the surface and arrange the tomatoes on top, cut side up. Season with a quarter of a teaspoon of salt and plenty of pepper, and scatter over the za’atar and sliced garlic. Drizzle with 1 tablespoon of oil and bake for about 25 minutes, until the tomatoes are tender and the cream is golden and bubbling round the edges. Leave to rest for five minutes.Serve with the remaining half a tablespoon of oil and some thyme sprinkled on top.Everyday granolaView image in fullscreenFood styling: Alice Wood.Photograph: Jonathan LovekinWe get spoiled in the test kitchen whenever my co-author Verena Lochmuller brings in one of her weekend “projects”. In fact, we’ve come to rely on them on a Monday morning. This granola came about this way. For the sake of simplicity, Verena had to trim down the ingredient list. That was somewhat painful, but you are more than welcome to start adding your favourites back in. Just take your pick from almonds, pecans, walnuts, ground cinnamon or ginger, or any dried fruit, stirred through once cooled. This granola is good for every occasion, even spooned over ice-cream. Make a big batch. It keeps for at least six weeks in an airtight container.Prep5 minsCook1 hr 15 minsMakesAbout 800g275g jumbo rolled oats150g blanched hazelnuts25g sesame seeds50g pumpkin seeds50g sunflower seeds110ml olive oil85g demerara sugar85ml maple syrup3 tbsp tahini1–2 very ripe bananas,finely mashed(150g)2 tsp vanilla bean paste or extractFine sea saltPreheat the oven to 160C (140C fan)/325F/gas 3.Combine the oats, nuts, seeds and half a teaspoon of salt in a large bowl.Put the oil, sugar and maple syrup into a small saucepan on a medium-low heat. Cook for about five minutes, whisking occasionally, until the sugar has melted (the oil might be separated on top, but that’s OK). Whisk in the tahini, banana and vanilla until combined, then pour over the oat mixture. Stir well and spread out on a large parchment-lined baking tray. Bake for about 1 hour and 10 minutes, stirring every 15 to 20 minutes, until browned and starting to crisp up. Leave to cool completely.Crisp up further before transferring to a jar or airtight container.Butter beans with Urfa chilli butterView image in fullscreenFood styling: Alice Wood.Photograph: Jonathan LovekinThis dish is for all the butter addicts – the word even appears twice in the title. The beans become so creamy and buttery that you’ll want to spoon them straight on to toast with nothing else.Prep5 minsCook15 minsServes450g unsalted butter1 tsp Urfa chilli flakes1 preserved lemon,seeds removed, finely chopped (20g)2 tsp lemon juice1 onion,thinly sliced (160g)2 garlic cloves,crushed1 tbsp biber salçasi (Turkish red pepper paste),mild or hot (or tomato paste with a pinch each of sugar and dried chilli flakes)1 tsp ground cumin1 tbsp double cream700g jar of butter beans,with the liquid, or 2 x 400g tinsFlaked sea saltPut 30g of butter into a small saucepan and place over a high heat. Cook, swirling the pan occasionally, for two to three minutes, until nutty and deeply brown. Take off the heat, carefully add the chilli flakes, preserved lemon and lemon juice, and set aside.For the beans, add the remaining 20g of butter to a large frying pan and place over a medium-high heat. When hot, add the onion and fry for about seven minutes, stirring occasionally, until starting to caramelise. Lower the heat to medium, add the garlic,biber salçasiand cumin, and cook for one minute. Add the cream, beans (including the liquid) and 60ml of water. Cook for about five minutes, until the liquid has thickened and lightly coats the beans.Drizzle over the Urfa butter, add a pinch of flaked sea salt and serve straight from the pan.Note on the ingredientsThe rest of the jar ofbiber salçasican be used in any recipe that calls for regular tomato paste – it adds a little more depth and flavour. Keep the jar in the fridge once opened.Ottolenghi Simple Too by Yotam Ottolenghi and Verena Lochmuller is published by Ebury (£30). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: ‘Simple, creamy and crunchy’: the best (and worst) supermarket coleslaw, tasted and rated | Food | The Guardian
description: Too cloying, too sweet or just right? Our tester works through the shop shelves to find the best slaw for your next barbecue, picnic or packed lunch
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Too cloying, too sweet or just right? Our tester works through the shop shelves to find the best slaw for your next barbecue, picnic or packed lunch
Content: The crunch bunch: 10 supermarket slaws were judged on appearance, aroma, texture and taste.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.View image in fullscreenThe crunch bunch: 10 supermarket slaws were judged on appearance, aroma, texture and taste.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterFoodReview‘Simple, creamy and crunchy’: the best (and worst) supermarket coleslaw, tasted and ratedToo cloying, too sweet or just right? Our tester works through the shop shelves to find the best slaw for your next barbecue, picnic or packed lunchThe best supermarket veggie burgersTom HuntSat 29 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIfind shop-bought coleslaw hard to stomach because it’s sharp, gloopy and often made with copious amounts of poor-quality mayonnaise and spirit vinegar. Pungent ingredients, such as cabbage and onion, are better eaten fresh, otherwise they break down and give off a disconcertingly sulphurous and sweaty aroma.I judged each product in this test on appearance, aroma, texture and, above all, taste, and awarded extra points for value. I marked down for an off-puttingly strong raw onion aroma.Preservatives and stabilisers aren’t essential (the better-tasting products don’t use them), and often give a slaw an unappealing, moussey texture. All that said, I was surprised to find some great products out there and most retained a surprisingly satisfying crunch.The best supermarket coleslawBest overall:Waitrose deli-style coleslaw with red onion and chivesView image in fullscreen£1.85 for 300g at Waitrose (62p/100g)★★★★☆A lovely, crunchy, finely shredded slaw with a creamy sauce and with no stabilisers or gums. Red onion and chives are present, but not dominant. The mayo includes a little whipping cream, free-range egg yolk and UK dairy.Best bargain:Aldi Specially Selected rich & indulgent coleslawView image in fullscreen£1.29 for 300g at Aldi (43p/100g), in store only★★★☆☆A creamy, chunky coleslaw that’s unctuous and moreish. Fresh, crunchy and well balanced with sweetness and acidity, this is cabbage-forward, with a little carrot and a subtle onion flavour, and a relatively straightforward mayo made with guar and xanthan gums.And the rest …Lidl Deluxe creamy coleslawView image in fullscreen£1.29 for 300g at Lidl (43p/100g), in store only★★★☆☆A veg-heavy, fine-cut cabbage and carrot slaw with a subtle onion twang and a refreshing sauce. A little tart, but arguably that’s what one wants from a slaw. Free-range egg, too. Flavoured with mustard, but also includes a preservative (potassium sorbate) and stabiliser (xanthan gum).Morrisons The Best extra crunchy coleslawView image in fullscreen£2 for 300g at Morrisons (67p/100g)★★★☆☆A medium-thick, crunchy coleslaw in a rich, free-range egg mayo. Sweet with some mild acidity and a subtle onion flavour. One of the simpler recipes (carrot, cabbage, onion, mayo), but it does contain xanthan gum.Tesco Finest coleslawView image in fullscreen£1.40 for 180g at Tesco (78p/100g)★★★☆☆A thinly shredded slaw that’s simple, creamy and crunchy, and has a nice balance of sweetness and acidity. Onion present, but not overpowering. No cream, but the thick mayo is thickened with citrus fibre, guar gum, xanthan gum and pectin.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionM&S Food deli-style coleslawView image in fullscreen£2.40 for 300g at Ocado (80p/100g)★★★☆☆Medium thick-cut slaw with a strong chive and onion flavour. Attractive with the pink cabbage, and one of the more mayo-heavy contenders. Includes a pinch of soft brown sugar, ground allspice and turmeric, though none is prominent. No gums, but potato starch and citrus fibre are added to stabilise.Asda Exceptional classic coleslawView image in fullscreen£1.94 for 300g at Asda (65p/100g)★★☆☆☆A rich, saucy, medium-thin slaw that’s sweet and crunchy but has a dominant onion and chive flavour. The mayo, made with xanthan gum and citrus fibre, is slightly moussey, though.Iceland Luxury coleslawView image in fullscreen£2.25 for 330g at Iceland (69p/100g)★★☆☆☆Finely shredded crunchy carrots, lots of sweet sauce made creamy by the addition of creme fraiche, and a sharp finish. Contains acetic acid, stabilisers (guar gum, xanthan gum) and a preservative (potassium sorbate).Co-op Irresistible deliciously rich coleslawView image in fullscreen£2.25 for 300g at Co-op (75p/100g)★★☆☆☆A finely shredded slaw with heaps of flavour, a warm dijon undertone, nice acidity from white-wine vinegar and great crunch. Colourful, with pink cabbage, carrot, red onion and chives, and a relatively strong onion flavour, but a slightly overcomplicated ingredients list, including potassium sorbate, maize starch and xanthan and guar gums.Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference coleslawView image in fullscreen£1.50 for 180g at Sainsbury’s (84p/100g)★★☆☆☆A ribbon-cut, saucy coleslaw made with a splash of single cream. Subtle acidity from lemon juice, but a complex recipe including stabilisers (guar gum and xanthan gum), potato starch and citrus fibre.For more, read thebest supermarket kimchi, tasted and ratedExplore more on these topicsFoodThe FilterVegetablesSaladSide dishesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meera Sodha’s recipe for spicy mozzarella, green bean and edamame salad | Vegetables | The Guardian
description: An enticing, slightly spicy, east/west fusion stacked with vigour and colour
Author: Meera Sodha
Headline: An enticing, slightly spicy, east/west fusion stacked with vigour and colour
Content: Meera Sodha’s spicy mozzarella, green bean and edamame salad.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.View image in fullscreenMeera Sodha’s spicy mozzarella, green bean and edamame salad.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.Meera Sodha recipesVegetablesMeera Sodha’s recipe for spicy mozzarella, green bean and edamame saladAn enticing, slightly spicy, east/west fusion stacked with vigour and colourMeera SodhaSat 29 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne thing I learned during the recent hot weather is that I don’t have enough “substantial but quick salads” in my locker. A salad one could call lunch (or a light dinner when served with other bits). On rotation in my “throw-together” category is myno-cook chickpea, tomato and cucumber salad, to which I’m also going to add my favouritesummer vegetable, bulgur and pesto salad, which isn’t quite an assembly job, but near-enough and a family favourite. To that line-up, I’m happy to introduce this gently spicy, green beauty.Spicy mozzarella, green bean and edamame saladMy recipe tester, Hannah, and I disagree on how much mozzarella a person can eat. I like a whole ball to myself, she prefers a half-ball. Adjust as you see fit.Prep10 minCook20 minServes21 tbsp rapeseed oil250g green beans, topped150g frozen edamame beans, defrosted100g frozen petit pois, defrosted2½ tbsp toasted sesame oil3 garlic cloves, peeled and minced1 tbsp sambal oelek1 tbsp light soy sauce½ tbsp light agave syrup½ tsp brown or red miso15g fresh mint, leaves picked and chopped2125g mozzarella ballsPut the rapeseed oil in a wide frying pan on a medium to high heat. Test the heat with a wooden spoon – when it’s hot enough, bubbles should form around the bottom of the spoon. Add the green beans to the pan, spacing them out, and leave for two minutes. Turn the beans, leave for another two minutes, then turn again and cook for a further two minutes, until blistered or blackened in places. Transfer the beans to a large bowl, then add the edamame beans and petit pois to the same bowl.To make the dressing, put the sesame oil in the same pan on a low to medium heat and, when it’s hot, add the garlic and stir for a minute. Add the sambal oelek, light soy sauce, agave and miso, stir well, cook for up to a minute, then take off the heat.Pour the dressing into the bean bowl, mix well to coat, then fold in the chopped mint.To serve, use tongs (or two forks) to lift the greens on to a platter, leaving behind the dressing. Tear open the mozzarella, arrange on top, then pour any remaining dressing over the cheese and salad.Explore more on these topicsVegetablesMeera Sodha recipesFoodSaladCheeseMain courseStarterHerbs and spicesfeaturesShareReuse this content
